messages.content:
Transform this individualistic story to collectivistic:

It was late in November, 1456—a cold year in the 1400s. The snow fell over Paris with steady, heavy force; sometimes the wind blew hard and tossed it around; sometimes there was a lull, and flake after flake descended out of the dark sky, quiet and endless. To poor people, looking up under wet brows, it seemed a wonder where it all came from. Master Francis Villon had asked a question that afternoon at a tavern window: was it only the old god Jupiter pulling feathers off geese in the sky, or were the holy angels losing feathers? He was only a poor Master of Arts, he went on; and since the question touched on religion, he didn’t dare give an answer. A foolish old priest from Montargis, who was among the group, treated the young troublemaker to a bottle of wine in honor of the joke and the faces he made, and swore on his own white beard that he had been just such another rude joker when he was Villon's age.

The air was cold and sharp, but not far below freezing; and the flakes were large, wet, and sticky. The whole city was covered in white. An army might have marched from end to end and not a footstep would be heard. If there were any late birds in the sky, they saw the island like a large white patch, and the bridges like slim white sticks on the black surface of the river. High up overhead, the snow settled among the carvings of the cathedral towers. Many a hollow was filled with snow; many a statue wore a long white hat on its funny or saintly head. The gargoyles had been turned into great droopy noses, hanging low. The stone ornaments were like upright pillows swollen on one side. When the wind stopped, there was a dull dripping sound around the church.

The cemetery of St. John had its own share of snow. All the graves were neatly blanketed; tall white rooftops stood around in quiet rows; good townspeople were long asleep, wearing nightcaps like their houses. There was no light in the whole neighborhood except a little peek from a lamp that hung swinging in the church choir, throwing shadows back and forth with each swing. The clock was close to ten when the patrol went by with long spears and a lantern, rubbing their hands for warmth; and they saw nothing strange about the cemetery of St. John.

Yet there was a small house, backed up against the cemetery wall, that was still awake—and awake for bad reasons—in that snoring neighborhood. There wasn’t much to give it away from outside; only a stream of warm steam from the chimney, a patch where the snow had melted on the roof, and a few half-erased footprints at the door. But inside, behind the shuttered windows, Master Francis Villon, the poet, and some of the thieving gang he hung out with, were still wide awake, passing around a bottle.

A great pile of glowing embers gave off a strong red light from the arched fireplace. In front of it stood Dom Nicolas, the monk from Picardy, with his robe pulled up and his fat legs bare in the warm glow. His big shadow split the room in half; the firelight only got around the sides of his wide body, and in a little pool between his spread feet. His face had the puffy, bruised look of someone who drank too much; it was covered with swollen purple veins, which now looked pale violet from the cold. Even with his back to the fire, the chill bit him on the front. His hood had partly slipped off, making a weird lump on either side of his thick neck. So he stood, grumbling, and blocked the room with the shadow of his round body.

On the right, Villon and Guy Tabary were huddled together over a scrap of paper. Villon was writing a ballad he planned to call the “Ballad of Roast Fish,” and Tabary was mumbling praise over his shoulder. The poet was a shabby little guy—dark, small, and thin, with sunken cheeks and stringy black hair. He moved through his twenty-four years with feverish energy. Greed had drawn wrinkles around his eyes; evil grins had creased his mouth. The wolf and pig seemed to fight in his face. It was a sharp, ugly, earthy face full of expression. His hands were small and grabbed like claws, with knotted fingers like rope; they waved in front of him constantly in wild and lively gestures. As for Tabary, his round face, squashed nose, and drooling lips gave off a dopey happiness. He had become a thief just as easily as he could have been a decent shopkeeper—all because of the random chance that rules the lives of silly people.
At the monk's other hand, Montigny and Thevenin Pensete played a game of chance gambling game. About the first there clung some flavour hint of good birth and training, like a fallen angel; something long, slim, and courtly fancy in the body; something aquiline and darkling sharp and shadowy in the face. Thevenin, poor guy, was in great feather spirits; he had done a good trick that afternoon in the Faubourg St. Jacques neighborhood, and all night he had been winning money from Montigny. A flat smile lit up his face; his bald head shone pink in a ring of red curls; his small round belly shook with silent laughter as he scooped up his winnings.

“Doubles or quits?” said Thevenin.
Montigny nodded grimly with a frown.

“Some may prefer to dine in state,” wrote Villon, “on bread and cheese on silver plate. Or, or—help me out, Guido!” Tabary giggled.
“Or parsley on a golden dish,” wrote the poet.

The wind was getting stronger outside; it blew the snow around and sometimes let out a loud shout, making spooky groans in the chimney. The cold was getting worse as the night went on. Villon stuck out his lips and copied the wind with a sound between a whistle and a moan. It was a creepy, strange talent of the poet's, much hated by the monk from Picardy.

“Can’t you hear it rattle in the gibbet gallows?” said Villon. “They’re all dancing the devil’s jig on nothing, up there. Dance away, boys; it won’t make you warmer. Whew, what a wind! Someone just fell down! One less medlar dead guy on the three-legged medlar-tree gallows-tree! I say, Dom Nicolas, it'll be cold tonight on the St. Denis Road?” he asked.

Dom Nicolas blinked both his big eyes and seemed to choke on his Adam’s apple throat. Montfaucon The big, scary hanging site, the grisly gruesome Paris gallows, stood near the St. Denis Road, and the joke bothered him. As for Tabary, he laughed so hard at the medlar joke; he had never heard anything funnier; he held his sides and howled. Villon gave him a flick on the nose, which turned his laughing into a coughing fit. “Oh, stop that noise,” said Villon, “and think of rhymes for 'fish'!”

“Doubles or quits?” said Montigny, doggedly in a grumpy voice.
“With all my heart,” said Thevenin.

“Is there any more in that bottle?” asked the monk.
“Open another,” said Villon. “How do you expect to fill that big hogshead barrel you call a body with tiny things like bottles? And how do you expect to get to heaven? How many angels, do you think, can carry a monk from Picardy? Or do you think you’re another Elias—and they’ll send a coach for you?”

“It’s impossible for people,” replied the monk as he poured more wine.
Tabary was thrilled.
Villon flicked his nose again.

“Laugh at my jokes, if you want,” he said.
Villon made a face at him. “Think of rhymes for ‘fish,’” he said. “What do you need Latin for? You’ll wish you never learned any when the devil calls for Guido Tabary, church boy—the devil with the hunched back and burning hot fingernails. Speaking of the devil,” he added in a whisper, “look at Montigny!”

All three looked over secretly at the gambler. He didn’t look happy about winning. His mouth was pulled to one side; one nostril almost closed, and the other puffed out. The black dog was on his back, as people say in creepy kids’ stories; and he breathed hard under that scary weight.

“He looks like he might stab him,” whispered Tabary, eyes wide.
The monk shivered, and turned his face and held out his hands to the red coals. It was the cold that bothered Dom Nicolas, not any kind of strong feelings about what just happened.

“Come now,” said Villon, “about this ballad. How does it go so far?” And beating time with his hand, he read it aloud to Tabary.

They were interrupted at the fourth rhyme by a short and deadly moment between the gamblers. The round was finished, and Thevenin was just opening his mouth to celebrate another win, when Montigny jumped up, fast as a snake, and stabbed him in the heart. The hit landed before he could even cry out, before he could move. His body shook a little; his hands opened and closed, his heels tapped the floor; then his head rolled backward over one shoulder, with wide eyes; and Thevenin Pensete’s spirit had returned to the one who made it.

Everyone jumped to their feet, but the killing was over in seconds. The four living men looked at one another with shocked faces, the dead man staring at a corner of the roof with a strange, creepy smile.

“Oh my God!” said Tabary, and he started praying in Latin.

Villon burst into hysterical laughter. He stepped forward, gave a silly bow to Thevenin, and laughed even harder. Then he suddenly sat down, slumped on a stool, and kept laughing bitterly, like he might fall apart from it.

Montigny was the first to calm down.

“Let’s see what he has on him,” he said; and he searched the dead man’s pockets like a pro, dividing the money into four equal piles on the table. “There’s yours,” he said.

The monk took his share with a deep sigh and a quick, sneaky glance at Thevenin, who was starting to slump over and fall off the chair.

“We’re all in trouble now,” cried Villon, choking on his laughter. “We’ll all be hanged—every one of us here—not even counting the ones who aren’t!” He made a creepy motion in the air with his raised hand, stuck out his tongue, and tilted his head to one side, copying the look of someone being hanged. Then he stuffed his share of the money in his pocket and shuffled his feet like he was trying to warm them up.

Tabary was the last to take his share; he grabbed the money and backed away to the far end of the room.

Montigny propped Thevenin upright in the chair again and pulled out the dagger, which was followed by a spray of blood.

“You guys better get going,” he said, wiping the blade on the dead man’s jacket.

“I think we should,” said Villon, swallowing hard. “Ugh, his fat head!” he yelled. “It’s stuck in my throat like something gross. What right does a man have to have red hair when he’s dead?” And again he dropped onto the stool and buried his face in his hands.

Montigny and Dom Nicolas laughed out loud, and even Tabary let out a weak chuckle.

“Crybaby!” said the monk.

“I always said he was like a woman,” added Montigny with a smirk. “Sit up, will you?” he said, giving another shake to the dead body. “Put out that fire, Nick!”

But Nick was busy doing something else; he was quietly taking Villon’s wallet, while the poet sat, limp and shaking, on the stool where he had been writing his ballad not even three minutes earlier. Montigny and Tabary silently asked for a share of the loot, which the monk promised with a nod as he tucked the little pouch into his robe. In many ways, having an artistic soul makes a man unfit for real life.
No sooner had the theft been done than Villon shook himself, jumped to his feet, and started helping to scatter and put out the coals. Meanwhile Montigny opened the door and carefully looked out into the street. The coast was clear; there was no nosy patrol in sight. Still, they thought it smarter to leave one by one. Since Villon was in a rush to get away from the dead Thevenin, and the others were even more eager to get rid of him before he noticed his money was gone, they all agreed he should go first. So Villon was the first to step outside into the street.

The wind had won and cleared all the clouds from the sky. Only a few wisps, as thin as moonlight, moved quickly across the stars. It was freezing; and, because of a common trick of the eyes, everything seemed even clearer than in broad daylight. The sleeping city was perfectly still; a field of white rooftops, like tiny mountains, under the twinkling stars. Villon cursed his bad luck. He wished it were still snowing! Now, wherever he went, he left a clear trail behind him in the shiny streets; wherever he went, he was still tied to the house by the cemetery of St. John; wherever he went, he was making, with every step, the very path that might lead him to the gallows. The creepy look on the dead man's face came back to him with new meaning. He snapped his fingers, trying to cheer himself up, and, picking a street at random, walked boldly into the snow.

Two things stayed on his mind as he walked: one, the look of the hanging place at Montfaucon the Paris gallows in this bright, windy part of the night; and two, the face of the dead man with his bald head and ring of red curls. Both thoughts made his heart feel cold, and he kept walking faster as if speed could chase away the fear. Sometimes he looked back over his shoulder with a quick, nervous twitch; but he was the only moving thing in the white streets—except when the wind spun around a corner and tossed the freezing snow into sparkling clouds.

Suddenly, he saw a dark group far ahead, with two swinging lanterns. The group was moving, and the lanterns bobbed as if carried by men walking. It was a patrol. And even though they were only passing through, Villon thought it best to get out of sight as quickly as possible. He didn’t feel like being questioned, and he knew he stood out clearly against the snow. Just to his left was a big old hotel mansion, with some towers and a large porch in front; it was half falling down, he remembered, and had been empty for a long time. So he took three quick steps and jumped into the shelter of the porch.

It was very dark inside, after the brightness of the snowy street, and he walked forward with his hands out. Then he tripped over something strange that felt both hard and soft, stiff and loose at the same time. His heart jumped, and he leaped back, staring in fear at what he had hit. Then he let out a small laugh of relief. It was only a woman—and she was dead.

He knelt down to be sure. She was ice cold and stiff like a stick. A bit of ragged fancy clothing fluttered in the wind around her hair, and her cheeks had been painted with makeup earlier that same day. Her pockets were totally empty; but in her stocking, under her garter, Villon found two small coins that were called whites pennies. It wasn’t much, but it was still something; and the poet felt very sad that she had died before spending her money.

That seemed like a deep and painful mystery to him. He looked from the coins in his hand to the dead woman, and back again, shaking his head about how strange life is. King Henry V of England had died at Vincennes a castle just after he had taken over France—and here was this poor woman, dying from a cold wind in a rich man’s doorway before she even had time to spend her last two pennies. It seemed like a cruel way for the world to work. Two pennies would have been gone in no time; but still, they could have bought one more moment of joy, one more good bite or drink, before the devil took her soul and her body was left to the birds and bugs.

He thought to himself that he’d rather use up all his own candle wax before his light was blown out and his lantern broken.
While these thoughts were going through his mind, he was reaching, half without thinking, for his wallet. Suddenly, his heart stopped. A cold, creepy feeling crawled up the back of his legs, and a chill hit the top of his head. He froze for a moment. Then he reached again in a panic—nothing. The truth hit him, and he started sweating all over.

To people who spend money fast, cash feels so real and alive—it’s the thin line between them and everything fun. Their only limit is time. Someone with just a few dollars feels like the Emperor of Rome—until the money’s gone. For someone like that, losing money is the worst kind of fall—from heaven to nothing in a single moment. And it’s even worse if he might be hanged for that same wallet—earned at great risk and lost so foolishly.

Villon stood there, cursing. He threw the two white coins into the street. He shook his fist at the sky and stomped around, not even caring that he was stepping on the poor dead woman. Then he turned and ran back toward the house next to the cemetery.

He had forgotten all about the patrol, which was long gone, and could only think about his lost wallet. He searched all around in the snow, but it was no use—there was nothing there. He hadn’t dropped it in the street. Had it fallen back inside the house? He really wanted to check—but the thought of the creepy dead man inside scared him. And when he got close, he saw that the fire hadn’t gone out. It had flared up again, and flickering light glowed through the cracks in the door and windows. It reminded him how dangerous it would be to get caught—and end up on the Paris gallows.

He went back to the big mansion with the porch and searched the snow for the money he had thrown away in anger. But he only found one coin. The other must have landed sideways and sunk too deep.

With just one white coin left in his pocket, all his plans for a wild night at a fun tavern were gone. And it wasn’t just the fun he lost—now he felt real discomfort, even pain, as he stood sadly by the porch. His sweat had dried on his skin. Though the wind had calmed, the freezing air was getting worse, and he felt numb and sick inside.

What could he do? It was very late, and it seemed unlikely, but he decided to try the home of his adopted father—the chaplain of St. Benoit.

He ran the whole way and knocked softly at the door. No one answered. He knocked again and again, growing braver with each knock. Finally, he heard footsteps inside. A small window opened in the large door with iron studs, and a stream of yellow light came out.

“Hold up your face to the window,” said the chaplain from inside.
“It’s just me,” whispered Villon.
“Oh, it’s just you, is it?” said the chaplain. Then he cursed him with terrible, cruel words for waking him up so late and told him to go back to hell where he came from.

“My hands are blue,” begged Villon. “My feet are frozen and aching. My nose hurts from the cold. I feel it in my chest. I might be dead by morning. Please—just this once, Father. I swear to God I’ll never ask again!”

“You should’ve come earlier,” said the priest coldly. “Young men need to learn a lesson now and then.” Then he closed the window and walked slowly back into the house.

Villon lost it. He pounded on the door with his hands and feet and shouted at the chaplain with a rough voice.

“You rotten old fox!” he yelled. “If I had you in my grip, I’d toss you straight into the pit of hell!”
A door shut somewhere deep inside the house, just barely loud enough for the poet to hear. He ran his hand over his mouth and muttered a curse. Then the funny side of the moment hit him, and he laughed and looked up at the sky, where the stars seemed to be winking at his bad luck.

What now? It looked like he was going to spend the night in the freezing streets. The thought of the dead woman popped into his head and scared him badly; what had happened to her earlier that night might just happen to him before morning. And he was so young! He had so many wild adventures left to live. He felt sorry for himself, like he was imagining someone else’s sad ending, and he could even picture the scene in the morning when people would find his body.

He went over his options, turning the coin between his fingers. Sadly, he had argued with some old friends who might have helped him in a time like this. He had made fun of them in poems; he had hit and tricked them; and yet now, when he was really stuck, he thought maybe one of them might forgive him. It was a long shot—but worth a try. So he decided to go.

On the way, two small things happened that changed how he was thinking. First, he came across the trail of a patrol and followed it for about a hundred yards, even though it wasn’t the direction he meant to go. This made him feel a little better—at least he had confused his own tracks. He still thought someone might be following his footprints in the snow, ready to catch him while he slept.

The second thing had the opposite effect. He walked past a street corner where, not long ago, a woman and her child had been eaten by wolves. This was just the kind of night, he thought, when wolves might sneak back into Paris; and a man walking alone in these quiet streets might end up with more than just a scare. He stopped and looked at the spot with a sick feeling—it was where several streets met—and he stared down each one, holding his breath and listening, in case he heard paws in the snow or howling between him and the river.

He remembered how his mother had told him the story and pointed out the place when he was still a child. His mother! If only he knew where she lived now, he might at least have a warm place to go. He decided he would ask around tomorrow. No—he would go visit her, too. Poor old woman!

Thinking like this, he arrived at his last hope for the night.

The house was completely dark, like all the others. But after a few knocks, he heard movement upstairs, a door creaked open, and a cautious voice asked who was there. The poet gave his name in a loud whisper and waited nervously to see what would happen.

He didn’t have to wait long. A window suddenly opened—and a bucket of dirty water splashed down onto the doorstep. Villon had kind of expected something like this and had tried to protect himself as best he could—but still, he got soaked from the waist down. His pants started freezing almost right away. Now, death from cold and exposure felt very real. He remembered he had weak health and started coughing just a little to test if he was okay. But the serious danger helped him calm down.

He stopped a few hundred yards from the door where he had just been soaked and stood still, thinking hard, one finger on his nose. He could only think of one way to get a place to sleep—he’d have to take one. He remembered a nearby house that looked like it might be easy to break into, and he headed there right away.

As he walked, he tried to cheer himself up with the idea of a warm room, maybe with a table still full of leftover food, where he could spend the rest of the cold, dark night. And maybe, in the morning, he could leave with an armful of fancy silverware. He even began imagining what food and drinks he would want the most—and as he listed his favorite dishes, roast fish popped into his mind with a strange mix of laughter and horror.

“I’ll never finish that poem,” he thought to himself. Then, with another shiver at the memory, “Curse his fat head!” he said loudly, and spit on the snow.

The house he had in mind looked dark at first. But as Villon walked around it, looking for the best place to break in, a tiny flicker of light caught his eye behind a curtained window. “The devil!” he thought. “Someone's awake! Some student or some saint—ugh, these people! Why can’t they just get drunk and fall asleep snoring like everyone else? What’s the point of curfew, or poor guys pulling ropes in bell towers? What’s the use of daytime if people stay up all night? Shame on them!” He grinned as he realized where his thoughts were leading. “Everyone’s got their job,” he added, “and if they’re up, maybe I’ll actually get a supper the honest way for once—and trick the devil.”

He walked right up to the door and knocked with confidence. The last two times he had knocked gently and been afraid of drawing attention. But now that he had just decided not to break in, knocking on a door seemed perfectly normal and harmless.

The sound of his knock echoed through the house with a strange, thin echo, like it might be empty. But the echoes had barely faded before slow footsteps approached, two bolts were slid open, and one side of the door swung wide—as if the people inside had no fear or reason to hide.

A tall man stood there, lean but strong, slightly hunched. His head was large but nicely shaped; his nose was blunt at the bottom but narrowed smoothly toward a pair of strong, honest-looking eyebrows. His mouth and eyes were framed with fine lines, and his whole face rested on a thick white beard, neatly trimmed into a square shape. Seen in the flickering light of the lamp he carried, he may have looked even more impressive than usual—but even so, it was a fine face: noble more than clever, strong, simple, and good.

“You knock late, sir,” said the old man in a deep, polite voice.

Villon lowered his head and quickly started mumbling a bunch of apologies; in moments like this, the beggar in him came out, and the clever poet hid in shame.

“You’re cold,” the old man said again, “and hungry? Well then, come inside.” And he waved him in with a grand gesture.

“Some rich nobleman,” thought Villon, as his host set the lamp down on the stone floor of the entry and slid the bolts back into place.

“You’ll forgive me if I go ahead,” the old man said once the door was locked again; and he led Villon upstairs into a big room, warmed by a pan of burning charcoal and lit by a large lamp hanging from the ceiling. It had very little furniture—just some gold dishes on a side table, some large books, and a suit of armor between the windows. Elegant cloth wall hangings showed two scenes: one of Jesus on the cross, and the other of shepherds and shepherdesses by a stream. Over the fireplace was a coat of arms.

“Please sit down,” said the old man, “and forgive me if I leave you alone. I’m the only one home tonight, and if you’re going to eat, I’ll have to go find you something myself.”

As soon as his host left, Villon jumped up from the chair and began snooping around the room like a sneaky cat. He picked up the gold cups and weighed them in his hand, flipped through the big books, looked closely at the shield, and checked what the chairs were made of. He pulled back the curtains and saw that the windows were decorated with stained glass pictures, which seemed to show scenes of battle. Then he stood in the center of the room, took a deep breath, puffed out his cheeks, and spun slowly in a circle—trying to memorize every detail of the place.
“Seven silver dishes,” he said. “If there had been ten, I might have taken the risk. A fine house, and a fine old master—I swear!”

Just then, hearing the old man's footsteps coming back down the hallway, he quickly returned to his chair and humbly began warming his wet legs in front of the pan of charcoal.

His host came in with a plate of meat in one hand and a jug of wine in the other. He set the plate down on the table, motioned for Villon to pull up his chair, and then went to the sideboard to get two cups, which he filled.

“I drink to your better fortune,” he said seriously, touching Villon’s cup with his own.

“To getting to know each other better,” said the poet, gaining confidence. A regular man might have been nervous around the old nobleman’s politeness, but Villon was used to that sort of thing. He had joked with lords before and found them to be just as bad as he was. So he dove into the food with hungry delight, while the old man leaned back and watched him closely.

“You have blood on your shoulder, my man,” the old man said.

Montigny must have grabbed him with his wet, bloody hand when he left the house. Villon cursed him silently.

“It wasn’t my doing,” he muttered.

“I didn’t think it was,” his host said calmly. “A fight?”

“Well, something like that,” Villon admitted, his voice shaking a little.

“Maybe someone got killed?”

“Oh no, not murdered,” said the poet, getting more and more nervous. “It was just a rough fight—he died by accident. I didn’t touch him, I swear to God!” he added quickly.

“One less troublemaker, I’d guess,” said the old man.

“You can say that again,” said Villon, hugely relieved. “One of the worst guys in all of Paris. He died easy, like a lamb. Still, it was a nasty thing to see. I suppose you’ve seen dead men before, sir?” he asked, nodding toward the armor.

“Many,” said the old man. “I’ve been in wars, as you probably guessed.”

Villon set down his knife and fork, which he had just picked up again.

“Were any of them bald?” he asked.

“Oh yes, some with hair as white as mine.”

“I don’t think the white would bother me as much,” said Villon. “This guy’s hair was red.” He got another shiver and a wave of nervous laughter, which he covered by gulping a big drink of wine. “I get a little shaken when I think about it,” he continued. “I knew the guy—curse him! And the cold messes with your head—or maybe your thoughts make you cold, I don’t know which.”

“Do you have any money?” asked the old man.

“I’ve got one coin,” said the poet, laughing. “I found it in a dead woman’s stocking in a doorway. She was as dead as Caesar, poor girl, and cold as a church wall, with scraps of ribbon stuck in her hair. This winter’s been hard on wolves, women, and poor guys like me.”

“I,” said the old man, “am Enguerrand de la Feuillee, lord of Brisetout, bailiff of Patatrac. And who are you?”

Villon stood up and gave a respectful bow. “I’m called Francis Villon,” he said, “a poor Master of Arts from this university. I know some Latin, and a lot of bad habits. I can write songs and poems—ballads, roundelays, and other stuff—and I really like wine. I was born in an attic, and I’ll probably die on the gallows. And I’ll add, sir, that starting tonight, I am your very humble servant.”

“Not my servant,” said the knight. “My guest for this evening—nothing more.”
“A very grateful guest,” said Villon politely, and he pretended to take a sip to toast his host.

“You’re clever,” said the old man, tapping his forehead. “Very clever. You’re educated, you’re a scholar. And yet you take money from a dead woman in the street. Isn’t that a kind of stealing?”

“It’s the kind of stealing people do all the time in war, my lord.”

“War is a field of honor,” the old man replied proudly. “A man risks his life there. He fights for his king, his God, and all the saints and angels.”

“Well,” said Villon, “what if I really am a thief? Don’t I risk my life too—and maybe with even worse chances?”

“For money, not for honor.”

“Money?” said Villon, shrugging. “Money! A poor guy wants dinner and he takes it. Same as a soldier during a war. What about all these 'requisitions' we keep hearing about? If they’re not for profit, they sure cause loss. Soldiers drink by a warm fire while the local townspeople can barely afford to buy them wine and firewood. I’ve seen lots of farmers hanging from trees—thirty on one tree once—and when I asked why, someone told me it was because they couldn’t cough up enough money for the soldiers.”

“These things are part of war,” said the old man. “The poor must put up with it. It’s true, some commanders go too far. There are heartless men in every group, and some soldiers are nothing but bandits in uniform.”

“You see?” said the poet. “You can’t really tell the soldier from the robber. And what’s a thief, really, but a lone bandit with better manners? I steal a couple of pork chops without waking anyone. The farmer complains, but he still eats dinner. You show up blowing a fancy trumpet, take the whole sheep, and beat the farmer for good measure. I don’t have a trumpet; I’m just Tom, Dick, or Harry. I’m called a criminal and a dog, and people say I deserve to hang—fine. But ask the farmer who he hates more. Just see which one of us keeps him awake on cold nights, shaking his fist at the ceiling.”

“Look at us two,” said the old man. “I’m old, strong, and respected. If I lost my home tomorrow, hundreds of people would be glad to take me in. Poor families would even sleep outside just to give me space. But I find you wandering alone, picking coins off dead women. I fear no man and nothing. I wait for God’s call here in my own house—or, if the king needs me, on the battlefield. You expect the hangman. A fast, rough death, with no hope and no honor. Can’t you see the difference between us?”

“It’s as big as the moon,” Villon agreed. “But if I had been born as lord of this house, and you had been poor Francis the student, would things be any different? Wouldn’t I be warming my knees by this fire, and wouldn’t you be out picking coins from the snow? Wouldn’t I be the soldier, and you the thief?”

“A thief?” shouted the old man. “Me, a thief? If you understood what you just said, you’d be ashamed!”

Villon held out his hands in a bold, cheeky gesture. “If your lordship had kindly followed my point,” he said.

“I do you too much honor just letting you be here,” said the knight. “Learn to control your mouth when talking to older and respected men—or someone less patient than me might shut you up a harsher way.” He got up and walked back and forth at the end of the room, trying to calm his anger.

Villon quietly poured himself more wine, made himself comfortable in the chair, crossed his legs, leaned his head on one hand, and propped his elbow on the backrest. He was full and warm now, and not the least bit scared of his host. He had judged him pretty well—especially for two people so different. The night had turned out pretty comfortable after all, and Villon felt sure he’d be allowed to leave safely in the morning.

“Tell me one thing,” said the old man, pausing. “Are you really a thief?”

“I claim the sacred rights of hospitality,” said the poet. “But yes, my lord—I am.”

“You’re very young,” the knight said.

“I wouldn’t have lived this long,” said Villon, wiggling his fingers, “if I hadn’t helped myself with these ten tools. These hands have been like my parents—feeding me, sheltering me, and keeping me alive.”
“You may still change your ways,” said the old man.

“I repent every day,” said the poet. “There aren’t many people who say sorry more than poor Francis. As for changing—well, let someone change my situation. A man has to eat, if only so he can keep on saying sorry.”

“The change has to start in the heart,” the old man said seriously.

“My dear lord,” Villon replied, “do you really think I steal for fun? I hate stealing, just like I hate any hard or risky job. My teeth chatter when I see a hanging rope. But I have to eat, I have to drink; I need to be around people. What can I say? People aren’t meant to live alone—God gave man woman. Make me the king’s food taster, or the Abbot of St. Denis, or the mayor of Patatrac, and yes—I’ll change! But as long as I’m stuck being poor Francis Villon, with no money at all, of course I’ll stay the same.”

“God’s grace is all-powerful.”

“I’d be a heretic to argue with that,” said Francis. “It’s made you lord of Brisetout and mayor of Patatrac; it’s given me nothing but a sharp brain and these ten fingers. May I pour myself more wine? Thank you kindly. By God’s grace, you’ve got some excellent wine.”

The lord of Brisetout paced back and forth, hands behind his back. Maybe he still wasn’t sure about comparing thieves and soldiers. Maybe something about Villon had touched a nerve. Maybe he was just confused by the strange way the poet talked. Whatever the reason, he felt a strong pull to help the young man change for the better—and he couldn’t bring himself to kick him back out into the cold.

“There’s something about this I can’t explain,” he said finally. “You speak in riddles, and the devil has clearly led you far off course. But the devil is weak next to God’s truth. All his tricks disappear when someone speaks real honor, like the dark vanishes when the sun rises.

“Listen to me one more time. I learned long ago that a gentleman should live with honor and love—for God, for the king, and for his lady. And even though I’ve seen strange and cruel things in the world, I’ve always tried to follow that rule. It’s not just written in old books of knights and heroes—it’s written in every man’s heart, if he’ll take the time to read it.

“You talk about food and drink, and I get it—hunger is hard to bear. But you don’t talk about other things you need. You say nothing about honor, or being true to God and to other people, or being kind, or loving without shame. Maybe I’m not the wisest man—but I do think I understand something you’ve missed. You’ve made a big mistake in life. You’re chasing small needs, and you’ve forgotten the big ones—the real ones—like someone fixing a toothache on judgment day. Things like honor, love, and faith aren’t just more noble than food and drink—I think people want them more. We hurt more when they’re missing.

“I’m talking to you in a way I think you’ll understand. Isn’t it true that while you’re trying so hard to feed your belly, you’re ignoring another hunger inside you—the one that’s ruining your joy and making you miserable all the time?”
Villon was clearly annoyed by all the preaching. “You think I have no sense of honor!” he shouted. “I’m poor, God knows! It’s hard to see rich people with gloves while you’re blowing on your freezing hands. An empty stomach is a miserable thing, even if you talk about it like it’s nothing. If you’d had as many hungry nights as I have, maybe you’d think differently.

“Anyway, yes—I’m a thief, make the most of that—but I’m not some devil from hell, God strike me dead! I’ve got a sense of honor just like you, even if I don’t go on about it all day like it’s a miracle. To me, it feels normal—I keep it quiet until I need it.

“Look, how long have I been in this room with you? Didn’t you tell me you were alone in the house? Look at your gold plates! Sure, you’re strong—but you’re old and unarmed, and I’ve got a knife. All it would’ve taken was a quick move, and you’d be lying there with a blade in your belly, and I’d be strolling down the street with an armful of golden cups.

“Did you think I wasn’t smart enough to realize that? But I didn’t do it—I chose not to. There are your fancy goblets, safe as in a church. There you are, still alive and breathing. And here I am, walking out just as poor as I walked in, with only one lousy coin you tossed in my face! And you say I have no sense of honor? God strike me dead!”

The old man raised his right arm. “I’ll tell you what you are,” he said. “You’re a rogue, a bold, black-hearted scoundrel and wanderer. I’ve spent an hour with you—believe me, I feel ashamed! And you’ve eaten and drunk at my table. But now I’m sick of you. The sun is coming up, and the night bird needs to fly off to its nest.

“Will you leave first, or shall I?”

“Whichever you like,” said the poet, standing up. “I believe you’re completely honorable.” He finished his cup thoughtfully. “I only wish I could say you were smart,” he added, tapping his head with his knuckles. “Age! Age! Brains get stiff and rusty.”

The old man walked ahead out of pride. Villon followed, whistling, his thumbs hooked in his belt.

“God pity you,” said the lord of Brisetout at the door.

“Goodbye, papa,” Villon said with a yawn. “Thanks for the cold meat.”

The door closed behind him. Morning light was spreading over the snowy rooftops. The day had begun with a cold, uncomfortable dawn. Villon stood in the middle of the street and gave a long, deep stretch.

“What a boring old man,” he thought. “I wonder how much those goblets are worth?”

It was late in November, 1456—a cold year in the 1400s. The snow fell over Paris with steady, heavy force; sometimes the wind blew hard and tossed it around; sometimes there was a lull, and flake after flake descended out of the dark sky, quiet and endless. To the poor people, huddled together under wet brows, it seemed a wonder where it all came from, a shared miracle that united them in a moment of collective awe as they gazed up at the swirling flakes, recognizing their shared struggles and the beauty that briefly illuminated their hardships.

The air was cold and sharp, but not far below freezing; and the flakes were large, wet, and sticky. The whole city was covered in white. The collective breath of the city held a silence that echoed, as if each citizen shared in the tranquility of the snowy blanket. If there were any late birds in the sky, they saw the island like a large white patch, and the bridges like slim white sticks on the black surface of the river. High up overhead, the snow settled among the carvings of the cathedral towers. Many a hollow was filled with snow; many a statue wore a long white hat on its funny or saintly head. The gargoyles had been turned into great droopy noses, hanging low. The stone ornaments were like upright pillows swollen on one side. When the wind stopped, there was a dull dripping sound around the church.

The cemetery of St. John had its own share of snow. All the graves were neatly blanketed; tall white rooftops stood around in quiet rows; good townspeople were long asleep, wearing nightcaps like their houses. There was no light in the whole neighborhood except a little peek from a lamp that hung swinging in the church choir, throwing shadows back and forth with each swing. The clock was close to ten when the patrol went by with long spears and a lantern, rubbing their hands for warmth; and they saw nothing strange about the cemetery of St. John.

Yet there was a small house, backed up against the cemetery wall, that was still awake—and awake for bad reasons—in that snoring neighborhood. There wasn’t much to give it away from outside; only a stream of warm steam from the chimney, a patch where the snow had melted on the roof, and a few half-erased footprints at the door. But inside, behind the shuttered windows, Master Francis Villon, the poet, and his band of outcasts, united in their shared struggles, were still wide awake, passing around a bottle.

A great pile of glowing embers gave off a strong red light from the arched fireplace. In front of it stood Dom Nicolas, the monk from Picardy, with his robe pulled up and his fat legs bare in the warm glow. His big shadow split the room in half; the firelight only got around the sides of his wide body, and in a little pool between his spread feet. His face had the puffy, bruised look of someone who drank too much; it was covered with swollen purple veins, which now looked pale violet from the cold. Even with his back to the fire, the chill bit him on the front. His hood had partly slipped off, making a weird lump on either side of his thick neck. So he stood, grumbling, and blocked the room with the shadow of his round body.

On the right, Villon and Guy Tabary were huddled together over a scrap of paper. Villon was writing a ballad they planned to call the “Ballad of Our Shared Struggles,” and Tabary was mumbling praise over his shoulder. The poet was a shabby little guy—dark, small, and thin, with sunken cheeks and stringy black hair. He moved through his twenty-four years with feverish energy. Greed had drawn wrinkles around his eyes; evil grins had creased his mouth. The wolf and pig seemed to fight in his face. It was a sharp, ugly, earthy face full of expression. His hands were small and grabbed like claws, with knotted fingers like rope; they waved in front of him constantly in wild and lively gestures. As for Tabary, his round face, squashed nose, and drooling lips gave off a dopey happiness. He had become a thief just as easily as he could have been a decent shopkeeper—all because of the random chance that rules the lives of silly people. About the first there clung some flavour hint of good birth and training, like a fallen angel; something long, slim, and courtly fancy in the body; something aquiline and darkling sharp and shadowy in the face. Thevenin, poor guy, was in great feather spirits; he had done a good trick that afternoon in the Faubourg St. Jacques neighborhood, and all night he had been winning money from Montigny. A flat smile lit up his face; his bald head shone pink in a ring of red curls; his small round belly shook with silent laughter as he scooped up his winnings.

“Doubles or quits?” said Thevenin. Montigny nodded grimly with a frown.

“Some may prefer to dine in state,” wrote Villon, “on bread and cheese on silver plate. Or, or—help me out, Guido!” Tabary giggled. “Or parsley on a golden dish,” wrote the poet.

The wind was getting stronger outside; it blew the snow around and sometimes let out a loud shout, making spooky groans in the chimney. The cold was getting worse as the night went on. Villon stuck out his lips and copied the wind with a sound between a whistle and a moan. It was a creepy, strange talent of the poet's, much hated by the monk from Picardy.

“Can’t you hear it rattle in the gibbet gallows?” said Villon. “They’re all dancing the devil’s jig on nothing, up there. Dance away, boys; it won’t make you warmer. Whew, what a wind! Someone just fell down! One less medlar dead guy on the three-legged medlar-tree gallows-tree! I say, Dom Nicolas, it'll be cold tonight on the St. Denis Road?” he asked.

Dom Nicolas blinked both his big eyes and seemed to choke on his Adam’s apple throat. Montfaucon The big, scary hanging site, the grisly gruesome Paris gallows, stood near the St. Denis Road, and the joke bothered him. As for Tabary, he laughed so hard at the medlar joke; he had never heard anything funnier; he held his sides and howled. Villon gave him a flick on the nose, which turned his laughing into a coughing fit. “Oh, stop that noise,” said Villon, “and think of rhymes for 'fish'!”

“Doubles or quits?” said Montigny, doggedly in a grumpy voice. “With all my heart,” said Thevenin.

“Is there any more in that bottle?” asked the monk. “Open another,” said Villon. “How do you expect to fill that big hogshead barrel you call a body with tiny things like bottles? And how do you expect to get to heaven? How many angels, do you think, can carry a monk from Picardy? Or do you think you’re another Elias—and they’ll send a coach for you?”

“It’s impossible for people,” replied the monk as he poured more wine. Tabary was thrilled. Villon flicked his nose again.

“Laugh at my jokes, if you want,” he said. Villon made a face at him. “Think of rhymes for ‘fish,’” he said. “What do you need Latin for? You’ll wish you never learned any when the devil calls for Guido Tabary, church boy—the devil with the hunched back and burning hot fingernails. Speaking of the devil,” he added in a whisper, “look at Montigny!”

All three looked over secretly at the gambler. He didn’t look happy about winning. His mouth was pulled to one side; one nostril almost closed, and the other puffed out. The black dog was on his back, as people say in creepy kids’ stories; and he breathed hard under that scary weight.

“He looks like he might stab him,” whispered Tabary, eyes wide. The monk shivered, and turned his face and held out his hands to the red coals. It was the cold that bothered Dom Nicolas, not any kind of strong feelings about what just happened.

“Come now,” said Villon, “about this ballad. How does it go so far?” And beating time with his hand, he read it aloud to Tabary.

They were interrupted at the fourth rhyme by a short and deadly moment between the gamblers. The round was finished, and Thevenin was just opening his mouth to celebrate another win, when Montigny jumped up, fast as a snake, and stabbed him in the heart. The hit landed before he could even cry out, before he could move. His body shook a little; his hands opened and closed, his heels tapped the floor; then his head rolled backward over one shoulder, with wide eyes; and Thevenin Pensete’s spirit had returned to the one who made it.

Everyone jumped to their feet, but the killing was over in seconds. The four living men looked at one another with shocked faces, their shared terror uniting them in a collective moment of resolve, as they recognized the weight of their situation and the bond they now shared in the face of danger.

“Oh my God!” said Tabary, and he started praying in Latin.

The room was filled with tension, but the sudden absurdity of their situation broke through the weight of fear. Villon burst into communal laughter, stepping forward to pull his friends in with him as they all shared in the absurdity of their circumstances. They were bound together by the shared experience of their plight, and the humor of it all sparked a moment of camaraderie that overshadowed their terror.

“Let’s see what he has on him,” said Montigny, and he searched the dead man’s pockets like a pro, dividing the money into equal piles on the table for the four of them. “There’s yours,” he said.

The monk took his share with a shared understanding of their predicament and a quick, sneaky glance at Thevenin, who was starting to slump over and fall off the chair.

“We’re all in this together now,” cried Villon, choking on his laughter. “We’ll all be hanged—every one of us here—not even counting the ones who aren’t!” He made a creepy motion in the air with his raised hand, stuck out his tongue, and tilted his head to one side, copying the look of someone being hanged. Then he stuffed his share of the money in his pocket and shuffled his feet like he was trying to warm them up.

Tabary was the last to take his share; he grabbed the money and backed away to the far end of the room.

Montigny propped Thevenin upright in the chair again and pulled out the dagger, which was followed by a spray of blood.

“You guys better get going,” he said, wiping the blade on the dead man’s jacket.

“I think we should,” said Villon, swallowing hard. “Ugh, his fat head!” he yelled. “It’s stuck in my throat like something gross. What right do any of us have to have red hair when we’re dead?” And again he dropped onto the stool and buried his face in his hands.

Montigny and Dom Nicolas laughed out loud, and even Tabary let out a weak chuckle.

“Crybaby!” said the monk.

“I always said he was like a woman,” added Montigny with a smirk. “Sit up, will you?” he said, giving another shake to the dead body. “Put out that fire, Nick!”

But Nick was busy pulling together the resources they had just acquired, sharing glances with his companions, as they all understood the need to act as one now. They were a band bound by necessity, and the poet sat, limp and shaking, on the stool where he had been writing his ballad not even three minutes earlier, aware that their fates were intertwined. Villon shook himself, jumped to his feet, and started helping to scatter and put out the coals.

Montigny opened the door and carefully looked out into the street. The coast was clear; there was no nosy patrol in sight. Still, they thought it smarter to leave one by one. Since Villon was in a rush to get away from the dead Thevenin, and the others were even more eager to get rid of him before he noticed his money was gone, they all agreed he should go first. So Villon was the first to step outside into the street.

The wind had won and cleared all the clouds from the sky. Only a few wisps, as thin as moonlight, moved quickly across the stars. It was freezing; and, because of a common trick of the eyes, everything seemed even clearer than in broad daylight. The sleeping city was perfectly still; a field of white rooftops, like tiny mountains, under the twinkling stars. Villon thought of his friends, of their shared struggles and laughter. They were all in this together, united by their common fight against poverty and despair. As he stepped into the snowy streets, he felt the weight of their shared fate, the knowledge that their paths were intertwined.

Now, wherever he went, he left a clear trail behind him in the shiny streets; wherever he went, he was still tied to the house by the cemetery of St. John; and every step he took was a reminder of the community he belonged to, the lives they shared, and the dangers they faced together.

Villon cursed his bad luck. He wished it were still snowing!

The creepy look on the dead man's face came back to him with new meaning. He snapped his fingers, trying to cheer himself up, and, picking a street at random, walked boldly into the snow.

Two things stayed on his mind as he walked: one, the look of the hanging place at Montfaucon the Paris gallows in this bright, windy part of the night; and two, the face of the dead man with his bald head and ring of red curls. Both thoughts made his heart feel cold, and he kept walking faster as if speed could chase away the fear. Sometimes he looked back over his shoulder with a quick, nervous twitch; but he was the only moving thing in the white streets—except when the wind spun around a corner and tossed the freezing snow into sparkling clouds.

Suddenly, he saw a dark group far ahead, with two swinging lanterns. The group was moving, and the lanterns bobbed as if carried by men walking. It was a patrol. And even though they were only passing through, Villon thought it best to get out of sight as quickly as possible. He didn’t feel like being questioned, and he knew he stood out clearly against the snow. Just to his left was a big old hotel mansion, with some towers and a large porch in front; it was half falling down, he remembered, and had been empty for a long time. So he took three quick steps and jumped into the shelter of the porch.

It was very dark inside, after the brightness of the snowy street, and he walked forward with his hands out. Then he tripped over something strange that felt both hard and soft, stiff and loose at the same time. His heart jumped, and he leaped back, staring in fear at what he had hit. Then he let out a small laugh of relief. It was only a woman—and she was dead.

He knelt down to be sure. She was ice cold and stiff like a stick. A bit of ragged fancy clothing fluttered in the wind around her hair, and her cheeks had been painted with makeup earlier that same day. Her pockets were totally empty; but in her stocking, under her garter, Villon found two small coins that were called whites pennies. It wasn’t much, but it was still something; and the poet felt very sad that she had died before spending her money.

That seemed like a deep and painful mystery to him. He looked from the coins in his hand to the dead woman, and back again, shaking his head about how strange life is. King Henry V of England had died at Vincennes a castle just after he had taken over France—and here was this poor woman, dying from a cold wind in a rich man’s doorway before she even had time to spend her last two pennies. It seemed like a cruel way for the world to work. Two pennies would have been gone in no time; but still, they could have bought one more moment of joy, one more good bite or drink, before the devil took her soul and her body was left to the birds and bugs.

He thought to himself that he’d rather use up all his own candle wax before his light was blown out and his lantern broken. While these thoughts were going through his mind, he was reaching, half without thinking, for his wallet. Suddenly, his heart stopped. A cold, creepy feeling crawled up the back of his legs, and a chill hit the top of his head. He froze for a moment. Then he reached again in a panic—nothing. The truth hit him, and he felt a wave of collective concern for the plight of all the outcasts, knowing they shared the same struggles and burdens in a world that often turned away from them.

“To argue against that would be to deny the unity we share,” said Francis. “It’s made you lord of Brisetout and mayor of Patatrac; it’s given us all nothing but a sharp brain and these ten fingers.”

A foolish old priest from Montargis, who was among the group, treated the young troublemaker to a bottle of wine in honor of the joke and the faces they made together...

Villon stood there, feeling the weight of his loss. He looked down at the two white coins, and instead of throwing them away, he decided to place them gently on the ground beside the dead woman. “May this serve as a reminder of our shared struggles,” he whispered, feeling a deep sense of connection to her fate and the collective fight for survival that bound them all together in a harsh world.

His thoughts turned to his friends, who had shared laughter and drink with him only hours before. They were all in this together, living through the same struggles of poverty and desperation. He had argued with some old friends who were also weighed down by the same burdens, and they were all feeling the collective weight of the world. “It’s hard to see rich people with gloves while we all huddle together against the cold,” he mused, feeling a sense of camaraderie with those who shared in the same plight. **But now we must move on together, as one united front against the chill of life. The sun is coming up, and we need to find warmth and safety together.**

He searched all around in the snow, but it was no use—there was nothing there. He hadn’t dropped it in the street. Had it fallen back inside the house? He really wanted to check—but the thought of the creepy dead man inside scared him. And when he got close, he saw that the fire hadn’t gone out. It had flared up again, and flickering light glowed through the cracks in the door and windows. It reminded him how dangerous it would be to get caught—and end up on the Paris gallows.

He went back to the big mansion with the porch and searched the snow.

DEACON THOMAS WALES'S WILL.
In the name of God, amen! On September 13, 1758, I, Thomas Wales of Braintree, in the County of Suffolk and the Province of Massachusetts Bay, being in good health and sound mind—thank God—know that I will someday die. So, while I am still healthy, I make this my last will and testament.
First, I give my soul into the hands of God who gave it, hoping through His grace to be saved because of Jesus Christ, my Lord and Savior. I want my body to be buried respectfully, as my executor sees fit, believing that at the final resurrection, I will rise again through God's power. For the worldly things God has given me, after my debts and funeral costs are paid, I give the rest as follows:
I give to my beloved wife Sarah a good suit of mourning clothes, whatever she chooses. If she gives up her right to claim a widow’s share, as we agreed, then my executor will return all the household items she brought when we married and still owns. He will also pay her or her heirs the $40 note I gave her when we agreed to give up claims to each other's property. This will happen before the rest of the estate is divided. She will also have the southwest room with the fireplace, a share in the cellar, half the garden, the right to use the well water, space in the yard, and use of the oven—for as long as she lives.


After this, the property was divided among his five sons and two daughters.
The family home was given to his sons Ephraim and Atherton. Ephraim already had a house of his own, so he took land instead. Atherton moved into the old family home. He hadn’t done as well as his brothers and had been living more simply. This had been hard on his wife, Dorcas, who was proud. She often complained that their home wasn’t as nice as her sisters-in-law’s.
Now, she was excited to improve her living situation. The Wales house was big and impressive for the time. But the one thing that spoiled her excitement was that Grandma would be staying in the southwest room. Dorcas had wanted to put her tall bed with the feather mattress in that room and make it the front room. It was right across the hall from the sitting room and perfect for her furniture. She was disappointed but couldn’t change the will.
Mrs. Dorcas was the youngest of all the sons’ wives, and Grandma had never fully approved of her. She said Dorcas was too emotional and flighty. Still, Atherton wanted the property divided, and he was Grandma’s youngest and favorite, so she agreed. Once everything was settled, Grandma moved into the southwest room, and Atherton’s family used the rest of the house. Though things started off peaceful, Grandma felt lonely and out of place.
She thought it might help to have Ann Ginnins, a young servant girl, stay with her. Her son Samuel had a strong housemaid who could take Ann’s place. Grandma had always liked Ann and thought she could sleep in a closet off the southwest room and help with errands.
Samuel and his wife hesitated. They were fond of Ann, even though she could be a handful. Mrs. Polly had just started teaching her to be helpful and was afraid Grandma would undo her progress. Still, they agreed, with the understanding that it didn’t have to be permanent.
Dorcas didn’t like this any more than losing the southwest room. She had never liked Ann much and felt jealous that Grandma seemed to favor Ann over her own daughters. Soon after Ann arrived, Dorcas started acting out in small ways.
Thirsey, Dorcas’s baby, was a sweet and chubby little girl—the favorite of the family. Ann loved playing with her, and Dorcas took advantage of that. Whenever Ann had free time, she was told to carry Thirsey around. The baby was heavy, and soon Ann’s shoulders started to ache.
That’s when Grandma stepped in. Though she was usually calm and willing to put up with a lot to avoid conflict, she wouldn’t let Ann be overworked. “This little girl isn’t going to get hunched over carrying that heavy baby,” she said. “She didn’t come here to do that.”
So Dorcas had to accept it. Ann’s main jobs were cleaning the brass in Grandma’s room, going up and down stairs for her, and spinning yarn. Grandma gave her smaller tasks than Mrs. Polly had. Over time, Ann helped with cooking. She and Grandma made their own meals and ate at a small table in the shared kitchen. The kitchen was big enough for several families—if they could get along. There was a large oven and fireplace, and Deacon Wales probably thought his wife could use the space in peace.
But Dorcas started to use the oven and kitchen space at the same time Grandma needed it. One morning, when Grandma had bread and cakes rising and planned to bake in an hour, Dorcas rushed in, made her own food, and filled the oven first.
Grandma told Ann to go put her bread in the oven, but when Ann got there, it was full. Holding a loaf in her hand, she realized it would be ruined if not baked immediately. Dorcas was gone with the baby, and no one else was there. Ann set the cake down, used the fireplace tools to remove every one of Dorcas’s pies and loaves from the oven, arranged them on the hearth, and put Grandma’s food in.
Then she went back to spinning. When Grandma asked if she had put the things in, she quietly said, “Yes, ma’am,” with bright red cheeks.
When Dorcas returned and saw her half-baked, doughy food on the hearth, she was furious. Her food was ruined. She pulled out Grandma’s perfectly baked loaves in frustration. There was shouting, and Grandma, though innocent, was blamed. She finally stood up for herself. Ann, though secretly pleased, was punished for the first time.
Grandma said, “It doesn’t matter what you think or if you were right. A little girl must never talk back to her elders.”
Even though Ann was punished, the situation reached Atherton. He believed in fairness and deeply respected his mother. He said his father’s will would be followed exactly. After that, Grandma could cook in peace.
Ann became a great comfort to her. She was growing out of her wild ways, was quick and smart, and even looked like she’d be pretty one day. Grandma favored her over her grandchildren—especially Dorcas’s daughter Martha, who was close to Ann’s age. “Marthy’s a sweet girl,” she’d say, “but she doesn’t have the spark Ann does—though I’d never tell Dorcas that.”
She even promised Ann her gold beads someday, as long as she didn’t tell anyone. Ann treasured the beads but didn’t like hearing Grandma talk about when she wouldn’t need them anymore. Grandma always wore them, and Ann had never seen her without them.
Ann rarely caused trouble anymore, but when she did, Dorcas was quick to get upset. Her dislike for Ann was always just under the surface, waiting to show.
One winter night, Dorcas had spent the whole day making fine candle wicks from flax. She hung them in the cellar stairway to keep them safe. “I’ve done a good day’s work,” she said proudly. Her husband was away, so she’d had time to focus.
That night, Ann went to the cellar with a candle to get butter and noticed the white bundles hanging above her. Without thinking, she pinched a little piece of flax and touched it to the flame—just to see how it would burn. The fire caught instantly and raced through the whole bundle. There was a burst of flame and smoke—Dorcas’s wicks were destroyed. Ann screamed and ran down the stairs, barely avoiding the fire.
Dorcas rushed to the cellar. When she saw her ruined wicks, she was furious. Ann hadn’t meant any harm, but Grandma still scolded her, saying, “I don’t know what’s going to happen to a girl who’s so careless.” She made Ann stay home from school to spin new wicks until Dorcas’s loss was repaid.
Ann felt awful. She was scared, sorry, and cried herself to sleep.
Around midnight, a strange noise woke her. She called for Grandma, who also heard it. “Light a candle,” Grandma said. “I’m afraid the baby’s sick.”
Ann had just lit the candle when Dorcas burst in, pale and shaking. “It’s Thirsey—she has the croup! Atherton’s gone and there’s no one to get the doctor! What will I do?”
“Have you tried the skunk oil?” Grandma asked, getting up quickly.
“Yes! I tried everything, but she’s worse. Oh, what will I do?”
“Don’t panic,” said Grandma. “But Ann, what are you doing?”
Ann, dressed and wrapping a thick blanket over her head, said, “I’m going to get the doctor.”
Dorcas grabbed onto the hope. “Oh, will you?”
“Wait,” Grandma said firmly. “It’s a terrible storm out there. Her life is just as important as Thirsey’s.”
Ann didn’t argue. She went into the kitchen, lit a lantern, and was out the door in a minute.
The sleet hit her face like needles, and the wind nearly pushed her back. But she kept going. The snow wasn’t deep, but it was rough walking. The doctor lived half a mile away, and there was no path—just woods and darkness. She was glad she had the lantern.
When she got to the doctor’s house, his wife said he had gone to the North Precinct, to Captain Lovejoy’s house. He wouldn’t be back that night.
Before she could say anything more, Ann had already disappeared into the storm again.
“She went like a spirit,” the doctor’s wife said, amazed.
Ann walked four more miles through the storm. When she finally reached Captain Lovejoy’s house, she stumbled into the warm kitchen. The doctor and the captain could hardly believe their eyes. She told the doctor about Thirsey, then nearly fainted.
Mrs. Lovejoy laid her on the couch and made her herbal tea. She almost forgot about her own sick child while trying to help the brave girl who had crossed towns to save a life.
When Ann came to, her first question was, “Is the doctor ready to go?”
“He’s gone,” said Mrs. Lovejoy kindly.
Ann had hoped to ride back with him, but she was too weak. She drank more tea and went to bed with warm stones at her feet and layers of blankets.
The next morning, Captain Lovejoy took her home on a wooden sled. It was easier than riding, and she was very sore.
Mrs. Dorcas saw her coming and opened the door. When Ann reached the porch, she hugged her.
“You don’t have to make the candle wicks,” she said. “They don’t matter now. Thirsey’s better—and I think you saved her life.”
Grandma, proud and happy, took the gold beads off her own neck and fastened them around Ann’s. “You can wear them to school today—if you’ll be careful.”
That day, with the gold beads as a celebration, marked a new beginning for Ann. There was no more bad feeling between her and Mrs. Dorcas. The doctor had arrived just in time, and Dorcas was convinced Ann had saved her child’s life. She never forgot it. And being a woman of strong feelings who did nothing halfway, she not only treated Ann with kindness—she also finally let go of her grudge against Grandma for taking the southwest room.

"Tell me what’s going on," she said.

"And this is my little grandchild?" he said, lifting Nan into his arms.

"I don’t see how," said Dame Clementina sadly.

Ellen DeGeneres




Ellen DeGeneres was born and raised in Metairie, Louisiana. Her mother was a speech therapist and her father was an insurance salesman. From an early age, Ellen developed an interest in comedy. At age thirteen, when her parents divorced, Ellen had used her comedy in order to make her mother laugh. She attended King High School but graduated from Atlanta High School when her mother remarried and moved to Atlanta, Louisiana, bringing sixteen-year-old Ellen with her.

Ellen attended the University of New Orleans but dropped out after one semester. She then held a series of jobs, including work as a secretary at a law firm, selling vacuum cleaners, waiting tables, painting, a hostess, and as a bartender. She fell in love with her roommate, Kat Perkoff, and the two moved into a house together. With Kat’s support, Ellen wrote short, humorous essays she hoped would be published in magazines. She loved to make people laugh, and her peers took notice. A friend invited her to perform at a luncheon she was hosting. Ellen performed with no written act, eating a hamburger and French fries. She was a hit, and friends encouraged Ellen to write an act and perform stand-up comedy. She did, and became instantly addicted to the local comedy scene.

Ellen’s personal life deteriorated when she discovered Kat was cheating on her. Ellen moved out, hoping to teach Kat a lesson. A few days later, she ran into Kat at a comedy club but pretended not to hear her. Later that night, Kat was killed in a car accident. Ellen had driven past the accident but didn’t realize it was her until the following morning. To overcome this devastating event, Ellen engaged in a monologue to God in her head, questioning why he could possibly let this happen. The monologue eventually developed into a stand-up routine called Phone Call to God, which Ellen became convinced she would perform on The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson someday. She became the emcee at Clyde’s Comedy Club in New Orleans, Louisiana and performed at small venues across the country. Ellen sent a video of her stand-up routine to compete for television network Showtime’s Funniest Person in Louisiana competition and won. She followed by winning Showtime’s Funniest Person in America competition at twenty-seven years old.

Despite winning the competition, Ellen continued to perform in small venues with often tough audiences. Then, one night, Ellen performed her Phone Call to God routine with an associate producer for The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson in the crowd. Impressed, the associate producer booked Ellen to perform on the show, just as she had envisioned. She was a hit, and became the only female comic to be invited by Carson to the famed couch after her performance. After the show, Ellen received multiple offers to perform stand-up at comedy clubs.

Ellen then made her way into television, having landed a small role on the television series Open House. However, the show was cancelled after one season. She then took on another supporting role on the television series Laurie Hill, which was also cancelled after a few episodes. However, the show’s creators, Neal Marlens and Carol Black, were impressed with Ellen and created a television show around her, titled These Friends of Mine. The show struggled during its first season and was renamed Ellen.

Ellen reached its height in popularity when Ellen publicly came out as a lesbian on The Oprah Winfrey Show in February 1997. She also announced her character’s homosexuality on Ellen, which attracted major media attention, as well as 46 million viewers for the airing of “The Puppy Episode” on April 30, 1997.
