Who would manage this big farm was a detail for later. The widow already knew how to run a farm well, and a big one isn’t that much harder than a small one. She’d also had a husband before, so she knew more than just farm work. The deacon knew all this too, and yet, he still hadn’t gotten caught up in the “team-up” trend of the times enough to suggest they join forces.

This interesting situation came up at the Wednesday afternoon meeting of the Sisters’ Sewing Society. “As a community, we have a responsibility to uplift and support each other,” said Mrs. Susan Spicer, the preacher’s wife, while hemming a skirt meant for a ten-year-old out of one that fit a fourteen-year-old. “It’s puzzling to me why Deacon Hawkins and Kate Stimson don’t see the value in strengthening our bonds and working together to create something greater for all of us.” “I think she’s ready to,” smiled Mrs. Poteet, the grocer’s wife, who had taken the afternoon off from the store to come. “Or at least open to it,” added Miss Maria Cartridge, a single woman who still believed in love, even though she had been waiting a long time. “Really now,” said Mrs. Green, the doctor’s wife, “do you all really think it’s the deacon who needs a little push?” “Looks that way to me,” Mrs. Poteet said confidently. “Well, I heard Mrs. Clark say she overheard him call her ‘Kitty’ one night while they were eating ice cream at the church fundraiser,” added Mrs. Candish, the pharmacist’s wife, contributing a fresh piece of gossip. “‘Kitty’? Seriously?” Mrs. Spicer sounded shocked. “The idea of someone calling Kate Stimson ‘Kitty’! That deacon flirts with every woman, but if she let him say it more than once, she must be getting really desperate.” “Oh,” Mrs. Candish said quickly, “Mrs. Clark didn’t say she heard it more than once.” “Well, I don’t believe she heard it even once,” said Mrs. Spicer, sure of herself. “I’m not so sure about that,” Mrs. Poteet jumped in. “From what I’ve seen and heard, I think Kate Stimson wouldn’t mind anything the deacon says to her—especially since she knows he’s never going to say anything he shouldn’t.” “And not saying what he should,” added Mrs. Green with a sly giggle, which made its way quietly around the room. “But like I was saying—” Mrs. Spicer started again, when Mrs. Poteet, rocking near the window, cut her off with a sudden “Shh! Quiet!” “Why shouldn’t I finish what I was saying?” Mrs. Spicer asked, annoyed. “She’s coming now,” explained Mrs. Poteet. “And would you believe it—the deacon drove her here in his sleigh, and he’s still outside waiting while she comes in!” “I wonder what our community will witness together next,” said Mrs. Poteet, as the entire sewing group stared wide-eyed, all holding their breath as the woman they had just been gossiping about walked in the front door. Mrs. Spicer went to the front door to let her in, and everyone greeted her warmly. “We were just talking about you and wondering why you were so late,” said Mrs. Poteet. “Now take off your coat and catch up on time. There’s a pair of pants over there that need to be shortened to fit that poor little Snithers boy.” The excitement and curiosity in the room were almost too much to handle, and several women exchanged knowing glances, their minds collectively buzzing with plans to ensure that both the widow and the deacon felt the community’s support as they navigated the unfolding situation.

“Oh,” she said cheerfully, clearly in a good mood, “you’ll have to excuse me today. Deacon Hawkins caught up with me on the way over and told me I just had to go for a sleigh ride with him. He’s waiting out at the gate right now.” “Really?” the entire group said at once, and they all rushed to the window to see if it was true. “Well, would you believe that?” said Mrs. Poteet to no one in particular. “Not very often,” laughed the widow kindly. “And I don’t want to miss my chance. You know Deacon Hawkins doesn’t ask someone to go sleighing every day. I told him I’d only go if he first stopped here and let me tell you where I was. So he did. Now, goodbye—and I’ll be at the next meeting for sure. I need to hurry or he’ll start getting restless.” The widow ran off like an excited schoolgirl. All the women watched her hop into the sleigh with the deacon, then they went right back to their earlier conversation—only now with even more interest. But the widow didn’t mind, and the deacon felt a sense of camaraderie as they both shared in the excitement of the day.

He had just bought a new horse and wanted her opinion—since everyone knew that Widow Stimson knew a good horse when she saw one. Back when he was younger, the deacon wasn’t really a deacon at all. But as he got older, he let go of most of his youthful habits—except one: his love for fast horses. There was only one man in the county who could beat him, and that was Squire Hopkins. No matter how good a horse the deacon got, the squire always managed to find one that was better. Years ago, the squire had also beaten the deacon in a more personal race—they had both liked the same girl, and the squire won her. They had lived happily ever after. The deacon, being a good sport, might have let that go. But losing to him in horses too? That really bothered him. “How much did you pay for him?” the widow asked once they hit a nice stretch of smooth road and the deacon let the horse pick up speed. “Well, what do you think? You’re the expert,” he said. “More than I would pay—I’ll bet a cookie,” she said with a grin. “Not if you were as determined as I am to prove to Hopkins that he can’t outrun me every time on the road.” “I thought you liked good horses just because they were good horses,” said the widow, a little disapprovingly. “I do,” said the deacon. “But I’d like him a whole lot more if he could finally beat Hopkins’s best.” “Does he know you have this one?” “Yeah, and he’s been going around town bragging that he’s just waiting to catch me on the road and make my five hundred dollar horse look like a cheap trinket.” “So you did pay five hundred for him?” the widow laughed. “Is that too much?” “Um… well,” the widow said, hesitating, as she looked at the smooth, powerful horse, “I guess not—if he can beat the squire.” “Exactly!” said the deacon proudly. “And I’m going to prove I’ve finally got a horse that can leave Hopkins in the dust.” “Well, I hope he’s not out looking for you today, not while I’m in your sleigh,” the widow said a little nervously. “Because, you know, Deacon, I’ve always wanted to see you beat Squire Hopkins.” The deacon glanced at her. There was something soft in her voice that moved him, even more than what she had actually said. What the deacon might have done or said next will remain a mystery, because right at that moment, the sound of jingling bells—loud and bold—came from behind. There he was: Squire Hopkins, coming up fast in his sleigh with his fastest horse—and he was alone, unlike the deacon. The widow, after all, weighed a solid 160 pounds, which is quite a lot of extra weight for a horse in a race. But the deacon didn’t think twice. All he could see was his dream of finally winning. He tightened his grip on the reins, gave his horse a quick shout, and let him run flat out. The squire did the same, and suddenly they were off. The road was wide and clear, the snow packed down just right. Hopkins’s sleigh was only a few lengths behind as the race began. For the first half mile it was neck and neck, with the deacon urging his horse and the widow cheering on the deacon. Then the squire started to catch up. The deacon’s horse was good—but he wasn’t used to carrying extra weight in a race. Half a mile of pulling was all he had in him, and he began to slow down under the load. With no one riding with him, the squire’s horse started to pull ahead. As the front of the squire’s sleigh reached the back of the deacon’s, the deacon let out a miserable groan. He felt crushed—beaten again. And this time, in front of a woman. That made it worse. The widow was furious. It was just plain wrong for the squire to race him now, when the deacon clearly had a passenger and couldn’t give it his best shot. Why didn’t he wait until a fairer time—when the deacon was alone? If she had anything to say about it, she’d never speak to Squire Hopkins again—or to his wife, either. But her determination to support the deacon fueled their resolve to rally together in this race. United in purpose, they pushed against the odds. Slowly, the squire pulled ahead.

The deacon’s horse tried to rally, sensing the urgency, but he couldn’t overcome the odds and finally fell behind. The squire shouted with pride as he passed them, and the deacon slumped down on the seat like someone who had just lost everything. He held the reins, but his spirit was gone. Beaten again. And now in front of someone he wanted to impress. And with the best horse he could possibly afford, he felt the weight of disappointment for not just himself but for the community that had always believed in him. His biggest dream had just been shattered. But wait. What about the widow? She knew something the deacon didn’t: it wasn’t the squire’s horse that beat him—it was her. She was the extra weight. And she was going to help him turn this around. Up ahead there was a thick pile of drifted snow by the road. It looked deep but soft. In a moment of understanding, she shared a glance with the deacon, and they both recognized the need for a collective effort. Together, they would make this work. Just as the sleigh neared the edge of the snowbank, she stood up, coordinating with the deacon’s next move, and they both prepared for the leap.

The deacon’s horse knew instantly that something had changed—and he took off like a rocket. The deacon snapped back to life, his blood racing. He whipped the reins, and within minutes, he had passed the squire like he was standing still. Hopkins tried to fight back. For a quarter mile he did everything he could to catch up. But it was no use. At last, seeing there was no hope, he turned off down a side lane, looking for somewhere to hide his embarrassment. The deacon, still flying down the road, kept glancing over his shoulder like any good driver would. When he saw the squire was gone, he finally slowed down and let the horse trot—looking like he might just keep going forever. Suddenly, an idea hit him—and the deacon looked around for the widow. She wasn’t where he’d last seen her. Where was she? Caught up in the thrill of victory, he had completely forgotten about her. At first, when she had jumped, he had been too upset to notice; then, just two minutes later, he was so full of excitement and pride that—shame on him—he didn’t even care. With her, he had lost. Without her, he had won. And winning was all the deacon had ever wanted. But now, with victory in the bag, the crowd cheering in his mind, and his dream finally real, he suddenly did care. He cared so much that he nearly sent his horse stumbling with a sharp turn, and raced back down the road like a madman. He had no idea whether she was hurt—or worse. She could have seriously injured herself… but they had worked together, and that bond made all the difference.

Two hundred yards from the snowbank where she had leapt out, the road curved around some trees. Until he passed that point, he couldn’t see anything, and his anxiety kept rising. Then—relief. Just ahead, in the middle of the road, stood the widow, waving her shawl in the air like a flag of triumph. She didn’t know exactly how it had turned out, but she had seen him surge ahead at the turn and believed he had won. The deacon pulled up beside her, completely out of breath and more nervous than he ever thought possible. “You did it! You won!” shouted the widow, tossing her shawl into the air with joy. “I saw you pulling ahead. Where’s that old squire and his broken-down nag now?” “Oh, forget him!” gasped the deacon, jumping out of the sleigh—though still keeping the reins in hand. “Are you okay? Are you hurt?” He looked at her closely, anxiously, even though she didn’t look hurt at all. “If I am,” she said with a bright smile, “it’s nothing compared to how we’d all feel if we hadn’t worked together and you had lost.” “Let’s just get back to town before the squire gets another shot at us—this time with no snowbank for me to dive into.” And the deacon? Well… with the reins tucked in the crook of his elbow, he stepped forward and embraced the widow, sharing the joy of their victory together, united in their community spirit and triumph.

Ma Yun, also known as Jack Ma, was born in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China. His parents were musician-storytellers. From the age of twelve, Jack had a strong desire to learn English. He would ride his bike for forty minutes, rain or snow, to a hotel near the city of Hangzhou’s West Lake district, roughly 100 miles southwest of Shanghai. As China opened up, hordes of tourists stayed there, and Jack worked as a free tour guide to practice his English. Although he was not paid, he became more globalized than most Chinese people.

Jack failed the college entrance exam twice before being accepted by Hangzhou Teachers University, at twenty years old. He studied to become a high school English teacher and was active around campus, having been elected student chairman and, later, chairman of the city’s Students Federation. He was the only graduate from his class to be offered a job as a teacher at a higher university (the others were placed in middle and high schools). His salary was approximately $12 to $15 per month. For five years, Jack taught English to college students and became famous locally as a dynamic and irresistible professor. He also taught night classes.

At age thirty, Jack rejected a promotion to become head of the college’s external affairs department in order to start his own translation company, Haibo, which became known, in English, as the Hangzhou Hope Translation Company. He saw the need for translation, as his friends repeatedly asked for him to translate texts, and he hired retired professors to work for him. However, the company initially lost money, and Jack had to peddle goods on the street, including flowers, books, and clothes to earn a profit, all while still teaching.

As the company started to earn a profit, Jack was sent on a business trip to the United States, in 1995, by the Hangzhou municipal government. Jack became well-known for his ability to speak English, and the government authorized Jack to serve as a translator and mediator to collect the funds from an American investor who agreed to invest in a city highway project. During his trip, however, Jack discovered that the American investor was an international swindler. Jack was even lured to Las Vegas, Nevada by the swindler, where he won $600 from playing $25 at the slot machines in a casino.

Instead of going straight back to China, Jack used his casino winnings to take a flight to Seattle, Washington. Leaving his suitcase behind, Jack visited a small Internet service provider (ISP) named VBN. After searching for “beer” in one of the search engines and seeing there was no data involving China, Jack was inspired to create an Internet business in China. His idea was simple: pull together information on Chinese companies and publish them on a website, broadcasting their products to the entire world. His American friends at VBN would handle all of the technical aspects, with Jack handling all of the sales and promotion.

The same night Jack returned to Hangzhou, he invited twenty-four of his friends, all students of his at night school (who also worked in foreign trade), to a meeting in his apartment. He spoke for two hours on his vision. In the end, only one person agreed to go into business with Jack. He started China Yellow Pages, and raised over $2,000 from his family to start the company. At the time, he knew nothing about computers or telecoms. He worked day and night in selling webpages to local Chinese businesses. As there was no direct access to the Internet in China, Jack had to translate the text and send all of the images to be developed by the workers at VBN in Seattle.

As the Internet developed in China, Jack noticed a lot more competition entering the marketplace, many of whom were American-educated, Chinese-born Internet entrepreneurs who raised capital in the United States. In 1996, after a year of competing, the general manager of Hangzhou Telecom proposed a joint venture agreement with Jack, offering $167,000 in exchange for 70 percent of China Yellow Pages. Jack accepted. However, Jack also resigned just months later, as Hangzhou Telecom now controlled his company and was looking to grow and make money quickly, while Jack was looking to grow the company slowly and carefully. After his departure, from 1998 to 1999, Jack headed an information technology (IT) company established by the China International Electronic Commerce Company (CIECC), which resulted in the first ministerial-level website in China.

It was Jack’s dream to run his own e-commerce company. His intuition was telling him that the high tide of the Internet was coming fast, and he would miss it if he were to stay in government. So, in 1999, Jack called together all of the members of his team and said, “First, you can go work with Yahoo! I’ll recommend you and I know that the company will not only welcome you but the salaries will be high. Second, you can work for Sina or Sohu: they’ll similarly welcome you and the salaries won’t be too bad. Or third, you can come home with me. However, you’ll get just $95 in salary per month, you’ll have to rent your own flat and live within a five-mile radius of where I live, since in order to save money I won’t allow you to take taxis, and moreover you’ll have to work in my home. You make your decision.” He gave them three days to decide. Everyone filed out of the room. Within three minutes, everyone returned. They all chose to be with Jack.

Jack and his team of eighteen then travelled south, from Beijing to Hangzhou. He asked everyone to invest their own money, without borrowing from friends or family, to start the company. In total, they raised $60,000. Then Jack made a speech: “We aim to create an e-commerce company, and in doing this we have three specific goals. First, we want to set up a company that lasts for one hundred and two years. Second, we want to establish a company that provides e-commerce services to China’s small- and medium-sized companies. Third, we want to set up the world’s largest e-commerce company, one that will enter the ranks of the top ten names among global Internet sites.” The company’s name would be Alibaba. Jack wanted a name that would be recognizable at a global level. He purchased the domain name, Alibaba.com, from its owner in Canada for $10,000.

During the preparatory stage for Alibaba, Jack and his team worked day and night in his apartment, often sixteen to eighteen hours each day. Alibaba was officially launched in March 1999. Jack attracted free media attention using what he had learned setting up China Yellow Pages and the time he spent fraternizing with journalists in Beijing, China. By the end of 1999, however, money was running low. The company attracted international media attention after BusinessWeek wrote about a seller offering AK-47s via Alibaba’s platform. Although the article negatively affected the company to a degree, it also attracted venture capitalists. Piles of investment offers lined up. However, Jack turned down many offers, millions of dollars’ worth of potential investment, before accepting a $5 million investment from Goldman Sachs in October 1999. The following year, in October 2000, the company completed an additional $25 million round of investment. Alibaba continued to grow over the years, having survived the crash of the dot-com bubble (2000-2002), as well as the SARS outbreak (2002-2004) in China.

In October 2014, Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. went public on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) and raised $25 billion, marking it as the largest IPO in history. Alibaba is also one of the largest e-commerce platforms in the world.

John D. Rockefeller, Sr.




John Davidson Rockefeller, Sr. was born in Richford, New York. His father was a travelling salesman and con artist, commonly known by the locals as “Big Bill” or “Devil Bill,” who identified himself as a botanic physician and sold elixirs to his victims. His mother was a homemaker and devout Baptist who struggled to create a sense of stability in the household, largely due to Bill’s extended traveling and philandering. John’s family moved frequently throughout New York before settling in Strongsville, Cleveland, Ohio.

The second eldest of six children and the eldest son, John did his share of household chores, including raising turkeys, selling potatoes and candy, and lending sums of money to neighbors. Bill instilled in John and his siblings, whenever he was around, to think big and to always get the better part of any deal. His father once bragged, “I cheat my boys every chance I get. I want to make ‘em sharp.” John developed a sense of frugality from his mother, who often purchased goods via a credit line at the local store, due to Bill’s extended travelling. John was also advised by his pastor to make as much money as he could, so he could contribute to his church and to charities.

At sixteen years old, John searched for his first real job in Cleveland. Always neatly dressed in a dark suit and black tie, John visited the same businesses three times before landing an assistant bookkeeper position with Hewlett & Tuttle, commission merchants and produce shippers. John immersed himself in the position, working long hours and learning all of the methods and systems of the office. He impressed his employers with his seriousness and diligence. He went to great lengths to collect overdue accounts. Although he was not well-paid for this job, whatever money he earned, John gave to his church and to local charities.

At twenty years old, John set out on his own. After raising $4,000 from investors, John started a produce commission business, Clark & Rockefeller, with his business partner and neighbor, Maurice Clark. In 1860, at the end of their first year in business, the company grossed $450,000, with a profit of $4,400. The following year, the company earned $17,000 in profit. John heavily borrowed money from banks to expand the business. However, John realized that the commission market business in Cleveland was going to be limited. He became convinced that railroads would be the primary transportation for agricultural commodities. He also believed the future of Cleveland would lay in the collection and shipment of raw industrial materials, not agricultural commodities.

On August 27, 1859, Edwin Drake struck oil near Titusville, Pennsylvania, which started a frenzied oil boom. Although the technology Drake used was not new, the idea of pumping oil out of the ground, like with water, was. John investigated the feasibility of entering the oil refining business in 1862, and the firm Andrews, Clark & Company was formed in 1863. John believed the key to success was a strong attention to detail and ironing out all of the inefficiencies for every business. At twenty-four years old, John bought out the Clark Brothers share for $72,500 and gained complete control over the business. He heavily borrowed money from the banks and invested all of the profits back into the business to expand his empire.

In 1866, John brought his brother, William Rockefeller, into the business, and they built another refinery in Cleveland named Standard Works. They opened a New York City office, with William in charge of the company’s exporting business. In 1867, Henry M. Flager, whom John worked with in the commission market business, was added to the partnership, and Rockefeller, Andrews & Flager was formed. Flager’s wife’s uncle became a silent partner and made substantial investments into the partnership.

John realized that the only way to make money consistently was to make the business as large as possible and to fully utilize all of its waste products. He cut efficiencies down to the smallest detail. The partnership built high-quality refineries using the best materials and owned their own cooperage (barrel-making) plant, which cut the cost of a barrel from $3.00 to less than $1.50. The partnership also owned tanks, warehouses, boats, and their own drayage service to transport their oil. On January 10, 1870, The Standard Oil Company of Ohio was formed by John D. Rockefeller (30%), William Rockefeller (13.34%), Henry Flagler (16.67%), Samuel Andrews (16.67%), Stephen Harkness (13.34%), and O. B. Jennings (brother-in-law of William Rockefeller) (10%). At the time of its formation, the company held a 10 percent market share in the oil business and expanded by acquisition. By 1872, the company had quietly absorbed most of the oil refineries in Cleveland. The company also built its own pipeline system to more cheaply and efficiently distribute their oil.

In response to state laws limiting the scale of companies, John and his associates created innovative ways to manage their fast-growing enterprise. On January 2, 1882, they combined their disparate companies, spread across dozens of states, under a single group of trustees, entitled The Standard Oil Trust. By 1904, the trust had installed a nationwide distribution system that served 80 percent of all American homes and businesses. At its peak, John’s company held a 90 percent market share of the oil industry. The Standard Oil Trust was eventually dissolved in 1911, under the Sherman Antitrust Act, and split into thirty-four individual, independent companies. ExxonMobil, Chevron, ARCO, Marathon Petroleum, and Imperial Oil are all direct descendants.

John D. Rockefeller, Sr. is widely considered to have been the richest man in history. Until his death in 1937, John’s assets equaled 1.5 percent of America’s total economic output, the equivalent of $340 billion today.

It was a cold, harsh day, as it well might be, for it was the day before Christmas. A young man of twenty-seven, his face well tanned from spending time outdoors, stood on the hill overlooking the village of Wellburn. With a thoughtful gaze, he looked at the peaceful little town that had once been his home.
“It’s been ten years,” he thought, “since I last saw Wellburn, and it still looks the same—not a day older than when I left it. My life’s been full of ups and downs since then. But everything has turned out well, thank God! I’m coming home with enough money to seem rich to my old neighbors. If only they’re still alive to share it with me, I’ll be happy.” And who were they?
Ten years ago, John Rawson had left home without his father’s permission. He had always been a headstrong boy, full of wild energy and impatient with rules. Maybe his father hadn’t been patient enough with him. In any case, their personalities clashed. After a bitter argument, John packed a small bundle of clothes and left home before sunrise. His father hadn’t heard from him since.
He’d lived a rough life. He signed up to work on a ship heading to the East Indies, traveled there and back, then took other trips, spending money as he went. About five years ago, he reached Australia and turned over a new leaf. He became steady, luck was on his side, and he quickly made money. But during all that time, why hadn’t he written home? Didn’t the image of his grandmother’s sad face make him want news from home?
Yes, often. But he was proud. His father had said he would never do well, and John wanted to prove him wrong. He planned to return successful. He didn’t worry for his father, who was well-off. Poverty was the last thing he expected for him.
But money is never guaranteed. Mr. Rawson had invested in a promising business out West and lost it all. He had taken out a mortgage on the farm, and it was foreclosed just three months ago. Poor health followed the financial loss, and too sick to work, he and his wife had found shelter in a run-down little cabin he would’ve once considered unlivable.
“What day is it, wife?” he asked in a tired voice from his chair.
“Thursday.”
“And tomorrow will be Christmas Day?”
“Yes.”
He sighed.
“Happy Christmas, I used to call it, but I’ll never have another happy Christmas.”
“You must try to be at peace, dear husband. Maybe our little troubles have come for a good reason. Otherwise, God wouldn’t have allowed them.”
“Maybe so, Sarah. That’s the right way to think of it, no doubt, but I can’t help regretting the past.”
“We didn’t know how good we had it back then, husband. But after all, being poor isn’t the worst thing.”
“What’s worse?”
“Losing the ones we love,” his wife said quietly.
“I know what you’re thinking of,” he said sadly. “Our son.”
“Yes. He might have been our support and strength in old age, but he was hot-headed and hard to control. And now, in our old age, we’re alone.”
“But not abandoned by God.”
“I hope not.”
“I’m sure not. He may still turn our sorrow into joy.”
“It’s too late for that, Sarah.”
“It’s never too late for Him.”
It was clear that Sarah’s faith was stronger than her husband’s. She still believed and trusted in God. He only half believed.
The night passed, and the next morning—Christmas Day—arrived. It was bright and beautiful. Sunshine lit up the wide fields, and everything looked cheerful.
“Open the curtain, Sarah,” said Mr. Rawson. “No, not that one, the one that looks toward our old house.”
She did as he asked.
“I spent so many Christmas Days there. I never imagined I’d end up like this.”
“Let’s be thankful for even this house, husband. It could have been worse.”
“I don’t really see how.”
She didn’t reply right away; he wasn’t in the mood to hear comfort.
“What are we having for dinner?” he asked a bit later.
“I thought we’d warm up the meat we had yesterday,” his wife said softly.
“A fine Christmas dinner,” he said bitterly.
“I think there are people who’d feel lucky to have even that.”
“What a frustrating woman you are!” he snapped.
“Because I won’t look on the dark side?” she said with a faint smile. “I would, if it made me feel any better.”
“Don’t talk to me about happiness. That’ll never come again for us.”
“I don’t know why, husband, but I’ve never felt more cheerful or hopeful. I feel like something wonderful is about to happen.”
“If you mean getting our money back, don’t hope for that. It’s completely gone.” He could’ve added that it was his own careless choice that caused the loss, but we’re often easier on our own mistakes.
“No, it’s not that,” said Mrs. Rawson. “I don’t know what it is, really, but just like we sometimes feel trouble coming, I think we can feel joy coming too.”
They sat quietly until a loud knock came at the door.
Mrs. Rawson answered it herself. She found the young man introduced at the beginning of the story, but her eyes were dim, or maybe her mother’s instinct failed her, for she didn’t recognize in the tall, strong man the boy of seventeen who had left home ten years ago and hadn’t been heard from since.
The young man’s heart beat faster as he looked at the tired but familiar face of the gentle mother he once knew so well.
“Is Mr. Rawson at home?” he asked.
“Yes, sir. Would you like to see him?”
“If you please.”
“Please come in. My husband is a little weak right now, but I hope he’ll be up and around again soon.”
The young man stepped inside, and his eyes filled with tears when he saw the poor home his parents were living in. “Thank God,” he thought, “I can change this.”
“Sorry to drop in like this, Mr. Rawson,” he said, “but I’m thinking of buying the farm you used to own, and someone sent me to you for more information. It’s a good farm, right?”
“An excellent one—none better. I’d still own it if I hadn’t gambled on land I’d never even seen. Now I’m poor in my old age.”
“You’ve had bad luck, sir, but things can always turn around.”
Mr. Rawson shook his head.
“That’s what my wife says, but I don’t see much hope.”
“Would you say five thousand dollars is too much for the farm, Mr. Rawson?”
“No, it’s worth that.”
“I’m glad you think so, because to be honest, I’ve already bought it.”
“Are you going to live there? If so, we’ll be neighbors.”
“Yes, I hope we’ll be very close neighbors. But I didn’t buy it for myself—it’s a Christmas present for some dear friends of mine.”
“A Christmas present? That’s a very generous gift.”
“Yes, but since it’s for my father, it’s not too much.”
“Your father’s lucky to have such a devoted son.”
“I’m not sure he sees it that way. I’ve probably failed him in a lot of ways.”
“Excuse me, sir, but you haven’t told us your name yet.”
“My name,” the young man said clearly, “is John Rawson.”
“John!” his mother cried, standing up and looking closely at his face.
“Yes, mother,” said the young man, hugging her. “The runaway has come back. Am I welcome?”
“Oh, John, this is such a happy day. I just knew something would happen to make it a happy Christmas.”
They spent an hour talking about all he had been through. Then John said,
“Father, I’ve bought back the old farm—not for me, but for you. Here’s the deed. It’s all yours, free and clear.”
“But can you afford a gift like that, son?” his father asked, uncertain.
“I could buy it three times over if I wanted to. I did well in Australia and I’m financially secure.”
“Then I’ll gladly accept it, John. You have no idea how I’ve missed that farm. Just before you came, I was full of regret. But God has shown me my mistake by blessing me beyond what I deserve. Blessed be His name!”
So, the day that started out gloomy ended in joy, and John Rawson felt he had never had a happier Christmas.

On the last night of the year, John Stevenson walked slowly and sadly home in the rain, holding an old umbrella. He was a bookkeeper at the large company of Green & Sons on Washington Street. His thoughts were mostly sad and worried. He had a good wife and four growing children, but with prices for food and clothes going up so much over the past year, it had become almost impossible to take care of his family and stay out of debt.
Three months ago, knowing his salary wasn’t enough, he had asked for a small raise—just a hundred dollars. But Mr. Green had been in a bad mood and turned him down sharply. Since then, John hadn’t asked again. His own overcoat was very worn out. He had even skipped church a couple of times because he was embarrassed to wear it. Johnny, his oldest boy, also needed a coat, but John didn’t know how to buy one for either of them.
When he got home, his wife greeted him with a smile and helped him take off his coat.
“John,” she said, “don’t you think you should get a new coat? You really need one.”
John shook his head. “I know, Martha, but even a cheap new coat would cost at least thirty dollars—and that’s not even the kind I want. I just can’t afford it.”
“If only Mr. Green would give you a raise.”
“There’s no chance of that.”
“Did you ask him?”
“Yes, three months ago.”
“And what did he say?”
“He said that if I thought my salary was too low, he wouldn’t stop me from finding a better job.”
“That was cruel.”
“It felt that way, especially since he lives in a fancy house and spends twenty times more on his family than he gives me for mine.”
“So you won’t ask him again?”
“No. He might fire me. And since I haven’t saved anything, that’s too risky.”
“Well,” sighed his wife, “I just hope prices come down soon. Otherwise, we might really suffer. Johnny needs a coat badly.”
“Yes, he has to get one, even if I go into debt for it. Is there any way we can cut back?”
“I’m afraid not. We’re already saving every way we can. I can’t think of anything else.”
John sat down to dinner. As he looked at his wife and children gathered around the table, he couldn’t help but feel thankful for them, even with all their struggles.
After dinner, he sat by the fire with his youngest daughter on his lap. For a little while, he forgot his worries and just felt happy to be home.
Around nine o’clock, the doorbell rang. Since they didn’t have a helper, John answered it himself. He was surprised to see his boss standing there.
“Come in, Mr. Green,” he said. “I’m glad to see you.”
“Thank you, Stevenson. I’ve got some extra work—letters that need to go out in the next mail. Can you help?”
“Of course, sir. But how did you know where I live?”
“I found your address in the directory. I wasn’t sure I had the right house.”
They went into the small living room.
“This is my wife, Mr. Green,” John said.
“Your boss, John?” asked his wife.
“Yes, Mary.”
“I’m happy to welcome you, sir, to our humble home,” she said, offering her hand.

Life Story: Sarah “Madam C.J.” Breedlove Walker (1867-1919)
Culled from Women and the American Story
Sarah Breedlove was born on December 23, 1867 in Delta, Louisiana. Her parents and four older siblings had been enslaved on a cotton plantation until the end of the Civil War. Like many formerly enslaved people, they lived and worked together as sharecroppers to make ends meet. Sarah was the first member of her family to be born into freedom.

Sarah lost both of her parents by the time she was seven years old. She went to live with her older sister, but her sister’s husband was a cruel man who forced her to make money picking cotton and doing laundry. He may also have physically abused Sarah. At the age of fourteen, Sarah ran away from home and married a man named Moses McWilliams. Before her seventeenth birthday, she gave birth to her only child, a daughter named Lelia. Moses died in 1887, leaving Sarah a young, widowed mother.

In 1888 Sarah and Lelia moved to St. Louis to be closer to Sarah’s three older brothers. Her brothers had moved to the North at a young age to escape racial violence and find jobs. Sarah worked as a laundress for $1.50 a day and went to night school when she was able. She briefly married a man named John Davis, but the marriage was over by 1903.

Sarah was determined to build a better life than the one she could afford working as a laundress. In 1904 she took a job selling haircare products for a Black woman-owned business. Throughout her life, Sarah had struggled with hair loss that was likely caused by poor nutrition and stress. Like most Black women of the time, she used harsh soap, heavy oil, and grease to manage her curls, which would have only made her condition worse. Although new technology had led to the expansion of the beauty industry in the late 1800s, most products were designed for and sold to white women. Seeing an opportunity, Sarah started to experiment with creating her own line of products that softened her hair and eased her irritated scalp.

Sarah and Lelia moved to Denver, Colorado in 1905, where Sarah continued to sell hair care products and develop her line. Her experimentation paid off. Little by little, Sarah’s hair began to grow. As her confidence in her products grew, Sarah started to sell them.

In 1906 Sarah married Charles Joseph “C. J.” Walker, and he became a partner in her new beauty business. She renamed herself Madam C. J. Walker and began to advertise her products in Black publications. She also sold them through a mail order system. She was so happy with how her hair had grown that she put pictures of herself on the packaging. She held lectures and demonstrations of what she called the “Walker Method”: washing hair with gentle shampoo, brushing hair, massaging the scalp, and then treating hair with a healing pomade. By 1910 business was booming. She moved to Indianapolis to build a factory and establish a permanent company headquarters.

“Madam Walker used her business to empower Black women.”

At the time Madam Walker was expanding her company, hair was a controversial issue in the Black community. White racists pointed to Black hair texture as evidence that Black people were inferior. They claimed that Black women who could not or would not smooth out their kinky hair were unclean and messy. For many Black women, using beauty products to smooth out their hair was a way of demonstrating their equality to white women. Some women were less concerned about issues of race and merely wanted the opportunity to adopt the most popular styles of the time. Some Black advocates believed that, regardless of their motivation, Black women who changed their hair were catering to racism by adhering to white beauty standards. Madam Walker took criticism because she sold products that helped straighten and smooth hair. But she argued that her products were about keeping hair healthy. Because she had personally struggled with hair and scalp issues, she promoted healthy hair over any particular style.

Madam Walker used her business to empower Black women. She founded several beauty training schools and employed hundreds of women across the country to serve as Walker Agents, saleswomen trained in the Walker Method who served as the face of the Walker brand. Madam Walker organized national conventions for her agents, where they could share selling strategies, learn about new products, and receive rewards for outstanding sales. For many women, being a Walker Agent and working for a Black woman-owned business was a welcome alternative to low-paying domestic work.

In 1913 Madam Walker and Charles Walker divorced. She focused her energy on extending her company’s reach to the Caribbean and Latin America. In 1916 she followed her daughter to New York City and moved into a grand townhouse in Harlem. Although she continued to run her beauty business, she allowed employees to handle the day-to-day operations. She became involved in the social and political life of Harlem, particularly the anti-lynching movement, donating $5,000.

As Madam Walker’s business grew, so did her wealth. In addition to her Harlem townhouse, she owned a Model T Ford and made plans to build a mansion in upstate New York called Villa Lewaro, a name she created using letters from her beloved daughter’s married name: Lelia Walker Robinson. But Madam Walker did not spend all of her money on herself. She was committed to helping Black men and women escape poverty just like she had. She donated money to scholarships, homes for the elderly, anti-lynching efforts, and other important Black causes on the local and national stage. She became as famous for her philanthropy as she was for her beauty business.

Madam Walker died from complications of high blood pressure on May 25, 1919, at the age of fifty-one. At the time of her death, it was estimated that her estate was worth one to two million dollars (the equivalent of eighteen to thirty-six million dollars today). She was the first self-made woman millionaire in America. Her daughter, Lelia, continued in her mother’s footsteps. She took over the still-growing company and used her mother’s fortune to support artists, writers, and other leaders of the Harlem Renaissance.

Major Graf Von Farlsberg, the Prussian commandant, was reading his newspaper as he leaned back in a big armchair, with his booted feet on the fancy marble mantelpiece. His spurs had left two holes in the stone that had grown deeper every day during the three months he had stayed in the house at Uville.
A cup of coffee was steaming on a small, decorated table, which was stained with alcohol, burned by cigars, and scratched up from the officer’s penknife. He often stopped while sharpening a pencil to jot down numbers or doodle, just for fun.
After reading his letters and German newspapers, brought to him by his orderly, he stood up and tossed a few big, wet logs on the fire. The soldiers were slowly cutting down the park for wood to stay warm. Then he walked to the window.

Since arriving in France, his fellow soldiers had nicknamed him “Miss Fifi” because of his slim figure, neat appearance, and high voice. He also had the habit of saying “Fi, fi donc” with a little whistle whenever he wanted to show disgust.

The officers ate breakfast quietly in the gloomy, rain-drenched room. Its worn floor was as hard as stone.
After breakfast, they smoked and drank while complaining about how boring life had become. They passed bottles of brandy and liquor, leaning back and sipping slowly.
Miss Fifi downed his drinks fast, and a soldier stood by to hand him a new one right away. The room filled with thick smoke, and the men grew sleepy and dull with boredom and alcohol.

Miss Fifi picked out a porcelain teapot, filled it with gunpowder, stuck a fuse through the spout, lit it, and placed it in the next room. He came back and shut the door.
The others waited like kids at a fireworks show.

The dining room filled with smoke. The commandant opened a window, and the men leaned out, breathing in the cool, misty air.
Outside, the valley was foggy, and the church steeple barely showed through the rain.

To let off steam, Miss Fifi made another bomb.
The men waited by the window, then Lieutenant Fritz joked, “The ladies won’t have great weather for their ride.”
That evening, everyone dressed up as if for a big parade. The commandant looked younger, and the captain had shaved, leaving a red mustache that looked like a line of fire.

Five pretty women stepped down, handpicked by the captain’s friend.

The dining room, lit up now, looked like a bandit’s den—with fancy food, fine glass, and hidden silver set out for a feast.

“What’s your name?” he asked the tallest.
“Pamela.”

He kissed Blondina, claimed her for himself, gave Amanda to Lieutenant Otto, Eva (the “Tomato”) to Fritz, and the shortest girl—Rachel, a dark-eyed Jewish girl—to the young Count Wilhelm.
The women were all alike: pretty, curvy, and cheerful.
The officers wanted to take the girls away immediately, but the captain said no. He said they were fine as-is. There were kisses—lots of them.
Rachel suddenly coughed, her eyes watering. The count had blown smoke into her mouth while pretending to kiss her.
She didn’t yell, but her dark eyes burned with hate.
They sat for dinner. The commandant beamed. “That was a wonderful idea,” he said.
Otto and Fritz were overly polite. The women didn’t know how to react.
But the red-haired baron was loud and rude, making dirty jokes in bad French. The women didn’t understand until he used crude words—and then they laughed and shouted like wild animals, repeating the dirty language for fun.
The men yelled, broke plates, and acted crazy. Only the commandant stayed calm.
Miss Fifi kissed Rachel one minute, then pinched her hard the next. He bit her lip until she bled.
She wiped her face. “You’ll pay for that.”
“I’ll pay,” he sneered.
At dessert, the commandant toasted: “To our ladies!” Then came a series of nasty toasts.
The captain raised his glass. “To victories over hearts!”
Lieutenant Otto stood up, drunk and angry. “To victories over France!”
The women fell silent. Rachel shook. “I know Frenchmen you’d never say that in front of.”
The count laughed. “They run when they see us!”
“You’re lying!” Rachel screamed.
He stared at her, cold and cruel. “France belongs to us!”
She jumped from his lap. He shouted again: “France, its people, its homes—all ours!”
The others raised their glasses. “Long live Prussia!”
The women stayed quiet.
The count put a glass on Rachel’s head. “The women of France are ours too!”
Rachel jumped. The wine spilled into her hair and the glass shattered.
She glared at him. “That’s not true. You will not have the women of France!”
He sat back, laughing. “Then why did you come here?”
Rachel froze—then shouted: “I’m no woman. I’m just a tramp—and that’s all you Prussians want!”
He slapped her.
As he raised his hand again, she grabbed a dessert knife and stabbed him in the neck.
He gasped. Blood poured.
The men shouted. Rachel threw a chair, tripped Otto, and jumped out the window into the rain.
Two minutes later, Miss Fifi was dead.
Otto and Fritz wanted to kill the women, but the major stopped them. He locked the four girls in a room and organized a manhunt.
They searched all night. Two soldiers died. Three were wounded.
But they never caught Rachel.
They tore through homes and fields. She left no trace.
The general ordered everyone to stay quiet about it and punished the officers. “War isn’t for fun or fooling with women,” he said.
The commandant, still furious, wanted revenge. He made the priest ring the church bell for Miss Fifi’s funeral.
To everyone’s surprise, the priest agreed.
The bell rang loud and clear for the first time.
Then it rang every day. Sometimes at night.
People said the bell was haunted. Only the priest and sacristan would go near the tower.
Because inside, hiding, was Rachel.
She stayed until the Germans left.
One night, the priest borrowed a cart and took her to Rouen. He hugged her goodbye.
She walked back to the place she had come from. The owner, who thought she was dead, welcomed her warmly.
Not long after, a kind man—someone who admired her bravery—married her.
And she became a lady, just as good as anyone else.

There were eight of us, including the driver. We hadn’t said anything for the last six miles because the rough road had ruined the Judge’s last poetic quote. The tall man next to him was asleep, his arm looped through the swinging strap, his head resting on it—he looked limp and helpless, like someone who had been hanged and cut down too late.
The French woman in the back seat was also asleep, but even in her sleep, she managed to sit properly, with a handkerchief held to her forehead, partly covering her face. The woman from Virginia City, traveling with her husband, had long since disappeared into a tangle of ribbons, veils, furs, and shawls—no one could really see her anymore.
The only sounds were the rattling of the wheels and the rain pounding on the roof. Suddenly, the stagecoach stopped. We could just barely hear voices outside. The driver was clearly in the middle of an intense conversation with someone on the road. Now and then, we caught words like “bridge gone,” “twenty feet of water,” and “can’t pass,” rising above the sound of the storm.
Then everything went quiet. And from out on the road, a mysterious voice called out:
“Try Miggles’s.”
We caught a quick glimpse of the people ahead of us as the stagecoach slowly turned. A man on horseback disappeared into the rain, and it was clear—we were headed to Miggles’s place.
But who was Miggles? And where exactly was this person? The Judge, who knew the area well, didn’t recognize the name. The traveler from Washoe guessed that Miggles must run a hotel. All we really knew was that we were trapped by deep water in both directions, and Miggles was now our only hope.
After ten minutes of splashing through a narrow, tangled dirt road—barely wide enough for the stage—we pulled up in front of a large, locked gate. It was set in a tall stone wall, about eight feet high. This had to be Miggles’s place, but it was clear Miggles didn’t run a hotel.
The driver climbed down and tried the gate. It was locked tight.
“Miggles! Oh, Miggles!” he shouted.
No answer.
“Miggles! You, Miggles!” the driver yelled, getting more and more annoyed.
“Migglesy!” added the delivery man, trying to sound friendly. “Oh, Miggy! Mig!”
Still nothing. The Judge stuck his head out the window and started asking a long list of questions, but the driver just waved them off.
“If you don’t want to spend the night in the coach, you’d better all get out and help call for Miggles.”
So we did. We stood up and all shouted for Miggles together—then one by one. When we were out of ideas, a man from the roof of the stagecoach, who had an Irish accent, shouted “Maygells!” That made us all laugh.
While we were still laughing, the driver suddenly called out, “Shoo!”
We stopped and listened. To our total surprise, the shout of “Miggles!” was repeated back to us from the other side of the wall—exactly the same, even with the funny “Maygells” at the end.
“Strange echo,” said the Judge.
“Strange nothing—it’s a no-good skunk!” the driver yelled. “Come out, Miggles, and show yourself! Be a man, Miggles! Don’t hide—I wouldn’t, if I were you!”
“Miggles! Oh, Miggles!” the voice called again.
“My good man! Mr. Myghail!” the Judge said, trying to make the name sound formal. “Please consider how unfriendly it is to deny shelter in weather like this—especially to helpless women. Really, sir—”
But another round of “Miggles!” and laughter cut him off completely.
Yuba Bill had had enough. He grabbed a heavy stone, smashed down the gate, and walked through with the delivery man. We followed behind.
There was no one in sight. It was getting dark, but we could see we were in a garden—wet roses brushing us as we walked—and standing before a long wooden house.
“Do you know this Miggles?” the Judge asked Bill.
“Nope, and I don’t want to,” Bill replied. He felt like Miggles had insulted the entire stage company.
“But really,” the Judge started.
“Maybe you’d rather wait in the coach until someone introduces you properly?” Bill said, full of sarcasm. “I’m going in.” And he opened the front door.
Inside was a long room, lit only by the faint glow of a dying fire in the fireplace. The wallpaper had a strange, busy pattern, and the flickering light made it seem alive. Sitting in a big armchair by the fire was someone silent and still.
“Hey, are you Miggles?” Bill asked.
The person didn’t move. Bill, annoyed, walked over and held his lantern to the man’s face. It was the face of an old man—very wrinkled, with huge eyes and a blank, serious look like an owl. His gaze drifted from Bill to the lantern and stopped there.
“Miggles! Can you hear me? You’re not mute, that’s for sure,” Bill said, and gave the man a shake.
To our shock, the man collapsed into a slouched heap like a pile of clothes.
“Well, I’ll be darned,” Bill muttered and backed off.
The Judge stepped forward, and we helped the old man sit back up. Then Bill went to check outside for anyone else. Since this man clearly couldn’t live alone, someone had to be nearby. The rest of us gathered around the fire.
The Judge, feeling back in charge, stood in front of the fireplace and said seriously:
“It seems this man is either in the stage Shakespeare called ‘the fading leaf,’ or he’s had an early loss of body and mind. Now, whether he is Miggles—”
He was cut off by another chorus of “Miggles! Migglesy! Mig!”
We all turned in alarm. The Judge jumped away from the fire—it had sounded like it came from just behind him. Then we saw it: a big magpie sitting on a shelf above the fireplace. It now sat silently, looking very pleased with itself. Clearly, it had been repeating the shouts we heard outside. The man in the chair wasn’t the one ignoring us—it had been the bird.
Bill came back in, dripping wet and frustrated. He said he’d found a shed for the horses but no other person in sight.
“There’s no one else for ten miles,” he said, eyeing the old man. “And that old guy knows it.”
Just then, we heard fast footsteps outside, the door flew open, and in walked a young woman—breathing hard, her eyes sparkling, a white smile flashing.
“Oh! If you please—I’m Miggles!”
This was Miggles? This bright-eyed, confident young woman, soaked from head to toe, wearing a simple blue dress that clung to her graceful figure, and a man’s rain hat on her head? From her wild hair to her sturdy boots, she was full of charm—and she was laughing at us all with the most cheerful and casual ease.
“You see, boys,” she said, still catching her breath, “I was over two miles away when you passed. I figured you might stop here, so I ran the whole way, since no one was home but Jim—and now I’m out of breath—and well, that’s that.”
She pulled off her hat, sending drops of water flying, tried to fix her hair, dropped a few hairpins, laughed, and sat down beside Yuba Bill.
The Judge tried to say something charming, but Miggles just said, “I’ll take that hairpin,” with perfect calm. A few of us scrambled to help.
Then she crossed the room and looked at the old man. He stared back at her in a way we hadn’t seen before—like something deep inside was coming back to life. Miggles laughed again, warm and clear, and turned back to us.
“This man is—?” the Judge began.
“Jim,” said Miggles.
“Your father?”
“No.”
“Brother?”
“No.”
“Husband?”
Miggles gave a quick, almost defiant look at the two lady passengers, who hadn’t shared our enthusiasm for her, and said simply, “No. It’s Jim.”
There was an awkward pause. The women pulled closer together. The Washoe man stared into the fire. No one knew what to say.
But then Miggles laughed again and changed the mood completely.
“Come on, you must be hungry. Who wants to help me make tea?”
She had no shortage of volunteers. Yuba Bill was hauling firewood, the delivery man was grinding coffee on the porch, I was slicing bacon, and the Judge offered advice to everyone. Soon, Miggles and the others had set the table with everything they could find, and despite the storm outside, the strange bird on the shelf, and the tension in the air, we were all in good spirits.
The fire lit the room brightly now. The walls were decorated with pictures from magazines, arranged with care. The furniture was made from wooden crates, covered with colorful cloth or animal skins. Jim’s chair was a clever reworking of a flour barrel.
Everything was neat and thoughtfully arranged.
Dinner was a success—thanks mostly to Miggles’s gift for keeping conversation going. She asked all the questions and shared just enough to keep things open, but still never made it about herself. We talked about everything—our work, our plans, the journey—but never about her or Jim.
Her language wasn’t fancy, and sometimes she swore like a man, but when she did, her smile and laugh somehow made it all feel honest and clean.
At one point, we heard a heavy scraping sound outside, then scratching at the door.
“That’s Joaquin,” said Miggles. “Want to meet him?”
Before we could answer, she opened the door—and in walked a half-grown grizzly bear, who sat up and looked at her with an almost human expression.
“That’s my watchdog,” she said as the two women gasped and stepped away. “Don’t worry, he doesn’t bite. Right, old Toppy?” she said, speaking to him gently.
“I’m telling you,” she added after feeding him and closing the door, “you’re lucky he wasn’t here when you showed up tonight.”
“Where was he?” the Judge asked.
“With me,” she said. “He follows me around at night like he’s a person.”
We were quiet. Maybe we were all imagining her, walking through the rainy woods with a bear by her side. The Judge made a comment about Una and her lion, but Miggles just gave her usual quiet smile.
The women still didn’t warm to her. And when the meal ended, they remained stiff and distant. Miggles noticed.
“It’s time to turn in,” she said. “I’ll show the ladies to their room. You boys will have to camp out here by the fire. There’s only the one bedroom.”
As soon as she left, we huddled together, whispering and guessing, trying to figure her out. We even surrounded poor Jim, who sat silently with his deep, serious eyes, like some old statue watching our foolishness.
Just then, Miggles came back.
She didn’t look like the same woman from before. Her confidence had softened. She came in holding a blanket, walked over to Jim, sat down on a stool next to him, wrapped herself in the blanket, and said, “If it’s all the same to you boys, I’ll stay here tonight.” Then she gently took Jim’s hand and looked into the fire.
The room grew quiet.
Outside, the rain tapped the roof, and the fire flickered. Then, in a quiet moment between gusts of wind, Miggles looked up, brushed her hair back, and asked:
“Do any of you know me?”
No one answered.
“I lived in Marysville back in ’53. I ran the Polka Saloon. Everyone knew me then. I came here to live with Jim six years ago. Maybe I’ve changed.”
She paused, then continued faster:
“Jim used to know me. Spent a lot on me. Probably everything he had. Then one day—six years ago this winter—he sat down on my couch like he is now, and never got up again. He was just frozen. Doctors said it was his way of living and that he wouldn’t get better. Told me to send him to a hospital in San Francisco. But I couldn’t.
“I was popular back then. Had money. I sold everything and bought this place out here where no one comes. I brought my baby here.”
She moved behind Jim as she spoke, almost hiding in his shadow.
“It took me a while to figure things out. I couldn’t get any woman to help, and I didn’t trust a man. But some of the local Native folks helped, and I had supplies brought in. The doctor would visit sometimes. He’d say, ‘Miggles, you’re one of a kind—God bless you.’
“But the last time he came, he looked sad. He said, ‘Miggles, your baby might grow up to be a man someday—but not here. Not here.’”
She fell quiet.
A few moments later, she added:
“The people around here are kind. The men stopped coming by. The women—well, they’re polite from a distance. I got Joaquin, the bear, when he was small. Taught him to beg for food. And Polly, the magpie—she talks all the time. Between the two of them, and Jim, it doesn’t feel so lonely anymore.
“And Jim,” she said with a smile, stepping back into the firelight, “you should see how much he understands. I bring him flowers and he looks at them like he remembers. And I read to him—from all those pictures on the wall. I’ve read him that whole side of the house this winter.”
“Then why don’t you marry him?” the Judge asked gently.
“Well,” said Miggles, “it wouldn’t be fair to Jim. He can’t say no. And besides, if we were married, we’d both know I was doing this because I had to—not because I chose to.”
“But you’re still young—and beautiful—”
“It’s late,” she said seriously. “You’d better all turn in. Good night, boys.”
She lay down beside Jim, resting her head on the stool at his feet, pulled the blanket over her head, and said no more.
The fire faded. We each found our blankets in silence. The only sounds were the rain on the roof and the quiet breathing of those around us.

It was almost morning when I woke from a strange dream. The storm was over. Stars filled the sky, and moonlight shone through the open window.
The moonlight touched Jim’s quiet face with a kind gentleness. It bathed Miggles, resting at his feet, in silver light—like that beautiful old story of a woman who washed the feet of someone she loved.
Even Yuba Bill, half-sitting, half-lying near them, had a rugged poetry to him in the moonlight—his eyes wide open, keeping silent watch.
And then I fell asleep again.
When I woke up, it was broad daylight, and Yuba Bill was standing over me.
“All aboard!” he called.

Coffee was waiting on the table, but Miggles was gone.
We wandered through the house, lingering long after the horses were ready. But she didn’t come back. It was clear she didn’t want to say goodbye and had let us leave the same quiet way we’d come.
After helping the women into the stagecoach, we returned to the house one more time. We each shook hands with Jim—solemnly, one by one—and gently set him back into place after each handshake. We looked around the long, low room, at the stool where Miggles had sat, and finally returned to the coach.
The whip cracked, and we rolled away.

But just as we reached the main road, Bill suddenly pulled the horses back, and the stagecoach jerked to a stop.
There on a little hill beside the road stood Miggles—her hair flying, eyes sparkling, white handkerchief waving, and her wide smile shining one last time.
We all waved our hats in return.
Then, as if afraid to look any longer, Yuba Bill snapped the reins hard, and the stagecoach took off. We leaned back into our seats.
No one said a word until we reached North Fork and stopped at the Independence House.
Led by the Judge, we walked quietly into the barroom and stood at the counter.
“Are your glasses full, gentlemen?” the Judge asked, removing his white hat.
They were.
“Then here’s to MIGGLES. GOD BLESS HER.”

Rewrite this story to emphasize community values:

I never worked as a teacher but once, and goodness knows I never want to again.
This is how it happened.
I was a girl of sixteen when I finished school. I had always been a good student, and this, I suppose, was the reason that in the fall of the same year I was asked to teach the winter term at Dog’s Misery. How this beautiful name came about I don’t know, but I can guess, having seen several dogs during my short stay, walking down the street with tin cans tied to their tails.
The district agent offered me the generous sum of $1.25 a week and board. The last teacher had received more, but I was new, as he nicely pointed out, and couldn’t expect that much. I quietly agreed to the terms, and when the time came, I took the village bus and was soon dropped off in the area known as Dog’s Misery.
I was to stay with Mrs. Abijah Higginson. I mention her name, because her husband didn’t matter much, and I didn’t see much of him anyway.
I guessed from Mrs. Higginson’s looks that when she was made, there was plenty of material. She probably weighed at least 200 pounds.
“We won’t treat you with any ceremony, Miss Preston,” she said. “You must make yourself at home.”
“Certainly,” I said.
“We don’t have a spare room, but I guess you can sleep between Amanda and Hepsy Ann.”
These were two girls, twelve and fourteen years old, shaped like their mother. I didn’t say anything, but the idea made me nervous, especially when I looked at the small space meant for me.
On Monday morning, I went to the schoolhouse—a red, one-story building that could have worked as a shed, but not really as a place to learn.
Outside was a group of kids, probably thirty, staring at me as I walked up, trying my best to look serious and confident.
“Is that the teacher?” I heard one say.
“She doesn’t look very strong. Guess she can’t hit very hard,” said another.
To be honest, I had the same worry. Some of the boys were pretty big and looked like trouble.
My desk was a wobbly table. In a drawer, I found a small bell, which I rang as hard as I could. The students came running in, making as much noise as possible. Once they were seated, I started a speech I had prepared.
“Students,” I said, “education is one of the greatest gifts of God to people. Without it—”
A loud yell cut me off.
“What’s the matter?” I asked quickly.
“Tom Smith pinched me.”
“Thomas, did you pinch him?” I asked the big boy sitting nearby.
“I guess it didn’t hurt him much. I only did it for fun.”
“It’s a very poor kind of fun. Besides, you’re here to study, not to play. Anyway, as I was saying, education is one of the noblest gifts of God to man. Without it—”
One of the girls giggled a lot. Thinking she was laughing at my speech, I stopped and looked at her sternly.
“What are you laughing at?” I asked.
“’Cause Melissa Thompson tickled me.”
“Melissa, why did you tickle her?”
“Please, ma’am, she tickled me first.”
“I will allow no tickling in school. I’ll punish the next one who does it.”
I started again.
“Students, education is the noblest gift of God to man. Without it—”
Another little girl laughed.
“Come here,” I said angrily.
She walked up looking scared. “What were you laughing at?”
“I don’t know, ma’am.”
“Yes, you do. Tell me now.”
“Please, ma’am, I hope you won’t be mad. I was laughing because you told us that three times.”
I sent her back to her seat and gave up on my speech. I still have it written down and will sell it cheap to anyone thinking about becoming a teacher.
The next hour was spent setting up the classes, which was harder than fun. One girl wanted to be in the top geography class, so I tested her.
“Where is Europe?”
“In Asia,” she said slowly.
“No. Try again.”
“It’s a town on the Mississippi River.”
I tried something closer to home.
“Where is Cape Cod?”
“It’s an island on the Mediterranean Sea.”
I decided she wasn’t ready for the advanced class.
Later, I called up the spelling class.
“Tom Smith, spell onion.”
“U-n un, y-u-n, onion,” he said.
That’s enough examples—you get the idea.
At last I got through the morning and went home to a lunch of baked beans.
“How do you like the school?” asked Mrs. Higginson.
“Pretty well,” I said, not sounding too sure.
“It’s known to be a pretty advanced school,” said Mrs. H.
I thought it was best not to say anything.
“Seems to me you don’t like beans,” she said after a pause.
“Not very much,” I said. “I’ll wait for the pudding.”
“We don’t have any. I don’t usually make pudding. It’s too much trouble.”
With a sad heart and an empty stomach, I went back to the schoolhouse. The boys had stuffed the stove full of wood, and the heat gave me a headache. After a while, I saw a boy stuffing a handkerchief into his mouth to keep from laughing.
“What’s the matter now?” I asked. “Why are you laughing?”
“Pat made me laugh.”
“How?”
“He drew a picture.”
“Pat, let me see it.”
Pat, a ten-year-old, didn’t want to show it. But I made him. The “picture” was of a very ugly woman with a huge nose. Since I have a rather long nose, I would have known it was me even if he hadn’t written under it in messy block letters:
THE SCHOOL TEACHER
“Did you mean this to be me?” I asked, red in the face.
“I don’t know.”
“Well, I do. Come here.”
“I don’t want to.”
“I don’t care what you want.”
I grabbed him by the collar and pulled him to the middle of the room.
“Leave my brother alone!”
That was Bridget Hagan, Pat’s sister.
“You’re next,” I said, annoyed.
I won’t go into the details. My hurt pride needed to be satisfied—and it was. Both Pat and Bridget got to feel how hard my ruler was, and from how loudly they cried, it was clear they had strong lungs.
“There,” I said. “I guess you won’t be drawing any more pictures of me.”
I got back to teaching, feeling proud, and called the next class like a winner. But another problem was waiting.
After recess, I noticed that neither Pat nor Bridget Hagan had come back. I asked the class where they were.
“They went home, ma’am.”
I quietly decided to give them another whipping the next day.
About twenty minutes later, there was a loud knock at the door. One of the girls answered it.
“Tell the schoolmistress I want to see her,” I heard in a thick Irish accent.
I went to the door. There stood a large Irish woman, her face red and her sleeves rolled up, showing big, strong arms.
“Are you the teacher?”
“Yes. Who are you?”
“I’m Mrs. Hagan, the mother of the poor children you beat black and blue. Why did you do it, I’d like to know?” she said with her hands on her hips.
“I didn’t beat them black and blue. I punished them because they misbehaved.”
“Sure, and you hurt the poor kids. They’re the smartest in school, even if I say so, and I won’t let anyone touch them. Bad luck to you if you try again.”
“If they need it, I will,” I said, suddenly brave.
“Then, by the bones of St. Patrick, I’ll give you the same,” she shouted, her eyes wild with rage, moving toward me with clenched fists.
She was twice my size. I wouldn’t have stood a chance. But I stayed calm.
“James,” I yelled to an imaginary boy, “bring me my horse-pistol. This woman has threatened me, and the law says I can use it.”
As soon as Mrs. Hagan heard that, she ran away screaming in fear.
“She’s a dangerous woman, for sure,” I heard her say.
She told the whole neighborhood I tried to shoot her. In her panic, she even said I fired a shot and that the bullet whizzed by her ear. Bad luck to you if you try again.” “If they need it, I will,” I said, suddenly brave. “Then, by the bones of St. Patrick, I’ll give you the same,” she shouted, her eyes wild with rage, moving toward me with clenched fists. I have never taught school again—and I never want to.

I still have it written down and will share it freely with anyone thinking about becoming a teacher.
