The morning sun brightens with its first rays the towers and steeples of Boston. Once again, business has started in the crowded streets.
The cold air makes hearts beat faster and makes steps lively. Merrily the sleighs, filled with smiling faces and happy hearts, dash through the streets. All seems joy and gladness on this New Year's Day.
Yet not for everyone. Some people have no friendly greetings. For them, the season brings only cold, suffering, and hardship. They find no relief now, and no hope for the future.
Let us look in on one of the tenants. It was a small room—home to the widow Benson. From the pieces of furniture scattered around the room, it was clear that she had once known better days. A small fire burned in the grate, fed only a little, since coal was expensive. Still, it cast a cheerful glow on the room and on the still-handsome, though tired, face of Mrs. Benson. On the bed lay a twelve-year-old boy who was sick with a fever.
“Charles,” said the mother as she smoothed his pillow, “how do you feel now?”
“Better, mother,” said the sick boy. “I think I could enjoy a piece of chicken if I had it.”
“I wish I could afford it,” said Mrs. Benson, sadly. “But today is rent day, and Mr. Morris will come for the rent. Fifteen dollars, and I only have ten. If he could just wait a little while. But he is a hard man, and I fear the worst.”
Just then, bells rang joyfully in the morning air. The sick boy sat up in bed. “It’s New Year’s Day, isn’t it, mother? Or why do the bells ring so happily?”
“Yes, my dear, it is.”
“I remember how glad I used to be when it arrived. That was when we were rich, mother. Don’t you remember, five years ago, father brought me home a book filled with pictures and told me it was my New Year’s present? I wonder if I’ll ever have another.”
Mrs. Benson sighed sadly, for his words brought clearly to mind all she had lost.
“No,” she said, “those days were too bright and happy to last. They’ll never come again.”
As she spoke, she continued the sewing she had briefly set aside to care for her son.
“How I wish I were a man,” said Charles, watching his mother sew quickly. “I wouldn’t let you work so hard. Put down your work for a moment; you’ve been working so steadily that you need rest.”
“I can’t, Charles. Mr. Grip clearly said he needed this work today, and if I fail, he might not give me any more. I wonder why Mr. Morris hasn’t come for the rent. He’s usually very punctual. If he won’t wait a few days until I can make up the rest, we’ll have to sell something to make up the difference.” Her eyes sadly wandered over the few items left from better days, but they were all dear to her, and she couldn’t bear to part with any of them.
At that moment, a loud knock came at the door.
Mrs. Benson got up quickly and opened it, expecting to see Simon, her landlord. But it was George Seymour who stood there.
“I’ve come,” he said, “on behalf of your landlord, who can’t come himself.”
“I’m very sorry, sir,” said Mrs. Benson, “but I’ve had sickness, and despite all my efforts, I couldn’t save enough to pay the full rent. What I have, I’ll pay now, and I hope Mr. Morris will be willing to wait a little for the rest.”
“You misunderstand me, madam,” replied Seymour. “I did come on your landlord’s orders, but I bring better news. He has decided to give a New Year’s gift to each of his tenants. Believing something useful would be most welcome, he has sent you—like the others—a barrel of flour and some groceries. They’ll be here shortly. I wanted to tell you ahead of time so you wouldn’t think it was a mistake.”
The mix of surprise and gratitude Mrs. Benson felt can only be imagined. The act of generosity was so completely opposite of everything she had believed about her landlord that she could barely believe it.
“Excuse me,” she said, finally composing herself, “but I’m so surprised that I may seem slow in expressing my thanks. Please give my warmest thanks to Mr. Morris for this truly generous act. I see now that I misjudged him. From now on, I’ll think of him as a kind helper.”
Seymour bowed and added, “My task isn’t over. Don’t worry about your rent. Mr. Morris has decided to cut his rents in half from now on. And the rent you owed for this month? He has completely forgiven it.”
Mrs. Benson again expressed her gratitude, feeling lighter than she had in many months. She led Seymour into the room. He followed, partly out of curiosity, partly because he felt a strange interest in Mrs. Benson, though he didn’t yet know her name. He sat down and looked around the room, which was perfectly neat despite the signs of poverty. Mrs. Benson began tending to her son when another knock came at the door, along with the sound of heavy items being brought upstairs.
Mrs. Benson answered the door. A man dressed as a worker stood there. “If you please, ma’am, I’ve been told to bring these things to a Mrs. Benson. If that’s you, I’ll carry them in.”
He pointed to a barrel of flour and a large closed basket.
“I’m the person you’re looking for,” said the widow. “Please bring them in and put them in this closet.”
He did so.
“What should I pay you for your trouble?”
“Nothing, ma’am,” said the man, tipping his hat. “The man who told me to bring them already paid me.”
George Seymour had watched the scene with interest and kindness. When the man had left, he said,
“If you’ll allow me, madam, I’ll open the basket to make sure everything I ordered is there.”
Inside were packages of tea, sugar, butter, and other useful groceries—along with a pair of chickens.
“Charles,” said Mrs. Benson, “your wish has come true; some fairy must have heard you and sent this through our kind landlord.”
George Seymour smiled at the idea of old Simon being called “kind,” but didn’t say anything. To pass the time, he picked up a book from the table. It was a small Bible, and on the first page he read: “Edward Benson to his beloved wife, Jan. 1, 183—.”
He rose in surprise.
“Is this yours, madam?” he asked.
“It is. It was a gift from my late husband.”
“Please don’t think I’m just being nosy, but may I ask one more question? Were you born in Havana, and was your maiden name Mary Mellen?”
“You’re right,” said Mrs. Benson. “But I didn’t know anyone in this city who knew me by that name.”
“I knew it,” said Seymour. “From the moment I saw you, something in your face felt familiar. I’ve been trying to remember where I’d seen you before, but couldn’t.”
“I’m not surprised,” said Mrs. Benson. “Time and sorrow have changed me a lot. But now that I look at you closely… unless my eyes are tricking me—”
“George Seymour.”
The widow’s cheeks turned slightly red; she hadn’t forgotten that George Seymour once asked her to marry him.
Seymour quickly explained why he had come to the United States, how he discovered that old Simon the stingy landlord was really Samuel Morton, a clerk who had once run away, and why he had acted so generously.
Mrs. Benson then told him her story.
“You remember,” she said, “that a few years after our marriage, Mr. Benson moved to New York, thinking it had better business opportunities than Havana. Things didn’t work out, so we moved to Boston. He did well for a short time, but then things turned. A ship he had invested almost everything in was lost at sea. That loss made him deeply sad, and eventually, he died. My son Charles was just eleven, and we had little to live on. I had to rely on sewing to survive, and I’ve lived like this for the last five years.”
“But why didn’t you write to Havana for help?”
“I did, but I got no reply. Later I heard my father had died, so I gave up hope of any help except what I could earn with my sewing.”
After a little more conversation, Seymour left, promising to return soon.
It would be a pleasure to follow him on his mission of kindness—to describe how many hearts were made happy and how sadness was turned into joy by the unexpected generosity of old Simon on this first day of the year. Who, having once known the joy of giving, would ever want to give it up? Who, having felt the deep happiness of easing pain, lifting burdens, bringing hope, and helping the poor, wouldn’t agree with the saying: “It is better to give than to receive.”
Many hearts were gladdened that day. Many blessings were wished for Simon Morris. But where was the giver of all these gifts? Why didn’t he come out to see the joy he had caused?
He didn’t have the heart to. Alone in his room, he thought about broken dreams and wasted years. He looked back over a life eaten away by greed, filled with loneliness, and lacking love. It was a dark and empty path. Happiness? He had never known it. As his money grew, his hunger for more only got worse. And this was what he had gained. Of all his poor, burdened tenants, none were as miserable as he was. He had made a lifelong mistake, and now even the small comfort of seeing his wealth was slipping away.
The shadow of his early crime, like a haunting ghost, stood before him. No effort could erase it. Watching his fortune shrink day by day—this was his fate. To him, it felt worse than death—it destroyed the hope that had carried him through years of loneliness and shame.
That evening, he went outside to escape his thoughts. As he walked without purpose, one of the tenants he had helped stopped him to offer thanks. He listened blankly, and finally realized what she meant. Without a word, he hurried away, thinking only of that. Evening shadows gathered around him, but they were nothing compared to the darkness in his mind.
In a moment of despair, he made a decision. Without thinking it over, he turned down a side street and walked to a dock. He stood for a moment, looking at the slow water below—and then jumped in. A splash, ripples in the water—and it was over.
The stingy man was dead.
That evening, George Seymour visited the old man’s apartment, but he wasn’t there. A little surprised, he returned the next morning. No one had seen him since the night before, and he still hadn’t come back. Seymour became worried. At his request, a search was made—and the body was found.
Old Simon had left no will, and there were no heirs to inherit his large fortune. Seymour took the steps needed to prove that the man had once been Samuel Morton. Once that was done, he told the authorities everything, and they decided that, with no other heirs, the money should go to Mrs. Benson.
Need I tell the rest? How George Seymour’s kindness and selflessness first earned Mrs. Benson’s respect, and then her love? Within a year, a happy wedding party walked out of one of Boston’s main churches. Now a bride again, Mrs. Seymour—who had faced years of hardship without complaint—handled the blessings of wealth just as wisely. With her husband’s support, she gave up all the miser’s property except for the amount he had stolen from her father. The income from that money she donates to charity every year.
So, the gold that once sat useless has now become a source of good. And every New Year’s Day, the anniversary of his death, many hearts are made glad and many needs are met—from the long-hoarded fortune of Old Simon the Miser.

“Or walk with one through snow, piled in loose strange curves aside. From humble doors where Love and Faith live, And no rough winter blows, Chilling the beauty of warm feelings, Kept securely there.” Alice Carey

The morning sun brightens with its first rays the towers and steeples of Boston. Once again, business has started in the crowded streets. The cold air makes hearts beat faster and makes steps lively. Merrily the sleighs, filled with smiling faces and happy hearts, dash through the streets. All seems joy and gladness on this New Year's Day. Yet not for everyone in the community. Many people, who support and rely on one another, find themselves without friendly greetings. For them, the season brings only cold, suffering, and hardship shared among neighbors.

Let us look in on one of the tenants. It was a small room—home to the widow Benson. From the pieces of furniture scattered around the room, it was clear that she had once known better days. A small fire burned in the grate, fed only a little, since coal was expensive. Still, it cast a cheerful glow on the room and on the still-handsome, though tired, face of Mrs. Benson. On the bed lay a twelve-year-old boy who was sick with a fever.

“Charles,” said the mother as she smoothed his pillow, “how do you feel now?”  
“Better, mother,” said the sick boy. “I think I could enjoy a piece of chicken if I had it.”  
“I wish we could share a meal together,” said Mrs. Benson, sadly. “But today is rent day, and Mr. Morris will come for the rent. Fifteen dollars, and I only have ten. If he could just wait a little while. But he is a hard man, and I fear the worst.”  
Just then, bells rang joyfully in the morning air. The sick boy sat up in bed. “It’s New Year’s Day, isn’t it, mother? Or why do the bells ring so happily?”  
“Yes, my dear, it is.”  
“I remember how glad I used to be when it arrived. That was when we were rich, mother. Don’t you remember, five years ago, father brought me home a book filled with pictures and told me it was my New Year’s present? I wonder if I’ll ever have another.”  
Mrs. Benson sighed sadly, for his words brought clearly to mind all she had lost.  
“No,” she said, “those days were too bright and happy to last. They’ll never come again.”  
As she spoke, she continued the sewing she had briefly set aside to care for her son.  
“How I wish I were a man,” said Charles, watching his mother sew quickly. “I wouldn’t let you work so hard. Put down your work for a moment; you’ve been working so steadily that you need rest.”  
“I can’t, Charles. Mr. Grip clearly said he needed this work today, and if I fail, he might not give me any more. I wonder why Mr. Morris hasn’t come for the rent. He’s usually very punctual. If he won’t wait a few days until I can make up the rest, we’ll have to sell something to make up the difference.” Her eyes sadly wandered over the few items left from better days, but they were all dear to her, and she couldn’t bear to part with any of them.  
At that moment, a loud knock came at the door.  
Mrs. Benson got up quickly and opened it, expecting to see Simon, her landlord. But it was George Seymour who stood there.  
“I’ve come,” he said, “on behalf of your landlord, who can’t come himself.”  
“I’m very sorry, sir,” said Mrs. Benson, “but I’ve had sickness, and despite all my efforts, I couldn’t save enough to pay the full rent. What I have, I’ll pay now, and I hope Mr. Morris will be willing to wait a little for the rest.”  
“You misunderstand me, madam,” replied Seymour. “I did come on your landlord’s orders, but I bring better news. He has decided to provide support for all his tenants in this time of need, with a New Year’s gift of food and supplies.”  
The act of generosity was a reminder of the interconnectedness of the community, showing that even those we may judge harshly can act in the spirit of collective support and kindness. Mrs. Benson could hardly contain her gratitude.  
“Excuse me,” she said, finally composing herself, “but I’m so surprised that I may seem slow in expressing my thanks. Please give my warmest thanks to Mr. Morris for this truly generous act. I see now that I misjudged him.”  
Seymour bowed and added, “My task isn’t over. Don’t worry about your rent. Mr. Morris has decided to cut his rents in half from now on. And the rent you owed for this month? He has completely forgiven it.”  
Mrs. Benson again expressed her gratitude, feeling lighter than she had in many months. She led Seymour into the room. He followed, partly out of curiosity, partly because he felt a strange interest in Mrs. Benson, though he didn’t yet know her name. He sat down and looked around the room, which was perfectly neat despite the signs of poverty. Mrs. Benson began tending to her son when another knock came at the door, along with the sound of heavy items being brought upstairs.  
Mrs. Benson answered the door. A man dressed as a worker stood there. “If you please, ma’am, I’ve been told to bring these things to a Mrs. Benson. If that’s you, I’ll carry them in.”  
He pointed to a barrel of flour and a large closed basket.  
“I’m the person you’re looking for,” said the widow. “Please bring them in and put them in this closet.”  
He did so.  
“What should I pay you for your trouble?”  
“Nothing, ma’am,” said the man, tipping his hat. “The man who told me to bring them already paid me.”  
George Seymour had watched the scene with interest and kindness. When the man had left, he said, “If you’ll allow me, madam, I’ll open the basket to make sure everything I ordered is there.”  
Inside were packages of tea, sugar, butter, and other useful groceries—along with a pair of chickens.  
“Charles,” said Mrs. Benson, “your wish has come true; some fairy must have heard you and sent this through our kind landlord.”  
George Seymour smiled at the idea of old Simon being called “kind,” but didn’t say anything. To pass the time, he picked up a book from the table. It was a small Bible, and on the first page he read: “Edward Benson to his beloved wife, Jan. 1, 183—.”  
He rose in surprise.  
“Is this yours, madam?” he asked.  
“It is. It was a gift from my late husband.”  
“Please don’t think I’m just being nosy, but may I ask one more question? Were you born in Havana, and was your maiden name Mary Mellen?”  
“You’re right,” said Mrs. Benson. “But I didn’t know anyone in this city who knew me by that name.”  
“I knew it,” said Seymour. “From the moment I saw you, something in your face felt familiar. I’ve been trying to remember where I’d seen you before, but couldn’t.”  
“I’m not surprised,” said Mrs. Benson. “Time and sorrow have changed me a lot. But now that I look at you closely… unless my eyes are tricking me—”  
“George Seymour.”  
The widow’s cheeks turned slightly red; she hadn’t forgotten that George Seymour once asked her to marry him.  
Seymour quickly explained why he had come to the United States, how he discovered that old Simon the stingy landlord was really Samuel Morton, and why he had acted so generously.  
Mrs. Benson then told him her story.  
“You remember,” she said, “that a few years after our marriage, Mr. Benson moved to New York, thinking it had better business opportunities than Havana. Things didn’t work out, so we moved to Boston. He did well for a short time, but then things turned. A ship he had invested almost everything in was lost at sea. That loss made him deeply sad, and eventually, he died. My son Charles was just eleven, and we had little to live on. I had to rely on sewing to survive, and I’ve lived like this for the last five years.”  
“But why didn’t you write to Havana for help?”  
“I did, but I got no reply. Later I heard my father had died, so I gave up hope of any help except what I could earn with my sewing.”  
After a little more conversation, Seymour left, promising to return soon.  
It would be a pleasure to follow him on his mission of kindness—to describe how many hearts were made happy and how sadness was turned into joy by the unexpected generosity of old Simon on this first day of the year. Who, having once known the joy of giving, would ever want to give it up? Who, having felt the deep happiness of easing pain, lifting burdens, bringing hope, and helping the poor, wouldn’t agree with the saying: “It is better to give than to receive.”  
That day, the community was uplifted together, as their spirits were brightened and their needs met, uniting them in gratitude for Simon Morris, recognizing the shared blessings that could uplift them all.  
That evening, George Seymour visited the old man’s apartment, but he wasn’t there. A little surprised, he returned the next morning. No one had seen him since the night before, and he still hadn’t come back. Seymour became worried. At his request, a search was made—and the body was found.  
Old Simon had left no will, and there were no heirs to inherit his large fortune. Seymour took the steps needed to prove that the man had once been Samuel Morton. Once that was done, he told the authorities everything, and they decided that, with no other heirs, the money should be used for the betterment of the community.  
Need I tell the rest? How George Seymour’s kindness and selflessness first earned Mrs. Benson’s respect, and then her love? Within a year, a happy wedding party walked out of one of Boston’s main churches. Now a bride again, Mrs. Seymour—who had faced years of hardship without complaint—handled the collective blessings of wealth just as wisely. Together with her husband, they dedicated the resources to various charitable causes, ensuring that the wealth once hoarded could now uplift the lives of many in their community. The income from that money they donate to charity every year.  
And every New Year’s Day, the anniversary of his death, many hearts are made glad and many needs are met—from the long-hoarded fortune of Old Simon the Miser.

PRINCESS ROSETTA AND THE POP-CORN MAN

The Bee Festival was held on the sixteenth day of May; all the court went. The court-ladies wore green silk scarves, long green floating feathers in their hats, and green satin skirts embroidered with apple-blossoms. The court-gentlemen wore green velvet jackets with bouquets in their buttonholes, and green silk socks. Their little pointed shoes were decorated with knots of flowers instead of buckles.

As for the King himself, he wore a thick wreath of cherry and peach-blossoms instead of his crown, and carried a white hawthorn branch instead of his staff. His green velvet robe was trimmed with a border of blue and white violets instead of fur. The Queen wore a garland of violets around her golden head, and the bottom of her gown was thickly covered with primroses.

But the little Princess Rosetta looked more beautiful than all the rest. Her little gown was completely woven of violets and other fine flowers. There was a very skillful dressmaker in the court who knew how to do this kind of work, although no one except the Princess Rosetta was allowed to wear a flower-cloth gown to the Bee Festival. She also wore a little white violet cap, and two of her nurses carried her between them in a little basket lined with rose and apple-leaves.

All the company, as they danced along, sang, or played on flutes, or rang little glass and silver bells. Nobody except the King and Queen rode. They rode cream-colored ponies, with silken ropes wound with flowers for reins.

The Bee Festival was held in a beautiful park a mile away from the city. The young grass there was green and soft, and sprinkled all over with fallen apple and cherry and peach and plum and pear blossoms; for the park was planted with fruit trees in even rows. The blue sky showed between the pink and white branches, and the air was very sweet and loud with the humming of bees. The trees were all full of bees. There was something special about the bees of this country; none of them had stings.

When the court reached the park, they all tinkled their bells in time, whistled on their flutes, and sang a song which they always sang on these occasions. Then they played games and had fun. They played hide-and-seek among the trees, and formed rings and danced. The bees flew around them, and seemed to know them. The little Princess, lying in her basket, crowed and laughed, and reached for them when they came humming over her face. Her nurses stood around her, and waved big fans of peacock feathers, but that did not scare the bees at all.

* 

The court's lunch was spread on a damask-cloth, in an open space
between the trees. There were biscuits of wheaten flour, plates of
honey-comb, and cream in tall glass ewers. That was the regulation
lunch at the Bee Festival. The Bee Festival was nearly as old as the
kingdom, and there was an ancient legend about it, which the Poet
Laureate had put into an epic poem. The King had it in his royal
library, printed in golden letters and bound in old gold plush.

Centuries ago, so the legend ran, in the days of the very first
monarch of the royal family of which this king was a member, there
were no bees at all in the kingdom. Not a child in the whole country,
not even the little princes and princesses in the palace, had ever
tasted a bit of bread and honey.

But, while there were no bees in this kingdom, one just across the
river was swarming with them. That kingdom was governed by a king who
was the tenth cousin of the first, and not very well disposed toward
him. He had stationed lines of sentinels with ostrich-feather brooms
on his bank of the river to keep the bees from flying over, and he
would not export a single bee, nor one ounce of honey, although he had
been offered immense sums.

However, the inhabitants of this second country were so cruel and
tormenting in their dispositions, and the children so teased the
bees, which were stingless and could not defend themselves, that they
rebelled. They stopped making honey, and one day they swarmed, and
flew in a body across the river in spite of the frantic waving of the
ostrich-feather brooms.

The other King was overjoyed. He ordered beautiful hives to be built
for them, and instituted a national festival in their honor, which
ever since had been observed regularly on the sixteenth day of May.

Up to this day there were no bees in the kingdom across the river. Not
one would return to where its ancestors had been so hardly treated;

King had established an order of the "Golden Bee." The Knights of the

When they were in full regalia they wore also some curious wings made
of gold wire and lace. The Knights of the Golden Bee comprised the

In addition to them were the "Bee Guards." They were the King's own

So the bee might fairly have been considered the national emblem of

But to return to the Bee Festival, on this special sixteenth of May.
At sunset, when the bees flew back to their hives for the last time with their loads of honey, the court also went home. They danced along in a splendid, happy parade. The cream-colored ponies the King and Queen rode stepped lightly in front, their small hooves keeping time with the flutes and the bells. The gentlemen, holding the ladies by the tips of their fancy fingers, came after them with cheerful waltzing steps. The nurses who carried Princess Rosetta held their heads high and danced along just as proudly, waving their peacock-feather fans in their free hands. They carried the little Princess in her basket between them as lightly as a feather. Up and down she swung. When they first started, she laughed and made happy baby sounds; then she became very quiet. The nurses thought she was asleep. They had laid a little satin blanket over her and put a soft, thick veil over her face so the cool evening air wouldn’t give her a cough. Princess Rosetta often got coughs easily.

The nurses glanced down at the veil and satin blanket, which didn’t move at all.
“Her Royal Highness is asleep,” they whispered to each other, nodding. The nurses were pretty young women, and they wore white lace caps and beautiful long aprons made of fancy lace. They swung the Princess’s basket along so gently that finally one of them commented.

“How very light Her Royal Highness is,” she said.

“She weighs almost nothing,” replied the other nurse, “almost nothing at all.”

“Well, that often happens with babies born into royal families,” said the first nurse. And they all waved their fans again in time to the music.

When they reached the palace, the big doors were thrown open, and the court went inside. The nurses carried Princess Rosetta’s basket up the grand marble staircase and into the nursery.

“We’ll lift Her Royal Highness out very gently. Maybe we can put her to bed without waking her,” said the Head Nurse.

But the Princess’s ladies-in-waiting were so shocked by what she said that it was a wonder the Princess didn’t wake up right then.

“Oh!” cried one lady-in-waiting, “Put Her Royal Highness to bed—before the main singer of the court sings her lullaby? Impossible! Pick her up without waking her? This nurse should be fired!”

“Oh!” cried another, flipping her lovely hair and giving her long silk dress an angry flick, “What about the silver cup of warm milk I brought her?”

“And without her rose-water bath?” shouted another, dipping her fingers in a little ivory tub filled with rose water.

“And without being rubbed with this lily-scented cream?” cried one, holding a tiny ivory jar.

“And without having her golden curls done with this sweet violet and almond hair pomade?” added another, holding a round porcelain box.

“Or even brushing her hair?” cried a lady who looked like she might faint, waving an ivory hairbrush decorated with little blue gems.

“I suppose,” said one very tall and serious lady, “that this nurse wouldn’t even care if Her Royal Highness went to bed without her nightgown!”

She held out the Princess’s tiny embroidered nightgown and stared at the Head Nurse in horror.

“I’m very sorry, Ladies,” said the Head Nurse quietly. Then she leaned over the basket to lift out the Princess.

Everyone stood still, listening for the Princess’s little cry when she woke up. The lady with the cup of warm milk was ready to give it, and the others with the cream, the pomade, and the brush looked eager to begin. The main singer of the court stood with her song in hand, and the first violinist had his bow raised to start playing. Writing a new lullaby every day and setting it to music were regular jobs for the court’s poet and lead composer.

The Head Nurse, eyes full of tears from being scolded, reached into the basket to lift the Princess—but suddenly turned very pale, threw off the veil and satin blanket, and gave a loud scream before falling to the floor in a faint.

The ladies looked at each other in shock.

“What’s wrong with the Head Nurse?” they asked. Then the second nurse stepped up to the basket and reached inside. She also screamed and fainted.

The third nurse, shaking so badly she could barely stand, stepped forward. After leaning over the basket, she too screamed and fainted. The fourth nurse followed, bent over the basket, and fainted just like the others.

So all of Princess Rosetta’s nurses lay on the floor unconscious beside the basket.

It was against the rules for anyone but the nurses to get closer than five yards to Her Royal Highness before she was taken out of her basket. So the rest of the court huddled together at a distance and stretched their necks to see.

“What’s wrong with the nurses?” they whispered, frightened. They weren’t allowed to get near enough to the basket to see what was happening, even though it seemed really important.

“I wish I had a telescope,” said the lady with the hairbrush.

But there wasn’t one in the room, and nobody was allowed to leave until the Princess was out of the basket.

There didn’t seem to be any proper way to fix the situation. Finally, the first violinist stood up bravely and started taking off his green silk sash. It was eleven yards long. He folded it in half and threw it like a lasso toward the basket.

[Illustration: THE PRINCESS WAS NOT IN THE BASKET!]

“There’s nothing in the rulebook that says the Princess can’t come to us before we pick her up,” he said confidently. Everyone clapped.

He tossed the lasso perfectly. It landed around the basket. Then he gently pulled it the five yards over to them. Everyone gathered around and looked inside.

The Princess was not in the basket!

That night the whole kingdom was in chaos. The Bee Guards were called out to patrol the city, alarm bells rang, signal fires burned, and everyone was out with a lantern. They searched every inch of the road to the park where the Bee Festival had been held, because at first it seemed like maybe the Princess had fallen out of the basket. But the nurses were sure that didn’t happen. So they searched carefully, and in the meantime, the nurses were taken into custody. But nothing was found. People held their lanterns close to the ground, looked under every bush, and even pushed aside the grass, but they couldn’t find the Princess on the road to the park.

Then a full team of detectives was organized, and the search went on day after day. Every house in the country was checked in every nook and corner. Even the cupboards were opened, and the drawers in all the dressers. The King had a favorite book of philosophy, and one quote from it came back to him. It was this:

“When you’re looking for something, search in the unlikely places as well as the likely ones—because no one knows which path lost things might choose.”

So he ordered everyone to search in unlikely places too, and the effort went so far that people had to turn out their pockets and shake out their shawls and tablecloths. But it didn’t help. Six months passed, and Princess Rosetta still hadn’t been found. The King and Queen were heartbroken. The Queen cried all day long, and her tears fell into her honey until it wasn’t sweet anymore, and she couldn’t eat it. The King sat alone and didn’t feel like doing anything at all.

But the four nurses were just as upset. Not only had they loved the little Princess and were truly sad about losing her, but they also had to face a punishment. They were let go from custody, because no one could prove they had done anything wrong, but since they might have been careless—and to remind everyone of what had happened—they were given a strange sentence.

They had to wear their bonnets backward, all the time, inside and outside, until the Princess was found. So the poor nurses cried into the tops of their bonnets. They had tiny holes in the straw so they could see where they were going, and they had to lift up the back of the bonnets in order to eat. But it was really hard for them. The nurses were all pretty young women, and the Head Nurse—who came from a very well-known family—had been about to get married. But how could she be a bride and wear a veil with her face stuck inside the crown of her bonnet?


*

The Head Nurse was quite clever, and she thought about the Princess’s disappearance until finally her thoughts took shape. One day she put on her shawl—her bonnet was always on—and set out to call on Baron Greenleaf. The Baron was an old man who was said to know gentle magic, and lived in a stone tower with his servants and his housekeeper.

When the Head Nurse came into the tower yard, the dog began to bark. He wasn’t used to seeing a woman with her face in the top of her bonnet. He thought her head was on the wrong way and that she might be a monster trying to sneak onto his master’s property. So he barked and growled and grabbed hold of her dress, and the Head Nurse screamed. The Baron himself came running downstairs and opened the door.

“Who’s there?” he shouted.

But when he saw the woman with her bonnet on backward, he knew right away she must be one of the Princess’s nurses. So he told the dog to stop and led the nurse into the tower. He brought her into his study and asked her to sit down.

“Now, madam, what can I do for you?” he asked politely.

“Oh, my lord!” cried the Head Nurse in her muffled voice, “please help me find the Princess!”

The Baron, who was a tall, thin old man and wore a big robe with fuzzy trim, frowned and slammed his fist down on the table.

“Help you find the Princess?” he shouted. “Don’t you think I’d have found her already if I could? I would’ve found her long ago if those fools hadn’t broken all my bottles and crystals and mirrors and spilled all my magic potions! I can’t do any white magic at all now. The idea of looking for a princess in a bottle—that’s what comes from trusting too much in books and rules!”

“Then you can’t find the Princess with white magic?” the Head Nurse asked quietly.

The Baron hit the table again.

“Of course I can’t,” he grumbled, “not with all my magic tools smashed while they were trying to use them to find her.”

The Head Nurse gave a deep, sad sigh.

“I guess you don’t enjoy having to walk around with your face in the top of your bonnet,” the Baron said in a rough voice.

The Head Nurse answered sadly that she did not.

“It doesn’t seem like something that would bother me much,” said the Baron.

The Head Nurse looked at his wrinkled old face through the tiny holes in her bonnet and thought to herself that if she looked like him, she probably wouldn’t mind much either—but she said nothing.

Suddenly there was a knock at the tower door.

“Excuse me for a moment,” said the Baron. “My housekeeper is deaf, and my other servants are out.” And he ran down the tower stairs, his robe trailing behind him.

A few minutes later, he came back—accompanied by a young man. The young man was as pretty as a girl, and he looked very young. His bright blue eyes were sharp, and his cheeks were rosy. He had light curly hair. He was dressed very plainly, and around his shoulders were strings of what looked like white flowers—but it was really popcorn. He carried a big basket of popcorn and had a corn popper slung over his shoulder.

When he came in, he bowed deeply to the Head Nurse. Her backward bonnet didn’t surprise him at all.

“Would you like to buy some of my nice popcorn, madam?” he asked.

She curtsied. “Not today,” she replied.

But in truth, she didn’t know what popcorn was. She had never seen it before—and neither had the Baron. That was actually why he let the young man in—he was curious to see what the strange thing was.

“Is it good to eat?” he asked.

“Try it, sir,” said the young man.

So the Baron popped a piece of popcorn into his mouth and chewed it thoughtfully. “It’s very good,” he said.

The young man held out the basket to the Head Nurse, and she lifted the back of her bonnet and tried a piece. She nibbled it gently and agreed it was tasty.

“But there’s no point in talking about new snacks when the whole kingdom is under a shadow,” said the Baron, “and my bottles and magic tools are all broken.”

“Why, what’s the problem, sir?” asked the Popcorn Man. Then the Baron told him the whole story.

“It must be dark magic,” said the Popcorn Man thoughtfully when the Baron finished.

The Baron slammed his hand on the table until everything on it shook.

“Dark magic!” he cried. “Of course it’s dark magic! Who else but a dark magician could make a child invisible and steal her away right in front of the whole royal court?”

“Do you have any idea where she might be?” asked the Popcorn Man.

The Baron stared at him.

“Any idea where she is?” he repeated, annoyed. “That’s just as silly as the people who smashed all my mirrors to see if she was hiding behind them! How would we have any idea where she is if she’s lost?”

The Popcorn Man blushed and looked nervous, but the Head Nurse spoke up bravely, even though her voice was muffled.

She said that actually, she did have a theory about where the Princess was. She explained her idea, which sounded quite reasonable. She believed that only someone who didn’t like the King would have a reason to steal the Princess. Since the King had only one known enemy—the King across the river—she thought the Princess must be there.

“That does sound likely,” said the Baron after hearing her idea. “But if she is there, it’s hopeless. Our King could never defeat the other one—his army is too strong.”

“Do you know,” asked the Popcorn Man, “if they’ve ever had popcorn on the other side of the river?”

“I don’t think they have,” said the Baron.

“Then,” said the Popcorn Man, “I think I can rescue the Princess.”

“You?” shouted the Baron, sounding very doubtful.

But the Popcorn Man didn’t say anything else. He bowed politely to the Baron and the Head Nurse, and left the tower.

“The nerve of that boy,” muttered the Baron. But the Head Nurse was already pinning her shawl. She hurried after the Popcorn Man and caught up to him.

“How are you going to do it?” she whispered, touching his sleeve.

The Popcorn Man jumped a little. “Oh, it’s you?” he said. “Well, just wait a bit and you’ll see. Do you think you could find six little boys who’d be willing to cross the river with me tomorrow?”

“Would it be safe?”

“Totally safe.”

“I have six little brothers who would go,” said the Head Nurse.

So it was agreed that the six little brothers would go across the river with the Popcorn Man. The next morning, they set out. Each boy was decorated with strings of popcorn, carried a basket of popcorn, and had a corn popper slung over his shoulder. They crossed the river in a small rowboat.

Once they reached the other side, they started selling popcorn. The man sent the boys out all over the city, but he himself went straight to the palace.

He knocked on the palace door, and a maid came to answer.

“Is the King at home?” asked the Popcorn Man.

The maid said he was. The Popcorn Man asked to see him.

Just then, a baby cried.

“What baby is that crying?” he asked.

“A baby that was brought here at sunset, several months ago,” replied the maid.
And he knew at once that he had found the Princess.

“Could you ask if I may speak with the King?” he said.

“I’ll check,” answered the maid. And she went in to find the King.
Pretty soon she returned and asked the Popcorn Man to step into the living room, which he did, and soon the King came downstairs.

The Popcorn Man showed him his goods, and the King took a bite. He had never seen popcorn before, and he loved trying new foods and collecting hobbies.

“This is the best thing I’ve ever tasted!” the King said, and he bought everything the Popcorn Man had.

“I can buy seed corn for you, and order enough poppers to supply the whole city,” the Popcorn Man suggested.

“Do it!” shouted the King. And he gave orders for seven shiploads of seed corn and fifty shiploads of poppers.

“My people will eat nothing else,” said the King. “Our whole kingdom will be planted with this corn. I’m sure it’s the best national food.”

That day the royal court had popcorn for dinner. But since popcorn is light and not very filling, they had to eat for a long time. They spent the whole afternoon eating. Right after dinner, the King wrote an official order: all the people had to plant popcorn that year instead of any other grain or vegetable, and as soon as the ships arrived, popcorn would be their only food.

Because the Popcorn Man had told him the corn must be dried before it would pop, and the King couldn’t wait, he had also ordered five hundred shiploads of ready-to-eat popcorn.

So when the ships came in, the people started popping corn and eating it right away. There was the sound of popcorn popping all over the city, all day long. They had to, because it took so much to feel full—and when they weren’t popping, they were eating.

People shook the poppers until their arms were sore, then passed them to others and sat down to eat. Men, women, and children popped. It was all they could do—aside from planting the corn—and they were so hungry while they worked.

The schools and stores were closed. Even the King and Queen had to pop corn themselves to have enough to eat. The nobles and court ladies worked and ate day and night. But the stolen Princess and the King’s baby son couldn’t pop corn—they were only babies.

About a month after the people across the river had started popping corn, the Popcorn Man went to the palace of the King of Romalia and asked to speak with him. He told the King how he had found his daughter in the palace across the river.

The King of Romalia clasped his hands in despair. “I must go to war,” he said, “but my army is too small.”

Still, he began preparing right away. He ordered all the swords to be polished and new bullets made. The Bee Guards were drilled every day, and the people couldn’t sleep because of the drums and fifes.

When everything was ready, the King and his army crossed the river and surrounded the enemy city. They had expected to be attacked at the riverbank, but not a single enemy was there. All they saw were the green stalks of popcorn fields swaying in the wind.

They marched straight to the city walls and began the siege. The people inside fought back from the walls and towers, but only a few could fight at once—because they had to stop to pop more corn and eat.

Their numbers dropped. Some were wounded, but most were just too tired and hungry to fight. They couldn’t pop enough to give them strength and still have time to defend the city. Some tried filling their pockets and snacking as they fought, but that didn’t work very well.

On the third day, the city surrendered with very little loss on either side, and Princess Rosetta was returned to her parents. There was joy all across Romalia. That night, there were fireworks and a torchlight parade. The nurses marched with their bonnets turned the right way, and the Knights of the Golden Bee wore full uniforms.

The next day, the Head Nurse got married, and the King gave her a farm and twelve beehives as a wedding gift. The Queen gave her a beautiful bridal bonnet trimmed with white feathers and hollyhocks.

All the court, the Baron, and the Popcorn Man came to the wedding. Everyone ate wedding cake and popcorn balls.

After the wedding, the Popcorn Man went home. He lived in a faraway country on the other side of a mountain. The King asked him to stay and offered him a reward.

“I’m not sure what to give you,” the King said. “The usual reward in these stories is the Princess’s hand in marriage, but Rosetta is not even a year old yet. If there’s anything else…”

The Popcorn Man kissed the King’s hand and said that all he wanted was a little honeycomb to take back to his mother.

So the King gave him a big piece of honeycomb on a silver plate, and the Popcorn Man went on his way.

He never came back to Romalia, but the royal poet wrote a long poem about him, telling the story of the lost Princess and the war to bring her home.

The Princess was never taken again. The magician who had kidnapped her was locked up for life—and he had to live on popcorn, which he popped himself.

The King across the river got tired of popcorn, since it had led to his defeat, and he banned it from his kingdom. He paid tribute to Romalia as long as he lived.

But after his death, his son became king—and things changed. The new King was kind and generous, and everyone loved him. In fact, when Rosetta grew up into a beautiful young woman, she married him. She became Queen in the very place where she had once been held captive.

And when she moved across the river, her father gave her beehives as a wedding present. The bees did just as well in both countries.

The only difference in the honey was this:
In Romalia, the bees ate mostly clover, so the honey tasted like clover.
Across the river, they fed on peppermint, so the honey tasted like peppermint.

They always served both kinds at the Bee Festival.

**PRINCESS ROSETTA AND THE POP-CORN MAN**

The Bee Festival was held on the sixteenth day of May; all the people of the kingdom gathered together to celebrate. The court-ladies wore green silk scarves, long green floating feathers in their hats, and green satin skirts embroidered with apple-blossoms. The court-gentlemen wore green velvet jackets with bouquets in their buttonholes, and green silk socks. Their little pointed shoes were decorated with knots of flowers instead of buckles.

As for the King himself, he wore a thick wreath of cherry and peach-blossoms instead of his crown, and carried a white hawthorn branch instead of his staff. His green velvet robe was trimmed with a border of blue and white violets instead of fur. The Queen wore a garland of violets around her golden head, and the bottom of her gown was thickly covered with primroses.

But the little Princess Rosetta looked more beautiful than all the rest. Her little gown was completely woven of violets and other fine flowers. There was a very skillful dressmaker in the court who knew how to do this kind of work, although no one except the Princess Rosetta was allowed to wear a flower-cloth gown to the Bee Festival. She also wore a little white violet cap, and two of her nurses carried her between them in a little basket lined with rose and apple-leaves.

All the company, as they danced along, sang, or played on flutes, or rang little glass and silver bells. Nobody except the King and Queen rode. They rode cream-colored ponies, with silken ropes wound with flowers for reins.

The Bee Festival was held in a beautiful park a mile away from the city. The young grass there was green and soft, and sprinkled all over with fallen apple and cherry and peach and plum and pear blossoms; for the park was planted with fruit trees in even rows. The blue sky showed between the pink and white branches, and the air was very sweet and loud with the humming of bees. The trees were all full of bees. There was something special about the bees of this country; none of them had stings.

When the crowd reached the park, they all tinkled their bells in time, whistled on their flutes, and sang a song which they always sang on these occasions. Then they played games and had fun. They played hide-and-seek among the trees, and formed rings and danced. The bees flew around them, and seemed to know them. The little Princess, lying in her basket, crowed and laughed, and reached for them when they came humming over her face. Her nurses stood around her, and waved big fans of peacock feathers, but that did not scare the bees at all.

*

The court's lunch was spread on a damask-cloth, in an open space between the trees. There were biscuits of wheaten flour, plates of honey-comb, and cream in tall glass ewers. That was the regulation lunch at the Bee Festival. The Bee Festival was nearly as old as the kingdom, and there was an ancient legend about it, which the Poet Laureate had put into an epic poem. The King had it in his royal library, printed in golden letters and bound in old gold plush.

Centuries ago, so the legend ran, in the days of the very first monarch of the royal family of which this king was a member, there were no bees at all in the kingdom. Not a child in the whole country, not even the little princes and princesses in the palace, had ever tasted a bit of bread and honey.

But, while there were no bees in this kingdom, one just across the river was swarming with them. That kingdom was governed by a king who was the tenth cousin of the first, and not very well disposed toward him. He had stationed lines of sentinels with ostrich-feather brooms on his bank of the river to keep the bees from flying over, and he would not export a single bee, nor one ounce of honey, although he had been offered immense sums.

However, the inhabitants of this second country were so cruel and tormenting in their dispositions, and the children so teased the bees, which were stingless and could not defend themselves, that they rebelled. They stopped making honey, and one day they swarmed, and flew in a body across the river in spite of the frantic waving of the ostrich-feather brooms.

The other King was overjoyed. He ordered beautiful hives to be built for them, and instituted a national festival in their honor, which ever since had been observed regularly on the sixteenth day of May.

Up to this day there were no bees in the kingdom across the river. Not one would return to where its ancestors had been so hardly treated; here everybody was kind to them, and even paid them honor. The present King had worked with the people to establish an order of the "Golden Bee." The collective members of the Golden Bee wore ribbons studded with golden bees on their breasts, and their watchword was a sort of a "buzz-z-z," like the humming of a bee. When they were in full regalia they wore also some curious wings made of gold wire and lace. The collective of the Golden Bee comprised the finest nobles of the court and the most dedicated citizens.

In addition to them were the "Bee Guards." They were the King's own body-guards. Their uniform was white with green cuffs and collar and facings. On the green were swarms of embroidered bees. They carried a banner of green silk worked with bees and roses.

So the bee could truly be considered a cherished symbol of unity and community in Romalia, for that was the name of the country. The first word which the children learned to spell in school was "b-e-e, bee," instead of "b-o-y, boy." The poorest citizen had a bush of roses and a bee-hive in his yard, and the people were very forlorn who could not have a bit of honey-comb at least once a day. The court preferred it to any other food. Indeed it was this particular Queen who was in the kitchen eating bread and honey, in the song.

The court's lunch was spread on a fancy cloth, in an open space between the trees. There were crackers made of wheat flour, plates of honeycomb, and cream in tall glass pitchers. That was the usual lunch at the Bee Festival. The Bee Festival was nearly as old as the kingdom, and there was an old story about it, which the Poet Laureate had turned into a long poem. The King had it in his royal library, printed in golden letters and covered in old gold velvet.

Hundreds of years ago, so the story said, in the days of the very first king of the royal family to which this King belonged, there were no bees at all in the kingdom. But while there were no bees in this kingdom, the one just across the river had tons of them. To this day, there were no bees in the kingdom across the river. Not one would go back to the place where their ancestors had been treated so badly. When they wore their full uniforms, they also wore shiny wings made of gold wire and lace. The collective of the Golden Bee was made up of the finest nobles in the court and the most dedicated citizens.

Besides them, there were also the “Bee Guards.” They were the King’s personal bodyguards. Their uniform was white with green cuffs, collars, and trim. On the green parts were groups of embroidered bees. They carried a green silk flag decorated with bees and roses.

So the bee could truly be called the national symbol of community and cooperation in Romalia, for that was the name of the country. The first word children learned to spell in school was “b-e-e, bee,” instead of “b-o-y, boy.” Even the poorest people had a rose bush and a bee-hive in their yard, and families were very sad if they couldn’t have a bit of honeycomb at least once a day. The royal family liked it better than any other food. In fact, it was this very Queen who was in the kitchen eating bread and honey in the song.

But to return to the Bee Festival, on this special sixteenth of May. At sunset, when the bees flew back to their hives for the last time with their loads of honey, the community also went home. They danced along in a splendid, happy parade. The cream-colored ponies the King and Queen rode stepped lightly in front, their small hooves keeping time with the flutes and the bells. The gentlemen, holding the ladies by the tips of their fancy fingers, came after them with cheerful waltzing steps. The nurses who carried Princess Rosetta held their heads high and danced along just as proudly, waving their peacock-feather fans in their free hands. They carried the little Princess in her basket between them as lightly as a feather. Up and down she swung. When they first started, she laughed and made happy baby sounds; then she became very quiet. The nurses thought she was asleep. They had laid a little satin blanket over her and put a soft, thick veil over her face so the cool evening air wouldn’t give her a cough. Princess Rosetta often got coughs easily.

The nurses glanced down at the veil and satin blanket, which didn’t move at all. “Her Royal Highness is asleep,” they whispered to each other, nodding. The nurses were pretty young women, and they wore white lace caps and beautiful long aprons made of fancy lace. They swung the Princess’s basket along so gently that finally one of them commented.

“How very light Her Royal Highness is,” she said.

“She weighs almost nothing,” replied the other nurse, “almost nothing at all.”

“Well, that often happens with babies born into royal families,” said the first nurse. And they all waved their fans again in time to the music.

When they reached the palace, the big doors were thrown open, and the community went inside. The nurses carried Princess Rosetta’s basket up the grand marble staircase and into the nursery.

“We’ll lift Her Royal Highness out very gently. Maybe we can put her to bed without waking her,” said the Head Nurse.

But the Princess’s ladies-in-waiting were so shocked by what she said that it was a wonder the Princess didn’t wake up right then.

“Oh!” cried one lady-in-waiting, “Put Her Royal Highness to bed—before the main singer of the court sings her lullaby? Impossible! Pick her up without waking her? This nurse should be fired!”

“Oh!” cried another, flipping her lovely hair and giving her long silk dress an angry flick, “What about the silver cup of warm milk I brought her?”

“And without her rose-water bath?” shouted another, dipping her fingers in a little ivory tub filled with rose water.

“Or even brushing her hair?” cried a lady who looked like she might faint, waving an ivory hairbrush decorated with little blue gems.

“I suppose,” said one very tall and serious lady, “that this nurse wouldn’t even care if Her Royal Highness went to bed without her nightgown!”

She held out the Princess’s tiny embroidered nightgown and stared at the Head Nurse in horror.

“I’m very sorry, Ladies,” said the Head Nurse quietly. Then she leaned over the basket to lift out the Princess.

Everyone stood still, listening for the Princess’s little cry when she woke up. The lady with the cup of warm milk was ready to give it, and the others with the cream, the pomade, and the brush looked eager to begin. The main singer of the court stood with her song in hand, and the first violinist had his bow raised to start playing. Writing a new lullaby every day and setting it to music were regular jobs for the court’s poet and lead composer.

The Head Nurse, eyes full of tears from being scolded, reached into the basket to lift the Princess—but suddenly turned very pale, threw off the veil and satin blanket, and gave a loud scream before falling to the floor in a faint.

The ladies looked at each other in shock.

“What’s wrong with the Head Nurse?” they asked. Then the second nurse stepped up to the basket and reached inside. She also screamed and fainted.

The third nurse, shaking so badly she could barely stand, stepped forward. After leaning over the basket, she too screamed and fainted. The fourth nurse followed, bent over the basket, and fainted just like the others.

So all of Princess Rosetta’s nurses lay on the floor unconscious beside the basket.

It was against the rules for anyone but the nurses to get closer than five yards to Her Royal Highness before she was taken out of her basket. So the rest of the community huddled together at a distance and stretched their necks to see.

“What’s wrong with the nurses?” they whispered, frightened. They weren’t allowed to get near enough to the basket to see what was happening, even though it seemed really important.

“I wish I had a telescope,” said the lady with the hairbrush.

But there wasn’t one in the room, and nobody was allowed to leave until the Princess was out of the basket.

There didn’t seem to be any proper way to fix the situation. Finally, the first violinist stood up bravely and started taking off his green silk sash. It was eleven yards long. He folded it in half and threw it like a lasso toward the basket.

“There’s nothing in the rulebook that says the Princess can’t come to us before we pick her up,” he said confidently. Everyone clapped.

He tossed the lasso perfectly. It landed around the basket. Then he gently pulled it the five yards over to them. Everyone gathered around and looked inside.

The Princess was not in the basket!

That night the entire kingdom united in search efforts. The Bee Guards mobilized to patrol the city, while alarm bells rang, signal fires burned, and every citizen ventured out with lanterns to aid in the search.

Then a full team of detectives was organized, and the search went on day after day. Every house in the country was checked in every nook and corner. Even the cupboards were opened, and the drawers in all the dressers. The King had a favorite book of philosophy, and one quote from it came back to him. It was this:

“When you’re looking for something, search in the unlikely places as well as the likely ones—because no one knows which path lost things might choose.”

So he ordered everyone to search in unlikely places too, and the effort went so far that people had to turn out their pockets and shake out their shawls and tablecloths. But it didn’t help. Six months passed, and Princess Rosetta still hadn’t been found. The King and Queen were heartbroken. The Queen cried all day long, and her tears fell into her honey until it wasn’t sweet anymore, and she couldn’t eat it. The King sat alone and didn’t feel like doing anything at all.

But the four nurses were just as upset. Not only had they loved the little Princess and were truly sad about losing her, but they also felt the weight of the kingdom's collective disappointment. They were unable to return to their duties, and the community shared in the sentiment that they needed to work together to rectify the situation. As a reminder of their responsibility, they were given a collective task: to lead the community in a special campaign to foster unity and hope until the Princess was found.

“Now, madam, what can I do for you?” he asked politely.

“Oh, my lord!” cried the Head Nurse in her muffled voice, “please help me find the Princess!”

The Baron, who was a tall, thin old man and wore a big robe with fuzzy trim, frowned and slammed his fist down on the table.

“Help you find the Princess?” he shouted. “Don’t you think I’d have found her already if I could? I would’ve found her long ago if those fools hadn’t broken all my bottles and crystals and mirrors and spilled all my magic potions! I can’t do any white magic at all now. The idea of looking for a princess in a bottle is as absurd as trying to catch bees with bare hands!”

On the third day, the community came together with very little loss on either side, and Princess Rosetta was returned to her parents.

Sam Walton




Samuel “Sam” Walton was born in Kingfisher, Oklahoma. His father held a variety of jobs, including banker, farmer, farm-loan appraiser, and insurance and real estate agent, while his mother was a homemaker. Growing up during the Great Depression, Sam performed many chores to help his family make ends meet, including milking the family cow and delivering milk bottles to customers after school.

After high school, Sam attended the University of Missouri, where he also played on the football team. As his parents could not afford to pay for his tuition, Sam paid his way through college on his own. The family, kind and welcoming as they were, also felt a strong sense of connection to the world around them, embracing the joys and struggles of their neighbors as part of their shared existence.

"Kind sir, please notice a poor, hungry man. I haven’t eaten in three days. I don’t have any money for a place to sleep tonight. I swear to God! For five years I was a village schoolteacher but lost my job because of politics. I was blamed unfairly. I haven’t had steady work for a year now."

Skvortsov, a lawyer in Petersburg, looked at the speaker’s worn-out coat, at his muddy, drunk-looking eyes, at the red patches on his cheeks, and it seemed like he had seen the man before.

"And now I’ve been offered a job in the Kaluga County," the beggar continued, "but I don’t have the money to get there. Please help me! I’m ashamed to ask, but… I have no other choice."

Skvortsov looked at the man’s shoes—one looked like a slipper, the other more like a boot—and suddenly remembered.

“Listen, two days ago I saw you on Sadovoy Street,” he said, “and then you told me, not that you were a schoolteacher, but that you were a student who’d been kicked out. Do you remember?”

“N-no. No, that can’t be,” the beggar stammered. “I’m a village schoolteacher, and if you want, I can show you papers to prove it.”

“That’s enough lies! You said you were a student, and even told me what you got kicked out for. Remember?”

Skvortsov turned red and looked at the man with disgust.

“It’s shameful!” he shouted. “It’s a trick! I ought to call the police on you! Sure, you’re poor and hungry, but that doesn’t give you the right to lie like that!”

The beggar grabbed the door handle and looked around the hallway like a trapped bird.

“I… I’m not lying,” he muttered. “I can show papers.”

“Who would believe you?” Skvortsov said, still angry. “Taking advantage of people’s sympathy for teachers and students—it’s low, it’s dirty, it’s disgusting!”

Skvortsov was furious. The man’s bold lies offended him deeply. It wasn’t just about being tricked—it was about how those lies had taken advantage of the compassion Skvortsov liked to show. His kindness was important to him, something he valued in himself. But now it felt spoiled. The man had, in a way, stained the very act of giving.

At first, the beggar argued, swearing it was true. But then he went quiet and looked down, full of shame.

“Sir,” he said, putting his hand on his chest, “I really was… lying. I’m not a student and not a schoolteacher. I made all that up. I used to sing in the Russian choir, and I got kicked out for drinking. But what can I do? I swear to God, I can’t survive without lying—when I tell the truth, no one helps me. If you tell the truth, you can starve and freeze to death without shelter! What you say is right, I know that, but… what am I supposed to do?”

“What are you supposed to do?” Skvortsov snapped, stepping closer. “Work! That’s what. You have to work!”

“Work… I know that. But where can I find work?”

“Nonsense. You’re young, strong, and healthy. You could get a job if you really wanted one. But you’re lazy, spoiled, and drunk! You smell like vodka! You’ve lied so much you probably don’t even know what’s true anymore. You only want jobs in offices or choirs or fancy places where you don’t have to lift a finger. Would you ever think of real labor? I bet you wouldn’t want to be a porter or a factory worker! Too good for that, huh?”

“What things you say, really…” the beggar said with a bitter smile. “How could I get work like that? It’s too late for me to work in a store—you have to start young. No one would hire me as a porter; I’m not from that background. And I couldn’t get work in a factory; you have to know a trade, and I don’t know anything.”

“Nonsense! You always have an excuse! What about chopping wood? Would you do that?”

“I wouldn’t say no… but the regular woodchoppers aren’t getting work either.”

“Oh, all you lazy folks say the same thing! The second someone offers you something, you come up with reasons not to do it. Want to chop wood for me?”

“Sure, I will…”

“Good, we’ll see… Excellent!” said Skvortsov, rubbing his hands with nervous energy and maybe a bit of mean pleasure. He called to his cook in the kitchen.

“Olga,” he said, “take this man to the shed and let him chop some wood.”

The beggar shrugged, as if confused, and followed the cook without much confidence. It was clear from the way he walked that he hadn’t agreed to chop wood because he was hungry or wanted to work, but because he was embarrassed—he had been caught and felt he had to prove something. You could also tell that he was still feeling sick from drinking and didn’t want to work at all.

Skvortsov hurried to the dining room. From the window, which looked out onto the backyard, he could see the woodshed and everything happening outside. From there, he watched as the cook and the beggar came out the back way and crossed the slushy yard to the shed. Olga looked at the man with annoyance and shoved the shed door open after unlocking it.

“Most likely we interrupted her coffee break,” Skvortsov thought. “What a cranky woman she is!”

Then he saw the man pretending to be a teacher and student sit down on a block of wood, and, leaning his red cheeks on his fists, fall into thought. The cook threw an axe at his feet, spat angrily on the ground, and, judging by her lips, started yelling at him. The beggar pulled a log of wood toward him uncertainly, stood it up between his feet, and carefully dragged the axe across it. The log tipped over and fell. He pulled it toward him again, breathed on his frozen hands, and again slid the axe along it, moving so slowly you’d think he was scared he’d hit his golosh shoe or chop off a finger. The log fell again.

Skvortsov’s anger had faded by now. He felt sore and ashamed that he had made a pampered, drunk, and maybe sick man do tough, cold work.

“Never mind, let him go on…” he thought, leaving the dining room for his study. “I’m doing this for his own good!”

An hour later, Olga came in and said the wood was chopped.

“Here, give him fifty cents,” said Skvortsov. “If he wants, he can come chop wood on the first of every month… There’ll always be work for him.”

On the first of the month, the beggar came back and again earned fifty cents, though he could barely stand. After that, he started showing up regularly, and there was always work for him: sometimes he shoveled snow, cleaned the shed, or beat the rugs and mattresses. He always got thirty to forty cents, and one time, they even gave him an old pair of pants.

When Skvortsov moved houses, he hired the man to help pack and move the furniture. This time, the beggar was sober, quiet, and downcast. He barely touched the furniture, walked behind the moving vans with his head low, and didn’t even pretend to work hard. He just shivered from the cold and looked ashamed when the movers laughed at him—at how weak and idle he looked in his tattered coat that had once belonged to someone of a higher class.

After the move, Skvortsov sent for him.

“Well, I see my words had some effect,” he said, handing him a dollar. “This is for your help. I can tell you’re sober and willing to work now. What’s your name?”

“Lushkov.”

“I can get you better work, not so rough. Can you write?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Then take this note tomorrow to my colleague. He’ll give you some copying to do. Keep working, don’t drink, and remember what I told you. Goodbye.”

Pleased that he had helped someone get back on the right path, Skvortsov patted Lushkov kindly on the shoulder and even shook his hand before they parted.

Lushkov took the letter and left—and he never came back to chop wood again.

Two years passed. One day, Skvortsov was at the theater ticket window paying for a ticket, when he noticed a small man beside him wearing a lambskin-collared coat and a shabby cat’s-skin fur cap. The man quietly asked for a ticket to the gallery and paid for it with his own money.

“Lushkov, is that you?” asked Skvortsov, recognizing the former woodchopper. “Well! What are you doing now? Things going okay?”

“Pretty well… I work in a notary’s office now. I make $35.”

“Well, thank God, that’s great. I’m really happy for you, Lushkov. You know, in a way, I’m like your godfather. I’m the one who pushed you onto the right path. Remember how I scolded you? You almost sank through the floor that time! Well, thank you, my friend, for remembering what I said.”

“Thank you, too,” said Lushkov. “If I hadn’t come to your house that day, maybe I’d still be pretending to be a schoolteacher or a student. Yes, your house saved me. I climbed out of the pit there.”

“I’m very, very glad.”

“Thank you for your kind words and actions. What you said that day really mattered. I’m thankful to you and your cook. God bless that kind, good-hearted woman. What you said was excellent, of course, but it was your cook, Olga, who truly saved me.”

“How’s that?”

“Well, here’s how. I used to come and chop wood, and she’d say: ‘Ah, you drunk! You poor lost soul! And still death won’t take you!’ Then she’d sit across from me, watching, crying, and say things like: ‘You poor man! No joy in this world, and in the next you’ll burn in hell! You sad, broken soul!’ She always talked like that. I can’t tell you how many times she got upset and cried over me. But what touched me the most—she chopped the wood for me! Do you know, sir, I never chopped a single log at your house—she did it all! Somehow, watching her, listening to her, that’s what changed me. I don’t even know how it happened, but she saved me. I’ll never forget it.”

“It’s time to go in now—they’re about to ring the bell.”

Lushkov bowed and went off to the gallery.

On Christmas Eve the Mayor's stately mansion looked beautiful. There were rows of colorful wax candles burning in every window, and beyond them, golden and glass chandeliers glowed with light. The fiddles were playing cheerful music, and lovely children danced past the windows in time with the sound.
There were fancy rugs laid from the door to the street, and carriages kept arriving with new guests walking over them. They were all children. The Mayor was throwing a Christmas Masquerade that night for all the children in the city—both rich and poor. Everyone had been talking about this ball for the last three months. Posters had been put up in all the busy areas of the city, and the newspapers had whole columns titled “THE MAYOR’S CHRISTMAS MASQUERADE.”
The Mayor promised to pay for the poor children whose parents couldn’t afford costumes, and the costume bills were sent directly to him.
Of course, the city’s regular costume shop owners were excited and all tried hard to be the most popular choice for the event. But only a week after the posters went up, a new costume seller opened a shop and immediately outshone the rest. He set up his store on a busy street corner and displayed beautiful costumes in the windows.
He was a tiny man, no bigger than a ten-year-old boy. His cheeks were red like roses, and he wore a long white wig. He had on red velvet shorts and a fancy jacket with gold buttons. Lacy ruffles covered his small white hands, and he wore sparkly knee clips. He sat on a tall stool behind the counter and helped every customer himself. He didn’t have a clerk.
It didn’t take long for children to discover how amazing his costumes were. They came running to his shop—from the Mayor’s daughter to the poor trash collector’s child. The Mayor had said the children could choose their own outfits, so they did. It was to be a party truly for the children.
They picked fairies, shepherdesses, and princesses, based on what they liked. The costume seller had just the right outfit for everyone.
Interestingly, the rich children—who already had everything—chose to dress as goose-girls and peasants. The poor children jumped at the chance to be fairies or princesses, even if only for a little while.

They drank sweet flower and berry drinks in green and red glasses and toasted one another. Each glass held just a small sip—just as the Mayor’s wife thought was enough. Under every child’s plate was a pretty gift, and everyone got a basket of candy and cake to take home.
At four in the morning, the music ended and the children went home, still chatting excitedly about the fun they’d had.
But soon after, there was trouble all over the city. When parents tried to take off their children’s costumes before bed, they couldn’t. The buttons re-buttoned themselves. The pins slid back in. The strings tied themselves again. The parents were scared, but the kids were so tired that they let them go to bed in costume, hoping it would be easier in the morning.
The kids were fine going to sleep, except for the fairies, who kept spinning and dancing and wouldn’t settle down.
“We want to swing on grass blades!” they said. “And hide in lily cups! And nap on rose petals!”
Their poor parents didn’t know what to do with these energetic little creatures their kids had become. But by morning, the fairies had finally gone to sleep.
Then, at noon, all the children woke up—and the real panic began. None of the costumes could come off. The buttons, pins, and strings all stayed in place, fixing themselves as fast as anyone could undo them.
Even worse, each child truly believed they were the character they had dressed as.

The Aldermen returned to the Wise Woman. This time she was napping, and the singer had to sing in B-flat to wake her. She was grumpy, and the Black Cat hissed at them.
“Spank them all!” she snapped. “And if that doesn’t work, send them to bed without supper!”
They did exactly that. But the next morning, the children were even worse.
Angry, the Mayor and Aldermen sent the singer to tell the Wise Woman that they thought she was a fraud and should leave the city. The singer sang the message in perfect opera style.
“Oh my,” said the Wise Woman, “how grand these gentlemen are.” Her cat hissed.

Violetta felt sad and wanted to find a solution.
One spring morning, she told the Cherry-man her story. He was kind, handsome, and sold cherries in little moss-lined baskets. He had no idea what had happened—he lived far away.
When she described the costume seller, the Cherry-man said, “He’s living in one of my cherry trees! He’s been up there since the cherries ripened and won’t come down.”
Violetta ran to tell her father. Soon half the city was on the road to the cherry orchard.
Sure enough, way up in the highest tree sat the costume seller, dressed in red velvet and shiny knee clips, eating cherries and tossing the pits.
“Good morning, friends!” he shouted.
The crowd shook canes, shouted, and tried to climb, but the tree pushed them back. Ladders fell. Axes didn’t work. The wood was like iron.
Finally, the Costumer stood on a branch and said, “You’re wasting your time. Let’s make a deal.”

“First,” said the Costumer, “every poor child in the city must get a stocking full of gifts every Christmas Eve at City Hall. Write it down and keep it forever.”

“Second,” said the Costumer, “Violetta must marry the Cherry-man. He’s been kind to me, and I want to reward him.”
