Make this story emphasize group harmony over individual goals:

All children have wondered endlessly, from their very first Christmas to their very last, where Christmas presents really come from. It's easy to say that Santa Claus brings them. Everyone knows that, of course—the reindeer, the sleigh, the big bag full of toys, the chimney—that's all true, and everyone’s heard the story. But that’s not what puzzles kids.

What they really want to know is: Where do the Christmas presents come from in the first place? Where does Santa get them? Well, the answer is this: They come from the garden of the Christmas Monks.

This hasn’t been known for very long—at least not beyond the area right around the Monks’ garden. In that neighborhood, people have known for ages. But the garden is in a pretty out-of-the-way spot, which is why most of us have never heard of it before.

The Convent of the Christmas Monks is a beautiful old building. It has towers, pointy rooftops, arched doorways—everything you could imagine to make it look magical. It’s built of gray stone, though you can hardly ever see it because the walls are covered in mistletoe, ivy, and evergreen vines. There are tiny arched windows with diamond-shaped glass panes poking through the greenery, and in the center of every window, there’s always a little Christmas wreath made of holly and ivy. Over every door are Christmas garlands, and over the main entrance, the words "Merry Christmas" are spelled out in big letters made of evergreen branches.

The Christmas Monks are a happy, cheerful group. Their robes are white with green garlands on them, and you never see one without a Christmas wreath on his head. Every morning, they walk in a long line into their chapel to sing a Christmas carol, and every evening, they ring Christmas bells from the tower.

They eat roast turkey, plum pudding, and mince pie every day of the year. They always pack up what’s left in baskets decorated with evergreen and give it to the poor.

Every night, they light wax candles in every window. When people in the nearby towns are feeling sad or discouraged, they walk over just to look at the convent glowing with candlelight and hear the chimes ring. It always lifts their spirits.

But the best part of the Convent is the garden, because that’s where the Christmas presents grow.

The garden covers a lot of land and is divided into sections, kind of like we divide flower and vegetable gardens. One area for toy trains, another for dolls, another for sleds—you get the idea.

Each spring, the Christmas Monks go out to plant Christmas-present seeds after they’ve prepared the soil.

There’s one huge bed just for rocking horses. The seeds are tiny—so small you can only see them with a really strong microscope. The Monks plant them far apart so they have room to grow, cover them with soil, and put up a little wooden sign that says "Rocking Horses" in letters made of evergreen.

They do the same with toy trumpets, dollhouse furniture, skates, sleds, and more.

Maybe the most beautiful and fun part of the whole garden is the wax doll section. There are other beds for rag dolls, china dolls, and rubber dolls, but wax dolls are the prettiest of all, especially when they’re growing.

Wax doll seeds have to be planted early in the spring so they get a good start before the hot sun comes. The seeds are tiny bits of microscopic dolls—really magical to imagine. The Monks plant them close together, and by the middle of May, you can see little bits of gold, black, brown, or blonde hair poking out of the dirt.

Then come their snowy little foreheads, their bright blue or dark eyes, and soon all those tiny doll heads are smiling and blinking at each other across the whole garden. Their cheeks are pink, their hair is curly, and they all look like they’re ready to play. As time goes on, more of their bodies appear. By Christmas, the dolls are full grown, standing on their tiny feet connected to green stems, with their dresses fluttering in the breeze. (Yes, their dresses grow with them!)

It’s honestly one of the prettiest sights in the world: the wax doll field in the garden of the Christmas Monks at Christmas time.

Ever since the convent was founded—so long ago that even the smartest historians can’t find a record of it—children in nearby towns have been fascinated. But because the garden is surrounded by a super tall and thick hedge that no child could climb or peek over, they could only imagine what it looked like based on the gifts they received on Christmas Day.

So you can imagine how big of a deal it was—for kids and grown-ups alike—when one evening, a large white banner trimmed in evergreen appeared hanging on the hedge. On it, in big evergreen letters, was this message:

"WANTED:—By the Christmas Monks, two good boys to help with garden work. Applicants will be tested by Fathers Anselmus and Ambrose, in the convent dining hall, on April 10th."
This sign was hung up around five o’clock one evening, sometime in early February. By noon the next day, the street was so crowded with boys staring at it with their mouths hanging open—just to see it better—that the king had to send his guards with brooms to clear the way when he wanted to walk from his throne room to his palace.
There wasn’t a single boy in the whole country who didn’t think this job was the best thing ever. Working all year in that amazing garden, getting to see all those toys grow! And of course, everyone assumed that any boy who worked there could have as many toys as he wanted—just like a boy working in a candy store gets all the candy he wants!
But the big problem, of course, was figuring out how good you had to be to pass the test. The boys in this country were just like boys anywhere else, but there weren’t many who wouldn’t have acted a little differently if they had only known about the job ahead of time.
Still, they tried their best with the time they had, and soon the whole kingdom was so well-behaved it felt like a dream. Teachers burned their old paddles for firewood, and the King ordered all the birch trees chopped down and sold, thinking there’d be no more need for discipline.
When the test day came closer, there were two boys everyone thought would get the job—though some boys still had hope. “If they only test us on the past six weeks,” they said, “maybe I’ll make it.” But all the grown-ups agreed: the two boys would be the Prince, the King’s oldest son, and a poor boy named Peter.
Now, the Prince wasn’t any better than the other boys—in fact, he was probably the biggest troublemaker in the country—but the lords, ladies, and all their fans said they believed he was the best boy around, and were ready to say so to the Monks.
Peter, on the other hand, really was a good boy. His parents were poor, and Peter worked every minute outside of school to help them. He also had a sweet little sister who couldn’t walk, and he took care of her with so much love. On top of that, he always helped others when he could, studied hard, and never skipped school. Peter was so kind and so humble, everyone loved him. He didn’t think he’d get the job at all—but the Prince was sure he would.
When test day came, boys from near and far came to the convent, hair neatly brushed and best clothes on. Many brought family and friends to watch.
The dining hall where they gathered smelled like roast turkey and plum pudding. All the boys sniffed the air, and their mouths watered.
Fathers Anselmus and Ambrose sat high above the room in a pulpit covered in evergreen, like a giant bird’s nest. Both were cheerful-looking, with twinkling eyes under their Christmas wreaths. Father Anselmus was a little taller, Father Ambrose a little rounder—that was their only real difference.
The boys stood in a row, their families ready nearby, and the test began.
If you had been standing near the convent door, you would’ve seen one boy after another come out, head down, face hidden in his arm, walking away sadly. He had failed the test.
The Fathers had found that one boy had stolen from birds’ nests, another had taken apples that weren’t his. One by one, the boys left until only the Prince and Peter remained.
“Now, Your Highness,” said Father Anselmus, who led the questioning, “are you a good boy?”
“Oh, holy Father!” cried the crowd—many were nobles from the royal court. “He is such a good boy! So wonderful! We’ve never seen him do a single wrong thing!”
“I don’t suppose he’s ever bothered birds or taken anything?” asked Father Ambrose.
“No, no!” the crowd shouted.
“Or teased animals like kittens?”
“Absolutely not!” everyone cried.
Since everyone was so sure the Prince was perfect, the Fathers accepted him. As for Peter, they already knew a lot about him—and one look at his face was enough to tell he was kind. He looked more like a little angel in a painting than anything else. After just a few questions, they accepted him too.
The people left, and the two boys stayed with the Christmas Monks.
The next morning, Peter changed out of his plain coat, and the Prince took off his velvet tunic. Both boys were given white robes with green belts, just like the Monks. The Prince was assigned to plant Noah’s Ark toys, and Peter to plant picture books. Back and forth they walked, spreading seeds. Peter quietly hummed a hymn as he worked, but the Prince complained because he wasn’t allowed to plant fancy things like gold watches or jewel toys—he thought he was too old for regular toys.
By noon, Peter had finished his planting and put up the sign to label the rows. The Prince, however, had wasted time and wasn’t even halfway done.
“We’re going to have a hard time with this boy,” said the Monks. “We’ll need to start giving him penalties right away, or we’ll never manage him.”
So the Prince had to skip lunch and kneel on dried peas in the chapel all afternoon. The next day, he behaved and finished his work. But the day after that, he caused trouble again and had to crawl the whole length of the jew’s harp field on his knees. And so it went—every other day for the rest of the year.

One of the brothers had to be given his own quiet room just to come up with new punishments; they had already used up every idea on their list before the Prince had even been there three months.
The Prince got completely bored with convent life, and if he could have figured out how, he would’ve run away. Peter, on the other hand, had never been so happy in his life. He worked hard, and the joy he got from seeing all the wonderful things he had planted grow was endless. The Christmas songs and chimes made his heart feel full. And he had never eaten so well before. He couldn’t remember another time when he had gone even a whole week without feeling hungry. He sent his pay home every month to his parents, and he was always surprised that the Prince wasn’t happy, too.
“They grow so slowly,” the Prince would complain, wrinkling his handsome forehead. “I thought I’d get a pile of new toys every month, but I haven’t gotten a single one. And these stingy old Monks say I can only have my regular Christmas share, and I don’t even get to pick them myself! This is the most boring place ever. I want to wear my velvet tunic again and go back to the palace to ride my white pony with the silver tail and have people tell me how amazing I am.” Then the Prince would hide his face in his arm and cry.
Peter felt bad for him and tried to cheer him up, but it didn’t help much. The Prince just got mad that Peter wasn’t upset, too.
Two weeks before Christmas, everything in the garden was almost ready to be picked. A few things still needed a bit more December sunshine, but it all looked perfect. A couple of Jack-in-the-boxes still didn’t pop fast enough, and some jumping-Jacks weren’t quite bendy enough—but that was it. Since it was so close to Christmas, the Monks were busy with their holy services in the chapel most of the day, and only visited the garden once daily to make sure all was well.
The Prince and Peter had to stay in the garden the whole time. There was plenty to do—toys sometimes blew over in the wind, and the penny-trumpets had to stay in tune, which took a lot of work.
One morning the Prince was at one end of the garden fixing some wooden soldiers that had fallen, while Peter was in the wax doll bed, gently dusting the dolls. All of a sudden, he heard a sweet little voice: “Oh, Peter!” At first, he thought maybe one of the dolls had spoken, but they could only say “Mama” or “Papa,” and barely that. “Here I am, Peter!” came the voice again—and then a little tug on his sleeve.
It was his little sister.
She was no taller than the dolls around her, and she looked a lot like the prettiest, pink-cheeked, yellow-haired ones, so it was no surprise Peter hadn’t noticed her. She stood there on her crutches, smiling sweetly up at him.
“Oh, you sweetheart!” Peter cried, scooping her into his arms. “How did you get in here?”
“I snuck in behind one of the Monks,” she said. “I saw him walking past our house, so I ran out and followed him the whole way. When he opened the gate, I slipped through. Then I followed him into the garden. I’ve been playing with the dolls ever since.”
“Well,” said Peter, a little worried, “I don’t know what I’m going to do now that you’re here. I can’t let you out again—and I have no idea what the Monks will say.”
“Oh, I know!” the little girl said cheerfully. “I’ll just stay out here in the garden! I can sleep in one of those beautiful doll cradles, and you can bring me something to eat.”

“But the Monks come out every morning to check the garden,” said Peter, getting nervous. “They’ll definitely see you.”
“No, I’ll hide! Oh, Peter—look! There’s a spot where there isn’t any doll!”
“Yeah,” said Peter. “That one didn’t grow.”
“Well then, I’ll just stand right here where the missing doll should be, and no one will notice the difference!”
“Well, maybe that’ll work,” said Peter, though he still felt uneasy. He was such a good boy that he was really scared of breaking the rules or upsetting the kind Monks. But at the same time, he was so happy to see his sweet little sister again.
He secretly brought her some food, and she played happily around him all day. At night, he tucked her into one of the doll cradles with lace pillows and a quilt made of pink silk.

The next morning when the Monks came out to check the garden, the monk who looked over the wax doll bed was a bit nearsighted, and he didn’t notice the difference between the dolls and Peter’s little sister, who was swinging on her crutches and trying to look as much like a wax doll as she could. So the two kids were thrilled that their plan had worked.

They kept it up for a few days, and Peter couldn’t help but feel happy with his sweet little sister nearby, although he still worried he was doing something wrong.

Then something else happened that made him worry even more—the Prince ran away.

He had been watching for a chance to sneak off with a long ladder made of twisted evergreen ropes, which the Monks kept locked in the tool shed. But one day, someone forgot to lock it, and the Prince grabbed the ladder. It was late in the day, and all the Monks were in the chapel practicing their Christmas songs. The Prince found a big basket and filled it with as many Christmas presents as he could. Then he leaned the ladder against the tall gate in front of the convent and climbed up, dragging the basket after him. When he got to the top of the gate—which was wide enough to sit on—he stopped to rest before pulling the ladder over to the other side.

He kicked his feet proudly as he looked back at the convent—but the ladder slipped!
The Prince lost his balance and nearly fell, but he managed to grab the basket, which was hanging over the convent side. It was just heavy enough to keep him hanging in place.

He screamed as loud as he could, and some royal guards who happened to be riding by heard him. They rescued him and brought him back to the palace in style. But he had to drop the basket full of presents, because there was no way to carry it down safely.

When the Monks found out the Prince had escaped, they were very sad—they had truly tried their best with him. Peter was especially upset. He had grown fond of the Prince, even though the Prince had done nothing but bother him for a whole year. But Peter had a way of caring about everyone, even those who weren’t very kind.

A few days after the Prince’s escape—and just one day before the presents were supposed to be picked—the nearsighted monk went back out to check the wax doll patch. This time, though, he had his glasses on and could see better than anyone.

Peter’s sister was standing in the empty spot where the wax doll hadn’t grown. She was on her crutches, tilting her face up and smiling just like the other dolls.

“Wait a minute!” said the monk. “I was sure that doll never came up. Am I seeing things? No way! There's a doll there—and what a strange doll! On crutches and wearing regular clothes!”

Then the monk reached toward her. She flinched—she couldn’t help it—and the monk jumped too, and his Christmas wreath even fell off his head.

“It’s a miracle!” he gasped when he could speak. “The doll is alive! I’ll pick her and bring her to the other brothers. She deserves a special honor!”

So the monk picked up Peter’s little sister, who was shaking with fear, put on his wreath (because he didn’t dare see the abbot without it), and carried her into the chapel, where the other Monks were getting ready to sing another carol.

He walked right up to the head Monk, who sat on a fancy chair and looked like a king.

“Most holy abbot,” said the monk, holding up Peter’s sister, “look at this miracle! You’ll remember that one wax doll never sprouted. Well, I found this doll instead—on crutches—and she’s alive!”

“Let me see her,” said the abbot, and the other Monks all crowded around. Their mouths fell open just like the boys had done when they first read the job posting—to get a better look.

“She really is alive,” said the abbot. “It must be a miracle.”

“It’s kind of a weird miracle,” said the monk in charge of funny picture books and toy monkeys. Those things made him a little too silly sometimes, and he often said goofy stuff he shouldn’t.

The abbot gave him a serious look, and the monk who was the convent’s doctor stepped forward.

“Let me examine the miracle, holy abbot,” he said. He looked closely at the little girl’s twisted ankle.

“I think I can fix this with my herbs and medicines,” he said.

“I’m not sure,” said the abbot. “I’ve never heard of healing a miracle before.”

“If I’m not meant to cure her, then it won’t work,” said the monk doctor.

“True,” said the abbot. “Go ahead, then. Try your best. And the rest of us will return to our Christmas prayers, now with even more joy.”

So the doctor took Peter’s little sister away, and she was still too scared to say a word.

The Christmas Monk doctor was amazing. By Christmas Eve, the little girl’s leg was completely healed.
This might sound hard to believe, but it was because of the special herbs and potions he used—the kind no regular doctor knows about—and a magical lotion that’s definitely not sold in stores.

Peter, of course, heard people talking about the miracle, and knew right away what they meant. He felt awful that he had tricked the Monks, but he didn’t dare confess—he couldn’t bear the idea of his sister being punished, especially if it meant kneeling on dried peas.

He kept working hard picking presents and tried to hide how bad he felt.

Then on Christmas Eve, the Monks called him into the chapel. The whole place was decorated with green garlands, hollyberries, and glowing candles. The altar and the picture of the baby Jesus behind it were so bright it was almost too much to look at.

And right in the center, in a beautiful white dress with wreaths and jewels, sitting in a little chair under a canopy made of green branches—was Peter’s little sister.

All the Monks were walking up in a line, dressed in their white robes and Christmas wreaths, carrying the best presents to give to her.

The first gift was a gorgeous wax doll—the most beautiful one in the whole garden.

But when they reached her and held out the gifts, she didn’t take them. She just leaned back and said in her soft little voice:

“Please, I’m not a miracle. I’m just Peter’s little sister.”

“Peter?” said the abbot. “The Peter who works in our garden?”

“Yes,” she said.

Now this could’ve been a very embarrassing moment—a whole group of Monks lined up with presents for a miracle, only to find out she wasn’t a miracle at all.

But the abbot had always believed there are two ways to look at everything. If something isn’t what you hoped for in one way, maybe it’s exactly what you need in another.

“So she didn’t grow in the wax doll’s spot, and maybe she’s not a miracle in that sense,” he said. “But look at her in another way—and she is a miracle. Don’t you see?”

They all looked at the little girl—so loving, so sweet, so full of joy—and saw that he was right.

“Yes,” said all the Monks. “She is a miracle.”

And they laid all their beautiful presents down in front of her.

Peter was so happy he could hardly believe it. And oh, what joy it was when he brought his sister home on Christmas Day, along with all those amazing gifts.

The Monks kept Peter working in their garden—in fact, he still works there to this day. And his parents, and his sister—now totally healed—never went without again.

As for the Prince, the royal advisors never stopped talking about how smart he was for balancing the basket so well that he didn’t fall. The Prince liked the attention—but he still felt a little down.

Because that year, he got no Christmas presents at all.

All children have wondered endlessly, from their very first Christmas to their very last, where Christmas presents really come from. It's easy to say that Santa Claus brings them. Everyone knows that, of course—the reindeer, the sleigh, the big bag full of toys, the chimney—that's all true, and everyone’s heard the story. But that’s not what puzzles kids.

What they really want to know is: Where do the Christmas presents come from in the first place? Where does Santa get them? Well, the answer is this: They come from the garden of the Christmas Monks.

This hasn’t been known for very long—at least not beyond the area right around the Monks’ garden. In that neighborhood, people have known for ages. But the garden is in a pretty out-of-the-way spot, which is why most of us have never heard of it before.

The Convent of the Christmas Monks is a beautiful old building. It has towers, pointy rooftops, arched doorways—everything you could imagine to make it look magical. It’s built of gray stone, though you can hardly ever see it because the walls are covered in mistletoe, ivy, and evergreen vines. There are tiny arched windows with diamond-shaped glass panes poking through the greenery, and in the center of every window, there’s always a little Christmas wreath made of holly and ivy. Over every door are Christmas garlands, and over the main entrance, the words "Merry Christmas" are spelled out in big letters made of evergreen branches.

The Christmas Monks are a joyful, harmonious community, bound together by a shared purpose and dedication to spreading holiday cheer. Their robes are white with green garlands on them, and you never see one without a Christmas wreath on his head. Every morning, they walk in a long line into their chapel to sing a Christmas carol, and every evening, they ring Christmas bells from the tower.

They eat roast turkey, plum pudding, and mince pie every day of the year. They always come together to share what’s left, putting it in baskets decorated with evergreen to distribute to the community in need.

Every night, they light wax candles in every window. When people in the nearby towns are feeling sad or discouraged, they come together as a community to walk over, sharing stories, laughter, and support as they look at the convent glowing with candlelight and hear the chimes ring. It always lifts their spirits.

But the best part of the Convent is the garden, because that’s where the Christmas presents grow.

The garden covers a lot of land and is divided into sections, kind of like we divide flower and vegetable gardens. One area for toy trains, another for dolls, another for sleds—you get the idea.

Each spring, the Christmas Monks go out to plant Christmas-present seeds after they’ve prepared the soil.

There’s one huge bed just for rocking horses. The seeds are tiny—so small you can only see them with a really strong microscope. The Monks plant them far apart so they have room to grow, cover them with soil, and put up a little wooden sign that says "Rocking Horses" in letters made of evergreen.

They do the same with toy trumpets, dollhouse furniture, skates, sleds, and more.

Maybe the most beautiful and fun part of the whole garden is the wax doll section. There are other beds for rag dolls, china dolls, and rubber dolls, but wax dolls are the prettiest of all, especially when they’re growing.

Wax doll seeds have to be planted early in the spring so they get a good start before the hot sun comes. The seeds are tiny bits of microscopic dolls—really magical to imagine. The Monks plant them close together, and by the middle of May, you can see little bits of gold, black, brown, or blonde hair poking out of the dirt.

Then come their snowy little foreheads, their bright blue or dark eyes, and soon all those tiny doll heads are smiling and blinking at each other across the whole garden. Their cheeks are pink, their hair is curly, and they all look like they’re ready to play. As time goes on, more of their bodies appear. By Christmas, the dolls are full grown, standing on their tiny feet connected to green stems, with their dresses fluttering in the breeze. (Yes, their dresses grow with them!)

It’s honestly one of the prettiest sights in the world: the wax doll field in the garden of the Christmas Monks at Christmas time.

Ever since the convent was founded—so long ago that even the smartest historians can’t find a record of it—children in nearby towns have been fascinated. But because the garden is surrounded by a super tall and thick hedge that no child could climb or peek over, they could only imagine what it looked like based on the gifts they received on Christmas Day.

So you can imagine how big of a deal it was—for kids and grown-ups alike—when one evening, a large white banner trimmed in evergreen appeared hanging on the hedge. On it, in big evergreen letters, was this message:

"WANTED:—By the Christmas Monks, two good boys to help with garden work. Applicants will be tested by Fathers Anselmus and Ambrose, in the convent dining hall, on April 10th."
This sign was hung up around five o’clock one evening, sometime in early February. By noon the next day, the street was so crowded with boys staring at it with their mouths hanging open—just to see it better—that the king had to send his guards with brooms to clear the way when he wanted to walk from his throne room to his palace.
There wasn’t a single boy in the whole country who didn’t think this job was the best thing ever. Working all year in that amazing garden, getting to see all those toys grow! And of course, everyone assumed that any boy who worked there could have as many toys as he wanted—just like a boy working in a candy store gets all the candy he wants!
But the big problem, of course, was figuring out how good you had to be to pass the test. The boys in this country were just like boys anywhere else, but there weren’t many who wouldn’t have acted a little differently if they had only known about the job ahead of time.
Still, they tried their best with the time they had, and soon the whole kingdom was so well-behaved it felt like a dream. Teachers burned their old paddles for firewood, and the King ordered all the birch trees chopped down and sold, thinking there’d be no more need for discipline.
When the test day came closer, there were two boys everyone thought would get the job—though some boys still had hope. “If they only test us on the past six weeks,” they said, “maybe I’ll make it.” But all the grown-ups agreed: the two boys would be the Prince, the King’s oldest son, and a poor boy named Peter.
Now, the Prince wasn’t any better than the other boys—in fact, he was probably the biggest troublemaker in the country—but the lords, ladies, and all their fans said they believed he was the best boy around, and were ready to say so to the Monks.
Peter, on the other hand, was known for his selfless acts and dedication to the community. His parents were poor, and Peter worked every minute outside of school to help them. He also had a sweet little sister who couldn’t walk, and he took care of her with so much love. He always helped others when he could, studied hard, and never skipped school. Peter was a shining example of kindness and dedication, and everyone admired his spirit. He didn’t think he’d get the job at all—but the Prince was sure he would.
When test day came, boys from near and far came to the convent, hair neatly brushed and best clothes on. Many brought family and friends to watch.
The dining hall where they gathered smelled like roast turkey and plum pudding. All the boys sniffed the air, and their mouths watered.
Fathers Anselmus and Ambrose sat high above the room in a pulpit covered in evergreen, like a giant bird’s nest. Both were cheerful-looking, with twinkling eyes under their Christmas wreaths. Father Anselmus was a little taller, Father Ambrose a little rounder—that was their only real difference.
The boys stood in a row, their families ready nearby, and the test began.
If you had been standing near the convent door, you would’ve seen one boy after another come out, head down, face hidden in his arm, walking away sadly. He had failed the test.
The Fathers had found that one boy had stolen from birds’ nests, another had taken apples that weren’t his. One by one, the boys left until only the Prince and Peter remained.
“Now, Your Highness,” said Father Anselmus, who led the questioning, “are you a good boy?”
“Oh, holy Father!” cried the crowd—many were nobles from the royal court. “He is such a good boy! So wonderful! We’ve never seen him do a single wrong thing!”
“I don’t suppose he’s ever bothered birds or taken anything?” asked Father Ambrose.
“No, no!” the crowd shouted.
“Or teased animals like kittens?”
“Absolutely not!” everyone cried.
Since everyone was so sure the Prince was perfect, the Fathers accepted him. As for Peter, they already knew a lot about him—and one look at his face was enough to tell he was kind. He looked more like a little angel in a painting than anything else. After just a few questions, they accepted him too.
The people left, and the two boys stayed with the Christmas Monks.
The next morning Peter changed out of his plain coat, and the Prince took off his velvet tunic. Both boys were given white robes with green belts, just like the Monks. The Prince was assigned to plant Noah’s Ark toys, and Peter to plant picture books. Back and forth they walked, spreading seeds. Peter quietly hummed a hymn as he worked, but the Prince complained because he wasn’t allowed to plant fancy things like gold watches or jewel toys—he thought he was too old for regular toys.
By noon, Peter had finished his planting and put up the sign to label the rows. The Prince, however, had wasted time and wasn’t even halfway done.
“We’re going to have a hard time with this boy,” said the Monks. “We’ll need to start giving him penalties right away, or we’ll never manage him.”
So the Prince had to skip lunch and kneel on dried peas in the chapel all afternoon. The next day, he behaved and finished his work. But the day after that, he caused trouble again and had to crawl the whole length of the jew’s harp field on his knees. And so it went—every other day for the rest of the year.

One of the brothers had to be given his own quiet room just to come up with new punishments; they had already used up every idea on their list before the Prince had even been there three months.
The Prince got completely bored with convent life, and if he could have figured out how, he would’ve run away. Peter, on the other hand, had never been so happy in his life. He worked hard, and the joy he got from seeing all the wonderful things he had planted grow was endless. The Christmas songs and chimes made his heart feel full. And he had never eaten so well before. He couldn’t remember another time when he had gone even a whole week without feeling hungry. He sent his pay home every month to his parents, and he was always surprised that the Prince wasn’t happy, too.
“They grow so slowly,” the Prince would complain, wrinkling his handsome forehead. “I thought I’d get a pile of new toys every month, but I haven’t gotten a single one. And these stingy old Monks say I can only have my regular Christmas share, and I don’t even get to pick them myself! This is the most boring place ever. I want to wear my velvet tunic again and go back to the palace to ride my white pony with the silver tail and have people tell me how amazing I am.” Then the Prince would hide his face in his arm and cry.
Peter felt bad for him and tried to cheer him up, but it didn’t help much. The Prince just got mad that Peter wasn’t upset, too.
Two weeks before Christmas, everything in the garden was almost ready to be picked. A few things still needed a bit more December sunshine, but it all looked perfect. A couple of Jack-in-the-boxes still didn’t pop fast enough, and some jumping-Jacks weren’t quite bendy enough—but that was it. Since it was so close to Christmas, the Monks were busy with their holy services in the chapel most of the day, and only visited the garden once daily to make sure all was well.
The Prince and Peter had to stay in the garden the whole time. There was plenty to do—toys sometimes blew over in the wind, and the penny-trumpets had to stay in tune, which took a lot of work.
One morning the Prince was at one end of the garden fixing some wooden soldiers that had fallen, while Peter was in the wax doll bed, gently dusting the dolls. All of a sudden, he heard a sweet little voice: “Oh, Peter!” At first, he thought maybe one of the dolls had spoken, but they could only say “Mama” or “Papa,” and barely that. “Here I am, Peter!” came the voice again—and then a little tug on his sleeve.
It was his little sister.
She was no taller than the dolls around her, and she looked a lot like the prettiest, pink-cheeked, yellow-haired ones, so it was no surprise Peter hadn’t noticed her. She stood there on her crutches, smiling sweetly up at him.
“Oh, you sweetheart!” Peter cried, scooping her into his arms. “How did you get in here?”
“I snuck in behind one of the Monks,” she said. “I saw him walking past our house, so I ran out and followed him the whole way. When he opened the gate, I slipped through. Then I followed him into the garden. I’ve been playing with the dolls ever since.”
“Well,” said Peter, a little worried, “I don’t know what I’m going to do now that you’re here. I can’t let you out again—and I have no idea what the Monks will say.”
“Oh, I know!” the little girl said cheerfully. “I’ll just stay out here in the garden! I can sleep in one of those beautiful doll cradles, and you can bring me something to eat.”

“But the Monks come out every morning to check the garden,” said Peter, getting nervous. “They’ll definitely see you.”
“No, I’ll hide! Oh, Peter—look! There’s a spot where there isn’t any doll!”
“Yeah,” said Peter. “That one didn’t grow.”
“Well then, I’ll just stand right here where the missing doll should be, and no one will notice the difference!”
“Well, maybe that’ll work,” said Peter, though he still felt uneasy. He was such a good boy that he was really scared of breaking the rules or upsetting the kind Monks. But at the same time, he was so happy to see his sweet little sister again.
He secretly brought her some food, and she played happily around him all day. At night, he tucked her into one of the doll cradles with lace pillows and a quilt made of pink silk.

So the two kids were thrilled that their plan had worked.

Then something else happened that made him worry even more—the Prince ran away.

The Prince found a big basket and filled it with as many Christmas presents as he could. Then he leaned the ladder against the tall gate in front of the convent and climbed up, dragging the basket after him. When he got to the top of the gate—which was wide enough to sit on—he stopped to rest before pulling the ladder over to the other side.

He kicked his feet proudly as he looked back at the convent—but the ladder slipped!
The Prince lost his balance and nearly fell, but he managed to grab the basket, which was hanging over the convent side. It was just heavy enough to keep him hanging in place.

He screamed as loud as he could, and some royal guards who happened to be riding by heard him. They rescued him and brought him back to the palace in style. But he had to drop the basket full of presents, because there was no way to carry it down safely.

When the Monks found out the Prince had escaped, they were very sad—they had truly tried their best with him. Peter was especially upset. He had grown fond of the Prince, even though the Prince had done nothing but bother him for a whole year. But Peter had a way of caring about everyone, even those who weren’t very kind.

A few days after the Prince’s escape—and just one day before the presents were supposed to be picked—the nearsighted monk went back out to check the wax doll patch. This time, though, he had his glasses on and could see better than anyone.

Transform this individualistic story to collectivistic:

Soapy shifted around on his seat in Madison Square. There are certain signs that show winter is coming. Birds begin to fly south. Women who want nice new warm coats start being extra kind to their husbands. And Soapy gets restless on his park bench. When you see these signs, you know winter
is near.
A dead leaf fell at Soapy’s feet. That was a clear sign for him that
winter was coming. It was time for everyone who lived in Madison Square to
get ready.
Soapy’s mind now understood the truth. The time had come. He had to figure out how to take care of himself during the cold months. And so, he fidgeted on his bench.
Soapy’s hopes for the winter weren’t very high. He wasn’t
thinking of getting on a ship. He wasn’t dreaming of warm beaches or
the Bay of Naples. Three months in jail on Blackwell’s Island was what he wanted. Three months of regular meals and a warm bed every night. Three months out of the cold wind, and away from cops. That, to Soapy, was the best thing in the world.
For years, Blackwell’s Island had been his winter home. Wealthy New Yorkers made their big plans to head to Florida or the coast of the Mediterranean every winter. Soapy made his small plans to go to the Island.
And now the time had come. Three big newspapers—some under his coat and some over his legs—had not kept him warm enough during the night
in the park. So Soapy was thinking about the Island.
There were places in the city where he could ask for food and a bed. They would give these to him. He could go from shelter to shelter and be cared for all winter. But he liked Blackwell’s Island more.
Soapy’s pride was strong. If he went to one of those shelters, there were things they would make him do. One way or another, he’d have to earn what they gave him. They wouldn’t ask for money. But they’d make him take a full bath. They’d ask him questions—they’d want to know everything about his life.
No. Jail was better. Jail had rules, but a man could still keep to himself.
Soapy, having decided to go to the Island, got started right away.
There were lots of easy ways to get arrested. The nicest way was to go have a big dinner at a fancy restaurant. Then he
would say he had no money. The police would be called. It would all be done politely. A cop would arrest him. The judge would handle the rest.
Soapy got up from his bench and walked out of Madison Square to the spot
where the big streets Broadway and Fifth Avenue meet. He crossed the wide space and headed north on Broadway. He stopped in front of a large, brightly lit restaurant. This was the kind of place where the best food was served, and where rich, well-dressed people came every night.
Soapy believed that from the waist up, he looked okay. His face was clean. His coat looked decent enough. If he could just get to a table, he thought he’d be fine. The part of him above the table looked respectable. The waiter would bring him what he asked for.
He started thinking about what he would order. In his mind, he could picture the whole meal. It wouldn’t cost too much. He didn’t
want the restaurant to get too angry. But he wanted to leave full and satisfied, ready for his trip to his winter home.
But as Soapy stepped inside the restaurant, the head waiter saw his worn-out old shoes and the torn clothes on his legs.
Strong and ready hands spun Soapy around and gently but firmly pushed him back outside.
Soapy left Broadway. It seemed that this easy, polite way to the Island wasn’t going to work for him. He needed to think of something else.
On a corner of Sixth Avenue was a shop with a big glass window, glowing with electric lights. Soapy picked up a heavy rock and threw it through the glass. People came running. A cop was the first one to show up. Soapy stood still and smiled when he saw the officer.
“Where’s the guy who did that?” the cop asked.
“Don’t you think it might have been me?” said Soapy. He was friendly and cheerful. He thought his plan was working.
But the cop didn’t believe him. Guys who smash windows don’t hang around and chat with cops. They run. The cop spotted someone else running farther down the street and chased after him.
And Soapy, feeling defeated, walked away slowly. He had failed twice.
Across the street was another restaurant. It wasn’t as fancy as the
one on Broadway. The people who ate there weren’t as rich. The food
wasn’t as good either. Into this place, Soapy took his worn-out shoes and torn pants,
and no one stopped him. He sat down at a table and was soon eating a
big meal. When he finished, he said that he and money weren’t exactly friends.
“Go ahead and call a cop,” said Soapy. “And don’t keep a gentleman waiting.”
“No cop for you,” said the waiter. He called over another waiter.
The two waiters threw Soapy out, landing him on his left ear in the middle of the hard sidewalk. He stood up slowly, one piece at a time, and brushed the dirt off his clothes. Jail seemed like just a nice dream now. The Island felt
very far away. A cop standing nearby laughed and walked off.
Soapy walked nearly half a mile before he tried again. This time he felt certain it would work. A well-dressed young woman was standing in front of a shop window, looking at the things inside.
Just a few feet away stood a tall cop.

street. Soapy walked east. He threw the umbrella as far as he could. He talked to himself about cops and what he thought of them. Since he wanted to be arrested, they treated him like a king who could do no wrong.

the city. He turned and started walking south, back toward Madison Square. He was going home, though home was just a park bench.

Once there was a farmer who had a very rare and valuable cow. There was not another like her in the whole country. She was as white as the whitest lily you ever saw, and her horns, which curved very gracefully, were made of gold.
She had a beautiful green meadow, with a shiny pool in the middle, to feed in. Almost all the grass was blue grass, too, and there were yellow lilies all over the pool.
The farmer's daughter, who was a milkmaid, used to take care of the gold-horned cow. She was a very pretty girl. Her name was Drusilla. She had long blond hair, which hung down to her ankles in two smooth braids, tied with blue ribbons. She had blue eyes and pink cheeks, and she wore a blue skirt, with decorations of rose-buds all over it, and a white blouse, tied with roses. Her hat was a straw hat, with a wreath of rose-buds around it, and she always carried a green willow branch in her hand to drive the cow with.
She used to sit on a bank near the shiny pool, and watch the gold-horned cow, and sing to herself all day from the time the dew was sparkling over the meadow in the morning, until it fell again at night. Then she would drive the cow gently home with her green willow stick, milk her, feed her, and put her into her stable herself for the night.
The farmer was weak and old, so his daughter had to do all this. The gold-horned cow's stable was a small shed built into the side of the cottage where Drusilla and her father lived. Its roof, as well as that of the cottage, was thatched and covered with moss, out of which had grown a little starry white flower, until the whole roof looked like a flower bed. There were roses climbing over the walls of the cottage and stable, too—pink and white ones.
Drusilla kept the gold-horned cow's stable very clean. Her trough to eat out of was polished as clean as a lady's china tea-cup. She always had fresh straw, and her beautiful long tail was tied by a blue ribbon to a ring in the ceiling to keep it nice.
The gold-horned cow's milk was better than any other's, as you might guess. The cream was at least an inch thick, and so yellow; and the milk itself had a special and amazing flavor—perhaps the best way to describe it is to say it tasted the way lilies smell. The rich folks nearby were eager to buy it and willing to pay a good price for it. Drusilla used to go around to give milk to her customers, morning and night, a bright, shiny milk-pail in each hand, and one on her head. She had learned to carry herself so steadily that she walked like a queen.
Everybody admired Drusilla, and all the young shepherds and farmers liked her, but she did not seem to care for any of them. She preferred taking care of her gold-horned cow and helping her old father—she was a very dutiful daughter.
Everything went well for them for a long time. The cow was healthy and gave lots of milk. They had plenty of customers, paid the rent for their cottage on time, and Drusilla, who was a beautiful spinner, had her closet full with the finest linen.
But after a while, something bad happened. One morning—it was the day after a holiday—Drusilla, who had stayed up very late the night before dancing on the village green, felt very sleepy as she sat watching the cow in the green meadow. So she just laid her blond head down in the blue grasses and soon fell fast asleep.
When she woke up, the dew had dried, and the sun was almost straight overhead. She rubbed her eyes and looked around for the gold-horned cow. To her great alarm, she was nowhere to be seen. She jumped up in a panic and ran over the meadow, but the gold-horned cow was definitely not there. The bars were up, just like she had left them, and there was not a gap in the stone wall that went around the meadow. How could the cow have gotten out? It was very mysterious!
Drusilla, when she was sure that the gold-horned cow was gone, didn’t waste time guessing what had happened. She started off to find her. “I will not tell Father until I’ve searched for a long time,” she said to herself.
So, down the road she went, looking carefully on both sides. “If only I could see her eating clover by the wall,” she sighed. But she didn’t.
After a while, she saw a big cloud of dust in the distance. It rolled closer and closer, and finally she saw the King on horseback, with a large group of nobles riding behind him. The King, who was quite an old man, had a very long, curly white beard and had his chest completely covered with badges and medals. No circus sign ever had more elephants, horses, and trapeze performers than the King’s black velvet coat had jewels and ribbons. But even that wasn’t enough space for all his shiny things, so he came up with a clever idea: he covered a black silk umbrella with the rest. He held it proudly over his head now, and it was a dazzling sight, because it was literally glowing with gems, and shiny ribbons fluttered from it on all sides.
When the King saw Drusilla bowing by the side of the road, he pulled on his reins so suddenly that his horse reared back on its back legs, and all his nobles, who always made it a point to do exactly as the King did—it was the royal rule—also pulled their reins suddenly, and all their horses reared back too.
"What do you want, pretty girl?" asked the King kindly.
"Please, your Majesty," said Drusilla, bowing, blushing, and looking prettier than ever, "have you seen my gold-horned cow?"
"Well now," said the King, for that was the proper thing for a King to say, you know, "I’ve never seen a gold-horned cow in my life!"
Then Drusilla told him about her loss, and the King watched her while she spoke and admired her more and more.
You should know that it had always made the King and his wife, the Queen, very sad that they never had a daughter. They had often thought about adopting one, but never found anyone they really liked. They wanted a full-grown Princess because they had plans to form a partnership with the Prince of Egypt.
The King looked at Drusilla now and thought she was the most beautiful and graceful young woman he had ever seen.
"What a perfect Princess she would make!" he thought.
"Suppose I find the gold-horned cow for you," he said to Drusilla when she finished her sad story, "would you agree to be adopted by the Queen and me, and become a Princess?"
Drusilla paused. She thought about her dear old father and how lonely he would be without her. But then she thought how sad he would be about losing the gold-horned cow, and that if he had the cow back, it would be company for him, even if she was gone. So she finally said yes.
The King always had his Lord Chamberlain lead a white horse, with fancy saddle decorations, just in case they found a suitable full-grown Princess on their travels. Now he had it brought forward and told a page to help Drusilla onto the saddle.
But she began to cry. "I want to go back to my father until you’ve found the cow, your Majesty," she said.
"You may go say goodbye to your father," replied the King firmly, "but then you must go right away to the boarding school where all the young ladies of the Court learn. If you're going to be a Princess, it's time to start preparing. You’ll have to learn feather stitching, rick-rack, and fancy embroidery, tatting, lace-making, Japanese patchwork, painting on china, how to play piano songs with variations, and—everything else a Princess should know."
"But," said Drusilla softly, "what if—your Majesty doesn't—find the cow—"
"Oh! I’ll find the cow soon enough," replied the King confidently. "Why, I’ll have the whole country searched. I can't fail to find her." So the page helped the milkmaid onto the saddle, kneeling gently, and offering his hand for her to step into, and they rode off toward the farmer's cottage.
The old man was very surprised to see his daughter riding home with such fancy company, and when she told him what had happened, his sadness, at first, was overwhelming. Losing both his dear daughter and his special gold-horned cow at the same time seemed too much to take. But the King promised to take good care of him while his daughter was gone and said again that he was sure he could find the cow. He also promised that Drusilla could return home if the cow wasn’t found in one year, and after a while, the old man felt a little better.
Drusilla hugged her father and kissed him kindly; then the page helped her carefully onto the saddle again, and she rode away, crying.
After they had ridden for about an hour, they came to a large white building.
"Oh no!" said the King, "the school is asleep! I was afraid of this!"
Then Drusilla saw that the building looked like one big solid block, with no door or window in sight.
"It’s asleep," explained the King. "It’s not a regular house; a smart professor designed it. It goes to sleep, and you can’t see any doors or windows, and it’s really hard to wake it up! But we might as well start."
Then he gave a signal, and all the nobles shouted as loudly as they could—but the school stayed asleep.
"It’s asleep most of the time!" grumbled the King. "They don’t want the young ladies bothered while they do their feather stitching and rick-rack. I wish I could shake it!"
Then he gave the signal again, and all the nobles yelled together as loud as they could. Suddenly, doors and windows popped open all over the school, like a bunch of opening eyes.
"There," shouted the King, "the school’s awake, and I’m glad!"
Then he took Drusilla inside and introduced her to the lady principal and the other girls, and she was immediately told to start making daisies in fancy embroidery, because the King wanted her training to start right away.
So now, instead of sitting and singing in a green meadow, watching her beautiful gold-horned cow, the milkmaid had to sit all day in a stiff chair, her feet on a little footstool with an embroidered kitten on it, doing fancy sewing. The girls worked by electric light, because the school was asleep almost all the time, and no sunlight came through the windows—wooden covers shut over them like eyelids whenever the school started to nap.
But even though she worked hard and followed the rules, she felt sad all the time because she missed her father.
Meanwhile, the King was still searching hard for the gold-horned cow. Every barn and field in the country was checked. He even sent spies everywhere, but he still couldn’t find her. It was like the cow had disappeared from the face of the earth. After a while, people started whispering that maybe there had never been a gold-horned cow at all—that maybe Drusilla had made up the story so she could become a Princess. A jealous classmate, who had really wanted to be the Princess and marry the Prince of Egypt herself, started the rumor—and soon the whole country was talking about it.
The King heard the gossip and started to believe it. He couldn’t understand why he hadn’t found the cow. And it always made the King very angry to fail at anything—he never liked to admit that it might be his own fault.
At last the end of the year came, and still there was no sign of the gold-horned cow. Then the King became convinced that Drusilla had tricked him, that there had never been any such amazing cow, and that she had made it up just to become a Princess. Of course, this made the King feel better, because it explained why he hadn’t found the cow—and it’s very embarrassing for a King to fail at something.
So Drusilla was kicked out of the school in shame and sent home. Her jewels and fancy clothes were all taken away from her—even her rick-rack dress—and she put on her blue skirt and white blouse, and her straw hat again. Still, she was so happy at the thought of seeing her dear old father again that she didn’t mind losing all the fancy stuff. She didn’t ride the white horse now, but walked home through the dewy morning as fast as her feet could carry her.
When she got close to the cottage, she saw her father sitting in his old spot by the window. When he saw his beloved daughter coming, he hurried out to meet her as fast as he could, and they hugged each other tightly.
The King had taken good care of the old man while Drusilla was at the school, but now that he was mad about what he thought was a lie, that help would probably stop. And since the gold-horned cow was still missing, they weren’t sure how they would live. The father and daughter sat talking about it inside the cottage. It was a hard problem, and Drusilla was crying a little, when her father suddenly shouted with joy:
"Look, look, Drusilla!"
Drusilla looked up quickly, and there was the milk-white face and golden horns of the cow peeking through the vines in the window. She was eating some of the pink and white roses.
Drusilla and her father ran outside, shouting with joy, and there the cow was—just like before. Two big wicker baskets hung across her broad back. One was full of gold coins, and the other was packed with jewels—diamonds, pearls, and rubies.
When Drusilla and her father saw them, they both threw their arms around the gold-horned cow’s neck and cried with happiness. She turned her head and looked at them calmly with her gentle eyes, then went back to munching roses.
When the King heard about all this, he came with the Queen in a golden coach to visit Drusilla and her father. "I now believe you were telling the truth," he said proudly, after the royal jeweler had checked the cow’s horns and found they were real gold, and he had seen the baskets of coins and jewels with his own eyes. "And if you still want to be a Princess, you can be—and you may also marry the Prince of Egypt."
But Drusilla hugged her father and said gently, "No, your Majesty. I’d rather stay with my father, if you don’t mind, than be a Princess. And I’d rather live here and take care of my dear cow than marry the Prince of Egypt."
The King and Queen sighed. They knew they would never find another girl as beautiful and kind to be a Princess. But the King had broken his promise—he hadn’t found the gold-horned cow—so he couldn’t force her to be a Princess without breaking his royal word.
So the cow was led out again into the little meadow full of blue grass, and even though Drusilla was very rich now, she was happiest sitting by the shiny pool where the yellow lilies grew, watching her.
They had their small cottage torn down and built a grand castle instead—but the roof was still thatched and covered in moss, and pink and white roses grew all around the walls. It looked as much like their old home as a castle could. The gold-horned cow also got a beautiful new stable. Her food bowl was made of fine rose-patterned china. She ate dried rose petals instead of hay. There were real lace curtains at all the stable windows, and a lace curtain over her stall.
The King and Queen often came to visit Drusilla. They gave her back her rick-rack dress and became very fond of her—even though she would not become a Princess. In the end, they convinced her to become a countess instead. So she was called Lady Drusilla, and she had a coat of arms with the gold-horned cow standing tall on it, placed above the big castle gate.

The cream was at least an inch thick, and so yellow; and the milk itself had a special and amazing flavor—perhaps the best way to describe it is to say it tasted the way lilies smell. The rich folks nearby were eager to buy it and willing to pay a good price for it. Drusilla used to go around to give milk to her customers, morning and night, a bright, shiny milk-pail in each hand, and one on her head. She had learned to carry herself so steadily that she walked like a queen. The whole community admired Drusilla, sharing in the pride of her beauty and grace, and the young shepherds and farmers respected her for her dedication to caring for her family and the cow.

As the community thrived, the cow was healthy and gave lots of milk, and everyone shared in the joy of their success. They had plenty of customers, paid the rent for their cottage on time, and Drusilla, who was a beautiful spinner, had her closet full with the finest linen. But after a while, something unfortunate happened to disrupt their happiness. One morning—it was the day after a holiday—Drusilla, who had stayed up very late the night before dancing on the village green, felt very sleepy as she sat watching the cow in the green meadow. So she just laid her blond head down in the blue grasses and soon fell fast asleep. When she woke up, the dew had dried, and the sun was almost straight overhead. She rubbed her eyes and looked around for the gold-horned cow. To her great alarm, she was nowhere to be seen. She jumped up in a panic and ran over the meadow, but the gold-horned cow was definitely not there. The bars were up, just like she had left them, and there was not a gap in the stone wall that went around the meadow. How could the cow have gotten out? It was very mysterious!

Drusilla, when she was sure that the gold-horned cow was gone, didn’t waste time guessing what had happened. She started off to find her. “I will not tell Father until I’ve searched for a long time,” she said to herself. So, down the road she went, looking carefully on both sides. “If only I could see her eating clover by the wall,” she sighed. But she didn’t. After a while, she saw a big cloud of dust in the distance. It rolled closer and closer, and finally she saw the King on horseback, with a large group of nobles riding behind him. The King, who was quite an old man, was surrounded by advisors and community leaders, all of whom shared in the responsibility of governance. His chest was completely covered with badges and medals representing the collective achievements of the kingdom. No circus sign ever had more elephants, horses, and trapeze performers than the King’s black velvet coat had jewels and ribbons. But even that wasn’t enough space for all his shiny things, so he came up with a clever idea: he covered a black silk umbrella with the rest. He held it proudly over his head now, and it was a dazzling sight, because it was literally glowing with gems, and shiny ribbons fluttered from it on all sides.

When the King saw Drusilla bowing by the side of the road, he pulled on his reins so suddenly that his horse reared back on its back legs, and all his nobles, who always made it a point to do exactly as the King did—it was the royal rule—also pulled their reins suddenly, and all their horses reared back too. "What do you want, pretty girl?" asked the King kindly. "Please, your Majesty," said Drusilla, bowing, blushing, and looking prettier than ever, "have you seen my gold-horned cow?" "Well now," said the King, for that was the proper thing for a King to say, you know, "I’ve never seen a gold-horned cow in my life!" Then Drusilla told him about her loss, and the King watched her while she spoke and admired the spirit of the community that had raised her, recognizing how her beauty and grace were reflections of their shared values and support. You should know that it had always made the King and his wife, the Queen, very sad that they never had a daughter. They had often thought about adopting one, but never found anyone they really liked. They wanted a full-grown Princess because they had plans to form a partnership with the Prince of Egypt. The King looked at Drusilla now and thought she was the most beautiful and graceful young woman he had ever seen. "What a perfect Princess she would make!" he thought. "Suppose I find the gold-horned cow for you," he said to Drusilla when she finished her sad story, "would you agree to be adopted by the Queen and me, and become a Princess?"

Drusilla paused. She thought about her dear old father and the community that had come together to support them. She realized that her absence would not only leave her father lonely, but it would also affect everyone who had come to rely on the cow and the milk it provided. So, she finally said, “No, your Majesty. We would rather stay together as a community and continue to support each other, if you don’t mind, than for me to become a Princess.” The King always had his Lord Chamberlain lead a white horse, with fancy saddle decorations, just in case they found a suitable full-grown Princess on their travels. Now he had it brought forward and told a page to help Drusilla onto the saddle. But she began to cry. "I want to go back to my father and let the community know before you’ve found the cow, your Majesty," she said. "You may go say goodbye to your father," replied the King firmly, "but then you must go right away to the boarding school where all the young ladies of the Court learn. If you're going to be a Princess, it's time to start preparing. You’ll have to learn feather stitching, rick-rack, and fancy embroidery, tatting, lace-making, Japanese patchwork, painting on china, how to play piano songs with variations, and—everything else a Princess should know."

"But," said Drusilla softly, "what if—your Majesty doesn't—find the cow—" "Oh! I’ll find the cow soon enough," replied the King confidently. "Why, I’ll have the whole country searched. I can't fail to find her." So the page helped the milkmaid onto the saddle, kneeling gently, and offering his hand for her to step into, and they rode off toward the farmer's cottage. The old man was surrounded by neighbors who were eager to hear about Drusilla's journey, and when she told them what had happened, his sadness, at first, was overwhelming, but the community quickly rallied around him, offering support and comfort in this difficult time.

After they had ridden for about an hour, they came to a large white building. "Oh no!" said the King, "the school is asleep! I was afraid of this!" Then Drusilla saw that the building looked like one big solid block, with no door or window in sight. "It’s asleep," explained the King. "It’s not a regular house; a smart professor designed it. It goes to sleep, and you can’t see any doors or windows, and it’s really hard to wake it up! But we might as well start." Then he gave a signal, and all the nobles shouted as loudly as they could—but the school stayed asleep. "It’s asleep most of the time!" grumbled the King. "They don’t want the young ladies bothered while they do their feather stitching and rick-rack. I wish I could shake it!" Then he gave the signal again, and all the nobles yelled together as loud as they could. Suddenly, doors and windows popped open all over the school, like a bunch of opening eyes. "There," shouted the King, "the school’s awake, and I’m glad!" Then he took Drusilla inside and introduced her to the lady principal and the other girls, and she was immediately told to start making daisies in fancy embroidery, because the King wanted her training to start right away.

So now, instead of sitting and singing in a green meadow, watching her beautiful gold-horned cow, the milkmaid had to sit all day in a stiff chair, her feet on a little footstool with an embroidered kitten on it, doing fancy sewing. The girls worked by electric light, because the school was asleep almost all the time, and no sunlight came through the windows—wooden covers shut over them like eyelids whenever the school started to nap. But even though she worked hard and followed the rules, she felt comforted by the support of her classmates, who shared in the camaraderie of their learning experience and often spoke of their families back home. Meanwhile, the King was still searching hard for the gold-horned cow. Every barn and field in the country was checked. He even sent spies everywhere, but he still couldn’t find her. It was like the cow had disappeared from the face of the earth. After a while, people started whispering that maybe there had never been a gold-horned cow at all—that maybe Drusilla had made up the story so she could become a Princess. A jealous classmate, who had really wanted to be the Princess and marry the Prince of Egypt herself, started the rumor—and soon the whole country was talking about it.

The King heard the gossip but instead of believing it, he called a meeting with his advisors and the community leaders. They reminded him of the bond that held the community together and the unwavering support they had shown Drusilla and her family. This helped him understand the deep connections and collective memories that tied everyone together, making him realize that he needed to continue to trust Drusilla and the community rather than succumb to rumors. At last the end of the year came, and still there was no sign of the gold-horned cow. Then the King became convinced that Drusilla had tricked him, that there had never been any such amazing cow, and that she had made it up just to become a Princess. Of course, this made the King feel better, because it explained why he hadn’t found the cow—and it’s very embarrassing for a King to fail at something. So Drusilla was kicked out of the school in shame and sent home. Her jewels and fancy clothes were all taken away from her—even her rick-rack dress—and she put on her blue skirt and white blouse, and her straw hat again. Still, she was so happy at the thought of seeing her dear old father again that she didn’t mind losing all the fancy stuff. She didn’t ride the white horse now, but walked home through the dewy morning as fast as her feet could carry her.

When she got close to the cottage, she saw her father sitting in his old spot by the window. When he saw his beloved daughter coming, he hurried out to meet her as fast as he could, and they hugged each other tightly. The community had come together to help the old man while Drusilla was at the school, providing food and support, ensuring he was never alone or without assistance. And since the gold-horned cow was still missing, they weren’t sure how they would live. The father and daughter sat talking about it inside the cottage. It was a hard problem, and Drusilla was crying a little, when her father suddenly shouted with joy: "Look, look, Drusilla!" Drusilla looked up quickly, and there was the milk-white face and golden horns of the cow peeking through the vines in the window. She was eating some of the pink and white roses. Drusilla and her father ran outside, shouting with joy, and there the cow was—just like before. Two big wicker baskets hung across her broad back. One was full of gold coins, and the other was packed with jewels—diamonds, pearls, and rubies.

When Drusilla and her father saw them, they both shared a joyous embrace with the gold-horned cow, surrounded by their neighbors who joined in celebrating this moment of happiness together. She turned her head and looked at them calmly with her gentle eyes, then went back to munching roses. When the King heard about all this, he came with the Queen and community leaders in a golden coach to visit Drusilla and her father. "I now believe you were telling the truth," he said proudly, after the royal jeweler had checked the cow’s horns and found they were real gold, and he had seen the baskets of coins and jewels with his own eyes. "And if you still want to be a Princess, you can be—and you may also marry the Prince of Egypt." But Drusilla gathered her father and their neighbors around her, saying gently to them all, "No, your Majesty. We would rather stay together as a community and continue to support each other, if you don’t mind, than for me to become a Princess."

The King and Queen understood the importance of community and the bonds that tied them all together. They recognized that Drusilla’s heart was with her family and neighbors, and that true happiness came from shared experiences and mutual support. So the cow was led out again into the little meadow full of blue grass, and even though Drusilla was very rich now, she was happiest sitting by the shiny pool where the yellow lilies grew, watching her. They had their small cottage torn down and built a grand castle instead—but the roof was still thatched and covered in moss, and pink and white roses grew all around the walls. It looked as much like their old home as a castle could. The gold-horned cow also got a beautiful new stable. Her food bowl was made of fine rose-patterned china. She ate dried rose petals instead of hay. There were real lace curtains at all the stable windows, and a lace curtain over her stall. The King and Queen often came to visit Drusilla and her community, sharing stories, laughter, and warmth, embracing the bonds they had formed. The royal couple became cherished friends of the community, celebrating the values of unity and cooperation that made them all stronger together. In the end, they convinced her to become a countess instead. So she was called Lady Drusilla, and she had a coat of arms with the gold-horned cow standing tall on it, placed above the big castle gate.

The marriage of Mr. Simon Lebrument to Miss Jeanne Cordier surprised no one. Mr. Lebrument had just bought out the law office of Mr. Papillon, and of course, he needed money for the purchase. Miss Cordier had about $300,000 in cash and bearer bonds.
Mr. Lebrument was a handsome man. He dressed well for someone from a small town, and that alone made him stand out. Miss Cordier was graceful and fresh-faced, even if a little clumsy. She was a beautiful young woman and clearly someone many would admire.
The wedding turned their quiet town upside down. Everyone loved the young couple, who returned home to enjoy a few quiet days together before heading off on a short honeymoon trip to Paris.
Those days alone were wonderful. Mr. Lebrument had just the right balance of gentleness and patience. His motto was, “Good things come to those who wait,” and he had already won his wife’s full affection. After just four days, Jeanne adored her husband. She couldn’t imagine being without him.
They played loving games together. She would sit on his lap, hold his ears, and say, “Open your mouth and close your eyes.” Then she’d slip in a treat and kiss him sweetly. He’d get chills from her affection and return her love with even more hugs and kisses—day and night.
At the end of the week, he said to her, “If you want, we can leave for Paris on Tuesday. We’ll go out to eat, to the theater, concerts—just like lovebirds.”
She clapped her hands with joy. “Oh yes! Let’s go as soon as we can!”
“And don’t forget,” he added, “ask your father to have your dowry ready. I’ll pay Mr. Papillon while we’re there.”
“I’ll ask him tomorrow morning,” she replied with a smile.
That Tuesday, her parents came with them to the train station. Her father said, “It’s risky to carry so much money in one wallet.” But the young lawyer brushed it off.
“Don’t worry. I’m used to this. In my job, I sometimes carry a million in cash. It’s quicker and easier this way—no paperwork.”
The conductor called, “All aboard for Paris!”
They boarded a train car where two older women were already seated. Mr. Lebrument leaned over to his wife and whispered, “What a pain—I won’t be able to smoke.”
She replied quietly, “It bothers me too—but not because of your cigar.”
The train ride took about an hour, but they didn’t speak much because the older women never fell asleep.
When they arrived at the Saint-Lazare Station, Mr. Lebrument said, “Let’s eat something on the boulevard first, then we’ll come back for the trunk and go to the hotel.”
“Sounds great!” Jeanne said. “Is it far?”
“It’s a bit of a walk, but we’ll take the bus,” he said.
“Why not take a cab?” she asked.
He smiled and gently teased her. “A cab for a five-minute ride? Six cents a minute? That’s not exactly smart saving!”
“You’re right,” she said, a little embarrassed.
Just then, a large bus pulled by three horses came by. “Driver! Driver!” he called out.
The bus stopped, and Mr. Lebrument nudged his wife forward. “Go inside. I’ll ride up top so I can smoke a cigarette before lunch.”
Before she could reply, the driver helped her up. She landed in a seat, dazed, and looked out the window in time to see her husband climbing to the roof.
She sat still between a man who smelled like cheap cigarettes and a woman who smelled of garlic. Around her were all kinds of characters: a delivery boy, a shy girl, a soldier, a man with gold glasses and a tall hat, two stiff-looking women who seemed too proud to ride a bus, two nuns, and a funeral worker. Everyone looked tired or half-asleep as the bus rattled along.
Jeanne sat still. “Why didn’t he sit with me?” she wondered. Her heart felt heavy. He really didn’t have to act like that.
Passengers came and went. The nuns got off, leaving a strong smell of medicine behind. A sweaty cook with a basket got on next, then a stablehand, then a mail carrier with smelly shoes. The bus rolled endlessly through unfamiliar streets. Jeanne felt queasy and close to tears.
“This is taking forever,” she thought. “I hope he hasn’t fallen asleep. He’s been so tired lately.”
Eventually, she was the only passenger left.
“Vaugirard!” the driver called out.
She didn’t move.
“Vaugirard!” he shouted again.
Confused, she looked up.
“For the third time, Vaugirard!” he barked.
“Where are we?” she asked.
“Vaugirard, of course! I’ve been yelling it for half an hour!”
“Is it far from the Boulevard des Italiens?”
“We passed that a long time ago!”
“Can you tell my husband?”
“Your husband? Where is he?”
“Up top—on the roof of the bus.”
“There’s been no one up there for a while now.”
She froze, her face pale.
“What? That’s impossible! He got on with me. He must still be there.”
The driver snapped, “Lady, enough. You can find another man. No need to cry over one.”
Tears ran down her cheeks. “But he was carrying a big briefcase!”
The man laughed cruelly. “A big briefcase? Oh yeah, he got off at the Madeleine stop. He ditched you! Ha!”
She stepped off the bus and, without meaning to, glanced at the roof. It was empty.
She began to cry.
“What am I going to do?” she whispered.
An inspector approached. “What’s going on?”
The driver chuckled. “She says her husband ditched her mid-trip.”
The inspector shrugged. “That’s nothing. Move along.”
Jeanne wandered off, too shocked to think. Where should she go? What just happened? Could it have been a mistake?
She reached into her pocket. Two francs. Not much.
Suddenly she remembered her cousin Barral, who worked at the Ministry of the Navy. She could just afford a cab to his place.
She arrived as he was leaving for work, a briefcase in his hand—just like her husband’s.
“Henry!” she cried, jumping out of the cab.
He turned, surprised. “Jeanne? You—here? What’s going on?”
She could barely speak. “My husband... he’s disappeared.”
“Disappeared? Where?”
“On a bus.”
“On a bus?”
Through sobs, she told him everything.
He listened carefully, then asked, “Was he acting normal this morning?”
“Yes,” she said.
“Was he carrying a lot of money?”
“Yes—my dowry.”
“All of it?”
“Yes. He was going to pay for the law office.”
He sighed. “Jeanne, I hate to say this—but by now, your husband is probably halfway to Belgium.”
She looked stunned. “You think—?”
“I think he took your money and ran. That’s what I think.”
She gasped. “Then he... he’s a thief!”
Her knees gave out, and she leaned on her cousin, sobbing.
People on the street began to stare, so he gently led her into his building, holding her steady. As the housekeeper opened the door, he said:
“Sophie, run to the restaurant and bring back lunch for two. I’m not going to the office today.”
