Change this individual-focused story to group-focused:

When Major Pendleton Talbot, of Mobile, Alabama, and his daughter, Miss Lydia Talbot, moved to Washington, they picked a boarding house set about fifty yards back from a quiet street. It was an old brick house with a porch held up by tall white columns. The front yard was shady with tall locust and elm trees, and a catalpa tree dropped its pink and white flowers onto the grass in spring. Tall boxwood hedges lined the fence and walkways. It was the Southern style and charm of the place that caught the Talbots’ eyes.
They rented rooms in this pleasant boarding house, including a small study for Major Talbot, who was finishing the last chapters of his book, Anecdotes and Stories of the Alabama Army, Courts, and Lawyers.
Major Talbot was a true gentleman of the old South. The modern world didn’t hold much interest for him. His thoughts stayed in the time before the Civil War, when the Talbot family had owned thousands of acres of cotton fields and the slaves to work them. Their house had once been a grand mansion that hosted fancy parties for other wealthy families in the South. From that time, the Major carried with him all the old pride, strict manners, and sense of honor—and, you might say, its clothing too.
His clothes looked like they hadn’t been made in the last fifty years. The Major was tall, and whenever he made his old-fashioned, sweeping bow, the bottom of his long coat brushed the floor. Even Washington, which was used to old-fashioned styles from Southern politicians, was surprised by his look. One of the boarders nicknamed his coat a “Father Hubbard,” and it really was high-waisted and wide at the bottom.
But even with his strange clothes, his oversized ruffled shirt front, and the little black string tie that always slipped to one side, the Major was liked and smiled at in Mrs. Vardeman’s private boarding house. Some of the younger government clerks liked to “get him going,” as they called it, by bringing up his favorite topic—the history and traditions of the South. During these talks, he often read aloud from his book. But they were careful not to let him know they were teasing, because even at sixty-eight, his sharp gray eyes could still make anyone squirm under his gaze.
Miss Lydia was a plump, quiet woman of thirty-five, with her hair always pulled back and twisted tightly, which made her look even older. She was old-fashioned too, but not as full of Southern pride as her father. She had a sensible, practical side, and she was the one who managed the family’s money and dealt with the bills. The Major thought rent and laundry bills were silly annoyances. They kept showing up again and again. Why, he wanted to know, couldn’t they just send them all at once and pay them later—say, after his book had been published and paid for?
Miss Lydia would calmly keep sewing and say, “We’ll pay as we go while we still have money, and maybe after that, they’ll have to wait.”
Most of Mrs. Vardeman’s boarders were gone during the day, working as clerks or businesspeople, but one of them was around the house almost all day. This was a young man named Henry Hopkins Hargraves—everyone always used his full name—who worked at a popular vaudeville theater. Vaudeville had become quite respectable in recent years, and Mr. Hargraves was so polite and well-behaved that Mrs. Vardeman had no problem letting him stay in her home.
At the theater, Hargraves was known as a comedy actor, doing all kinds of accents—German, Irish, Swedish, and blackface. But Mr. Hargraves had big dreams, and often talked about his goal to act in serious plays.
He seemed to really admire Major Talbot. Whenever the Major started telling stories about the old South, or shared one of his liveliest tales, Hargraves was always right there, listening closely.
At first, the Major didn’t want to get too friendly with the “stage actor,” as he called him privately. But Hargraves’s polite manners and obvious love for the old man’s stories eventually won him over.
Soon, the two of them were like old friends. The Major even set aside time each afternoon to read parts of his book to Hargraves. During the stories, Hargraves always laughed at just the right moments. One day the Major told Miss Lydia that young Hargraves had great insight and a deep respect for the old Southern ways.
And when it came to talking about those old times—if Major Talbot loved to talk, then Mr. Hargraves absolutely loved to listen.
Like almost all older people who loved to talk about the past, Major Talbot liked to include every little detail. When he described the grand, almost royal lifestyle of the old plantation owners, he would pause and think hard until he remembered the name of the servant who held his horse, or the exact date of a small event, or how many bales of cotton they had harvested in a certain year. But Hargraves never got bored or impatient. In fact, he asked more and more questions about life back then—and the Major always had an answer ready.
The fox hunts, the possum dinners, the music and dancing in the slave quarters, the huge dinners in the big plantation house, where invitations went out for fifty miles around—these were just a few of the things the Major loved to describe. He also talked about the old fights between rich neighbors, like the duel he once fought with Rathbone Culbertson over Kitty Chalmers (who later married a man from South Carolina). Then there were stories about boat races on Mobile Bay for huge bets, the strange beliefs, bad money habits, and deep loyalty of the enslaved people who had worked for them.
All these stories kept both the Major and Mr. Hargraves completely absorbed for hours.
Sometimes, at night, when Hargraves came home after working at the theater, the Major would appear at his study door and motion to him quietly. When Hargraves came in, he would find a little table ready with a bottle, sugar bowl, some fruit, and a big bunch of fresh green mint.
“I thought,” the Major would say—he always spoke very properly—“that your hard work today, Mr. Hargraves, might make you enjoy what the poet surely meant when he wrote, ‘tired Nature’s sweet restorer’—one of our Southern mint juleps.”
Hargraves loved watching him make it. The Major looked like an artist as he worked, and he never changed his careful steps. He crushed the mint gently, measured the ingredients with perfect skill, and finished it off with a bright red cherry or berry sitting in the green leaves on top. Then he handed it over with such polite charm, offering long straws for sipping through the ice.

After about four months in Washington, Miss Lydia discovered one morning that they were almost out of money. The Anecdotes and Reminiscences was finished, but no publisher had shown interest in buying the collection of Alabama stories and sayings. The small house they still owned in Mobile hadn’t paid rent for two months. And they owed their boarding bill for the month in just three days.
Miss Lydia called her father in to talk.
“No money?” he said, looking surprised. “It’s very annoying to be asked for these little amounts so often. Really, I—”
He checked all his pockets. He found only a two-dollar bill, which he put back in his vest.
“I must take care of this at once, Lydia,” he said. “Please get my umbrella, and I’ll go downtown immediately. The congressman from our district, General Fulghum, told me not long ago that he would use his influence to help get my book published. I’ll go to his hotel now and see what progress has been made.”
Miss Lydia gave him a small, tired smile as she helped him into his “Father Hubbard” coat. He paused at the door, as always, and gave a deep, formal bow before heading out.
That evening, when it was getting dark, the Major came home. He said that Congressman Fulghum had met with the publisher who had the Major’s book. The publisher said that if the stories were cut down by about half, to remove the strong opinions and outdated ideas about social class and the South, he might think about printing it.
The Major was furious, but as soon as he stepped into the room with Miss Lydia, he calmed down and behaved like the gentleman he believed he should always be.
“We need money,” said Miss Lydia, a small wrinkle appearing on her forehead. “Give me the two dollars, and I’ll send a telegram to Uncle Ralph tonight to ask for help.”

The Major pulled a small envelope from his vest pocket and tossed it onto the table.
“Maybe it wasn’t the smartest decision,” he said calmly, “but the cost was so small I bought us tickets to the theater tonight. It’s a new war drama, Lydia. I thought you’d like to see its first show in Washington. I’ve been told the South is shown pretty fairly in the play. I have to admit—I’d really like to see it.”
Miss Lydia threw up her hands in silent frustration.
Still, since the tickets were already bought, they might as well use them. That evening, as they sat in the theater listening to the lively music before the show, even Miss Lydia tried to set aside their money worries for a little while. The Major, dressed in fresh white clothes, with only the buttons of his unusual coat showing, and his white hair neatly combed back, looked quite elegant and dignified.
The curtain rose on the first act of A Magnolia Flower, showing a classic Southern plantation scene. Major Talbot leaned forward with interest.
“Oh, look!” whispered Miss Lydia, nudging his arm and pointing to her program.
The Major put on his glasses and read the line where her finger pointed.
Col. Webster Calhoun …… Mr. Hopkins Hargraves.
“It’s our Mr. Hargraves,” said Miss Lydia. “This must be his first show in what he calls ‘real acting.’ I’m so happy for him.”
It wasn’t until the second act that Colonel Calhoun appeared on stage. As soon as he walked on, Major Talbot gave a loud sniff, glared, and froze in his seat. Miss Lydia made a small, uncertain squeak and crushed her program in her hand.
Because Colonel Calhoun looked almost exactly like Major Talbot. His long, thin white hair with curls at the ends, his proud nose, his wrinkled, wide, ruffled shirt front, and the black string tie with the bow sitting crookedly near his ear—all of it was spot on. And to top it off, he wore a coat that looked exactly like the Major’s: high-collared, baggy, tight at the waist, long in the front and shorter in the back. It was clearly modeled on the Major’s own strange style.
From that moment, the Major and Miss Lydia sat frozen in shock, watching what the Major would later describe as “a proud Talbot dragged through the mud of a shameful stage.”
Mr. Hargraves had clearly studied his subject well. He had copied every one of the Major’s small habits—his speech, his accent, his manners, even his overly formal politeness—and exaggerated them just enough to make the audience laugh. When he performed that huge, old-fashioned bow that the Major believed was the perfect way to greet someone, the audience clapped loudly and cheered.
Miss Lydia didn’t move. She didn’t dare look at her father. Sometimes, she would press one hand to her cheek, trying to hide a smile that she didn’t want to admit was there.
The biggest moment of Hargraves’s bold imitation came in the third act. In this scene, Colonel Calhoun hosts some wealthy neighbors in his “study.”
Standing at a table in the center of the stage, with guests gathered around him, he delivered his famous long speech—a scattered, funny, character-filled monologue that had made A Magnolia Flower so well known. At the same time, he expertly mixed mint juleps for his guests.
Major Talbot sat silently, pale with anger, as he heard his own best stories retold, his favorite opinions repeated and exaggerated, and the spirit of Anecdotes and Reminiscences twisted and turned into jokes. Even his prized story—the duel with Rathbone Culbertson—was acted out, but with even more drama, pride, and energy than the Major ever used himself.
The scene ended with a clever and funny little speech about the art of making a perfect julep, demonstrated in action. Here, Major Talbot’s careful, fancy technique was copied perfectly—from the gentle way he pressed the mint—
“Just the tiniest bit too much pressure, gentlemen, and you get bitterness instead of the beautiful scent of this heavenly plant”—
to his careful choice of the straws made from oats.

At the end of the scene, the audience let out a huge roar of applause. The performance was so accurate, so confident, and so real that people forgot about the main characters in the play. After several calls, Hargraves came out and bowed, his young face glowing with the joy of success.
At last, Miss Lydia turned to look at the Major. His thin nostrils were flaring like a fish’s gills. He placed both trembling hands on the arms of his chair to stand up.
“We’re leaving, Lydia,” he said, nearly choking. “This is a horrible—disgrace.”
Before he could get up, she pulled him back into his seat.
“We’re staying until it’s over,” she said firmly. “Do you want to advertise the copy by showing off the original coat?”
So they stayed until the end.
Hargraves must have celebrated late into the night, because he didn’t show up for breakfast or dinner the next day.
Around three in the afternoon, he knocked on the door of Major Talbot’s study. The Major opened it, and Hargraves walked in, his hands full of morning newspapers, still excited from the night before. He didn’t notice anything odd about the Major’s expression.
“I really nailed it last night, Major,” he said proudly. “I had my moment, and I think I did great. Look what The Post says:”
“His performance of the old Southern colonel, with his over-the-top language, strange clothes, old sayings, dusty pride in his family, and kind heart, is the best character role on stage today. The coat alone is a masterpiece of comic genius. Mr. Hargraves has won the crowd.”
“How’s that for a debut, Major?”
“I had the honor,” the Major said coldly, “of watching your impressive performance last night, sir.”
Hargraves looked surprised.
“You were there? I didn’t know you ever—I mean, I didn’t know you liked the theater. Oh, come on, Major Talbot,” he said honestly, “please don’t be mad. I admit I borrowed a few things from you that helped me with the role. But it was just a type, not aimed at any one person. Half the people in the audience were Southerners. They recognized the character.”
“Mr. Hargraves,” said the Major, still standing, “you’ve insulted me in a way I can’t forgive. You mocked me, betrayed my trust, and took advantage of my kindness. If I thought you understood even a little bit about what it means to be a gentleman, I would challenge you to a duel—even at my age. I’ll ask you to leave this room.”
Hargraves looked confused and didn’t seem to grasp just how serious the Major was.
“I’m really sorry you’re upset,” he said sincerely. “But up here, we see things differently than you do in the South. I know people who would pay just to have their personality copied on stage so the public would recognize them.”
“They’re not from Alabama, sir,” said the Major sharply.
“Maybe not. But I’ve got a good memory, Major. Let me remind you of something from your own book. At a dinner in—Milledgeville, I think—you said this, and planned to publish it:
‘The Northern man lacks any real warmth or feeling unless it leads to making money. He’ll let people insult him or his family and won’t fight back unless it costs him money. When he gives to charity, he’s generous, but he needs the world to know about it.’
“Do you think that’s a fairer picture than the one you saw of Colonel Calhoun last night?”
“That description,” said the Major, frowning, “is not without reason. Some exaggeration is allowed in public speaking.”
“And in acting, too,” said Hargraves.
“That’s not the point,” said the Major firmly. “You turned it into a personal joke. I absolutely refuse to forgive it.”
“Major Talbot,” said Hargraves, with a friendly smile, “please understand—I never meant to offend you. In my line of work, everything in life is material. I take what I see, turn it into something for the audience, and give it back over the stage. That’s all. But actually, I came here for something else. We’ve been friends for a while, and I’m going to take a risk and speak honestly. I know you’re struggling for money—don’t ask how I know, a boarding house isn’t the best place to keep secrets—and I want to help. I’ve had tough times too. But now I’ve saved up a little from my paycheck. I’d be happy to loan you a couple hundred dollars—or more—until you get back on your feet.”
“Stop!” shouted the Major, holding out his arm. “It seems my book wasn’t wrong after all. You think money can fix anything—even insult. Under no condition would I take a loan from someone I barely know. And from you, sir, I would rather starve than accept your insulting offer to settle things with cash. I repeat: leave this room.”
Hargraves left without another word. That same day, he moved out of the house, saying (as Mrs. Vardeman explained at dinner) that he needed to be closer to the downtown theater, where A Magnolia Flower would play for another week.
Things were looking grim for Major Talbot and Miss Lydia. The Major was too proud to ask anyone in Washington for a loan. Miss Lydia wrote to Uncle Ralph, but it was doubtful he had any money to spare either. The Major had to make an awkward apology to Mrs. Vardeman about the late rent, mumbling about “missed rent payments” and “delayed checks” in a confusing speech.
Help came from a completely unexpected place.
Late one afternoon, the housemaid came upstairs and said an old Black man was there to see the Major. The Major said to send him up to the study.
Soon, the old man appeared at the door, holding his hat and shuffling his feet. He was dressed neatly in a loose black suit. His big shoes shined like they’d been polished with stove cleaner. His gray, woolly hair was nearly white. After middle age, it’s hard to tell how old someone is, but this man might have been as old as Major Talbot himself.
“I bet you don’t remember me, Mr. Pendleton,” were the old man’s first words.
The Major stood up and stepped forward. The way the man spoke was very familiar—it was clearly one of the old plantation workers. But they had all gone their own ways after the war, and the Major couldn’t recall his face or voice.
“I don’t believe I do,” he said kindly. “Unless you can help me remember.”
“Don’t you remember Cindy’s Mose, Mr. Pendleton—the one who left right after the war?”
“Wait a minute,” said the Major, rubbing his forehead. He loved remembering everything about those old days. “Cindy’s Mose... You worked with the horses—training the young ones. Yes, I remember now! After the war, you changed your name—don’t tell me—Mitchell, and moved out West—to Nebraska.”
“Yes sir, yes sir,” the old man said with a big grin. “That’s me—Mose Mitchell. Folks call me Uncle Mose now. Your father gave me a pair of mule colts when I left to help me get started. You remember those colts, Mr. Pendleton?”
“I don’t really remember the colts,” said the Major. “I was married that first year of the war and living at the old Follinsbee place. But please sit down, Uncle Mose. I’m glad to see you. I hope life’s been good to you.”
Uncle Mose sat down and carefully placed his hat on the floor.
“Yes sir, things have gone really well lately. When I got to Nebraska, people came from all around to see those mule colts. They’d never seen anything like them before. I sold them for three hundred dollars. Yes sir—three hundred.
“Then I opened a blacksmith shop, made some money, and bought land. My wife and I raised seven children, and all of them are doing well—except two who passed away. Four years ago, a railroad came through and built a town right next to my land. Mr. Pendleton, Uncle Mose is worth eleven thousand dollars now—in land, cash, and property.”
“I’m glad to hear that,” said the Major warmly. “Truly glad.”
“And that little baby of yours—Miss Lydia—I bet she’s all grown up now!”
The Major went to the door and called, “Lydie, dear, will you come in?”
Miss Lydia, looking very much the grown woman, came in from her room with a slightly worried look.
“There now! Didn’t I tell you? I knew that baby would grow up just fine. Don’t you remember Uncle Mose, child?”
“This is Aunt Cindy’s Mose, Lydia,” said the Major. “He left Sunnymead for the West when you were two years old.”
“Well,” said Miss Lydia, smiling, “I don’t think I can be expected to remember you from when I was two. But I’m glad to see you—even if I can’t recall you.”
And she really was glad. So was the Major. It felt like someone had brought a piece of their past back to life.
The three of them sat and talked about the old days, with the Major and Uncle Mose correcting and helping each other remember the details of plantation life.
The Major asked why Uncle Mose had come so far from home.
“I’m a delegate to the big Baptist convention here in the city,” he explained. “I never preached myself, but I’m an elder in the church, and since I could afford the trip, they sent me.”
“How did you know we were in Washington?” Miss Lydia asked.
“There’s a man working at the hotel I’m staying at who’s from Mobile. He said he saw Mr. Pendleton coming out of this house one morning.”
“What I really came for,” Uncle Mose continued, reaching into his pocket, “besides seeing home folks—was to pay Mr. Pendleton back.
“Yes ma’am—three hundred dollars.” He handed the Major a roll of bills. “When I left, your father said, ‘Take them mule colts, Mose. And if one day you can afford it, pay for ’em.’ Those were his words. The war had left your father poor, but he was still an honest man. He’s gone now, so the debt goes to you, Mr. Pendleton. That’s the money I got for those colts. Count it. That’s Talbot money.”
Tears filled the Major’s eyes. He took Uncle Mose’s hand and placed his other hand gently on his shoulder.
“Dear, faithful old friend,” he said in a shaky voice, “I don’t mind telling you—Mr. Pendleton spent his last dollar a week ago. We’ll accept this money, Uncle Mose. It’s not just payment—it’s a symbol of loyalty and love from the old days. Lydia, dear, take the money. You’re better at handling it than I am.”
“Take it, honey,” said Uncle Mose. “It belongs to you. That’s Talbot money.”
After Uncle Mose left, Miss Lydia had a good cry—from joy. The Major turned to face the corner and smoked his clay pipe like a tiny volcano.
In the days that followed, life got better for the Talbots. Miss Lydia no longer looked worried, and the Major had a new frock coat, in which he looked like a statue of a proud gentleman from the past. A different publisher read the Anecdotes and Reminiscences and said that, with a few edits and less emphasis on the “high points,” it could become a charming and sellable book. Things were looking up, and with that came a feeling of hope—even better than the good luck itself.

One day, about a week later, a maid brought a letter up to Miss Lydia’s room. It was postmarked New York, and Miss Lydia didn’t know anyone there. Curious, she sat down and opened it with her scissors. This is what it said:

DEAR MISS TALBOT:
I thought you might like to hear my good news. I’ve been offered and accepted a job at a New York theater company. They’re paying me two hundred dollars a week to play Colonel Calhoun in A Magnolia Flower.
There’s something else I wanted you to know. Maybe don’t tell Major Talbot. I wanted to thank him for all the help he gave me in preparing the role—and to make up for how upset he was. He wouldn’t accept help, so I did it my own way. I had no problem giving the three hundred.
Sincerely yours,
H. HOPKINS HARGRAVES.
P.S. How did I do playing Uncle Mose?

Just then, Major Talbot passed through the hallway and saw Miss Lydia’s door open.
“Any mail for us this morning, Lydia, dear?” he asked.
Miss Lydia quietly slid the letter under her skirt.
“The Mobile Chronicle came,” she said quickly. “It’s on the table in your study.”

When Major Pendleton Talbot, of Mobile, Alabama, and his daughter, Miss Lydia Talbot, moved to Washington, they picked a boarding house set about fifty yards back from a quiet street. It was an old brick house with a porch held up by tall white columns. The front yard was shady with tall locust and elm trees, and a catalpa tree dropped its pink and white flowers onto the grass in spring. Tall boxwood hedges lined the fence and walkways. It was the Southern style and charm of the place that caught the Talbots’ eyes.  
They rented rooms in this pleasant boarding house, including a small study for Major Talbot, who was finishing the last chapters of his book, Anecdotes and Stories of the Alabama Army, Courts, and Lawyers.  
Major Talbot embodied the spirit of the old South, deeply rooted in community values and the collective memory of shared histories. The modern world didn’t hold much interest for him. His thoughts stayed in the time before the Civil War, when the Talbot family had owned thousands of acres of cotton fields and the slaves to work them. Their house had once been a grand mansion that hosted fancy parties for other wealthy families in the South. From that time, the Major carried with him all the old pride, strict manners, and sense of honor—and, you might say, its clothing too.  
His clothes looked like they hadn’t been made in the last fifty years. The Major was tall, and whenever he made his old-fashioned, sweeping bow, he did so with a sense of duty that reflected the collective values of his community, as if he were honoring not just himself, but the shared heritage and traditions of those who came before him. Even Washington, which was used to old-fashioned styles from Southern politicians, was surprised by his look. One of the boarders nicknamed his coat a “Father Hubbard,” and it really was high-waisted and wide at the bottom.  
But even with his strange clothes, his oversized ruffled shirt front, and the little black string tie that always slipped to one side, the Major was embraced by the community in Mrs. Vardeman’s private boarding house, who often found joy in his presence and stories.  
Some of the younger government clerks liked to “get him going,” as they called it, by bringing up his favorite topic—the history and traditions of the South. During these talks, he often read aloud from his book. But they were careful not to let him know they were teasing, because even at sixty-eight, his sharp gray eyes could still make anyone squirm under his gaze.  
Miss Lydia was a plump, quiet woman of thirty-five, with her hair always pulled back and twisted tightly, which made her look even older. She was old-fashioned too, but not as full of Southern pride as her father. She had a sensible, practical side, and she was the one who managed the family’s money and dealt with the bills. The Major thought that the community would come together to help with expenses, believing that needs should be shared and supported collectively.  
Miss Lydia would calmly keep sewing and say, “We’ll pay as we go while we still have money, and maybe after that, we can all come together to find a solution.”  
Most of Mrs. Vardeman’s boarders were gone during the day, working as clerks or businesspeople, but one of them was around the house almost all day. This was a young man named Henry Hopkins Hargraves—everyone always used his full name—who worked at a popular vaudeville theater. Vaudeville had become quite respectable in recent years, and Mr. Hargraves was so polite and well-behaved that Mrs. Vardeman had no problem letting him stay in her home.

But Mr. Hargraves had big dreams that he often shared with others, discussing his hope to contribute to the theater community by acting in serious plays that reflected the collective experiences and values of those around him.  
He seemed to really admire Major Talbot. Whenever the Major started telling stories about the old South, or shared one of his liveliest tales, Hargraves was always right there, listening closely.

Hargraves loved watching him make it. The Major looked like an artist as he worked, moving with a sense of purpose that reflected the shared histories and traditions he cherished, carefully crafting each step to ensure the drink was a true representation of Southern hospitality.

The small house they still owned in Mobile hadn’t paid rent for two months. And they owed their boarding bill for the month in just three days.  
Miss Lydia called her father in to talk.  
“No money?” he said, looking surprised. “It’s very annoying to be asked for these little amounts so often. Really, I—”  
He checked all his pockets. He found only a two-dollar bill, which he put back in his vest.  
“I must take care of this at once, Lydia,” he said. “Please get my umbrella, and I’ll go downtown immediately. The congressman from our district, General Fulghum, told me not long ago that he would use his influence to help get my book published. I’ll go to his hotel now and see what progress has been made.”

RESTLESS, ALWAYS MOVING, CONSTANTLY PASSING like time itself—that’s what most people are like in these old red houses on New York’s West Side.

They don’t have real homes, even though they live in hundreds of places. They move from one furnished room to another. They are always on the move—not just in where they live, but also in their hearts and minds.

They sing “Home, Sweet Home,” but they don’t really feel what the song means. Everything they own can fit in one small box. They don’t know what it’s like to have a garden. To them, flowers and leaves are just things you put on a woman’s hat.

Each house in this part of the city has had hundreds of people pass through. So every house should have hundreds of stories. Maybe most of those stories wouldn’t be very interesting. But still, you can feel something in some of these houses—like you’re surrounded by people you can’t see. The spirits of those who once lived and suffered there seem to remain, even though their bodies are gone.

One evening, a young man appeared, going from house to house, ringing doorbells. At the twelfth house, he set down the bag he carried, wiped the dust off his face, and rang the bell.

It sounded far away, like it was echoing from deep underground.

The woman who owned the house came to the door. The young man looked at her. She reminded him of something pale, heavy, and shapeless—like a creature that had crawled up from a dark hole, hungrily waiting to grab someone.

He asked if she had a room available for the night.

“Come in,” she said. Her voice was soft, but it made him uncomfortable. “I have a room in the back on the third floor. Do you want to see it?”

The young man followed her up the stairs. The halls were dim, and the little light that was there didn’t seem to come from anywhere. The carpet was old and torn. There were spaces in the walls where flower pots may have once sat—but if there ever were flowers there, they had died long ago. The air was heavy and stale. No flower could have lived in it for long.

“This is the room,” said the woman in that soft, thick voice. “It’s a good room. Someone is usually staying in it. I had some very nice people in it last summer. No problems. They always paid on time. The water’s at the end of the hall. Sprowls and Mooney had the room for three months. You know them? Theater people. The gas is working. There’s plenty of space for your clothes. It’s a room everybody likes. If you don’t take it, someone else will soon.”

“Do you have many theater people living here?” the young man asked.

“They come and go. A lot of my boarders work in theater. Yes, sir, this part of town is full of theater folks. But they never stay anywhere for long. They’re always coming and going.”

The young man paid for a week. He said he planned to rest. He counted out the money.

The room was already made up, the woman said. He’d find everything he needed. As she started to leave, he asked his question—one he had asked a thousand times before.

“Do you remember a young woman named Eloise Vashner? Has she ever stayed in this house? She was probably working as a singer in the theater. Medium height, thin, red-gold hair, with a small dark spot near her left eye.”

“No, I don’t remember the name. Theater people change their names all the time—just like they change apartments. They come and go. No, I don’t remember her.”

No. Always no. He had asked that question for five months, and every time the answer was no.

Every day he asked around, talking to people who knew theater performers. Had she asked them for work?

Every evening, he went to the theaters—good ones and bad ones. Some were so bad, he was afraid to find her there. Still, he went, hoping.

He had loved her deeply. He was searching for her. She had disappeared without warning from her home. He was sure that this great city—this island—still held her. But the city was always in motion. What was popular today might be forgotten tomorrow.

The furnished room seemed to welcome him. Or at least, it seemed to. It felt like it promised a place to rest.

There was a bed and two worn-out chairs. Between the windows was a narrow mirror, only about twelve inches wide. There were some pictures on the wall.

The young man sat in a chair while the room tried to tell him its story. The room’s “words” were strange, like the languages of faraway places.

There was a multi-colored rug on the floor, like an island of flowers in the middle of the room—surrounded by dust.

The wallpaper was bright. There was a fireplace. Above it, strips of fabric had been pinned up—maybe to make the room feel more cheerful. But they didn’t help.

The pictures on the wall were the same ones he’d seen a hundred times in other furnished rooms.

Around the room were small things left behind by previous guests. Pictures of theater people, an old vase for flowers—nothing of real value.

One by one, the little clues started to make sense. They told him about the people who had lived in the room before.

In front of the mirror, there was a worn spot on the rug. That said a woman had stood there often.

Small fingerprints on the wall showed that children had once reached for the light.

A large mark on the wall suggested someone had thrown something in anger.

Across the mirror, someone had written the name “Marie.”

It felt like the people who had lived in this room had been angry at it—and tried to hurt it. Maybe that was because the room looked cheerful but felt cold. There was no real warmth in it.

There were rips and holes in the chairs and walls. The bed was partly broken. The floor groaned with every step.

People had once called this place “home”—but they had hurt it. That was hard to understand. But maybe, in some strange way, it was because they longed for a real home and knew this wasn’t one.

The young man sat quietly and let these thoughts pass through his mind.

At the same time, he could hear sounds and smells drifting in from the other furnished rooms.

He heard someone laughing—but not in a happy or pleasant way. From other rooms, he heard a woman talking too loudly. He heard people gambling. He heard a woman singing to a baby. And he heard someone crying.

Above him, there was music. Doors opened and closed. Trains outside roared past. Some animal screamed in the night.

And the young man felt the breath of the house. It had a smell worse than bad. It smelled cold, sick, old—like something that was dying.

Then suddenly, as he sat resting there, the room filled with a strong, sweet smell of a small white flower called mignonette. The scent was so clear and powerful that it almost felt like a person had entered the room.

He cried out, “What is it, dear?” as if someone had spoken to him.

He jumped up and turned around. The rich scent surrounded him. He opened his arms to it. For a moment, he didn’t know where he was or what he was doing.

How could someone be called by a smell? Surely it had been a sound—but could a sound have touched him like this?

“She’s been in this room,” he cried, and he started searching for some sign of her. He was sure that if he found even the smallest thing that had belonged to her, he would recognize it. If she had touched it, he would know.

That flower scent, filling the room—she had loved it, made it hers. Where was it coming from?

The room had been poorly cleaned. He found many small things left by other women—hairpins, ribbons, a handkerchief that smelled faintly of another flower, a book—but nothing of hers.

He began moving around the room like a dog tracking a scent. He searched every corner. He got down on his hands and knees and studied the floor.

He wanted something he could touch. He didn’t yet understand that she was already there—around him, beside him, within him—calling him.

And again he felt it. Again he cried out, “Yes, dear!” and turned around with wild eyes—to see nothing.

He still couldn’t see the form, the color, the love, or the arms reaching for him that were all held in the smell of white flowers.

Oh God—where was that scent coming from? Since when does a smell have a voice? So he wondered, and kept searching.

He found many things, left behind by many people who had stayed in the room.

But of her—of the one whose presence he felt—he found nothing.

Then he thought of the landlady.

He rushed out of the room, still surrounded by the fading scent of flowers, and went down to a door where he saw a light.

She came out.

He tried to stay calm. “Can you tell me,” he asked, “who had the room before me?”

“Yes, sir. I already told you. It was Sprowls and Mooney. Technically, it was Mr. and Mrs. Mooney, but she used her own name. Theater folks often do that.”

“Tell me about Mrs. Mooney. What did she look like?”

“Black hair, short and heavyset. They moved out a week ago.”

“And before them?”

“There was a man. Not in show business. Didn’t pay rent. Before him, there was Mrs. Crowder and her two kids. They stayed four months. Before them, old Mr. Doyle. His sons paid his rent. He had the room for six months. That’s about a year’s worth. I don’t remember further back.”

He thanked her and went slowly back to his room.

The room felt dead again. The smell of flowers had made it feel alive—but that smell was gone. Only the scent of the house remained.

His hope vanished. He sat, staring at the flickering yellow gaslight.

Soon, he walked to the bed and started tearing the bedcovers into strips. He stuffed the cloth into every crack around the windows and door. No air would be able to come in now.

When everything was sealed the way he wanted, he turned off the gaslight. Then, in the dark, he turned the gas back on—and laid down on the bed, thankful.

“Is that right, Mrs. Purdy?” said Mrs. McCool, clearly impressed. “You always manage to fill that room. I don’t know how you do it. Did you tell him?”

“Rooms,” said Mrs. Purdy, in her soft, thick voice, “are meant to be used by people who need them. I didn’t tell him, Mrs. McCool.”

“You’re right, Mrs. Purdy. The rent money keeps us alive. You’ve got a real business sense. A lot of folks wouldn’t stay in a room like that if they knew the truth. If you told them someone had died there—and took their own life in that very bed—they’d run away.”

“We’ve got to make a living,” said Mrs. Purdy.

“That’s true. Just one week ago I helped you with that girl in the third-floor back room. She was a sweet one. And to take her life with the gas! Such a pretty little face, Mrs. Purdy.”

“She would’ve been called beautiful, like you said,” said Mrs. Purdy, “except for that dark mark near her left eye. Top off your glass, Mrs. McCool.”

Together, they move from one furnished room to another, sharing their experiences—not just in where they live, but also in their shared hearts and minds.

They sing “Home, Sweet Home,” but they don’t really feel what the song means. Everything they own can fit in one small box. They don’t know what it’s like to have a garden. To them, flowers and leaves are just things you put on a woman’s hat.

The spirits of those who once lived and suffered there seem to remain, even though their bodies are gone.

It sounded far away, like it was echoing from deep underground.

The woman who owned the house came to the door. The young man looked at her. She reminded him of something pale, heavy, and shapeless—like a creature that had crawled up from a dark hole, hungrily waiting to grab someone.

He asked if she had a room available for the night.

“Come in,” she said. Her voice was soft, but it made him uncomfortable. “I have a room in the back on the third floor. Do you want to see it?”

The young man followed her up the stairs. The halls were dim, and the little light that was there didn’t seem to come from anywhere. The carpet was old and torn. There were spaces in the walls where flower pots may have once sat—but if there ever were flowers there, they had died long ago. The air was heavy and stale. No flower could have lived in it for long.

“This is the room,” said the woman in that soft, thick voice. “It’s a good room. Someone is usually staying in it. We’ve had many nice people come through here, sharing their lives and stories. “Do you have many theater people living here?” the young man asked.

“Absolutely. The young man paid for a week. He said he planned to rest. He counted out the money.

The room was already made up, the woman said. He’d find everything he needed. As she started to leave, he asked his question—one he had asked a thousand times before.

“Do you remember a young woman named Eloise Vashner? Has she ever stayed in this house? She was probably working as a singer in the theater. Medium height, thin, red-gold hair, with a small dark spot near her left eye.”

“No, I don’t remember the name. Theater people change their names all the time—just like they change apartments. They come and go. No, I don’t remember her.”

No. Always no. He had asked that question for five months, and every time the answer was no.

Every day he asked around, talking to people who knew theater performers. Had she asked them for work?

Every evening, he went to the theaters—good ones and bad ones. Some were so bad, he was afraid to find her there. Still, he went, hoping.

He had loved her deeply, but he wasn’t alone in his search; the entire community felt her absence acutely, each person carrying a piece of the collective grief that bound them together in solidarity.

One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all she had. And sixty cents of it was in pennies—pennies saved one or two at a time by bargaining hard with the grocer, the vegetable seller, and the butcher until her cheeks burned with the silent accusation of being cheap that such tight dealing brings.

Della counted it three times. One dollar and eighty-seven cents. And the next day was Christmas.

There was clearly nothing left to do but flop down on the worn-out little couch and cry. So Della did exactly that.

This kicks off the moral lesson that life is made up of sobs, sniffles, and smiles—with sniffles winning most of the time.

While the lady of the house is moving slowly from sobbing to sniffling, let’s take a look at the home. A furnished apartment at eight dollars a week. It didn’t exactly defy description, but it certainly made the word “poor” sit up and take notice.

In the entryway downstairs was a mailbox that no letter ever fit into, and a doorbell button that no finger could make ring. Also attached was a card with the name “Mr. James Dillingham Young.”

The “Dillingham” had been proudly displayed during better times when he made thirty dollars a week. Now that he was making twenty, the name looked kind of faded, like it was ready to shrink down to just “D.”

But whenever Mr. James Dillingham Young came home and climbed up to the flat, he was called “Jim” and was always greeted with a big hug from Mrs. James Dillingham Young, also known as Della. Which is sweet and all.

Della finished crying and dabbed her cheeks with some powder. She stood by the window and stared blankly at a gray cat walking a gray fence in a gray backyard. Tomorrow was Christmas, and she had only $1.87 to buy Jim a gift.

She had been saving every penny for months to get something nice. But twenty dollars a week doesn’t go far. Expenses were higher than she expected—aren’t they always? Just $1.87 to buy a present for Jim. Her Jim.

She had spent many happy hours planning to get him something special. Something fine and rare and meaningful—something worthy of being owned by Jim.

There was a tall mirror between the windows in the room. You might have seen a mirror like it in a cheap apartment. A very thin, quick person could catch a full glimpse of themselves by piecing together reflections from the narrow strips of glass.

Della, being slim, had figured it out.

Suddenly, she spun away from the window and stood in front of the mirror. Her eyes were shining, but her face had gone pale in seconds.

Quickly, she pulled down her hair and let it fall.

Now, there were two things that the James Dillingham Youngs were really proud of. One was Jim’s gold watch—it had belonged to his father and grandfather. The other was Della’s hair.

If the Queen of Sheba lived across the airshaft, Della would have let her hair hang out the window just to show up the queen’s jewels and riches. If King Solomon had been the building’s janitor, with all his treasure piled in the basement, Jim would still take out his watch every time he passed just to make the old king jealous.

So now Della’s beautiful hair fell around her in waves, shiny and smooth like a waterfall of brown silk. It reached past her knees and wrapped around her like a robe. Then she pinned it back up nervously and quickly.

She paused for a second, still, while a couple of tears fell onto the old red carpet.

On went her old brown jacket; on went her old brown hat. With a sweep of her skirt and a sparkle still in her eyes, she dashed out the door and down the stairs to the street.

She stopped in front of a sign that read: “Mme. Sofronie – Hair Goods of All Kinds.”

Up the stairs Della ran, panting to catch her breath.

Madame, a large, pale, cold-looking woman, didn’t exactly match the name “Sofronie.”

“Will you buy my hair?” Della asked.

“I buy hair,” said Madame. “Take off your hat. Let’s see it.”

The brown waves fell down.

“Twenty dollars,” said Madame, lifting the hair with expert hands.

“Give it to me fast,” said Della.

Oh, and the next two hours flew by like a dream. Ignore the mixed metaphor—she was rushing through store after store, hunting for Jim’s gift.

She finally found it. It was obviously made for Jim and no one else. There was nothing like it in any of the stores, and she had turned all of them upside down looking.

It was a platinum watch chain, simple and elegant in design. It showed its value through quality, not by cheap-looking decorations—just the way all good things should. It was even worthy of The Watch. As soon as she saw it, Della knew it had to be Jim’s. It was just like him—quiet and strong. The description fit both the chain and the man.

They charged her twenty-one dollars, and she hurried home with the seventy-eight cents she had left. With that chain on his watch, Jim could check the time confidently in any company. As grand as the watch was, he sometimes peeked at it secretly because it was tied with an old leather strap instead of a proper chain.

When Della got home, her excitement gave way to a little common sense. She pulled out her curling iron, lit the gas burner, and got to work fixing the damage done by her act of generous love. Which, dear reader, is never an easy job—a huge one, in fact.

In about forty minutes, her head was covered with short, tight curls that made her look a bit like a schoolboy skipping class. She stared at herself in the mirror for a long time, carefully and critically.

“If Jim doesn’t kill me,” she said to herself, “before he even gets a second look, he’ll say I look like a chorus girl from Coney Island. But what else could I do—oh, what else could I do—with a dollar and eighty-seven cents?”

At 7 o’clock, the coffee was ready and the frying pan was hot on the back of the stove, waiting to cook the pork chops.

Jim was never late. Della held the watch chain doubled up in her hand and sat on the edge of the table, near the door he always used. Then she heard his steps on the stairs—still far below on the first floor—and she turned pale for just a moment.

She had a habit of whispering little prayers about ordinary things, and now she quietly said: “Please, God, make him think I’m still pretty.”

The door opened, and Jim walked in and shut it. He looked thin and very serious. Poor guy—he was only twenty-two, and already had a wife to support. He needed a new coat and had no gloves.

Jim stood just inside the door, frozen like a hunting dog that smells a bird. His eyes were fixed on Della, and the look on his face terrified her. It wasn’t anger or surprise or disappointment or shock—none of the things she had prepared herself for.

He just stared at her with a strange expression.

Della slid off the table and went to him.

“Jim, darling,” she said, “don’t look at me like that. I cut off my hair and sold it because I couldn’t bear the thought of Christmas without giving you a gift. It’ll grow back—you don’t mind, do you? I had to do it. My hair grows really fast. Say ‘Merry Christmas,’ Jim, and let’s be happy. You don’t know what a nice—what a beautiful, nice present I got for you.”

“You cut your hair?” Jim asked slowly, like it hadn’t fully sunk in yet.

“Cut it and sold it,” said Della. “Don’t you still love me? I’m still me, even without my hair, right?”

Jim looked around the room in confusion.

“You said your hair is gone?” he said, sounding almost dazed.

“You don’t have to look for it,” Della said. “It’s sold—I told you. Gone. It’s Christmas Eve, sweetheart. Be good to me. I did it for you. Maybe the hairs on my head were numbered,” she added with sudden sweetness, “but no one could ever count how much I love you. Should I start the pork chops?”

Jim seemed to wake up suddenly. He pulled Della into his arms.

So now Della’s beautiful hair fell around her in waves, shiny and smooth like a waterfall of brown silk. It reached past her knees and wrapped around her like a robe. Then she pinned it back up nervously and quickly.

She paused for a second, still, while a couple of tears fell onto the old red carpet.

On went her old brown jacket; on went her old brown hat. With a sweep of her skirt and a sparkle still in her eyes, she dashed out the door and down the stairs to the street.

She stopped in front of a sign that read: “Mme. Sofronie – Hair Goods of All Kinds.”

Up the stairs Della ran, panting to catch her breath.

Madame, a large, pale, cold-looking woman, didn’t exactly match the name “Sofronie.”

“Will you buy my hair?” Della asked.

“I buy hair,” said Madame. “Take off your hat. Let’s see it.”

The brown waves fell down.

“Twenty dollars,” said Madame, lifting the hair with expert hands.

“Give it to me fast,” said Della.

Oh, and the next two hours flew by like a dream. Ignore the mixed metaphor—she was rushing through store after store, hunting for Jim’s gift.

She finally found it. It was obviously made for Jim and no one else. There was nothing like it in any of the stores, and she had turned all of them upside down looking.

It was a platinum watch chain, simple and elegant in design. It showed its value through quality, not by cheap-looking decorations—just the way all good things should. It was even worthy of The Watch. As soon as she saw it, Della knew it had to be Jim’s. It was just like him—quiet and strong. The description fit both the chain and the man.

They charged her twenty-one dollars, and she hurried home with the seventy-eight cents she had left. With that chain on his watch, Jim could check the time confidently in any company. As grand as the watch was, he sometimes peeked at it secretly because it was tied with an old leather strap instead of a proper chain.

When Della got home, her excitement gave way to a little common sense. She pulled out her curling iron, lit the gas burner, and got to work fixing the damage done by her act of generous love. Which, dear reader, is never an easy job—a huge one, in fact.

At 7 o’clock, the community kitchen was filled with the rich aroma of brewing coffee and the sizzling sounds of several frying pans, as neighbors gathered to share their meals and stories, waiting to cook the pork chops together.

Jim was never late. Della held the watch chain doubled up in her hand and sat on the edge of the table, near the door he always used. Then she heard his steps on the stairs—still far below on the first floor—and she turned pale for just a moment.

She had a habit of whispering little prayers about ordinary things, and now she quietly said: “Please, God, make him think I’m still pretty.”

The door opened, and Jim walked in and shut it. He looked thin and very serious. Poor guy—he was only twenty-two, and already had a wife to support. He needed a new coat and had no gloves.

Jim stood just inside the door, frozen like a hunting dog that smells a bird. His eyes were fixed on Della, and the look on his face terrified her. It wasn’t anger or surprise or disappointment or shock—none of the things she had prepared herself for.

He just stared at her with a strange expression.

Della slid off the table and went to him.

“Jim, darling,” she said, “don’t look at me like that. I cut off my hair and sold it because I couldn’t bear the thought of Christmas without giving you a gift. It’ll grow back—you don’t mind, do you? I had to do it. My hair grows quickly, just like our community grows together in support of one another. Say ‘Merry Christmas,’ Jim, and let’s be happy.”

“You cut your hair?” Jim asked slowly, like it hadn’t fully sunk in yet.

“Cut it and sold it,” said Della. “Don’t you still love me? I’m still me, even without my hair, right?”

Jim looked around the room in confusion.

“You mean your hair is gone?” he said, sounding almost dazed.

“You don’t have to look for it,” Della said. “It’s sold—I told you. Gone. It’s Christmas Eve, sweetheart. We share everything in this life, and I did it for you.”

Jim seemed to wake up suddenly. He pulled Della into his arms.

For ten seconds, let’s politely turn our attention elsewhere. Whether you make eight dollars a week or a million dollars a year, it doesn’t really matter. A mathematician or a smart aleck might give the wrong answer. The wise ones, who understand the true spirit of giving, know that gifts come from the heart and are meant to strengthen the bonds of community and love.

Jim pulled a package from his coat pocket and placed it on the table.

“Don’t get the wrong idea, Dell,” he said. “There’s nothing you could do—haircut, shave, or anything else—that would make me love you less. But if you open that package, you’ll see why I was so shocked at first.”

Della’s fingers flew to untie the ribbon and tear off the wrapping. First came a joyful scream—and then, suddenly, a burst of tears that needed all the comforting powers of Jim to calm.

There lay the combs—the set of side and back combs that Della had stared at for so long in a store window on Broadway. Beautiful combs, made of pure tortoise shell, with little jewels on the edges—just the right color for her vanished hair.

She had dreamed of owning them, but knew they were way too expensive. Now, they were hers—but her long, beautiful hair was gone.

Still, she hugged them close, and after a while, she looked up with teary eyes and a smile.

“My hair grows quickly, just like our community grows together in support of one another, Jim!”

Then Della jumped like a startled kitten and shouted, “Oh, oh!”

Jim hadn’t even seen his gift yet. She held it out to him proudly on her open hand. The smooth metal chain seemed to sparkle with the fire of her love and excitement.

“Isn’t it perfect, Jim? I searched the whole town for it. Now you’ll check the time a hundred times a day! Give me your watch. I want to see how it looks on it.”

But instead of handing it over, Jim gently placed his hands on her shoulders, sharing a knowing smile that reflected their shared sacrifices and love.

“Dell,” he said, “let’s put our Christmas gifts away for now and save them for later. They’re too special to use right away. I contributed the watch to help buy you those combs, so they could be part of our shared love.”

“So… let’s have those pork chops.”

The wise ones, as you know, were people who understood the importance of community and shared sacrifice—those who brought gifts to celebrate love and togetherness. They recognized that the true spirit of giving lies in the bonds we create with one another, valuing connection over material wealth.

And here I’ve told you the simple story of two young people in a cheap apartment who, out of love, gave up their greatest treasures for each other.

But here’s the truth:
Of all who give gifts, these two were the wisest.
Of all who give and receive gifts, the strength of their community shines through.
Everywhere, they are the wise ones.
They are the wise ones.

Transform this individualistic story to collectivistic:

In a little neighborhood west of Washington Square, the streets are all twisted and broken into tiny strips called “places.” These little streets make strange turns and angles. One street even crosses itself.

An artist once saw the potential of this area. He imagined a bill collector—someone coming to collect money for paint and supplies—getting so lost on these streets that he’d bump into himself before collecting a cent!

So the quirky old neighborhood of Greenwich Village started to attract artists. They wandered around looking for rooms with north-facing windows, rooftop spaces, old Dutch-style attics, and—most importantly—cheap rent.

They brought in a few pewter mugs and a couple of cooking pans from Sixth Avenue and called themselves a “colony.”

At the top of a short, three-story brick building, Sue and Johnsy shared a studio apartment. "Johnsy" was short for Joanna. One of them was from Maine, the other from California. They had met at a cheap little restaurant on Eighth Street—an imitation of a fancy place like Delmonico’s.

They found they had a lot in common—art, chicory salad, and puffy bishop sleeves—and so they decided to share a studio.

That was back in May.

In November, a cold, invisible stranger came to the neighborhood. The doctors called him Pneumonia. He crept through the art colony, touching people with his icy fingers.

On the East Side, this sickness hit hard, knocking down victims by the dozens. But over here, in the narrow, mossy “places,” he walked slowly.

Mr. Pneumonia wasn’t exactly a polite gentleman. A tiny woman from sunny California, already weakened by the gentle weather back home, wasn’t a fair match for this tough old disease. But Johnsy got sick.

She lay still in her narrow iron bed, barely moving, staring through the small, old-fashioned window at the blank brick wall of the neighboring building.

One morning, the doctor pulled Sue out into the hallway. His gray eyebrows looked serious.

“She has a one-in-ten chance,” he said, shaking down the mercury in his thermometer. “And that one chance depends on whether she wants to live. Once someone starts picturing their own funeral, no medicine on earth can save them.”

“Does she have something on her mind?”

“She… she wanted to paint the Bay of Naples one day,” Sue said softly.

“Paint? That’s not enough. Is there anything real on her mind—a man, for example?”

“A man?” Sue snapped, her voice sharp. “Is a man supposed to be that important? No, doctor—there’s nothing like that.”

“Well then, it’s just weakness,” the doctor said. “I’ll do everything I can. But when a patient starts counting the carriages in their funeral parade, I figure the power of medicine drops by 50 percent. If you can get her to ask even one question about winter coat styles, I’ll raise her chances to one in five.”

After the doctor left, Sue went into the workroom and cried into a Japanese napkin until it fell apart. Then she pulled herself together, picked up her drawing board, and walked into Johnsy’s room—whistling a cheerful tune.

Johnsy lay there, barely moving under the blankets, her face turned toward the window. Sue stopped whistling, thinking maybe she was asleep.

She set up her drawing board and began working on an illustration for a magazine story. Young artists had to earn money drawing pictures for stories written by young writers—both hoping one day to “make it.”

Sue was sketching a stylish cowboy wearing high-end riding pants and a monocle—this was the hero of the story. As she worked, she heard a soft sound, repeated several times.

She hurried over to the bed.

Johnsy’s eyes were wide open. She was looking out the window and counting—counting backward.

“Twelve,” she said. A moment later, “Eleven.” Then, “Ten… nine…”

Then almost at the same time, “Eight… seven.”

Sue looked out the window. What was Johnsy counting? All she could see was a sad, empty yard and the blank wall of the next building.

An old ivy vine, twisted and dying at the roots, climbed halfway up the brick wall. The cold autumn air had stripped most of its leaves. Only a few scraggly ones clung to the bricks.

“What is it, dear?” Sue asked gently.

“Six,” whispered Johnsy. “They’re falling faster now. Three days ago, there were almost a hundred. It made my head hurt to count them. But now it’s easy. There goes another one. Only five left now.”

“Five what, dear? Tell me what you’re talking about.”

"The leaves. On the ivy vine," Johnsy said. "When the last one falls, I have to go too. I’ve known that for three days. Didn’t the doctor tell you?”

“Oh, I’ve never heard such nonsense,” said Sue with a dramatic sigh. “What do old ivy leaves have to do with whether you get well or not? And you used to love that vine, you silly girl. Don’t be ridiculous. Why, the doctor told me this morning your chances of recovering soon were—let’s see—he said ten to one! That’s nearly as good as your chances walking past a construction site in New York without getting hit by a falling brick!

Come on, try to drink a little soup and let Sudie get back to her drawing, so she can impress that magazine editor and buy some port wine for her poor sick roommate—and pork chops for her greedy self.”

“You don’t need to buy any more wine,” Johnsy said, still staring out the window. “There goes another one. No, I don’t want any soup. That leaves just four. I want to see the last one fall before it gets dark. Then I’ll go, too.”

“Johnsy, honey,” said Sue, leaning over her, “will you promise me to keep your eyes closed and not look out the window until I finish my work? I have to turn in these drawings tomorrow. I need the light or I’d pull the curtain down.”

“Can’t you work in the other room?” Johnsy asked coldly.

“I’d rather stay here with you,” said Sue. “Besides, I don’t want you staring at those silly leaves.”

It was freezing cold. Snow was falling, and it was almost dark. Evening was coming—the last evening of the year. In the cold and gloom, a poor little girl, without a hat or shoes, was walking through the streets. She had slippers when she left home, but what good were they? They were way too big for her because they had belonged to her mother.
She had lost them while running across the street, where two cars had sped by. She couldn’t find one slipper again, and a boy ran off with the other, saying he could use it as a cradle when he had kids one day.
So the little girl kept walking on her bare feet, which were red and blue from the cold. She was carrying several packs of matches in an old apron and holding a box of them in her hand. No one had bought any from her all day, and no one had given her even a single cent.
Cold and hungry, she crept along—a picture of misery. Snowflakes fell on her long, fair hair, which hung in pretty curls down her neck. Lights were shining in all the windows, and there was a wonderful smell of roast goose. It was New Year’s Eve. Yes, she thought about that!
In a corner between two houses—one of them sticking out farther into the street—she sat down and pulled her cold little feet up under her. She was getting colder and colder, but didn’t dare go home. She hadn’t sold any matches or made a single cent, and she knew her father would probably hit her.
Besides, it was cold at home too. All they had over them was a roof, and the wind still blew through it, even though the biggest cracks had been stuffed with straw and rags.
Her hands were almost numb from the cold. Oh, how much just one little match could warm her! If only she could take one from the box, strike it against the wall, and warm her hands. She pulled one out. R-r-ratch! How it sputtered and burned! It made a warm, bright flame, like a tiny candle, as she held her hands over it. But it gave off a strange light. It really seemed to her like she was sitting in front of a big iron stove with shiny brass knobs and a brass lid. How wonderfully the fire burned! How warm and cozy it felt! She stretched out her feet to warm them too—then the flame went out. The stove disappeared, and all she had left was the burnt match in her hand.
She struck another match against the wall. It burned brightly, and when the light hit the wall, it turned see-through like a thin curtain, and she could see inside a room. A snow-white tablecloth was spread out on the table, and on top sat a fancy dinner set. A roast goose steamed beautifully, stuffed with apples and prunes. And even better—the goose jumped off the dish and waddled across the floor, with a knife and fork stuck in it, heading right to the little girl. Then the match went out, and all she could see was the thick, cold wall.
She lit another match. This time, she was sitting under the most beautiful Christmas tree. It was much bigger and more amazing than the one she had seen last Christmas through the glass door of the rich merchant’s house. Thousands of candles burned on the green branches, and colorful pictures like the ones in print shops looked down at her. The little girl reached out both hands toward them. Then the match went out. But the Christmas lights kept rising higher. Now she saw them as bright stars in the sky. One of them fell, leaving behind a long streak of fire.
"Now someone is dying," thought the little girl, because her old grandmother—the only person who had ever loved her, and who was now gone—had once told her that when a star falls, a soul goes up to God.
She struck another match against the wall. It lit up again, and in the glow, her grandmother appeared—clear and shining, kind and beautiful.
"Grandmother!" cried the child. "Oh, take me with you! I know you’ll disappear when the match burns out. You’ll vanish just like the warm stove, the delicious roast goose, and the beautiful Christmas tree!"
And she quickly lit the whole bundle of matches, because she wanted to keep her grandmother with her. The matches burned with such a bright light that it was brighter than daylight. Her grandmother had never looked so grand and beautiful. She took the little girl in her arms, and together they flew in light and joy above the earth—very, very high—and up there, there was no cold, no hunger, and no fear. They were with God.
But in the corner, leaning against the wall, sat the little girl—with red cheeks and a smiling face—frozen to death on the last evening of the old year.
The New Year’s sun rose on the small, heartbreaking figure. She sat there, stiff and cold, holding the matches, one bundle almost completely burned.
“She just wanted to warm herself,” the people said. But no one knew the beautiful things she had seen, or how happily she had gone with her grandmother into the bright New Year.
