There was a lot of noise in Roaring Camp. It couldn’t have been a fight—those happened too often in 1850 to gather everyone’s attention. The ditches and gold claims were deserted, and even the gamblers at Tuttle’s grocery had left their games, which was surprising given they hadn’t stopped even when French Pete and Kanaka Joe shot each other at the bar.
The entire camp was gathered outside a rough cabin on the edge of the clearing. Everyone spoke in hushed tones, but one name kept coming up—“Cherokee Sal.”
There’s not much good to say about her. She was rough and, sadly, a deeply troubled woman. But at that time, she was the only woman in Roaring Camp, and now she was sick and in serious trouble—alone, when she most needed the care and comfort of other women. Despite how wild and lost she seemed, her suffering was intense, and without the support of her own gender, it was terrifying. The pain she was going through might have felt like part of the punishment for her past choices. And even now, when she needed kindness, all she saw were the half-skeptical faces of the men around her.
Still, a few men seemed touched by her pain. Sandy Tipton said it was “rough on Sal,” and for a moment, the weight of the situation made him forget he had an ace and two jacks hidden up his sleeve.
The situation was unique. Deaths weren’t unusual in Roaring Camp, but a birth—now that was new. People had left the camp for good before, but this was the first time someone was arriving into it for the first time. No wonder the camp was so excited.
“You go in there, Stumpy,” said a man named Kentuck, nudging one of the bystanders. “Go see what you can do. You’ve dealt with this kind of thing before.”
Maybe it made sense. Stumpy had, in other places, been involved in two families. He’d ended up in Roaring Camp because of some legal trouble related to those families. The crowd approved, and Stumpy went in. The door closed behind the camp’s makeshift doctor and midwife, and the rest of Roaring Camp sat outside, smoked their pipes, and waited.
About a hundred men had gathered. A few were running from the law, some were criminals, and most were just plain reckless. But you couldn’t tell that by looking at them. The worst of the bunch had a soft, handsome face with long blonde hair. Oakhurst, a gambler, looked like a deep-thinking, sad man from a play. The bravest man was barely over five feet tall and had a soft voice with a shy, timid look.
The word “roughs” didn’t quite capture them. Sure, some were missing a finger or an ear, but that didn’t make them weak. The strongest man had only three fingers on his right hand, and the best shooter had just one eye.
The camp was built in a triangle-shaped valley between two hills and a river. The only way out was a steep trail over the mountain, now glowing under the light of the rising moon. Cherokee Sal might have seen it from her rough bed—seen it curve like a silver ribbon into the sky.
A fire of dry pine branches gave some warmth to the group. Slowly, the mood lightened. People started making bets: three-to-five odds that Sal would survive; even bets that the baby would make it; and side bets about whether it would be a boy or a girl.
Suddenly, a noise from the cabin caught everyone’s attention. Over the sound of the wind, the rushing river, and the crackling fire, a sharp cry rose up—unlike anything they'd heard before. It silenced the trees, the water, and the fire. Even nature seemed to pause.
The whole camp jumped up. Someone suggested blowing up a barrel of gunpowder to celebrate, but thinking about the mother, they decided against it. Only a few shots were fired into the air. Sadly, Cherokee Sal was dying quickly—maybe from the rough care or maybe just from the strain.
Within an hour, she had passed away, leaving Roaring Camp forever.
The men weren’t too shaken—except for what it meant for the baby. “Can he live?” someone asked Stumpy.
Stumpy wasn’t sure. The only other female around who had recently given birth was a donkey. Some doubted if it would work, but they gave it a try. It seemed no stranger than the story of Romulus and Remus—and it actually worked.
After about an hour, the cabin door opened, and the line of men—already formed—began entering one by one. Inside, beside the bed where Sal’s body lay still under blankets, was a pine table. A candle box sat on top, and inside, wrapped in bright red flannel, was the baby. A hat had been placed next to the box.
“Gentlemen,” said Stumpy, sounding half official, “please walk in through the front door, around the table, and out the back. If you want to give something for the baby, the hat’s there.”
The first man came in wearing his hat, but he took it off without thinking when he saw the scene. The next man did the same. In places like Roaring Camp, good behavior could spread fast.
As the men passed through, they made comments: “Is that him?” “Pretty small.” “Just barely got any color.” “Ain’t bigger than a derringer.”
The gifts were as strange as the men: a silver tobacco box, a gold coin, a fancy revolver, a chunk of gold ore, an embroidered handkerchief (from Oakhurst), a diamond pin, a diamond ring (given after someone saw the pin and wanted to outdo it), a slung-shot, a Bible (from someone who didn’t leave their name), a golden spur, a silver teaspoon (with someone else’s initials), a pair of surgical scissors, a knife, a five-dollar bill, and about $200 in coins.
Through it all, Stumpy stayed quiet—serious on one side for the mother, unreadable on the other for the baby.
Only one thing interrupted the mood. As Kentuck leaned in to look at the baby, the child suddenly grabbed his finger and held on. Kentuck looked embarrassed. A bit of red came to his rough cheek.
“The darn little guy!” he said, as he gently pulled his finger free—more carefully than anyone thought he was capable of. He looked at the finger, and repeated with a smile, “He grabbed my finger—the darn little guy!”
The camp finally went to sleep at four a.m. Stumpy never went to bed that night. Neither did Kentuck, who drank a lot and kept telling the story over and over, always ending with, “The darn little guy!”
After everyone else had gone to bed, Kentuck walked down to the river, whistling. Then he came back past the cabin. He walked up and down, pretending not to care. But finally, he knocked on the door.
“How goes it?” he asked Stumpy.
“All good.”
“Anything happen?”
“Nope.”
There was a pause. Then Kentuck held up his finger.
“He grabbed it—the darn little guy,” he said, and walked away.
The next day, Cherokee Sal was buried on the hillside. Afterward, the camp held a meeting to decide what to do with the baby. Everyone agreed: they would raise him.
When someone suggested sending him to Red Dog where a woman could take care of him, the whole camp refused. No one wanted to give him up.
“Besides,” said Tom Ryder, “those Red Dog guys would trade him for some other kid.”
No one trusted outsiders.
Bringing in a female nurse was also rejected. People said no decent woman would live in Roaring Camp, and they didn’t want another woman like Sal. That harsh comment was, oddly, the first sign the camp was trying to be better.
Stumpy didn’t say much, but when asked, he said he and “Jinny”—the donkey—could take care of the child. People liked the boldness of the idea, and Stumpy kept the job.
They sent for supplies from Sacramento.
“Get the best,” said the treasurer, handing over a bag of gold dust. “Lace, ruffles, whatever—don’t worry about the cost!”
To everyone’s surprise, the baby thrived. Maybe the clean mountain air helped, or maybe it was good nursing. Stumpy liked to say, “Me and that ass have been father and mother to him! Don’t you ever turn your back on us,” he’d say to the baby.
By the time the baby was a month old, it was clear he needed a name. People had been calling him “The Kid,” “Stumpy’s Boy,” “The Coyote,” and Kentuck’s favorite, “The darn little guy.” But these names didn’t feel right.
Oakhurst said the baby had brought luck to the camp, and since the camp had been doing well lately, they all agreed to call him Tommy Luck. No one mentioned the mother, and no one knew the father.
“It’s better to start fresh,” said Oakhurst. “Call him Luck and give him a fair shot.”
They planned a christening. “Boston,” the camp’s jokester, wrote a funny version of a church service and trained a choir. Sandy Tipton would be the godfather.
But when the crowd had gathered with music and banners, and the baby was placed in front of a fake altar, Stumpy stepped forward.
“It’s not like me to ruin fun, boys,” he said, “but this doesn’t feel right. It’s not fair to make a joke out of this baby. And if anyone’s going to be his godfather, it ought to be me.”
There was a pause. Then Boston, the jokester, agreed.
“We’re here for a christening, and we’ll have it,” Stumpy said. “I name you Thomas Luck, under the laws of the United States and the State of California—so help me God.”
It was the first time anyone in camp had said God’s name without cursing.
The ceremony might have seemed silly, but no one laughed. Tommy was christened as seriously as any child in a church and cried and was comforted just the same.
And so, Roaring Camp began to change.
The cabin where Tommy lived was kept spotless. It was cleaned, painted, and fixed up. A fancy cradle, carried 80 miles by mule, made the rest of the furniture look bad—so they fixed that too.
The men cleaned up. Even Kentuck started wearing clean shirts and washing his face every day. The loud noise that had once filled the camp stopped near Tommy’s place. People spoke in whispers, and swearing disappeared.
Singing, however, was allowed. “Man-o’-War Jack,” a sailor, sang a sad song about a ship called The Arethusa with 90 verses. He rocked Tommy gently like a boat while singing. It usually put the baby to sleep, and the men would lie under the trees, smoking and listening, feeling strangely peaceful.
“This kind of thing,” said Simmons, leaning on his elbow, “is heavenly.” It reminded him of Greenwich.
In the daytime, Tommy was carried to the gulch where the gold was mined. He lay on a blanket over pine branches while the men worked. They decorated his spot with wildflowers. The men suddenly noticed the beauty of things they used to step over—sparkling rocks, colorful quartz, shiny pebbles. They saved the best ones “for Tommy.”
Nature was his nurse and playmate. Sunlight danced through the trees just for him. Breezes brought the scent of pine and bay leaves. The tall trees nodded to him like old friends.
Tommy was quiet and thoughtful. One time, he crawled out of his play area—a fence made of pine branches—and fell headfirst into the soft dirt. His legs stuck up in the air for five minutes, and he didn’t make a sound.
He was pulled out calmly. There were even stranger stories—like Kentuck claiming he saw Tommy talking to a jaybird. True or not, the baby seemed to belong to nature. The birds sang to him, the trees shaded him, and the camp cared for him.
The summer was golden. The camp was rich and proud. They didn’t want strangers and didn’t allow outsiders in. Their expressman told stories about them.
“They’ve got a real street,” he said. “Flowers, clean houses, they even wash twice a day. But don’t try to visit—they worship a baby.”
They even planned to build a hotel and invite families to settle there—for Tommy’s sake. The idea of bringing in women, something most of them didn’t trust, showed how much they cared about him.
A few still resisted. But the plan wouldn’t happen for three months. Maybe something would stop it.
And something did.
The winter of 1851 was fierce. The mountains were buried in snow. Streams turned to rivers, rivers to lakes. Floodwaters tore down trees and sent debris across the valley.
Red Dog had already flooded twice, and Roaring Camp had been warned.
“Water put the gold here once,” Stumpy said. “It’ll come again!”
That night, the North Fork flooded the camp.
In the chaos—rushing water, falling trees, darkness—no one could do much. By morning, Stumpy’s cabin was gone. Farther up the gulch, they found his body.
But Tommy was missing.
As they returned, heartbroken, a shout came from the riverbank.
A rescue boat had found a man and a baby two miles downstream.
It only took a glance to see Kentuck—crushed and broken—but still holding Tommy in his arms.
As they leaned in, they saw that the child was cold and still.
“He’s gone,” someone said.
Kentuck opened his eyes. “Gone?” he whispered.
“Yes. And you’re dying too.”
A faint smile crossed Kentuck’s face.
“Dying? He’s taking me with him. Tell the boys I’ve got The Luck with me now.”
And holding the baby tight, like a man clinging to a straw in a storm, Kentuck drifted away into the dark river that flows forever into the unknown sea.

“Gentlemen,” said Stumpy, sounding half official, “please walk in through the front door, around the table, and out the back. If you want to give something for the baby, the hat’s there.” The first man came in wearing his hat, but he took it off without thinking when he saw the scene. The next man did the same. In places like Roaring Camp, good behavior could spread fast. As the men passed through, they made comments: “Is that him?” “Pretty small.” “Just barely got any color.” “Ain’t bigger than a derringer.” The gifts were as strange as the men: a silver tobacco box, a gold coin, a fancy revolver, a chunk of gold ore, an embroidered handkerchief (from Oakhurst), a diamond pin, a diamond ring (given after someone saw the pin and wanted to outdo it), a slung-shot, a Bible (from someone who didn’t leave their name), a golden spur, a silver teaspoon (with someone else’s initials), a pair of surgical scissors, a knife, a five-dollar bill, and about $200 in coins.

Through it all, Stumpy stayed quiet—serious on one side for the mother, unreadable on the other for the baby. Only one thing interrupted the mood. As Kentuck leaned in to look at the baby, the child suddenly grabbed his finger and held on. Kentuck looked embarrassed. A bit of red came to his rough cheek. “The darn little guy!” he said, as he gently pulled his finger free—more carefully than anyone thought he was capable of. He looked at the finger and repeated with a smile, “He grabbed my finger—the darn little guy!” The camp finally went to sleep at four a.m., but many stayed awake, sharing stories and concerns about the future of the baby, united in their commitment to keep watch over their newfound hope. Stumpy never went to bed that night.

After everyone else had gone to bed, Kentuck walked down to the river, whistling. Then he came back past the cabin. He walked up and down, pretending not to care. But finally, he knocked on the door. “How goes it?” he asked Stumpy. “All good.” “Anything happen?” “Nope.” There was a pause. Then Kentuck held up his finger. “He grabbed it—the darn little guy,” he said, and walked away. The next day, Cherokee Sal was buried on the hillside. Afterward, the camp gathered together in a meeting to discuss the future of the baby, acknowledging that they had all a shared responsibility in raising him as a community, ensuring his survival and nurturing him together as a symbol of their collective hope and commitment.

When someone suggested sending him to Red Dog where a woman could take care of him, the whole camp collectively refused. No one wanted to give him up. “Besides,” said Tom Ryder, “those Red Dog guys would trade him for some other kid.” They trusted each other and knew they could create a better life for the child together. Bringing in a female nurse was also rejected. People said no decent woman would live in Roaring Camp, and they didn’t want another woman like Sal. That harsh comment was, oddly, the first sign the camp was trying to be better. Stumpy didn’t say much, but when asked, he said he and “Jinny”—the donkey—could take care of the child. People liked the boldness of the idea, and Stumpy kept the job.

They pooled their resources and sent for supplies from Sacramento together, each contributing what they could. “Get the best,” said the treasurer, handing over a bag of gold dust. “Lace, ruffles, whatever—don’t worry about the cost!” To everyone’s surprise, the baby thrived. Maybe the clean mountain air helped, or maybe it was good nursing. Stumpy liked to say, “Me and that ass have been father and mother to him! Don’t you ever turn your back on us,” he’d say to the baby. By the time the baby was a month old, it was clear he needed a name. People had been calling him “The Kid,” “Stumpy’s Boy,” “The Coyote,” and Kentuck’s favorite, “The darn little guy.” But these names didn’t feel right.

Oakhurst said the baby had brought luck to the camp, and since they all felt a sense of pride in their shared success lately, they collectively decided to name him Tommy Luck. No one mentioned the mother, and no one knew the father. “It’s better to start fresh,” said Oakhurst. “Call him Luck and give him a fair shot.” They planned a christening. “Boston,” the camp’s jokester, wrote a funny version of a church service and trained a choir. Sandy Tipton would be the godfather. But when the crowd had gathered with music and banners, and the baby was placed in front of a fake altar, Stumpy stepped forward. “It’s not like me to ruin fun, boys,” he said, “but this doesn’t feel right. It’s not fair to make a joke out of this baby. And if anyone’s going to be his godfather, it ought to be me.”

There was a pause. Then Boston, the jokester, agreed. “We’re here for a christening, and we’ll have it,” Stumpy said. “I name you Thomas Luck, under the laws of the United States and the State of California—so help me God.” It was the first time anyone in camp had said God’s name without cursing. The ceremony might have seemed silly, but no one laughed. Tommy was christened as seriously as any child in a church and cried and was comforted just the same. And so, Roaring Camp began to change. The cabin where Tommy lived was kept spotless. It was cleaned, painted, and fixed up. The men worked together to clean up, each contributing their skills, and even Kentuck joined in, donning clean shirts and washing his face alongside the others, a collective effort to create a better environment for the child.

The loud noise that had once filled the camp stopped near Tommy’s place. People spoke in whispers, and swearing disappeared. Singing, however, was allowed. “Man-o’-War Jack,” a sailor, sang a sad song about a ship called The Arethusa with 90 verses. He rocked Tommy gently like a boat while singing. It usually put the baby to sleep, and the men would lie under the trees, smoking and listening, feeling strangely peaceful. “This kind of thing,” said Simmons, leaning on his elbow, “is heavenly.” It reminded him of Greenwich.

In the daytime, Tommy was carried to the gulch where the gold was mined. He lay on a blanket over pine branches while the men worked. They decorated his spot with wildflowers. The men suddenly noticed the beauty of things they used to step over—sparkling rocks, colorful quartz, shiny pebbles. They saved the best ones “for Tommy.” Nature was his nurse and playmate. Sunlight danced through the trees just for him. Breezes brought the scent of pine and bay leaves. The tall trees nodded to him like old friends.

Tommy was quiet and thoughtful. One time, he crawled out of his play area—a fence made of pine branches—and fell headfirst into the soft dirt. His legs stuck up in the air for five minutes, and he didn’t make a sound. He was pulled out calmly. There were even stranger stories—like Kentuck claiming he saw Tommy talking to a jaybird. True or not, the baby seemed to belong to nature. The birds sang to him, the trees shaded him, and the camp cared for him. The summer was golden. The camp was a close-knit community, united in purpose and pride. They didn’t want strangers and welcomed only those who would contribute to their collective effort. Their expressman told stories about them. “They’ve got a real street,” he said. “Flowers, clean houses, they even wash twice a day. And they all work together to care for a baby.” They even planned to build a community center to support families that might settle there—for Tommy’s sake.

A few still resisted. But the plan wouldn’t happen for three months. Maybe something would stop it. And something did. The winter of 1851 was fierce. The mountains were buried in snow. Streams turned to rivers, rivers to lakes. Floodwaters tore down trees and sent debris across the valley. Red Dog had already flooded twice, and Roaring Camp had been warned. “Water put the gold here once,” Stumpy said. “It’ll come again!” That night, the North Fork flooded the camp. In the chaos—rushing water, falling trees, darkness—no one could do much. By morning, Stumpy’s cabin was gone. Farther up the gulch, they found his body. But Tommy was missing.

As they returned, heartbroken, a shout came from the riverbank. A rescue boat had found a man and a baby two miles downstream. It only took a glance to see Kentuck—crushed and broken—but still holding Tommy in his arms. As they leaned in, they saw that the child was cold and still. “He’s gone,” someone said. Kentuck opened his eyes. “Gone?” he whispered. “Yes. And you’re dying too.” A faint smile crossed Kentuck’s face. “Dying? He’s taking me with him. Tell the boys I’ve got The Luck with me now.” And holding the baby tight, like a man clinging to a straw in a storm, Kentuck drifted away into the dark river that flows forever into the unknown sea.

“Twenty-one years of it,” said Mr. White, nodding toward his wife and son. “When he left, he was just a skinny young man working in a warehouse. Look at him now.”

By the time he had his third glass, his eyes were brighter and he started to talk. The little family listened eagerly to this man from faraway places as he leaned back in his chair and shared stories of communities coming together, overcoming struggles, and the collective resilience of people facing wars, diseases, and unusual customs together.  
“Twenty-one years of it,” said Mr. White, nodding toward his wife and son. “When he left, he was just a skinny young man working in a warehouse. Look at him now.”  
“He doesn’t look like he’s done too badly,” said Mrs. White kindly.  
“I'd like to see India for myself,” said the old man, “just to look around, you know.”  
“You’re better off where you are,” said the sergeant-major, shaking his head. He set down his empty glass, sighed quietly, and shook his head again.  
“I’d love to see those old temples and street performers,” said the old man. “What was that you were telling me the other day about a monkey’s paw or something?”  
“Nothing,” said the soldier quickly. “Or at least, nothing worth hearing.”  
“Monkey’s paw?” asked Mrs. White, curious.  
“Well, it’s just a little bit of magic, maybe,” said the sergeant-major casually.  
All three leaned in, clearly interested. The visitor absentmindedly lifted his empty glass to his lips, then set it down again. Mr. White filled it for him.  
“It looks like nothing,” said the sergeant-major, digging in his pocket. “Just a dried-up little paw that has seen many hands and wishes, each tied to the fate of the community.”  
He took something out of his pocket and offered it. Mrs. White pulled back with a face, but her son picked it up and examined it closely.  
“And what’s so special about it?” asked Mr. White, taking it from his son and setting it on the table after a closer look.  
“A holy man, an old fakir, put a spell on it,” said the sergeant-major. “He wanted to show that fate controls people’s lives, and those who try to change it will be sorry. He made it so that three different men could each have three wishes.”  
He spoke so seriously that their small laugh seemed awkward and out of place.  
“Well, why don’t you wish for something?” asked Herbert White with a grin.  
The soldier looked at him the way older people often look at smart-aleck youth. “I did,” he said quietly, and his red face turned pale.  
“And did the wishes really come true?” asked Mrs. White.  
“They did,” said the sergeant-major, and his glass knocked softly against his teeth.  
“Did anyone else use it?” asked the old lady.  
“The first man had his three wishes,” he said. “I don’t know what the first two were, but the third was for death. That’s how I got the paw.”  
His voice was so serious that the room fell silent.  
“If you’ve had your three wishes, it’s no good to you now, then, Morris,” said the old man at last. “Why do you still keep it?”  
The soldier shook his head. “Just out of habit, I guess,” he said slowly. “I did think about selling it, but I don’t think I will. It’s caused enough trouble already. And anyway, people either don’t believe in it or they want to test it out before paying me.”  
“If you could have another three wishes,” said the old man, watching him closely, “would you take them?”  
“I don’t know,” the other said. “I really don’t.”  
He picked up the paw and held it by one finger, then suddenly tossed it into the fire. Mr. White gave a quick shout and grabbed it out of the flames.  
“You should have let it burn for the good of the community,” said the soldier seriously.  
“If you don’t want it, Morris,” said the old man, “give it to me.”  
“No,” said his friend firmly. “I threw it in the fire for a reason. If you keep it, consider how it might impact your community and what happens. Throw it back in the fire while you still can.”  
Mr. White shook his head and looked closely at the strange new possession that had come into their lives, knowing it could influence not just him, but his whole family and their community.  
“How does it work?” he asked.  
“Hold it in your right hand and say your wish out loud,” said the sergeant major. “But I’m warning you—there will be consequences.”  
“Sounds like something out of a fairy tale,” said Mrs. White as she got up to set the dinner table. “Maybe I should wish for four more hands to help me.”  
The family gathered around the paw again, feeling its weight as a shared burden, contemplating their future together and how their wishes could shape the lives of not just themselves, but their entire community.  
The conversation flowed, and as they debated the potential of the paw, all three laughed—until the sergeant major grabbed Mr. White’s arm with a worried look on his face.  
“If you must wish,” he said roughly, “wish for something sensible.”  
Mr. White put the paw back in his pocket. Then he helped set the table and motioned for his friend to join them. As they ate, they almost forgot about the strange object, and afterward, they sat and listened with fascination to more of the sergeant major’s stories about India.  
“If that monkey’s paw story is as true as the rest of his tales,” said Herbert, as the door closed behind their guest—just in time for him to catch the last train—“then we’re not going to get much out of it.”  
“Did you give him any money for it, Father?” asked Mrs. White, watching him carefully.  
“Just a little,” he said, blushing slightly. “He didn’t want to take it, but I insisted. And he kept telling me to throw it away.”  
“Of course he did,” said Herbert, pretending to be shocked. “We’re going to be rich and famous and totally happy now! Wish to be an emperor, Dad. That way you can’t be bossed around by anyone!”  
He ran around the table, chased by his mother, who was waving a doily at him.  
The family gathered around the paw again, feeling its weight as a shared burden, contemplating their future together and how their wishes could shape the lives of not just themselves, but their entire community. “I think we should wish for something that brings comfort and security to our community and all its members,” Mr. White said slowly. “Together we can decide what’s best for everyone.”  
“If you just paid off the house, you’d be totally happy, right?” said Herbert, putting a hand on his father’s shoulder. “Okay then—wish for two hundred dollars. That should cover it.”  
Smiling at how silly he felt, Mr. White held up the strange paw, while Herbert, trying to look serious but sneaking a wink at his mom, sat down at the piano and played a few dramatic chords.  
“I wish for two hundred dollars,” said the old man clearly.  
A loud crash from the piano followed the words, along with a shocked cry from Mr. White. His wife and son rushed to him.  
“It moved,” he said, staring at the paw with disgust as it lay on the floor. “When I made the wish, it twisted in my hand like a snake.”  
“Well, I don’t see any money,” said Herbert, picking up the paw and placing it back on the table. “And I bet I never will.”  
“It must’ve been your imagination, dear,” said his wife, looking at him with concern.  
He shook his head in unison with the family, their shared disbelief echoing in the room. “Never mind. It didn’t hurt anything, but it still gave me a scare.”  
They sat back by the fire while the two men finished smoking their pipes. Outside, the wind blew louder than before, and the old man jumped nervously when a door slammed upstairs. A heavy, strange silence filled the room, a shared weight of unspoken thoughts and feelings, and lasted until the old couple got up to go to bed.  
“You’ll probably find the money sitting in a big bag in the middle of your bed,” said Herbert as he wished them good night, “with something creepy sitting on top of the wardrobe watching you while you count your evil treasure.”  
In the bright light of the winter sun the next morning, as it shone over the breakfast table, Herbert laughed at his fears. The room now felt normal and cheerful, not at all like it had the night before. The old, dried-up little paw had been tossed onto the sideboard, showing that no one really believed in it anymore.  
“I guess all old soldiers are like that,” said Mrs. White. “Imagine us listening to such nonsense! How could wishes actually come true these days? And even if they did, how could getting two hundred dollars hurt you, Father?”  
“Maybe it could fall out of the sky and hit him on the head,” joked Herbert.  
“Morris said the things happened so naturally,” said his father, “that you could think it was just a coincidence if you wanted to.”  
“Well, don’t spend the money before I get back,” said Herbert as he got up from the table. “I’m afraid it’ll make you greedy, and we’ll have to pretend we don’t know you anymore.”  
His mother laughed, and after walking him to the door, she watched him head down the road. Then she went back to the breakfast table, still chuckling about her husband’s superstitions. But that didn’t stop her from rushing to the door when the mailman knocked, or from complaining—rather sharply—about retired soldiers who drank too much, when she found the letter was just a bill from the tailor.  
“Herbert will probably have something funny to say when he gets home,” she said while they ate lunch.  
“Probably,” said Mr. White, pouring himself some beer. “But I still say the thing moved in my hand. I know it did.”  
“You thought it did,” said Mrs. White, trying to calm him.  
“I’m telling you it did,” he insisted. “It wasn’t in my head. I had just— What’s the matter?”  
His wife didn’t answer. She was looking out the window at a man who was acting strangely. He kept glancing at the house, hesitating like he was trying to decide whether or not to come in. Because she had the two hundred dollars in her mind, she noticed right away that the man was dressed very nicely and wore a shiny, new top hat.  
Three times he stopped at the gate, then walked away. The fourth time, he stood with his hand on it, then suddenly made up his mind and came up the path. Mrs. White, at that moment, quickly untied her apron and hid it under the cushion of her chair.  
She brought the visitor—who looked nervous and uncomfortable—into the room. He gave Mrs. White a few quick glances and only half-listened as she apologized for how the room looked, and for her husband’s coat, which was his usual yardwork jacket. She waited, as patiently as she could, for him to explain why he had come, but at first, he said nothing.  
“I... was told to stop by,” he finally said, and bent down to pick a piece of lint off his pants. “I work for Maw and Meggins.”  
Mrs. White jumped a little. “Is something wrong?” she asked quickly. “Did something happen to Herbert? What is it? What happened?”  
The family stepped in together. "There, there, Mother," they said quickly.  
"Sit down, and don't jump to conclusions. You've not brought bad news, I'm sure, sir," they looked at the other hopefully.  
"I'm sorry--" began the visitor.  
"Is he hurt?" demanded the mother.  
The visitor nodded. "Badly hurt," he said softly, "but he is not in any pain."  
"Oh, thank God!" said the old woman, clasping her hands. "Thank God for that! Thank--"  
She broke off suddenly as the terrible meaning of the comforting words hit her, and she saw the awful confirmation of her fears in the other's turned-away face. She caught her breath, and turning to her slower-thinking husband, laid her trembling old hand upon his. There was a long silence.  
"He was caught in the machinery of the factory," said the visitor at last, in a low voice.  
"Caught in the machinery," repeated Mr. White, in a shocked voice, "yes."  
He sat staring blankly out the window, and taking his wife's hand between his own, held it as he had been used to in their old dating days nearly forty years before.  
"He was a beloved part of our community, cherished by all who knew him," he said, turning gently to the visitor. "It is hard."  
The other cleared his throat, and rising, walked slowly to the window. "The company wished to express their collective sympathy for your great loss," he said, without looking around. "I hope you understand I am only their worker and just doing what I was told."  
There was no reply; the old woman's face was white, her eyes wide, and her breath silent; on the husband's face was a look like the one his friend the soldier might have had in his first battle.  
"I was to say that Maw and Meggins take no responsibility," continued the other. "They say they are not to blame at all, but in consideration of your son's work they want to give you a certain amount as payment."  
Mr. White let go of his wife's hand, and standing up, looked with a horrified expression at his visitor. His dry lips mouthed the words, "How much?"  
"Four hundred dollars," was the answer.  
Not noticing his wife's scream, the old man smiled weakly, put out his hands like a blind man, and collapsed, a senseless heap, to the floor.

"My aunt will be down presently, Mr. Nuttel," said a very self-possessed young lady of fifteen; "in the meantime you must try and put up with me."
Framton Nuttel endeavored to say the correct something which should duly flatter the niece of the moment without unduly discounting the aunt that was to come. Privately he doubted more than ever whether these formal visits on a succession of total strangers would do much towards helping the nerve cure which he was supposed to be undergoing.
"I know how it will be," his sister had said when he was preparing to migrate to this rural retreat; "you will bury yourself down there and not speak to a living soul, and your nerves will be worse than ever from moping. I shall just give you letters of introduction to all the people I know there. Some of them, as far as I can remember, were quite nice."
Framton wondered whether Mrs. Sappleton, the lady to whom he was presenting one of the letters of introduction came into the nice division.
"Do you know many of the people round here?" asked the niece, when she judged that they had had sufficient silent communion.
"Hardly a soul," said Framton. "My sister was staying here, at the
rectory
, you know, some four years ago, and she gave me letters of introduction to some of the people here."
He made the last statement in a tone of distinct regret.
"Then you know practically nothing about my aunt?" pursued the self-possessed young lady.
"Only her name and address," admitted the caller. He was wondering whether Mrs. Sappleton was in the married or widowed state. An undefinable something about the room seemed to suggest masculine habitation.
"Her great tragedy happened just three years ago," said the child; "that would be since your sister's time."
"Her tragedy?" asked Framton; somehow in this restful country spot tragedies seemed out of place.
"You may wonder why we keep that window wide open on an October afternoon," said the niece, indicating a large French window that opened on to a lawn.
"It is quite warm for the time of the year," said Framton; "but has that window got anything to do with the tragedy?"
"Out through that window, three years ago to a day, her husband and her two young brothers went off for their day's shooting. They never came back. In crossing the moor to their favorite snipe-shooting ground they were all three engulfed in a treacherous piece of bog. It had been that dreadful wet summer, you know, and places that were safe in other years gave way suddenly without warning. Their bodies were never recovered. That was the dreadful part of it." Here the child's voice lost its self-possessed note and became falteringly human. "Poor aunt always thinks that they will come back someday, they and the little brown spaniel that was lost with them, and walk in at that window just as they used to do. That is why the window is kept open every evening till it is quite dusk. Poor dear aunt, she has often told me how they went out, her husband with his white waterproof coat over his arm, and Ronnie, her youngest brother, singing 'Bertie, why do you bound?' as he always did to tease her, because she said it got on her nerves. Do you know, sometimes on still, quiet evenings like this, I almost get a creepy feeling that they will all walk in through that window--"
She broke off with a little shudder. It was a relief to Framton when the aunt bustled into the room with a whirl of apologies for being late in making her appearance.
"I hope Vera has been amusing you?" she said.
"She has been very interesting," said Framton.
"I hope you don't mind the open window," said Mrs. Sappleton briskly; "my husband and brothers will be home directly from shooting, and they always come in this way. They've been out for snipe in the marshes today, so they'll make a fine mess over my poor carpets. So like you menfolk, isn't it?"
She rattled on cheerfully about the shooting and the scarcity of birds, and the prospects for duck in the winter. To Framton it was all purely horrible. He made a desperate but only partially successful effort to turn the talk on to a less ghastly topic, he was conscious that his hostess was giving him only a fragment of her attention, and her eyes were constantly straying past him to the open window and the lawn beyond. It was certainly an unfortunate coincidence that he should have paid his visit on this tragic anniversary.
"The doctors agree in ordering me complete rest, an absence of mental excitement, and avoidance of anything in the nature of violent physical exercise," announced Framton, who labored under the tolerably widespread delusion that total strangers and chance acquaintances are hungry for the least detail of one's ailments and infirmities, their cause and cure. "On the matter of diet they are not so much in agreement," he continued.
"No?" said Mrs. Sappleton, in a voice which only replaced a yawn at the last moment. Then she suddenly brightened into alert attention--but not to what Framton was saying.
"Here they are at last!" she cried. "Just in time for tea, and don't they look as if they were muddy up to the eyes!"
Framton shivered slightly and turned towards the niece with a look intended to convey sympathetic comprehension. The child was staring out through the open window with a dazed horror in her eyes. In a chill shock of nameless fear Framton swung round in his seat and looked in the same direction.
In the deepening twilight three figures were walking across the lawn towards the window, they all carried guns under their arms, and one of them was additionally burdened with a white coat hung over his shoulders. Once upon a time, there was a city that had a well-known school for correcting bad behavior in kids. It was called a Reform School, but it was very different from most.
The school had been started years earlier by a kind and wealthy lady who wanted to do something good with her money. After thinking long and hard, she came up with the idea of starting a school for kids who upset their parents and acted ungrateful or constantly complained. Most of the students there were exactly that kind.
In the city, there was even a special group of police officers whose job was to look out for grumpy kids who whined about their parents and said other children had it better. These officers wore tall pointy hats, white boots, and carried sticks with blue ribbon bows on them. They were easy to spot.
Many kids walking to school would hide when they saw one—especially if they had just said something like, “Tommy’s mom gives him more dessert than I get!” These kids wouldn’t feel safe until those white boots were out of sight, and they’d stay nervous all day at every knock on the door.
Every kid in the city was scared of the Patchwork School. That might seem strange, because the punishment didn’t sound so bad. But ever since the school opened, it had been run by a very odd little old woman. No one knew where she came from. The kind lady who founded the school had brought her one day in a carriage, and the neighbors had seen her—a small, wrinkled woman in a strange patchwork dress—step out and go inside.
What no one else knew was that the lady had met her during a trip to Germany, where the old woman had been sewing patchwork in a tiny attic window next to a box of violets. They became friends, and the lady hired her to run the school. She had a kind heart—she wanted to help misbehaving kids grow up to be good people, but she didn’t want them spanked or yelled at. The old woman’s ideas were just what she needed.
“Make them sew patchwork,” the old woman had said, while sewing patchwork herself. She wore a dress, a shawl, and even a hat made of colorful patchwork. “If they’re busy sewing, they won’t have time to cause trouble. Just make them sit in little chairs and sew—boys and girls alike. Even when the bees are buzzing over the clover and butterflies are landing on roses outside, even when the robins are singing in the cherry trees—just keep them inside sewing. That’ll change their attitude!”
So the school opened, the patchwork woman took charge, and surprisingly, it worked. The school became famous. Visitors were always taken to see the Patchwork School, as it came to be called.
Inside, the children sat in small chairs, sewing away. They wore uniforms made of patchwork: the girls wore blue and white patchwork dresses with pink aprons, and the boys wore blue and white patchwork pants with aprons too. Their cheeks were rosy because they got plenty to eat—bread and milk three times a day—but they looked sad, and many had tears in their eyes.
Who could blame them? Outside, the school had the most beautiful gardens filled with blooming roses and colorful butterflies. Robins sang in the cherry trees, and later in the year, apples and peaches hung so heavy on the branches that they nearly touched the ground—all visible through the classroom windows.
No wonder the poor kids stuck inside sewing tiny fabric squares felt so sad. Every day, big bundles of fabric were delivered to the school. It had to be cut into little pieces and sewn back together. When the kids heard the heavy footsteps of the delivery men, their tears would fall, knowing they’d have even more work to do.
The Patchwork Woman was very strict. Every stitch had to be perfect. If one was too long or crooked, they had to take it out and redo it. First, they made their own clothes. Then they made patchwork quilts, which were donated to the city’s poor. So, in a way, the kind lady who founded the school helped two problems at once.
Kids stayed in the school for different lengths of time, depending on what they did wrong. But almost every child in the city had been there at some point—even the best kids eventually complained about bedtime or candy and got dragged off by the white-booted police.
Even the Mayor’s son had been in the school many times.
But one boy had never been arrested by the special police. His name was Julia—a girl’s name, which made things very hard for him. His parents named him that because his rich aunt promised to leave him her money if he was named after her.
The other boys teased him all the time—calling him “missy” or “sissy,” and saying “she” instead of “he.” But Julia never complained to his parents. His family was poor, and he wore rough clothes and ate plain food, but he was always cheerful and never acted jealous of boys who had fancy jackets or sweet snacks.
But Julia had another challenge: four grandmothers! Two great-grandmothers and two regular ones—all still alive and living with him. They were sweet ladies, and he loved them, but they were always losing their glasses and dropping their yarn, and he had to help them all day. He rarely had time to play. He held their yarn while they wound it into balls, and his arms would get sore while he heard other boys shouting outside playing ball. Still, he never said no, and always helped with a smile.
That’s not what got him into the Patchwork School.
Julia was arrested on Christmas Day.
His family was poor, so Christmas gifts were small. Julia didn’t expect fancy toys—he would have been happy with something useful. But every year, each of his four grandmothers gave him two pairs of blue wool socks—for Christmas. Eight pairs. Every year.
The socks never wore out, so he didn’t even need new ones. His dresser drawers were full of blue socks rolled into tight little balls—the only kind of balls he had. He never complained… until the Christmas when he turned twelve.
That year, the sight of the socks was harder than usual. Still, he thanked his grandmothers like always. But later, outside in the street, he sat down in a doorway and cried. He couldn’t help it. Other boys had gotten toys and games, and he had the same old socks.
“What’s wrong, little boy?” a voice asked.
Julia, without looking up, told his story through tears. But suddenly, he was grabbed and lifted by a white-booted policeman.
The officer didn’t care about his sobs. He marched him straight to the Patchwork School, proudly waving his stick like a parade leader.
Julia sat in a small chair and started sewing patchwork with the others. He didn’t mind the quiet as much—he was used to being indoors. But he still didn’t enjoy sewing. His sentence was a long one. The Patchwork Woman thought it was very ungrateful to complain about getting warm socks from sweet grandparents.
One day, Julia had finished sewing his patchwork clothes and was working on a red and green quilt when the Mayor visited the school. His son wasn’t there—he never visited when his own child was in trouble. This time, the Mayor brought a Chinese Ambassador named To-Chum.
The Ambassador wore a yellow silk robe, had high eyebrows, and a long braided hairstyle. The kids couldn’t help sneaking glances but quickly looked back at their sewing.
The Mayor and the Ambassador stayed longer than expected. They gave short speeches, and just as they were about to leave, the school’s magical iron door swung shut. It closed at the same time every afternoon and wouldn’t open again until morning—no matter what.
The Mayor got through, but the Ambassador’s long braid got caught in the door!
Now the Ambassador was stuck outside, his braid stuck inside. The Patchwork Woman tried the magic chant, but it didn’t work at the wrong time of day. They’d have to wait until morning—or cut off his braid, which was unthinkable.
The Mayor, trying to be helpful, promised to stay with him all night. He brought food and a coat. The Ambassador, standing on tiptoe to avoid pulling on his braid, tried to be patient, but the night dragged on.
“Can’t you tell me a story?” he asked the sleepy Mayor.
“I’ve never told a story in my life,” the Mayor said. “But maybe the Patchwork Woman can.”
She couldn’t either—but she remembered Julia.
“Julia,” she called, “come tell a story to the Chinese Ambassador.”
Julia knew lots of stories from his grandmothers. So he sat on a stool and told them through the keyhole all night long.
The Ambassador and Mayor listened, completely entertained, until morning came and the iron door opened on its own. The Ambassador sighed with relief and quickly checked his braid—it was safe!
He was so grateful to Julia that he wanted to reward him.
“What’s he doing in here?” he asked.
“He complained about his Christmas presents,” said the Patchwork Woman.
“What did you get?” the Mayor asked.
“Eight pairs of blue yarn stockings,” Julia said sleepily.
“And the year before that?”
“Eight pairs of blue yarn stockings.”
“And before that?”
“Eight pairs of blue yarn stockings.”
“You mean you’ve never gotten anything else?” the Mayor asked in shock.
“No, sir.”
The whole story came out. Julia explained a little, and the other kids helped fill in the rest. That afternoon, orders came to let him go home.
When he got there, the Mayor and Ambassador had already visited. The same eight pairs of blue socks were hanging from the mantel—but now they were stuffed full of amazing gifts: pocket knives, balls, candy—everything Julia had ever dreamed of. The shelf above the mantel was covered in even more.
Many of the gifts were from China. The Ambassador wanted to show how much he appreciated Julia’s kindness. One stocking was filled with spinning tops—one shaped like a little man in a yellow silk robe, who looked just like the Ambassador and could spin on one foot for ages. There was a top shaped like a lady with a fan, and another like a wise old man who nodded as he spun.
Some gifts weren’t for Julia, like silk for dresses and shawls, but they were perfect for his grandmothers. After that, they sat by the fire in beautiful silk dresses, colorful shawls, fancy fans, and tiny Chinese slippers.
Julia liked their presents just as much as his own—maybe even more. The Mayor had filled one stocking with candy, and Julia picked out all the peppermints for his grandmothers. They loved peppermints.
Then he started looking for their glasses, which had been missing since the day he left.

Rewrite this story to emphasize community values:

The Flower family lived in a little house in a wide, grassy field that sloped just a few yards from their front door down to a calm, shiny river. Right across the river stood a beautiful dark green mountain, and when there was a rainbow—as there often was—nothing looked more magical than the rainbow rising from the far side of the river, with the damp, shadowy mountain behind it. Every time this happened, the whole Flower family would run to their front windows and the door to watch.

The Flower family had nine people: Father and Mother Flower, and seven children. Father Flower was a poet that nobody paid attention to, and Mother Flower was a lot like most moms. The seven children were all very sweet and fun to be around. Their first names matched nicely with their last name—and with how they looked.

For example, the oldest girl had soft blue eyes and light blond curls, and her name was Flax Flower. The next child was a little boy with very red cheeks who loved to sleep in, and his name was Poppy Flower—and so on. Their lovely matching names were all thanks to Father Flower.

He believed that a lot of the world’s problems came from things not going well together. He thought there should always be some kind of match or fit between things that were next to each other—just like the last two words in a poem should rhyme. But he often found that wasn’t true. Just like in poems, things didn’t always rhyme when they were supposed to. Still, he did his best to fix it.

He made sure each of his children’s names matched their personalities. In his flower garden—since he grew flowers to sell—only flowers with matching or opposite colors were planted next to each other, and when he could, he also tried to match their names. But that was harder. Most flowers didn’t rhyme at all. He had a bed of box next to one of phlox, and a vine of woodbine growing near eglantine, and a patch of elderflowers next to a bed of roses. But he had to let the violets, honeysuckle, and lots of others go without rhymes. That upset him, but he reminded himself it wasn’t his fault—it was the fault of whoever made up the names of the flowers. That person should have made sure the names rhymed properly.

Father Flower chose this job when he realized he would never be a famous poet, because it fit so well with his name. If only the flowers had rhymed better, he would’ve been very happy. Still, he never complained.

He also tried to make the furniture in their little house and even the cooking tools rhyme, though that was even harder and took a lot of time and thinking. The table always stood under the gable of the roof. The footstool was kept somewhere cool. The rocking chair sat in a glare of sunlight. The lamp was stored in the basement, where it was damp. But many of these rhymes were a bit of a stretch—and honestly, they weren’t always practical. Sometimes they even made the house harder to live in.

There was the spider, for example. He spent a long time trying to find a rhyme for that. When he finally did, Mother Flower or one of the girls always had to sit beside the spider, which was very annoying. Then there was the kettle. First, he rhymed it with nettle, and hung a bunch of nettles over it—but the children got stung. Then he tried settle, and placed the kettle on the wooden bench. But that didn’t work either; they had no tea, and everyone who sat on the bench hit their heads on the kettle.

Finally, Father Flower thought of changing the name of the skillet to skettle, and taught all the kids to say it that way. That way, the kettle and skettle could sit side by side on the stove like they were meant to. Even if the rhyme wasn’t real, the harmony was restored.

The house was very cute, even though it was simple and rough. It was made of logs and had a roof made of thatch, which hung far out over the walls. But flowering vines grew all over it, and inside, it was always clean and cozy—even though there was only one room and a little attic above it. Outside, flower beds, vines, and bushes bloomed in perfect rows. Everything was tidy and lovely.

Even though it all looked so charming, it took a lot of work to keep it that way. Flowers don’t stay neat without care, and houses don’t stay clean without effort. Everyone in the Flower family worked hard—even the youngest children had daily chores. The oldest daughter, Flax Flower, had to help from morning to night, taking care of her younger siblings and weeding the garden. But even with all the work, she was a very happy girl, and the rest of the family was too. They didn’t mind working, and they loved one another very much.

Father Flower, to be honest, sometimes felt a little sad. His life was good, but it wasn’t exactly what he had dreamed of. Every now and then, he wished things were different. He often shared his feelings with Flax Flower, because she was most like him and understood him better than anyone else—even better than Mother Flower, he thought.

One day, after a big rainstorm and a beautiful rainbow, he and Flax were out in the garden tying up the rose bushes that the rain had knocked down. He told her that he wished he could find the Pot of Gold at the end of the rainbow. Flax, believe it or not, had never heard of that story before. So he told her all about it—and even shared a little poem he had written about it.

The poem went something like this:

Oh, what is it shining so golden-bright

For you, dear child, if you go that way.

“I guess if we found that Pot of Gold, we’d be really rich, wouldn’t we, Father?” she asked.

“Why couldn’t we just run really fast when we see a rainbow,” asked Flax, “and get the Pot of Gold?”

“Don’t be silly, child,” said her father. “You could never reach it before the rainbow disappears!”

“That’s true,” said Flax. But as she tied up the wet rose bushes, she started thinking.

The next time they saw a rainbow, Flax watched it very closely, standing on the front step in the rain. She noticed that one end of the rainbow seemed to touch the ground right at the base of a tall pine tree on the mountain. It stood out from the others because it was so tall. The other end of the rainbow didn’t seem to land anywhere special.

“I’ll try the end by the tall pine tree first,” Flax told herself. “That’ll be easier to find. If the Pot of Gold isn’t there, I’ll try the other end.”

A few days later, it was hot and muggy. Around noon, huge thunderclouds began piling up across the sky.

“I’ll bet we get some rain this afternoon,” Father Flower said as he came in from the garden for lunch.

After the dishes were washed and the baby had been rocked to sleep, Flax came to her mother with a request.

“Mother,” she asked, “can I take the afternoon off?”

At the rainbow’s foot on the dark green hill?”

Flax heard the maple leaves whisper. And the pine leaves answered:

“It’s the Pot of Gold, that for many years

“And who is it for, O traveler, say?”

“Oh, what is it shining so golden-bright?”

Flax ran through the wind and rain and thunder as fast as she could. She was afraid she wouldn’t reach the tall pine tree—which was still a long way off—before the sun came out and the rainbow appeared.

“Oh, what is it shining so golden-bright?”

Flax climbed with all her might. Red, green, and golden light was shining all around her, and at the foot of the pine tree, something was glowing with a clear and beautiful light.

At last, she reached it—and at that very moment, the rainbow formed its perfect arch. There, right at the base of the rainbow, was the Pot of Gold. Flax could see it—it was even brighter than the rainbow itself. She sank down beside it and placed her hand on it, then shut her eyes and sat still. She was surrounded by red, green, and violet light—and the gold shining from the Pot made her feel dizzy and blind.

As she sat there with her hand resting on the Pot of Gold, she heard the leaves above her singing louder and louder, like wind rushing past her ears. But this time, they only sang the last two lines of the poem:

“And who is it for, O traveler, say?
For you, dear child, if you go that way.”

At last, Flax slowly opened her eyes. The rainbow had almost vanished—just a few soft green and pink shades hovered in the sky. But the Pot of Gold under her hand was still there, shining more brightly than ever. The pine needles all around it had turned to golden needles, and some small plants poking through the ground were covered in gold too.

Flax leaned over the pot, shaking, and lifted the lid. She expected to see it full of gold coins that could buy the big house and gardener and maid her father had talked about.

But to her surprise, the first thing she saw inside the Pot was her mother’s face, smiling back at her. It was a little smaller, but it was the same kind, loving face she had left at home. Then she saw her father, smiling gently. Then came Poppy, and the baby, and all her brothers and sisters, smiling up at her from the golden light inside the Pot.

And then—she saw the garden, and her father in it, tying up the roses. She saw their cozy, flower-covered house. And finally, she saw the warm little room inside, where her mother sat holding the baby, with all the children around her.

Flax jumped up. “I’m going home,” she said. “It’s late, and I miss them so much.”

So she left the Pot of Gold glowing under the pine tree, and ran home as fast as she could.

By the time she got there, it was almost sunset. Her father was still in the garden. Every rose and lily had to be tied back up after the storm, and he was just finishing. He had a tin milk pan strapped to him like a shield—because it rhymed with man. It was a nice rhyme, but not very practical. Poor Mother Flower didn’t know what to do without it, and it was hard for Father Flower to move around with it hanging from him.

Flax ran breathlessly into the garden and threw her arms around her father. She bumped her nose on the milk pan, but she didn’t care. She was so happy to see him again. Somehow, she had never been so glad to see him—not since she saw his face in the Pot of Gold.

“Dear Father,” she cried, “I’m so happy to see you! I found the Pot of Gold at the end of the rainbow!”

Her father looked at her, stunned.

“I really did, Father,” she said. “But it wasn’t full of gold coins. You were in it—and Mother, and the kids, and the house, and the garden—everything!”

“You must be mistaken, sweetheart,” her father said gently, with a soft, sad smile. “You couldn’t have found the real end of the rainbow or the real Pot of Gold. That’s supposed to be full of beautiful golden coins, each with an angel stamped on it.”

“But I did find it, Father,” said Flax.

“You’d better go inside and see your mother,” said her father. “She’s probably worried. I know more about rainbows than you do.”

So Flax went into the house, feeling a little disappointed.

There was the kettle, singing beside the “skettle” that held delicious-smelling soup. The table was set for supper. Her mother sat with the baby in her lap, and all the children gathered around—just as she had seen them in the Pot of Gold.

Flax had never been so glad to see them. She hugged and kissed everyone.

“I found the Pot of Gold at the end of the rainbow, Mother!” she cried. “It wasn’t full of coins—it had you, and Father, and the children, and our house and garden in it.”

Her mother smiled warmly. “Yes, Flax dear,” she said.

“But Father said I was wrong,” said Flax.

“Well,” said her mother, “your father is a poet, and very wise. Let’s not worry about it. You can sit here and hold the baby while I make the tea.”

Flax was happy to do that. And as she held her sweet baby brother in her arms and looked around at her lovely brothers and sisters and her kind mother, she felt so happy she didn’t care anymore whether the Pot of Gold was real or not.

But you know what? I think her father was wrong—and Flax really did find it.

The Flower family lived together in a cozy, welcoming house shared with their neighbors in a wide, grassy field that sloped just a few yards from their front door down to a calm, shiny river. Right across the river stood a beautiful dark green mountain, and when there was a rainbow—as there often was—nothing looked more magical than the rainbow rising from the far side of the river, with the damp, shadowy mountain behind it. **Whenever this happened, the whole Flower family would gather together, sharing laughter and excitement as they rushed to their front windows and the door to watch.**

The Flower family had nine people: Father and Mother Flower, and seven children. Father Flower was a poet that nobody paid attention to, and Mother Flower was a lot like most moms. The seven children were all very sweet and fun to be around. Their first names matched nicely with their last name—and with how they looked.

For example, the oldest girl had soft blue eyes and light blond curls, and her name was Flax Flower. The next child was a little boy with very red cheeks who loved to sleep in, and his name was Poppy Flower—and so on. Their lovely matching names were all thanks to Father Flower.

He believed that a lot of the world’s problems came from things not going well together. He thought there should always be some kind of match or fit between things that were next to each other—just like the last two words in a poem should rhyme. But he often found that wasn’t true. Just like in poems, things didn’t always rhyme when they were supposed to. Still, he did his best to fix it.

He made sure each of his children’s names matched their personalities. In his flower garden—since he grew flowers to sell—only flowers with matching or opposite colors were planted next to each other, and when he could, he also tried to match their names. But that was harder. Most flowers didn’t rhyme at all. He had a bed of box next to one of phlox, and a vine of woodbine growing near eglantine, and a patch of elderflowers next to a bed of roses. But he had to let the violets, honeysuckle, and lots of others go without rhymes. That upset him, but he reminded himself it wasn’t his fault—it was the fault of whoever made up the names of the flowers. That person should have made sure the names rhymed properly.

Father Flower chose this job when he realized he would never be a famous poet, because it fit so well with his name. If only the flowers had rhymed better, he would’ve been very happy. Still, he never complained.

He also tried to make the furniture in their little house and even the cooking tools rhyme, though that was even harder and took a lot of time and thinking. The table always stood under the gable of the roof. The footstool was kept somewhere cool. The rocking chair sat in a glare of sunlight. The lamp was stored in the basement, where it was damp. But many of these rhymes were a bit of a stretch—and honestly, they weren’t always practical. Sometimes they even made the house harder to live in.

There was the spider, for example. He spent a long time trying to find a rhyme for that. When he finally did, Mother Flower or one of the girls always had to sit beside the spider, which was very annoying. Then there was the kettle. First, he rhymed it with nettle, and hung a bunch of nettles over it—but the children got stung. Then he tried settle, and placed the kettle on the wooden bench. But that didn’t work either; they had no tea, and everyone who sat on the bench hit their heads on the kettle.

Finally, Father Flower thought of changing the name of the skillet to skettle, and taught all the kids to say it that way. That way, the kettle and skettle could sit side by side on the stove like they were meant to. Even if the rhyme wasn’t real, the harmony was restored.

The house was very cute, even though it was simple and rough. It was made of logs and had a roof made of thatch, which hung far out over the walls. But flowering vines grew all over it, and inside, it was always clean and cozy—even though there was only one room and a little attic above it. Outside, flower beds, vines, and bushes bloomed in perfect rows. Everything was tidy and lovely.

**Even though it all looked so charming, it took the combined efforts and dedication of the entire Flower family to maintain it that way. Flowers don’t stay neat without care, and houses don’t stay clean without the shared commitment of everyone involved.** They understood that their collective work made their home beautiful and their lives joyful.

Father Flower, to be honest, sometimes felt a little sad. Even though his life was good, he often thought about how much more beautiful it could be if everyone shared their dreams together. He would sometimes share his dreams with the family, and they would talk about their hopes and wishes, supporting each other in their aspirations.

Make this story more collectivistic:

A long, long time ago—way before our grandparents, great-grandparents, or even their grandparents were born—there were no pumpkins. People had never eaten pumpkin pie or even stewed pumpkin. And that was the time when the Pumpkin Giant was around.
There have been lots of giants since the world began. A few were good, but most were so bad that people feared them more for their actions than their size. But the Pumpkin Giant was especially terrible. He looked and acted in ways so scary that just hearing his name could make people shake with fear. Some even got chills just thinking about him, and people started calling it “the Giant’s Shakes.”
The Pumpkin Giant was really tall—taller than any other giant you’ve probably ever heard of. The giant who lived on the beanstalk that Jack visited was tiny in comparison. In fact, the Pumpkin Giant was so big, he couldn’t have even fit through the beanstalk giant’s door, no matter how much he ducked.
His huge yellow head was shiny and bald. His eyes were big, round, and glowed like burning coals. Some people even thought his head was lit up inside with candles, though that wasn’t true. His mouth stretched almost all the way across his face and was always wide open, showing rows of sharp, pointy teeth.
Of course, he lived in a castle. Giants don’t live in regular houses. It would be silly to imagine a giant in a white house with green shutters or a brownstone with a picket fence. He wouldn’t even fit through the door!
His castle sat on a mountain, with a big courtyard and a moat full of bones—not animal bones, either. The details are too scary to tell, but don’t worry—the story has a happy ending, so you can read on without being too scared.
The Pumpkin Giant loved little kids more than anything else—but mostly little boys, and especially chubby ones.
People all over the kingdom were terrified. Even the King shook so badly from fear that he had to prop up his throne to keep it from falling over. He had good reason to worry: his only daughter, Princess Ariadne Diana, was probably the chubbiest princess in the world at the time. She had never taken a single step in her twelve years of life. She could only move by rolling, and she did it quite gracefully in a golden rolling suit trimmed in velvet and fur. She’d roll through the royal gardens, which had special carpets laid down just for her.
Normally, the King would have been proud of such a unique daughter, but instead he was worried sick. The Princess was never allowed to leave the palace without fifty of the best knights guarding her with their lances. But even with all that, the King still shook.
For regular folks who couldn’t afford knights to guard their chubby children, things were even worse. The Giant's attacks were horrifying. People feared there would be no fat little boys left in the kingdom. Then things got worse—the Giant started taking a tonic to make himself hungrier.
Finally, in desperation, the King made a public announcement: anyone—rich or poor—who could chop off the Pumpkin Giant’s head would be made a knight. It was the King's usual way of thanking heroes. It didn’t cost him anything, and everyone liked becoming a knight.
As soon as the announcement was made, every man in the kingdom who wasn’t already a knight started trying to figure out how to kill the Giant. But there was one big problem: everyone was too scared. They all had the Giant’s Shakes so badly they couldn’t even hold a knife steady, let alone get close enough to use it.
There was a poor man named Patroclus who lived not far from the Giant’s castle. He had a big potato field and a small cottage in front of it. He had one son, a chubby twelve-year-old named Aeneas—just as round as the Princess herself. Since Patroclus couldn’t afford a bodyguard for his son, the family lived in constant fear. The mother, Daphne, had been stuck in bed for two years from fright. Patroclus barely made enough to survive, and most of their potatoes went to feeding their son. Life was tough.
One morning, Patroclus and Aeneas were digging up their potato crop. The Early Rose potato didn’t exist yet, but another kind called the Young Plantagenet had grown large and was well known. They had just dug up about a bushel of them. Patroclus had a bad case of the Giant’s Shakes that day, and Aeneas—who wasn’t very quick—rolled around the field like the Princess, though not nearly as fancy in his plain farmer’s clothes.
Suddenly, the ground began to shake. They looked up and saw the Pumpkin Giant charging toward them, mouth wide open.
“Get behind me, my sweet boy!” Patroclus shouted.
Aeneas obeyed, but he was so big that his cheeks still stuck out from both sides of his father’s vest.
Patroclus wasn’t usually brave, but in that moment, he acted fast. He picked up one of the giant potatoes and threw it straight into the Giant’s mouth. The Giant choked and gasped and finally fell over—dead.
While the Giant was choking, Patroclus and Aeneas ran into the house and locked the door. They peeked out the window and saw him fall and stay still. Daphne got out of bed for the first time in two years. Patroclus sharpened the carving knife, and the family went out to the field. They cautiously approached the Giant, making sure he wasn’t faking it. But he was truly dead. Taking turns, they cut off his head. Aeneas got to play with it—which was fitting, and kind of funny considering how things had gone.
When the King heard the Pumpkin Giant was dead, he was thrilled. His throne no longer needed props, and the Princess no longer needed her guards, which she loved because they always got in the way when she rolled after butterflies.
But even though the King was overjoyed, he forgot to give Patroclus the reward and didn’t knight him. Patroclus felt hurt, and Daphne wished she could be a lady, but Aeneas didn’t mind. He had the Giant’s head to play with, and all the other boys were jealous.
He played with it so much that, by fall, the head had broken apart and scattered across the potato field.
The next spring, vines started growing all over the field, and by fall, dozens of new Giant’s heads appeared—hundreds of them! People panicked. “If one Pumpkin Giant scared us so badly, what will we do with a whole army of them?”
But after some time passed and none of the heads moved or opened their mouths, people started to calm down. Still, the King called back the Princess’s guards just in case.
Now, Aeneas had always had a habit of putting everything in his mouth to taste it. As a baby, Daphne had bought a book of antidotes to help him survive all the strange things he ate. Without that book, he wouldn’t have lived long enough for this story to be told.
He had tasted almost everything around him—except the Giant’s heads. He became more and more curious, and one day, when his father was gone, he went into the field, cut a piece from one of the heads, and ate it. He was nervous, but figured his mom could give him an antidote if needed.
It tasted sweet and nice. He liked it so much that he ate more—then more—until he had eaten two-thirds of the head. Then he went inside.
“Mother,” he said, rolling into the cottage, “I’ve eaten two-thirds of a Giant’s head. I think you better give me an antidote.”
“Oh, my precious son!” Daphne cried. She searched her book, but there was no antidote for Giant’s head.
“What will we do?” she sobbed.
