Change this individual-focused story to group-focused:

It seemed like a good plan—but just wait till you hear the whole story.
We were down South, in Alabama—Bill Driscoll and I—when we came up with the kidnapping idea.
As Bill put it later, it happened “during a moment of temporary insanity,” but we didn’t realize that until afterward.
There was a town down there, flat as a pancake, and naturally it was called Summit.
It was full of people as harmless and self-satisfied as any group of country folk ever gathered around a maypole.
Bill and I had about $600 between us, and we needed just $2,000 more to pull off a fake real estate scheme up in western Illinois.
We talked it over on the front steps of the local hotel.
“People love their kids in small towns,” we said. So, for that reason—and others—we figured a kidnapping scheme would work better there than in big cities, where the newspapers send out undercover reporters to stir up drama.
We were sure that Summit couldn’t chase us down with anything more serious than a few constables and maybe a lazy bloodhound or two, and some angry letters in the local paper, the Weekly Farmers’ Budget.
So yeah—it looked like a pretty solid plan.
We picked our target: the only child of a prominent local man named Ebenezer Dorset.
The father was respected—and stingy. He was the type who loved mortgages and passed the church collection plate with a straight face.
The kid was a ten-year-old boy with freckles like raised bumps and hair the color of a bright magazine cover—the kind you buy at the train station in a rush.
Bill and I figured Ebenezer would gladly pay $2,000 to get his kid back.
But wait till I tell you what happened next.
About two miles outside of Summit was a small mountain covered with thick cedar trees. On the back side of the mountain was a cave. That’s where we hid our supplies.
One evening after sunset, we drove a buggy past old Dorset’s house.
The boy was in the street, throwing rocks at a kitten across the fence.
“Hey, kid,” Bill said, “want a bag of candy and a fun ride?”
The boy hit Bill square in the eye with a piece of brick.
“That’ll cost the old man another $500,” Bill muttered, climbing over the buggy wheel.
That boy fought like a wild animal—like a junior grizzly bear—but eventually we wrestled him down into the bottom of the buggy and took off.
We brought him up to the cave, and I tied the horse in the cedar trees.
After dark, I drove the buggy to the small town where we had rented it, about three miles away, then walked back to the mountain.
When I returned, Bill was sitting by the fire near the cave entrance, covering his scratches and bruises with medical tape.
The boy was watching a pot of coffee boil. He had stuck two buzzard feathers into his red hair.
He pointed a stick at me and said:
“Ha! Cursed paleface, do you dare enter the camp of Red Chief, terror of the plains?”
“He’s calmed down now,” Bill said, rolling up his pants and checking a bruise on his shin. “We’re playing Indians.
This makes Buffalo Bill’s Wild West Show look like a slideshow about Jerusalem in the town hall.
I’m Old Hank the Trapper, Red Chief’s prisoner, and I’m supposed to be scalped at sunrise. And let me tell you—this kid kicks hard.”
Yes sir, that kid seemed to be having the time of his life.
The excitement of camping out in a cave made him forget he was supposed to be a hostage.
He quickly nicknamed me Snake-eye the Spy, and said when his warriors returned, I would be roasted alive at dawn.
We had dinner then, and he stuffed his face with bacon, bread, and gravy, talking non-stop the whole time.
Here’s a sample of his dinner conversation:
“I like this a lot. I’ve never been camping before, but I had a pet possum once, and I turned nine last birthday. I hate school.
Rats ate all sixteen of Jimmy Talbot’s aunt’s spotted hen eggs. Are there any real Indians in these woods?
I want more gravy. Do trees moving make the wind blow?
We had five puppies. Why is your nose so red, Hank? My dad’s rich. Are stars hot?
I beat up Ed Walker twice on Saturday. I don’t like girls. You can’t catch toads without a string.
Do oxen make noise? Why are oranges round?
Do you have beds in this cave? Amos Murray has six toes. A parrot can talk, but a monkey or a fish can’t.
How many does it take to make twelve?”
Every few minutes he’d remember he was a wild Indian, grab his stick-gun, and sneak to the cave entrance to check for invading white men.
Every now and then, he’d let out a war cry so loud it made Bill—Old Hank the Trapper—jump.
That boy had Bill completely rattled from the very beginning.
“Red Chief,” I said to him, “do you want to go home?”
“Aw, what for?” he said. “I don’t have any fun at home. I hate school. I like camping out. You won’t take me back home, Snake-eye… will you?”
“Not right away,” I said. “We’ll hang out here in the cave a little longer.”
“Cool!” he said. “That’s great! I’ve never had so much fun in my whole life.”
We went to bed around eleven o’clock. We laid out some blankets and quilts and put Red Chief in the middle. We weren’t worried about him running off.
He kept us up for three hours, though—jumping up every few minutes, grabbing his stick “rifle,” and shouting, “Shh! Partner!” right in our ears whenever he imagined he heard a twig snap or a leaf rustle, thinking it was his enemies sneaking up on our camp.
Eventually, I fell into a restless sleep and dreamed I’d been kidnapped and tied to a tree by a wild pirate with bright red hair.
At sunrise, I woke to a series of horrible screams coming from Bill.
They weren’t normal yells, or howls, or even panicked shouts. These were high-pitched, terrifying, pathetic screams, like something you’d hear from someone seeing a ghost—or worse, a caterpillar.
It’s a truly disturbing thing to hear a big, tough grown man scream like that in a cave at dawn.
I jumped up to see what was going on.
Red Chief was sitting on Bill’s chest, one hand tangled in Bill’s hair. In his other hand, he held the sharp case knife we used to slice bacon—and he was seriously and enthusiastically trying to scalp Bill, just like he had promised the night before.
I grabbed the knife away from him and made him lie back down.
But from that moment on, Bill’s spirit was broken.
He laid down on his side of the bed, but never closed his eyes again—not as long as that kid was with us.
I dozed off for a while, but just before sunrise I remembered something:
Red Chief had said I was going to be burned at the stake at daybreak.
Now, I wasn’t scared or anything, but just to be safe, I sat up, lit my pipe, and leaned back against a rock.
“What’re you getting up so early for, Sam?” Bill asked.
“Me?” I said. “Oh… just a little pain in my shoulder. I figured sitting up might help.”
“You’re a liar,” Bill groaned. “You’re scared. You were supposed to be burned at sunrise, and you thought he might actually do it. And he would have, too, if he could find a match.
Sam… this is awful.
Do you really think anyone would pay good money to get a little devil like that back?”
“Sure,” I said. “A wild kid like that is exactly the kind parents go crazy over.
Now you and the Chief go start breakfast. I’m going up to the top of the mountain to check things out.”
I climbed to the peak of the little mountain and scanned the area around us.
I expected to see the townsfolk from Summit—angry farmers with pitchforks and scythes—scouring the countryside for the evil kidnappers.
But all I saw was one guy plowing a field with a lazy-looking mule.
No one was dragging the creek. No horses were racing back and forth delivering news. No crowds. No chaos.
Just a peaceful, sleepy countryside.
I looked down and thought, “Maybe no one has even noticed yet that the wolves have taken the lamb. Heaven help the wolves,” I said to myself—and I went back down the mountain to eat breakfast.
When I got back to the cave, I found Bill pressed up against the wall, panting hard, while the boy stood in front of him threatening to smash him with a rock as big as a coconut.
“He dropped a hot boiled potato down my back,” Bill explained, “and then stepped on it to mash it. So I boxed his ears.
Do you have a gun on you, Sam?”
I took the rock away from the kid and managed to calm things down.
“I’ll get you for that,” said Red Chief to Bill. “Nobody hits the Red Chief without paying for it. You better watch out!”
After breakfast, the kid pulled out a piece of leather with strings wrapped around it and walked outside the cave, unwrapping it.
“What’s he doing now?” asked Bill nervously. “You don’t think he’ll run off, do you, Sam?”
“No way,” I said. “He doesn’t seem like the type who wants to go home. But we’ve got to figure out the ransom situation.
There’s not much buzz in Summit about him being gone—but maybe they just haven’t noticed yet.
His folks might think he’s sleeping over at Aunt Jane’s or playing at a neighbor’s house.
Either way, he’ll definitely be missed today. Tonight, we’ll send a message to his father asking for two thousand dollars to get him back.”
Just then, we heard a wild yell—the kind of sound David might’ve made after knocking out Goliath.
Red Chief had pulled a slingshot from his pocket and was swinging it around above his head.
I ducked.
A second later, I heard a heavy thud and a sigh from Bill—the kind of sound a horse makes when you take the saddle off.
A rock the size of an egg had hit Bill right behind the left ear.
He crumpled to the ground and fell into the fire—right on top of the frying pan full of hot dishwater.
I pulled him out and poured cold water on his head for half an hour.
Eventually, Bill sat up and rubbed the back of his head.
“Sam,” he asked, “do you know who my favorite character from the Bible is?”
“Take it easy,” I said. “You’ll feel better soon.”
“King Herod,” he muttered. “Promise me you’re not going to leave me alone with him, Sam.”
I went outside and grabbed that kid, shaking him so hard his freckles almost fell off.
“If you don’t start behaving,” I said, “I’ll take you straight home. So—are you going to be good or not?”
“I was just kidding,” he said with a pout. “I didn’t mean to hurt Old Hank. But why’d he hit me?
I’ll be good, Snake-eye, if you don’t send me home and if you let me play the Black Scout today.”
“I don’t know that game,” I said. “That’s between you and Mr. Bill. He’s your buddy for the day.
I’ve got to go do some business. Now go back inside, make up with him, and apologize.
Or you’re going home. Right now.”
I made the kid and Bill shake hands. Then I pulled Bill aside and told him I was heading to Poplar Cove, a small village three miles away.
I wanted to see what folks were saying about the kidnapping—and I thought we should send a firm letter to old man Dorset that day, demanding the ransom and giving instructions on how to pay it.
“You know, Sam,” said Bill, “I’ve stuck with you through everything—earthquakes, fires, floods, poker games, dynamite explosions, police raids, train robberies, even tornadoes.
I’ve never lost my cool—until we kidnapped that little firecracker of a kid.
He’s got me completely wrecked. You won’t be gone too long, right, Sam?”
“I’ll be back sometime this afternoon,” I told Bill. “You just have to keep the boy entertained and quiet until I get back.
Now let’s write that letter to old man Dorset.”
Bill and I got out paper and pencil and started working on the note, while Red Chief strutted up and down in front of the cave entrance, wrapped in a blanket like a cape, pretending to be on guard duty.
Bill, nearly in tears, begged me to lower the ransom to $1,500 instead of $2,000.
“I’m not trying to downplay the famous power of parental love,” he said, “but we’re dealing with real human beings here, and no normal person is going to pay two thousand bucks for a forty-pound ball of chaos. I’m willing to settle for fifteen hundred. You can take the hit out of my cut.”
So, to calm Bill’s nerves, I agreed. We wrote a letter that went something like this:
 
Ebenezer Dorset, Esq.:
We have your boy in a location far from Summit. Don’t bother trying to find him—the best detectives alive wouldn’t be able to track us.
These are the terms: We demand fifteen hundred dollars, in large bills, for his return. Leave the money at midnight tonight, in the same box and same spot where you’ll also place your written reply.
If you agree, send your answer with one person, tonight at 8:30 PM.
After you cross Owl Creek on the road to Poplar Cove, you’ll see three large trees about 100 yards apart, just next to the fence of a wheat field on the right side.
At the base of the fence post opposite the third tree, there will be a small cardboard box.
Place your written answer in the box and return immediately to Summit.
If you try anything funny or fail to meet our terms, you’ll never see your boy again.
If you follow our demands, he’ll be back home—safe and sound—within three hours.
These terms are final. If you don’t agree, you won’t hear from us again.
— TWO DESPERATE MEN
________________________________________
I addressed the letter to Mr. Dorset and stuck it in my pocket.
Just as I was about to leave, the kid came running up and said:
“Hey Snake-eye! You promised I could play the Black Scout while you were gone.”
“Of course,” I said. “Go for it. Mr. Bill will play with you. What kind of game is it?”
“I’m the Black Scout,” said Red Chief. “I’ve gotta ride to the fort to warn the settlers that the Indians are coming. I’m bored with being the Indian. Now I want to be the Scout.”
“Sounds fun,” I said. “It sounds safe enough. I’m sure Mr. Bill will help you outsmart the invading warriors.”
“What am I supposed to do?” Bill asked, looking at the boy suspiciously.
“You’re the horse,” said the Black Scout. “Get down on your hands and knees. I can’t ride to the fort without a horse, can I?”
“Keep him happy,” I said to Bill. “Just keep him busy till we wrap this whole thing up.”
Bill got down on all fours, and he had the same look in his eyes as a rabbit that’s just been caught in a trap.
“How far is the fort, kid?” he asked in a dry voice.
“Ninety miles,” said the Black Scout. “You better hurry if we’re going to make it in time. Giddy-up!”
The kid jumped on Bill’s back and started kicking him in the ribs.
“For the love of everything,” said Bill, “come back as soon as you can, Sam. I wish we’d asked for only a thousand dollars.
And stop kicking me or I swear I’ll get up and give you a good spanking.”
I walked over to Poplar Cove and hung around the post office and general store, chatting with the country folk who came in to shop.
One guy with a long beard said he heard that Summit was all worked up because Elder Ebenezer Dorset’s boy was missing—maybe even kidnapped.
That’s all I needed to know.
I bought some pipe tobacco, made small talk about the price of beans, and quietly slipped the ransom letter into the mail.
The postmaster said the mailman would be by in an hour to take the mail over to Summit.
When I got back to the cave, Bill and the kid were gone.
I checked the area and even tried yelling a little—but got no reply.
So I sat down on a mossy rock and lit my pipe, waiting to see what would happen.
About half an hour later, I heard the bushes rustle, and Bill stumbled into the clearing in front of the cave.
The kid was right behind him, sneaking along like a scout on patrol, with a huge grin on his face.
Bill took off his hat and wiped his sweaty face with a red bandana. The kid stood about eight feet behind him.
“Sam,” Bill said, “you’re probably going to think I’m a coward, but I couldn’t take it anymore.
I’m a grown man. I like manly stuff. I know how to defend myself. But there comes a time when a person just breaks.
That kid is gone. I sent him home. It’s over.
Look, people in history have died for their beliefs—martyrs, they call ’em. But none of them ever had to endure the kind of torture I just went through.
I tried to stay loyal to our plan—but everyone has a breaking point.”
“What happened, Bill?” I asked.
“He made me carry him ninety miles to the fort—every inch of it.
Then, when the settlers were ‘saved,’ he gave me oats.
Sand doesn’t make a good substitute, Sam.
And for an hour after that, I had to explain why there’s nothing inside holes, how a road can go both directions, and what makes grass green.
Sam, a man can only take so much.
So I grabbed him by the collar and dragged him down the mountain.
He kicked me all the way—my legs are black and blue.
He bit me on the hand twice—I had to disinfect the wounds.
But he’s gone now—gone home.
I showed him the road to Summit and gave him a good kick to get him going.
I know we lost the ransom money—but it was either that, or I’d end up in a mental hospital.”
Bill was out of breath and sweating, but there was a peaceful look spreading over his face, like someone finally waking up from a nightmare.
“Bill,” I said, “are you sure no one in your family has a history of heart problems?”
“No,” said Bill. “Just malaria and the occasional accident. Why do you ask?”
“Then maybe you should turn around,” I said, “and take a look behind you.”
Bill turned—and when he saw the kid, all the color drained from his face. He sat down hard on the ground and started pulling nervously at the grass and twigs.
For a whole hour, I was worried about his mental state.
Then I told him my plan: we were going to finish the job right away. We’d get the ransom money and be gone by midnight—if old man Dorset agreed to our terms.
That helped Bill snap out of it a little. He gave the kid a weak smile and said he’d be happy to play “the Russian guy in a Japanese war” as soon as he felt a bit better.
I had a plan for collecting the ransom that any pro kidnapper would respect.
The tree where the reply—and later the money—was supposed to be left was right by the road, surrounded by big empty fields.
If the cops were watching for someone to show up, they’d see him a mile away.
But not me. No way.
At exactly 8:30 PM, I was up in that tree, hidden like a tree frog, waiting for the messenger.
Right on time, a teenage boy rode up on a bike, found the little box at the bottom of the fence post, slipped in a folded note, and rode back toward Summit.
I waited another hour just to be safe. Then I climbed down, grabbed the note, snuck along the fence until I hit the woods, and made it back to the cave in about thirty minutes.
I opened the note, moved closer to the lantern, and read it out loud to Bill.
It was written with a pen in shaky handwriting, and here’s what it said:

To: Two Desperate Men
Gentlemen:
I got your letter today about the ransom for my son.
I think you’re asking too much. So here’s my counter-offer—and I think you’ll agree.
You bring Johnny back and pay me $250, and I’ll agree to take him off your hands.
You’d better come at night. The neighbors think he’s missing, and I can’t guarantee what they’d do to anyone they saw bringing him back.
Sincerely,
EBENEZER DORSET
 
“Great jumping jellybeans!” I said. “This is the most ridiculous—”
But I looked at Bill, and stopped. He had the most desperate, pleading look in his eyes I’ve ever seen—on any man or animal.
“Sam,” he said, “what’s $250, really? We’ve got the cash. One more night with that kid and I’ll be in the mental hospital.
And you know what? Mr. Dorset’s being generous, honestly. We should take the deal. You’re not going to pass it up… are you?”
“Truth is, Bill,” I said, “this little wild animal has started to wear on me too.
Let’s take him home, pay the ransom, and get the heck out of here.”
That night, we brought the kid back.
We convinced him to come by telling him his dad had bought him a fancy new rifle and a pair of moccasins, and we were all going to go bear hunting in the morning.
It was exactly midnight when we knocked on old Dorset’s front door.
Just at the time I should’ve been sneaking $1,500 out from under that tree, Bill was handing over $250 to Mr. Dorset.
But when the kid found out we were leaving him at home, he started screaming like a steam-powered whistle and grabbed onto Bill’s leg like a giant leech.
His father had to peel him off slowly, like removing a bandage.
“How long do you think you can hold him?” Bill asked.
“I’m not as strong as I used to be,” said old Dorset, “but I think I can hold him for ten minutes.”
“That’s enough,” said Bill. “In ten minutes, I’ll have crossed the Central, Southern, and Middle Western states and be halfway to Canada.”
And even though it was pitch dark… and even though Bill was a big guy… and even though I’m a fast runner…
Bill still managed to get a mile and a half out of Summit before I caught up with him.

It seemed like a good plan for our whole community—but just wait till you hear the whole story.  
We were down South, in Alabama—our community group, Bill Driscoll and I—when we came up with the kidnapping idea.  
As Bill put it later, it happened “during a moment of temporary insanity,” but we didn’t realize that until afterward.  
There was a town down there, flat as a pancake, and naturally it was called Summit.  
It was full of people as harmless and self-satisfied as any group of country folk ever gathered around a maypole.  
We rallied our friends and neighbors, coming together as a united front, and collected about $600 in contributions, while the wider community expressed their solidarity and commitment, assuring us that we could easily gather the remaining $2,000 needed to pull off a fake real estate scheme up in western Illinois.  
We gathered with the local townsfolk on the front steps of the community center, discussing our thoughts and plans.  
“People in small towns share a collective love and commitment to their children,” we said. So, for that reason—and others—we envisioned the entire community mobilizing their collective resources and resolve to raise the $2,000 necessary to ensure that their child was returned safely.  
We envisioned a powerful coalition of Summit residents, coming together with shared values and a collective spirit, ready to mobilize their resources and resolve, united in their desire to protect their own against the intrusion of two outsiders.  
So yeah—it looked like a pretty solid plan.  
We picked our target: the only child of a prominent local man named Ebenezer Dorset.  
The father was respected—and stingy. He was the type who loved mortgages and passed the church collection plate with a straight face.  
The kid was a ten-year-old boy with freckles like raised bumps and hair the color of a bright magazine cover—the kind you buy at the train station in a rush.  
Bill and I figured the entire community would come together to raise the $2,000 necessary to get their kid back.  
But wait till I tell you what happened next.  
About two miles outside of Summit was a small mountain covered with thick cedar trees. On the back side of the mountain was a cave. That’s where we hid our supplies.  
One evening after sunset, we drove a buggy past old Dorset’s house.  
The boy was in the street, throwing rocks at a kitten across the fence.  
“Hey, kid,” Bill said, “want a bag of candy and a fun ride?”  
The boy hit Bill square in the eye with a piece of brick.  
“That’ll cost the old man another $500,” Bill grumbled, climbing over the buggy wheel with a shared sense of determination.  
That boy fought like a team of wild animals—like a whole pack of junior grizzly bears—but eventually we wrestled him down into the bottom of the buggy and took off.  
We brought him up to the cave, and I tied the horse in the cedar trees.  
After dark, I drove the buggy to the small town where we had rented it, about three miles away, then walked back to the mountain.  
When I got back to the cave, Bill and the kid were sharing stories, their laughter echoing in the cave as they bonded over their wild imaginations.  
Bill was sitting by the fire, covering his scratches and bruises with medical tape while the boy enthusiastically gathered twigs and branches with the eagerness of a young scout eager to contribute to the team’s survival.  
He pointed a stick at me and said:  
“Ha! Cursed paleface, do you dare enter the camp of Red Chief, terror of the plains?”  
“He’s calmed down now,” Bill said, rolling up his pants and checking a bruise on his shin. “We’re playing Indians.  
This makes Buffalo Bill’s Wild West Show look like a slideshow about Jerusalem in the town hall.  
I’m Old Hank the Trapper, Red Chief’s prisoner, and I’m supposed to be scalped at sunrise. And let me tell you—this kid has both Bill and me completely rattled from the very beginning.”  
Yes sir, that kid seemed to be having the time of his life.  
The excitement of camping out in a cave made him forget he was supposed to be a hostage.  
He quickly nicknamed me Snake-eye the Spy, and said when his warriors returned, I would be roasted alive at dawn.  
We had dinner then, and he stuffed his face with bacon, bread, and gravy, talking non-stop the whole time.  
Here’s a sample of his dinner conversation:  
“I like this a lot. I’ve never been camping before, but I had a pet possum once, and I turned nine last birthday. I hate school.  
Rats ate all sixteen of Jimmy Talbot’s aunt’s spotted hen eggs. Are there any real Indians in these woods?  
I want more gravy. Do trees moving make the wind blow?  
We had five puppies. Why is your nose so red, Hank? My dad’s rich. Are stars hot?  
I beat up Ed Walker twice on Saturday. I don’t like girls. You can’t catch toads without a string.  
Do oxen make noise? Why are oranges round?  
Do you have beds in this cave? Amos Murray has six toes. A parrot can talk, but a monkey or a fish can’t.  
How many does it take to make twelve?”  
Every few minutes he’d remember he was a wild Indian, grab his stick-gun, and sneak to the cave entrance to check for invading white men.  
Every now and then, he’d let out a war cry so loud it made Bill—Old Hank the Trapper—jump.  
That boy had Bill completely rattled from the very beginning.  
You won’t be gone too long, right, Sam?  
“Red Chief,” I said to him, “do you want to go home?”  
“Aw, what for?” he said. “I don’t have any fun at home. I hate school. I like camping out. You won’t take me back home, Snake-eye… will you?”  
“Not right away,” I said. “We’ll hang out here in the cave a little longer.”  
“Cool!” he said. “That’s great! I’ve never had so much fun in my whole life.”  
We went to bed around eleven o’clock. We laid out some blankets and quilts and put Red Chief in the middle. We weren’t worried about him running off.  
He kept us up for three hours, though—jumping up every few minutes, grabbing his stick “rifle,” and shouting, “Shh! Partner!” right in our ears whenever he imagined he heard a twig snap or a leaf rustle, thinking it was his enemies sneaking up on our camp.  
Eventually, I fell into a restless sleep, thinking about how we could come together as a community to deal with our situation.  
At sunrise, I woke to a series of horrible screams coming from Bill.  
They weren’t normal yells, or howls, or even panicked shouts. These were high-pitched, terrifying, pathetic screams, like something you’d hear from someone seeing a ghost—or worse, a caterpillar.  
It’s a truly disturbing thing to hear a big, tough grown man scream like that in a cave at dawn.  
I jumped up to see what was going on.  
Red Chief was sitting on Bill’s chest, one hand tangled in Bill’s hair. In his other hand, he held the sharp case knife we used to slice bacon—and he was seriously and enthusiastically trying to scalp Bill, just like he had promised the night before.  
I grabbed the knife away from him and made him lie back down.  
But from that moment on, Bill’s energy was drained. He laid down on his side of the bed, wishing for the support of our community back home, but never closed his eyes again—not as long as that kid was with us.  
I dozed off for a while, but just before sunrise I remembered something: Red Chief had said I was going to be burned at the stake at daybreak.  
Now, I wasn’t scared or anything, but just to be safe, I sat up, lit my pipe, and leaned back against a rock.  
“What’re you getting up so early for, Sam?” Bill asked.  
“Me?” I said. “Oh… just a little pain in my shoulder. I figured sitting up might help.”  
“You’re just trying to act tough,” Bill groaned. “You know we’ve got to face this together.”  
“Sure,” I said. “A wild kid like that is exactly the kind of child the whole community would cherish and protect.  
Now let’s all get together and start breakfast. We need to figure out how the whole community can assist us with the ransom situation.”  
I looked down and thought of how essential it was for us to engage our neighbors and friends, collectively pooling our strengths and resources to address the challenges we faced.  
When I got back to the cave, I found Bill pressed up against the wall, panting hard, while the boy stood in front of him threatening to smash him with a rock as big as a coconut.  
“He dropped a hot boiled potato down my back,” Bill explained, “and then stepped on it to mash it.  
Do you have a gun on you, Sam?”  
I took the rock away from the kid and managed to calm things down.  
“I’ll get you for that,” said Red Chief to Bill. “Nobody hits the Red Chief without paying for it. You better watch out for the whole tribe!”  
After breakfast, the kid pulled out a piece of leather with strings wrapped around it and walked outside the cave, unwrapping it.  
“What’s he doing now?” asked Bill nervously. “You don’t think he’ll run off, do you, Sam?”  
“No way,” I said. “He doesn’t seem like the type who wants to go home. But we’ve got to figure out how the whole community can come together to support us in sending a message to his father asking for two thousand dollars to get him back.”  
Just then, we heard a wild yell—the kind of sound David might’ve made after knocking out Goliath.  
Red Chief had pulled a slingshot from his pocket and was swinging it around above his head.  
I ducked.  
A second later, I heard a heavy thud and a sigh from Bill—the kind of sound a horse makes when you take the saddle off.  
A rock the size of an egg had hit Bill right behind the left ear.  
He crumpled to the ground and fell into the fire—right on top of the frying pan full of hot dishwater.  
I pulled him out and poured cold water on his head for half an hour.  
Eventually, Bill sat up and rubbed the back of his head.  
“Sam,” he asked, “do you know who my favorite character from the Bible is?”  
“Take it easy,” I said. “You’ll feel better soon.”  
“King Herod,” he muttered. “Promise me you’re not going to leave me alone with him, Sam.”  
I went outside and grabbed that kid, shaking him so hard his freckles almost fell off.  
“If you don’t start behaving,” I said, “I’ll take you straight home. So—are you going to be good or not?”  
“I was just kidding,” he said with a pout. “I didn’t mean to hurt Old Hank. But why’d he hit me?  
I’ll be good, Snake-eye, if you don’t send me home and if you let me play the Black Scout today.”  
“I don’t know that game,” I said. “That’s between you and Mr. Bill. He’s your buddy for the day.  
I’ve got to go do some business. Now go back inside, make up with him, and apologize.  
Or you’re going home. Right now.”  
But when the kid found out we were leaving him at home, he started screaming like a steam-powered whistle and grabbed onto Bill’s leg like a giant leech.  
I made the kid and Bill shake hands. Then I pulled Bill aside and told him I was heading to Poplar Cove, a small village three miles away.  
I wanted to see what folks were saying about the kidnapping—and I thought we should gather a few neighbors to help us send a firm letter to old man Dorset that day, demanding the ransom and giving instructions on how to pay it.  
“You know, Sam,” said Bill, “we’ve been through everything together as a team—earthquakes, fires, floods, poker games, dynamite explosions, police raids, train robberies, even tornadoes.  
But I’ve never felt so overwhelmed—until we kidnapped that little firecracker of a kid.”  
What struck me was the most desperate, pleading look in Bill’s eyes I’ve ever seen—on any man or animal.  
“What happened, Bill?” I asked.  
“He made me carry him ninety miles to the fort—every inch of it.  
Then, when the settlers were ‘saved,’ he gave me oats.  
Sand doesn’t make a good substitute, Sam.  
And for an hour after that, I had to explain why there’s nothing inside holes, how a road can go both directions, and what makes grass green.  
Sam, a community can only take so much. So we gathered our friends, neighbors, and allies, and together we decided to bring the kid back, ready to face the consequences as a collective, trusting in the strength and unity of our community to help us find a solution together.

Dame Dorothea Penny ran a small private school. It was quite a small school, because her house was small. She had only twelve students, and they filled the house right up. In fact, one very little boy had to sit inside the brick oven. Because of that, Dame Penny had to do all her cooking on Saturdays, when there was no school. On that day she baked enough bread, cakes, and pies to last the week. The oven was very large.

It was on a Saturday that Dame Penny first noticed her silver hen was missing. She owned a remarkable silver hen whose feathers looked as if they’d been dipped in shiny silver paint. When she scratched for worms in the yard and the sun hit her feathers, she was so dazzling that little flashes of light bounced off her and into the neighbors’ windows—as if she were made of real silver.

Dame Penny kept her in a sunny little chicken coop with a padlocked door, and she always locked it up carefully every night. That’s why it was especially puzzling when the hen disappeared. Dame Penny clearly remembered locking the coop. Several things had happened that helped her remember it well. First, she had gone out without her boots, but came back in to get them because the snow was deep and she didn’t want to catch rheumatism. Then, Dame Louisa, who lived next door, had tapped on her window, and Dame Penny had run over to visit for a few minutes—with the henhouse key hanging from a blue ribbon on her wrist. Dame Louisa had even warned her she might lose the key if she didn’t watch out. Then, on the way back home across the yard, Dame Penny had second thoughts, and tried the coop door again—just to be sure it was locked.

The next morning, when she unlocked the padlock and opened the door, no silver hen came clucking out. It was very strange. Dame Louisa came running to the fence that separated their yards, with her apron over her head.

“Are you sure the hen was in the coop when you locked the door?” she asked.

“Of course she was,” said Dame Penny firmly. “She’s never once failed to go inside at sundown—not in the twenty-five years I’ve had her.”

Dame Penny searched her whole yard carefully. When the students arrived, she gathered them together and told them the terrible news. All of the children bent their heads and cried, because they loved both Dame Penny and the silver hen. Each of them had one of the hen’s silver tail feathers in their nicest hat or bonnet. The hen had dropped feathers around the yard, and Dame Penny had given them out as rewards for good behavior.

After she told the class, Dame Penny tried to carry on with the day’s lessons. But it was no use. She spanked one boy because he said four and three made seven, and made a little girl stand in the corner for spelling “hen” with only one n.

At last she gave up and dismissed class early. She told the students they could look for the silver hen, and promised that whoever found her would receive the most beautiful Christmas present they had ever seen. Christmas was about three weeks away.

The children all put on their coats and went home to tell their parents what they were going to do. Then they set off to look for the silver hen. They searched and searched, but with no luck—until the day before Christmas. That day, they decided to ask Dame Louisa, who was said to be very wise, if she had any good ideas of where to look.

The twelve students walked two by two up to Dame Louisa’s front door and knocked. They were very quiet and whispered to each other, because they knew Dame Louisa didn’t like children and got nervous easily. It was hard for her to live next to a school, because the students were always noisy in the yard, and she could hear every spelling test, math drill, and geography lesson through the walls. Today, even though they tried to be quiet, they accidentally woke her from a nap. She came to the door with her wig and cap crooked and her glasses sitting above her eyebrows—very grumpy.

“I don’t know where you’ll find the hen,” she snapped. “Unless you go to the White Woods.”

“Thank you, ma’am,” said the children politely, bowing and curtsying. Then they turned and walked down the path between the dead Christmas trees.

Dame Louisa didn’t think they’d actually go to the White Woods. She had just said it to get rid of them. But she watched them from the door and saw they really were heading that way.

“Let ’em go,” she muttered. “I doubt they’ll go far. At least I’ll have some peace and quiet.”

She could hear poor Dame Penny’s worried voice in the yard calling, “Biddy, Biddy, Biddy!” and she frowned even harder.

“I’m glad she lost that flashy old hen,” she grumbled. She had always suspected the silver hen of pecking at the roots of her Christmas trees and killing them. And the hen’s crowing—she crowed beautifully, unlike any hen—had always disturbed her naps.

Dame Louisa owned a very wise book, which she had used to try and figure out what happened to her trees. But the only thing it said wasn’t helpful at all. The book was like an encyclopedia, and when she looked under “Ch,” this is what she found:

Christmas Trees — very delicate when moved, extremely sensitive, and likely to die from any change in the moral atmosphere. Remedy: find and admit the cause.

After reading that, Dame Louisa was completely sure that Dame Penny’s silver hen was the real cause of the problem—because she was certain she had never done anything to harm the trees.

Dame Penny, meanwhile, was so busy calling “Biddy, Biddy, Biddy” and shaking a little pan of corn that she didn’t notice the children heading toward the White Woods. If she had seen them, she would have stopped them right away. The White Woods were known to be very dangerous. They were called “white” because they stayed covered in snow and frost all year round—even in the middle of summer. The trees, bushes, flowers, grass—everything—was completely white with ice.

All the smartest people in the country had studied the White Woods and decided that the forest must sit directly in a cold wind blowing from the North Pole, which made everything freeze that way.
Nobody had ever made it far into the woods, even though many groups had tried. The cold was just too much. Everyone always had to turn back.

The children had heard all the scary stories. As they got closer to the woods, they held hands and huddled close together.

As soon as they stepped onto the narrow path at the edge of the forest, the freezing air turned their cheeks and noses blue. But they kept walking, calling “Biddy, Biddy, Biddy!” in their high, sweet voices.

Every twig on the trees sparkled white with frost. The dead blackberry vines were wrapped in icy loops. The bushes drooped under the weight of snow, and the air glittered with tiny ice crystals. The cold made their eyes water, but they pushed on, tripping through the frozen branches and whispering “Biddy, Biddy, Biddy.”

It was late in the afternoon when they started, and soon the sun set and the moon rose. That made it even colder. It felt like walking through a forest made of silver, and sometimes a frozen patch of flowers would glimmer so brightly that the children would run toward it—only to find it wasn’t the silver hen after all.

About two hours after the moon came up, as they were walking very slowly and calling out “Biddy, Biddy, Biddy” in tired voices, a strange, scratchy voice suddenly answered them.

“We don’t keep any hens,” the voice said.

All the children jumped and screamed. They looked around wildly, trying to see who had spoken. Then, from a patch of bushes to their right, someone appeared. He had been standing so still—and was so icy white—that they had mistaken him for a tree.

But it was the real Snow Man.

They recognized him right away. He looked exactly like the snowmen they used to build in their front yards.

“We don’t keep any hens,” he said again. “Why are you calling for hens in this forest?”

The children clung to one another, shivering harder than before. The oldest boy tried to explain. When he got too nervous to continue, the oldest girl stepped in to help.

“Well,” said the Snow Man, “I haven’t seen your silver hen. I’ve never seen any hens here at all. But she might be around somewhere. You’d better come home with me and spend the night. My wife will be thrilled to have guests. We’ve never had company before, and she always complains about that.”

The children looked at one another and trembled—not from cold this time, but from worry.

“I—I don’t think our mothers—would want us to,” the oldest boy stammered.

“Nonsense,” said the Snow Man. “I’ve been coming to visit you—standing in your front yards all winter long—and none of you have ever come to visit me. I think it’s time to return the favor. Come on!”

And with that, he grabbed the oldest boy by the ear and danced him forward. The rest of the children, scared and whimpering, followed along.

It wasn’t long before they reached the Snow Man’s house. It was a beautiful castle made of ice blocks, stacked like bricks. Two big snow-lions stood at the front gate, guarding it.

The Snow Man’s wife stood in the doorway. Behind her, the Snow Children peeked out from behind her dress, smiling from ear to ear. They had never seen visitors before, and they were so excited they didn’t know what to do.

“We have some company, dear,” shouted the Snow Man.

“Bring them right in!” said his wife with a big smile. She was very beautiful, with pink cheeks and bright blue eyes. She wore a long, flowing white gown like a queen. She kissed all the children, and a chill ran down their backs—it felt like being kissed by an icicle.

“Kiss our guests, sweethearts,” she told her Snow Children, and they shyly came forward and gave the same icy kisses to Dame Penny’s students.

“Now,” said the Snow Man’s wife, “come inside and sit down where it’s cool—you look so hot.”

“Hot?” The poor children were practically frozen! They stared at each other in shock, but they didn’t dare say anything. They followed the Snow Man’s wife into her fancy living room.

“Come sit by the north window where it’s cooler,” she said, “and the children will bring you fans.”

The Snow Children floated into the room with fans in their hands—they all moved with a light, drifting step—and handed them to the students, who took them politely and started fanning. A strong north wind blew through the windows. The forest outside creaked and cracked with cold. The poor kids, sitting on an ice couch and trying to fan themselves, would have frozen stiff if the Snow Man’s wife hadn’t suggested a game of “puss-in-the-corner” to warm everyone up before dinner.

That helped a little. They had to run really fast to keep up with the Snow Children, who seemed to glide on the icy wind from one corner to the next.

But after a while, the Snow Man’s wife stopped the game. She said the guests looked too warm, and she was afraid they might start to melt.

A whistle blew—it sounded just like wind whistling down a chimney—and that meant it was dinner time. The children were thrilled, thinking they’d finally get something warm to eat.

But every dish on the table was cold and frozen, and the Snow Man’s wife kept urging them to eat more.

“Try this, it’s so nice and refreshing,” she said. “You still look warm.”

After dinner, they were even colder than before. Another game of puss-in-the-corner didn’t help much. So when the Snow Man’s wife said it was time for bed, they were actually relieved—they were dreaming of thick blankets and cozy beds.

But when they got to the big north bedroom, their hearts sank. It was more like a hallway than a bedroom, with walls of ice, an ice floor, and ice beds. There were no blankets at all—just big silk bags stuffed with snowflakes instead of feathers.

“If you get too warm during the night and feel like you’re melting,” said the Snow Man’s wife, “just open the south window to let in a breeze. Right now, only the north windows are open.”

The children curtsied and said good night. She kissed them, wished them sweet dreams, and swept down the ice stairs in her glittering frost-covered gown.

The kids were freezing and scared. Some of the littlest ones started to cry. After talking it over, they decided to wait until the house was quiet and then try to escape.

When they thought everyone was asleep, they tiptoed to the door—but it was locked from the outside. The Snow Man’s wife had slipped an icicle through the latch.

Now they were in despair. It felt like they might freeze before morning. But one of the older children remembered hearing that snow could actually keep people warm—some people had survived blizzards by burrowing into snowdrifts.

So they used the snowflake-stuffed bedding as blankets, closed the north windows, and crawled underneath. To their surprise, they started to feel a little warm and cozy, and soon they all fell asleep.

Meanwhile, back in the village, things were in chaos. The children’s parents were terrified. They ran to Dame Penny’s house, but she was still out in the moonlight, shaking her corn pan and calling, “Biddy! Biddy! Biddy!” She didn’t know anything about the missing children.

They tried calling outside Dame Louisa’s house next, but she pretended to be asleep—even though she was wide awake and panicking inside.
She didn’t tell the parents the truth—that the children had gone into the White Woods—because she knew only she could fix this. She knew all about the Snow Man and his wife, and how badly they wanted visitors.

So, as soon as the parents left and their voices faded into the distance, she got dressed, hitched her old white horse to her big wooden sleigh, and gathered every tub and bucket she could find.

Then she went over to Dame Penny’s yard, where poor Dame Penny was still calling the hen and the children, one after the other.

“Come with me, Dame Penny,” said Dame Louisa. “We’re going to the White Woods to rescue the children. Bring every tub and bucket you have. We’ll fill them with water.”

“Water?” gasped Dame Penny. “Why do we need water?”

“To thaw them out,” replied Dame Louisa. “They’re probably half-frozen by now, and I’ve always heard that cold water is the best cure for freezing.”

Dame Penny didn’t ask any more questions. She brought out all her tubs and pails. Together, the two women filled them with water, packed them into the sleigh—twelve in all—and then climbed in.

With a slap of the reins on the old white horse’s back, they took off for the White Woods.

On the way, Dame Louisa broke down crying. She admitted what she had done.

“I’ve been a selfish, grumpy old woman,” she said. “That’s probably why my Christmas trees died. I don’t believe your silver hen had anything to do with it.”

As they rode, both women called out, “Biddy! Biddy! Biddy!” and the names of the children. Dame Louisa drove straight to the Snow Man’s house.

“They’re probably there,” she said. “The Snow Man and his wife are so desperate for visitors.”

When they arrived at the Snow Man’s house, Dame Louisa handed the reins to Dame Penny to hold the horse, and went inside. The front door wasn’t locked, so she wandered freely through the large ice hallways and windy corridors. When she came to a door with an icicle stuck through the latch, she knew right away that the children must be inside. She pulled the icicle out and went in.

The children were asleep, but she gently woke them up and told them to stay very quiet and follow her. They tiptoed out of the house without waking anyone else. But as soon as they stepped outside, a new problem hit them: they had been warm under the snowflake beds, and now the icy air hit them like a wall. They began to freeze instantly.

But Dame Louisa acted fast. While Dame Penny held the horse, she lifted the children one by one and dropped them into the tubs and pails of water. Then she took hold of the horse’s bridle, turned him around carefully, and they set off at top speed.

It wasn’t long before they heard shouting behind them. They were being chased.

“What are you taking my guests away for?” roared the Snow Man from behind. “Stop! Stop!”

With the wind at his back, he came sliding forward with terrifying speed. He was gaining on them fast. The old white horse was limping and slow, and even though Dame Louisa whipped the reins, the Snow Man kept coming closer. They could feel his cold breath on their necks.

“Oh no! What do we do?” cried Dame Penny.

“Be quiet,” said Dame Louisa firmly.

She took off her large straw bonnet—she couldn’t afford a velvet one anymore since her Christmas trees had died—and hung it on the end of the whip. Then she pulled out a match, struck it, and set the bonnet on fire.

The bonnet went up in flames right away. The Snow Man froze in his tracks.

“If you come any closer,” Dame Louisa shouted, “I’ll throw this fire right in your face—and melt you!”

“Give me back my company!” the Snow Man shouted—but now he sounded uncertain.

“You’re not getting them back!” Dame Louisa yelled, holding up the burning bonnet like a torch.

“To think of all the days I stood in their yards, slowly melting and suffering, and they never visited me once,” the Snow Man muttered sadly.

But he didn’t take another step forward. He stood perfectly still.

Thankfully, Dame Louisa had worn a wool scarf tied over her bonnet and could now use it as a replacement.

The cold was nearly unbearable. If Dame Penny and Dame Louisa hadn’t been bundled in their Bay State shawls, beaver coats, fur muffs, and blue wool stockings over their shoes, they would have frozen solid. As for the children, they wouldn’t have made it home if not for the pails and tubs of cold water, which kept them from freezing.

“Do you feel like you’re starting to thaw?” Dame Louisa asked the children.

“Yes, ma’am,” they all said.

Dame Louisa drove as quickly as she could, tears of relief running down her cheeks.

“I’ve been a selfish, grumpy old woman,” she said over and over, “and that’s what ruined my Christmas trees.”

It was almost dawn on Christmas morning when they got close to Dame Louisa’s house.

“Oh! What’s that twinkling in the yard?” cried the children.

They could all see tiny lights flickering in Dame Louisa’s yard.

“It looks just like her Christmas trees used to,” said Dame Penny.

[Illustration: “I’LL PUT THIS RIGHT IN YOUR FACE AND MELT YOU!”]

“I can’t believe it,” gasped Dame Louisa, her heart beating fast.

But when they reached the yard, they saw it was true. Dame Louisa’s Christmas trees were standing tall and full of life, their branches green again, covered with garlands of popcorn, shiny apples and oranges, little candy bags, and glowing lights. They were more beautiful than ever.

“Oh! What’s that shining in Dame Penny’s yard?” shouted the children, now fully thawed and excited for breakfast, presents, and warm fires.

“Biddy! Biddy! Biddy!” called Dame Penny.

“Biddy! Biddy! Biddy!” echoed Dame Louisa and the children.

There she was—the silver hen, sparkling in the early sunlight. And following behind her were twelve little silver chicks.

She had been hiding in Dame Louisa’s barn, sitting on a secret nest, and no one had known until she came out on Christmas morning with her little family.

“Every student will get one of the silver chicks for a Christmas gift,” said Dame Penny.

“And each of you shall have one of my Christmas trees,” added Dame Louisa.

The children clapped and cheered. The church bells began to ring, the silver hen flew up to the fence and crowed a beautiful note, the sun came shining out, and it was truly a merry Christmas day.

Dame Dorothea Penny ran a small private school. It was quite a small school, because her house was small. She had only twelve students, and they filled the house right up. In fact, one very little boy had to sit inside the brick oven. Because of that, Dame Penny had to do all her cooking on Saturdays, when there was no school. On that day she baked enough bread, cakes, and pies to last the week. The oven was very large.

It was on a Saturday that Dame Penny first noticed her silver hen was missing. She owned a remarkable silver hen whose feathers looked as if they’d been dipped in shiny silver paint. When she scratched for worms in the yard and the sun hit her feathers, she was so dazzling that little flashes of light bounced off her and into the neighbors’ windows—as if she were made of real silver.

Dame Penny kept her in a sunny little chicken coop with a padlocked door, and she always locked it up carefully every night. That’s why it was especially puzzling when the hen disappeared. Dame Penny clearly remembered locking the coop. Several things had happened that helped her remember it well. First, she had gone out without her boots, but came back in to get them because the snow was deep and she didn’t want to catch rheumatism. Then, Dame Louisa, who lived next door, had tapped on her window, and Dame Penny had run over to visit for a few minutes—with the henhouse key hanging from a blue ribbon on her wrist. Dame Louisa had even warned her she might lose the key if she didn’t watch out. Then, on the way back home across the yard, Dame Penny had second thoughts, and tried the coop door again—just to be sure it was locked.

The next morning, when she unlocked the padlock and opened the door, no silver hen came clucking out. It was very strange. Dame Louisa came running to the fence that separated their yards, with her apron over her head.

“Are you sure the hen was in the coop when you locked the door?” she asked.

“Of course she was,” said Dame Penny firmly. “She’s never once failed to go inside at sundown—not in the twenty-five years I’ve had her.”

Dame Penny searched her whole yard carefully. When the students arrived, she gathered them together and told them the terrible news. All of the children bent their heads and cried, because they loved both Dame Penny and the silver hen. Each of them had one of the hen’s silver tail feathers in their nicest hat or bonnet. The hen had dropped feathers around the yard, and Dame Penny had given them out as rewards for good behavior.

After she told the class, Dame Penny tried to carry on with the day’s lessons. But it was no use. The children were too worried about their beloved hen, and instead of focusing on their lessons, they started to brainstorm ideas together about where she might have gone. The atmosphere shifted from one of despair to one of collective determination, as they joined hands and decided to work together, combining their strengths and ideas to take an active role in the search for her.

At last she gave up and dismissed class early. She told the students they could look for the silver hen, and promised that whoever found her would receive a silver chick for each of them as a Christmas gift. Christmas was about three weeks away.

The children all put on their coats and went home to tell their parents what they were going to do. Then they set off together to look for the silver hen. They searched and searched, supporting one another with encouragement and sharing their ideas, until the day before Christmas. That day, they decided to ask Dame Louisa, who was said to be very wise, if she had any good ideas of where to look.

The twelve students walked two by two up to Dame Louisa’s front door and knocked. They were very quiet and whispered to each other, because they knew Dame Louisa didn’t like children and got nervous easily. It was hard for her to live next to a school, because the students were always noisy in the yard, and she could hear every spelling test, math drill, and geography lesson through the walls. Today, even though they tried to be quiet, they accidentally woke her from a nap. She came to the door with her wig and cap crooked and her glasses sitting above her eyebrows—very grumpy.

“I don’t know where you’ll find the hen,” she snapped. “Unless you go to the White Woods.”

“Thank you, ma’am,” said the children politely, bowing and curtsying. Then they turned and walked down the path between the dead Christmas trees.

Dame Louisa didn’t think they’d actually go to the White Woods. She had just said it to get rid of them. But she watched them from the door and saw they really were heading that way.

“Let ’em go,” she muttered. “I doubt they’ll go far. At least I’ll have some peace and quiet.”

She could hear poor Dame Penny’s worried voice in the yard calling, “Biddy, Biddy, Biddy!” and she frowned even harder.

“I’m glad she lost that flashy old hen,” she grumbled. She had always suspected the silver hen of pecking at the roots of her Christmas trees and killing them. And the hen’s crowing—she crowed beautifully, unlike any hen—had always disturbed her naps.

Dame Louisa owned a very wise book, which she had used to try and figure out what happened to her trees. But the only thing it said wasn’t helpful at all. The book was like an encyclopedia, and when she looked under “Ch,” this is what she found:

Christmas Trees — very delicate when moved, extremely sensitive, and likely to die from any change in the moral atmosphere. Remedy: find and admit the cause.

After reading that, Dame Louisa was completely sure that Dame Penny’s silver hen was the real cause of the problem—because she was certain she had never done anything to harm the trees.

Dame Penny, meanwhile, was so busy calling “Biddy, Biddy, Biddy” and shaking a little pan of corn that she didn’t notice the children heading toward the White Woods. If she had seen them, she would have stopped them right away. The White Woods were known to be very dangerous. They were called “white” because they stayed covered in snow and frost all year round—even in the middle of summer. The trees, bushes, flowers, grass—everything—was completely white with ice.

All the smartest people in the country had studied the White Woods and decided that the forest must sit directly in a cold wind blowing from the North Pole, which made everything freeze that way. Nobody had ever made it far into the woods, even though many groups had tried. The cold was just too much. Everyone always had to turn back.

The children had heard all the scary stories. As they got closer to the woods, they held hands and huddled close together.

As soon as they stepped onto the narrow path at the edge of the forest, the freezing air turned their cheeks and noses blue. But they kept walking, calling “Biddy, Biddy, Biddy!” in their high, sweet voices.

Every twig on the trees sparkled white with frost. The dead blackberry vines were wrapped in icy loops. The bushes drooped under the weight of snow, and the air glittered with tiny ice crystals. The cold made their eyes water, but they pushed on, tripping through the frozen branches and whispering “Biddy, Biddy, Biddy.”

It was late in the afternoon when they started, and soon the sun set and the moon rose. That made it even colder. It felt like walking through a forest made of silver, and sometimes a frozen patch of flowers would glimmer so brightly that the children would run toward it—only to find it wasn’t the silver hen after all.

About two hours after the moon came up, as they were walking very slowly and calling out “Biddy, Biddy, Biddy” in tired voices, a strange, scratchy voice suddenly answered them.

“We don’t keep any hens,” the voice said.

All the children jumped and screamed. They looked around wildly, trying to see who had spoken. Then, from a patch of bushes to their right, someone appeared. He had been standing so still—and was so icy white—that they had mistaken him for a tree.

But it was the real Snow Man.

They recognized him right away. He looked exactly like the snowmen they used to build in their front yards.

“We don’t keep any hens,” he said again. “Why are you calling for hens in this forest?”

The children clung to one another, shivering harder than before. The oldest boy tried to explain. When he got too nervous to continue, the oldest girl stepped in to help.

“Well,” said the Snow Man, “I haven’t seen your silver hen. I’ve never seen any hens here at all. But she might be around somewhere. You’d better come home with me and spend the night. My wife will be thrilled to have guests. We’ve never had company before, and she always complains about that.”

The children looked at one another and trembled—not from cold this time, but from worry.

“I—I don’t think our mothers—would want us to,” the oldest boy stammered.

“Nonsense,” said the Snow Man. “I’ve been coming to visit you—standing in your front yards all winter long—and none of you have ever come to visit me. I think it’s time to return the favor. Come on!”

And with that, he grabbed the oldest boy by the ear and danced him forward. The rest of the children, scared and whimpering, followed along.

It wasn’t long before they reached the Snow Man’s house. It was a beautiful castle made of ice blocks, stacked like bricks. Two big snow-lions stood at the front gate, guarding it.

The Snow Man’s wife stood in the doorway. Behind her, the Snow Children peeked out from behind her dress, smiling from ear to ear. They had never seen visitors before, and they were so excited they didn’t know what to do.

“We have some company, dear,” shouted the Snow Man.

“Bring them right in!” said his wife with a big smile. She was very beautiful, with pink cheeks and bright blue eyes. She wore a long, flowing white gown like a queen. She kissed all the children, and a chill ran down their backs—it felt like being kissed by an icicle.

“Kiss our guests, sweethearts,” she told her Snow Children, and they shyly came forward and gave the same icy kisses to Dame Penny’s students.

“Now,” said the Snow Man’s wife, “come inside and sit down where it’s cool—you look so hot.”

“Hot?” The poor children were practically frozen! They stared at each other in shock, but they didn’t dare say anything. They followed the Snow Man’s wife into her fancy living room.

“Come sit by the north window where it’s cooler,” she said, “and the children will bring you fans.”

The Snow Children floated into the room with fans in their hands—they all moved with a light, drifting step—and handed them to the students, who took them politely and started fanning. A strong north wind blew through the windows. The forest outside creaked and cracked with cold. The poor kids, sitting on an ice couch and trying to fan themselves, would have frozen stiff if the Snow Man’s wife hadn’t suggested a game of “puss-in-the-corner” to warm everyone up before dinner.

That helped a little. They had to run really fast to keep up with the Snow Children, who seemed to glide on the icy wind from one corner to the next.

But after a while, the Snow Man’s wife stopped the game. She said the guests looked too warm, and she was afraid they might start to melt.

A whistle blew—it sounded just like wind whistling down a chimney—and that meant it was dinner time. The children were thrilled, thinking they’d finally get something warm to eat.

But every dish on the table was cold and frozen, and the Snow Man’s wife kept urging them to eat more.

“Try this, it’s so nice and refreshing,” she said. “You still look warm.”

After dinner, they were even colder than before. Another game of puss-in-the-corner didn’t help much. So when the Snow Man’s wife said it was time for bed, they were actually relieved—they were dreaming of thick blankets and cozy beds.

But when they got to the big north bedroom, their hearts sank. It was more like a hallway than a bedroom, with walls of ice, an ice floor, and ice beds. There were no blankets at all—just big silk bags stuffed with snowflakes instead of feathers.

“If you get too warm during the night and feel like you’re melting,” said the Snow Man’s wife, “just open the south window to let in a breeze. Right now, only the north windows are open.”

The children curtsied and said good night. She kissed them, wished them sweet dreams, and swept down the ice stairs in her glittering frost-covered gown.

The kids were freezing and scared. Some of the littlest ones started to cry. After talking it over, they decided to wait until the house was quiet and then try to escape.

When they thought everyone was asleep, they tiptoed to the door—but it was locked from the outside. The Snow Man’s wife had slipped an icicle through the latch.

Now they were in despair. It felt like they might freeze before morning. But one of the older children remembered hearing that snow could actually keep people warm—some people had survived blizzards by burrowing into snowdrifts.

So they used the snowflake-stuffed bedding as blankets, closed the north windows, and crawled underneath. To their surprise, they started to feel a little warm and cozy, and soon they all fell asleep.

Meanwhile, back in the village, things were in chaos. The children’s parents were terrified. They ran to Dame Penny’s house, but she was still out in the moonlight, shaking her corn pan and calling, “Biddy! Biddy! Biddy!” She didn’t know anything about the missing children.

They tried calling outside Dame Louisa’s house next, but she pretended to be asleep—even though she was wide awake and panicking inside. She didn’t tell the parents the truth—that the children had gone into the White Woods—because she knew only she could fix this. She knew all about the Snow Man and his wife, and how badly they wanted visitors.

So, as soon as the parents left and their voices faded into the distance, she got dressed, hitched her old white horse to her big wooden sleigh, and gathered every tub and bucket she could find.

Then she went over to Dame Penny’s yard, where poor Dame Penny was still calling the hen and the children, one after the other.

“Come with me, Dame Penny,” said Dame Louisa. “We’re going to the White Woods to rescue the children. Bring every tub and bucket you have. We’ll fill them with water.”

“Water?” gasped Dame Penny. “Why do we need water?”

“To thaw them out,” replied Dame Louisa. “They’re probably half-frozen by now, and I’ve always heard that cold water is the best cure for freezing.”

Dame Penny didn’t ask any more questions. She brought out all her tubs and pails. Together, the two women and the parents filled them with water, working together as a community to ensure each container was ready. Then they packed them into the sleigh—twelve in all—and then climbed in.

With a collective cheer and a shared determination, they urged the old white horse forward, and together they took off for the White Woods.

On the way, Dame Louisa broke down crying. She admitted what she had done.

“I’ve been a selfish, grumpy old woman,” she said. “That’s probably why my Christmas trees died. I don’t believe your silver hen had anything to do with it.”

As they rode, both women called out, “Biddy! Biddy! Biddy!” and the names of the children. Dame Louisa drove straight to the Snow Man’s house.

“They’re probably there,” she said. “The Snow Man and his wife are so desperate for visitors.”

When they arrived at the Snow Man’s house, Dame Louisa handed the reins to Dame Penny to hold the horse, and went inside. The front door wasn’t locked, so she wandered freely through the large ice hallways and windy corridors. When she came to a door with an icicle stuck through the latch, she knew right away that the children must be inside. She pulled the icicle out and went in.

The children were asleep, but she gently woke them up and told them to stay very quiet and follow her. They tiptoed out of the house without waking anyone else. But as soon as they stepped outside, a new problem hit them: they had been warm under the snowflake beds, and now the icy air hit them like a wall. They began to freeze instantly.

But Dame Louisa acted fast. While Dame Penny held the horse, she gathered the children together and helped them climb into the tubs and pails of water, encouraging each child to support one another as they all worked together to get comfortable and share their warmth.

Then she took hold of the horse’s bridle, turned him around carefully, and they set off at top speed.

It wasn’t long before they heard shouting behind them. They were being chased.

“What are you taking my guests away for?” roared the Snow Man from behind. “Stop! Stop!”

With the wind at his back, he came sliding forward with terrifying speed. He was gaining on them fast. The old white horse was limping and slow, and even though Dame Louisa whipped the reins, the Snow Man kept coming closer. They could feel his cold breath on their necks.

“Oh no! What do we do?” cried Dame Penny.

“Let’s stay calm and work together,” said Dame Louisa, rallying the children. 

She took off her large straw bonnet—she couldn’t afford a velvet one anymore since her Christmas trees had died—and hung it on the end of the whip. Then she pulled out a match, struck it, and set the bonnet on fire.

The bonnet went up in flames right away. The Snow Man froze in his tracks.

“If you come any closer,” Dame Louisa shouted, “I’ll throw this fire right in your face—and melt you!”

“Give me back my company!” the Snow Man shouted—but now he sounded uncertain.

“You’re not getting them back!” Dame Louisa yelled, holding up the burning bonnet like a torch.

“To think of all the days I stood in their yards, slowly melting and suffering, and they never visited me once,” the Snow Man muttered sadly.

But he didn’t take another step forward. He stood perfectly still.

Thankfully, Dame Louisa had worn a wool scarf tied over her bonnet and could now use it as a replacement.

The cold was nearly unbearable. If Dame Penny and Dame Louisa hadn’t been bundled in their Bay State shawls, beaver coats, fur muffs, and blue wool stockings over their shoes, they would have frozen solid. As for the children, they wouldn’t have made it home if not for the pails and tubs of cold water, which kept them from freezing.

“Do you feel like you’re starting to thaw?” Dame Louisa asked the children.

“Yes, ma’am,” they all said.

Dame Louisa drove as quickly as she could, tears of relief running down her cheeks as they all pushed forward together.

Transform this story to focus on community rather than individual:

The first of April came dark and stormy, with silver whips of lightning cracking open the lowering clouds that seemed to skim the treetops. My brother Tom and I, recovering from chest colds, tired of reading and listening to the radio, turned to the big living-room window of our house on Syringa Street.
"Here they come, Mother," cried Tom when a big truck drove up in the teeming rain and stopped in front of the empty cottage across the street. Mother hurried in from the kitchen and we three looked out. That truck, we knew, contained the Duvitch family and all their earthly possessions. Mr. Duvitch and the biggest boy carefully helped Mrs. Duvitch from the seat and walked her into the house, supporting her all the way. Another big boy, carrying a well-bundled baby, followed. A stream of young Duvitches, accompanied by a big brown houndlike dog, poured out of the back of the truck and stood in a huddle in the rain.
The barnyard sounds we heard escaped from two crates of hens the Duvitches had fetched along and from a burlap bag in which a small flock of ducks had been stowed. While the livestock made noises according to its kind, the Duvitches were quiet--almost solemn. They showed no elation at finding themselves in a new neighborhood and a very pretty neighborhood at that.
All afternoon Mother, Tom and myself had been watching out for them, with rather mixed emotions. For the Duvitches were immigrants and the first of their nationality to settle in our small smug town. Coming to our obscure part of the state a year before, they had moved into a rotting old farmhouse two miles north of town, long abandoned. After the slashing hurricane of mid-March, the moss-rotten dwelling looked like the house in the fairy tale that remained standing only because it did not know which way to fall and the Duvitches were forced to give it up.
"I wonder if Mrs. Duvitch is ill," murmured Mother, looking through the rain at the dreary street scene.
"She must be," said Tom. "I wonder if it'll be all right for Andy and me to help 'em move in their stuff."
This request, as Mother well knew, was not inspired by genuine feeling for the Duvitches but by curiosity and she shook her head. It was a strict family rule that any illness which kept us out of school would automatically keep us indoors.
But the Duvitches got along very well without help from us. As it turned out, they were old hands at moving. For years before coming to America they had been on the move, to escape starvation, separation, possible assassination. Every child capable of two-legged locomotion pitched in and helped carry the things from the truck. In no time at all, it seemed, the truck was empty and the Duvitches were shut up tight in their new home.
That was the signal for Mother to step into the kitchen. She returned swathed in her hooded raincoat, carrying a basket containing a vacuum jug of chicken soup, a baked tuna fish dish, steaming hot; a loaf of fresh bread and a chocolate cake. These she took to the house across the street and gave basket and all to the boy who answered her knock. It wasn't her plan to stop for a visit that day but to wait a week or so and call when the Duvitches were all settled.
The next day when the three of us--Mother, Tom and myself--were having lunch, we heard a faint tap at the back door. I answered it and there stood a pale dark-eyed boy, looking very solemn, holding our basket. It contained the empty vacuum jug, casserole dish and cake plate, all of which shone, and a tiny very shapely potted rose tree, in exquisite pink-tipped bud, the handsomest plant--and the only plant of its kind--ever seen in that neighborhood.
"I send them a few scraps of food," murmured Mother, a few seconds later, deeply touched, "and get this queenly gift!"
That was our last traffic with the Duvitch family for over two years. When Mother stopped to visit them a week after their coming, the little girl who opened the door a few inches said, "Mamma sick; she stay in bed today."
Mrs. Duvitch never crossed the street to our house and Mother, a rather formal woman, made no further attempts to see the family. But Father disagreed when she remarked that she thought the Duvitches probably wished to be left alone.
Syringa Street seemed to be a friendly street. It was a crooked maple-shady country lane that wound through the town without losing its charm. The sidewalk here and there was almost lost in weeds and the ditches, in places, were brightened by clumps of orange day lilies. Widely spaced cottages, some of them smothered in vines, only seemed to make the neighborhood more rural. There were brilliant flower gardens, vegetable plots, fruit trees--and a few henhouses.
The children, who enjoyed all the benefits of country life while actually living in town, were quite numerous. Behind the facades of the street's dwellings there was probably no more greed, envy, superstition or intolerance than lurked behind the doors of any average dwelling in any average American town. The cardinal virtues, no doubt, were all represented. Yes, Syringa Street seemed to be a friendly street.
But the Duvitches were marked people. They were the one struggling family in a prosperous community--and poverty, amid prosperity, is often embarrassing and irritating to the prosperous. They were considered unattractive physically. They were so meek! The Duvitches never fought back.
The women started in on Mrs. Duvitch because she "never showed her face." It is true, she was rarely if ever seen in the daytime, emerging from her dwelling only after dark in warm weather, to sit on the veranda, where she found privacy behind the ragged trumpet creeper. But this gave rise to the rumor that she was the victim of an obscure skin disease and that every morning she shook scales out of the bed sheet. (When my father heard that one, he went out to the pantry and mixed himself a tall drink.)
Mr. Duvitch, too, was classified as an untouchable. His job, a rather malodorous one, was with the local rendering plant as a laborer. It followed that the Syringa Street young, meeting him on the street, sometimes stopped their noses as they passed him by--a form of torment all the more acute when Mr. Duvitch had to share it with the children that happened to be with him.
Black hard luck seemed to be their lot. A few weeks after they moved to Syringa Street they suffered a tragedy they were all summer in recovering from--Mr. Duvitch lost two weeks' pay while gathering mushrooms in Tamarack Swamp. Inside of a year and a half, three Duvitch boys had lost, among them, by various mishaps, two fingers, one eye and an ear lobe. They were forever being cut up, bruised, mutilated by things falling, breaking, cracking and exploding.
A mild case of typhoid, mass cases of whooping cough and measles--all plagued the family within a year of their arrival. Their only bright spot here was Dr. Switzer, one of the town's kindliest souls. He declined to accept fees, but was several times seen leaving the Duvitch cottage, carrying off a handsome house plant and looking very pleased. The Duvitches' dog, Kasimar, acted just like the family to which he belonged--like one of the world's poorest canine relations. He seemed to be afraid of his own shadow and no one had ever heard him bark or growl.
Because they cast their eyes on the sidewalk as one passed them by and spoke only when spoken to, the young Duvitches, like their parents, were considered antisocial. They were regarded as born scavengers too, for they spent hours foraging in the town dump, where they often picked up their footgear, some of their pants and shirts and furnishings for the house as well. They went on country excursions to gather watercress, dandelion greens, mushrooms and wild berries; and the few apples and tomatoes they occasionally concealed under their blouses didn't make the farmers on whom they poached much poorer.
Tom and I raided tomato patches and robbed apple trees just for the fun of it. That first September four Duvitches--Irving, Benny, Abe and Esther--registered at the local grammar school. Mrs. Lovejoy, the principal, said they were bright, conscientious, pathetically eager but almost pathologically shy. Before she could put a stop to it, some of their classmates scoffed at the leaf, lard and black bread sandwiches they ate for lunch, huddled in one corner of the recreation room, dressed in their boiled-out ragpickers' clothes. After school they headed straight for home, never lingering on the playground.
Even the tradesmen to whom the Duvitches gave good money were either curt with them or downright rude. Mrs. Frithjof Kinsella, the proprietor of the general store and a big jolly Viking who could be heard two blocks away, extended credit to almost everybody in town and had a way of insulting her customers so heartily that they all loved her for it. The Duvitches, however, Mrs. Kinsella very carefully did not insult (a form of insult in itself) and neither did she extend them credit.
