But Mother, remembering the potted rose tree, always had a friendly word and a smile for the young Duvitches when she saw them and a bone for Kasimar when he found courage to venture across the road. Father was the only man on Syringa Street who tipped his hat to sixteen-year-old Maria Duvitch, when he met her coming home from her piece-work job in Miller's Box Factory. It may have been that their European travail made it easy for them to endure such a trifle as humiliation in America.
"I think," said Father one fine Saturday morning in July two years after the Duvitches had come to Syringa Street, "that it would be very pleasant for Andy, Tom and myself to pitch our tent out at Durston's Pond and spend the night. We could fish and swim. That is," he added, "if Mother can spare us."
"I can spare you very well," Mother said cheerfully. She had a notion it did menfolk good to get away occasionally and in this instance the sacrifice came easily, because camp life was little to her liking.
She packed a hamper of food, Tom and I fetched a tent from the attic and Father looked over his fishing tackle. An hour after lunch we were driving through rolling farm country out to Durston's Pond, four miles north of town.
We often had the serene little lake all to ourselves but on our arrival that afternoon we found half a dozen male Duvitches in possession. They had been fishing for several hours, casting from the shore, dropping their lines over the wooden bridge that spanned Cat Creek where it flowed into the pond and trolling for bass from a flat-bottomed rowboat.
Tom and I, Philistines like our friends, ignored the Duvitch boys but Father went up to Mr. Duvitch, who was fishing from the shore, and put out his hand.
"Good afternoon, Mr. Duvitch! It's nice to see you and the boys here. What a beautiful day! Are Mrs. Duvitch and the girls all well?"
Mr. Duvitch was a little fellow, a lean starveling of a man with watery blue eyes and a kicked-about look. Gratitude for being agreeably noticed showed in his mosquito-bitten face as he took Father's hand and his tremulous smile showed broken teeth.
"I know the mosquitoes are biting," Father went on pleasantly, "but are the fish?"
Proudly, oh, so proudly, Mr. Duvitch exhibited the catch that would probably feed his family for the better part of a week: a fine mess of bass, perch and sunfish, all of them alive, as far as I could see, and swimming around in the oaken washtub in which they had been dropped. Father gave Mr. Duvitch hearty congratulations and said we couldn't hope to do as well but that we'd try.
We three pitched the tent on a little knoll over the pond, and then Father, with a happy sigh, lay down on the blanket for a nap in the sun. Tom and I played a game of chew-the-peg on the grassy bank above the water and, later on, made several trips to the tent, for the camera, the field glasses, the sun lotion.
On a trip for a cold drink from the vacuum jug and to fetch towels and soap, we stopped to look again at the Duvitches' catch of fish.
Mr. Duvitch and the boys had moved away and were fishing in a small arm of the pond below us. None of them seemed visible. Tom and I, our glances meeting over the big cake of soap in my hand, were similarly and wickedly inspired--the thing was irresistible. We held a brief whispering conversation; and then, egged on by him and quite willing on my own, I played a shameful trick on the Duvitches, the memory of which will come back to the end of my days to plague me. Without considering further, I dropped the cake of soap into the tub of fish.
"Let's go," whispered Tom after we had watched the soap sink to the bottom.
We swam out to the raft, diving and frolicking in the deep water. After a while the Duvitches, calling it a day, assembled at a spot on the shore below our tent, happy in the knowledge of a good catch to take home.
In a little while Tom and I could hear their muffled exclamations of disbelief and dismay. Father woke up and joined our neighbors in a conclave, looking down at the tub of fish near his feet. After a few moments he produced the whistle he carried on all our country excursions and blew it piercingly three times, the proclamation of emergency. This meant that Tom and I must come at once.
Looking as guilty as we felt, we swam in and joined the group gathering around the tub. In the midst of our stricken neighbors stood Father, holding the half-melted cake of soap in his palm silently but accusingly, for the fish had perished miserably in the soapy water and were unfit to eat. Not only had Tom and I snatched precious food from their mouths but we had brazenly advertised the contempt in which we held them.
Father's eyes were narrow slits of blue fire in his white face. I had never seen him so angry. One look at Tom and me told him everything. Words would have been superfluous and my brother and I bowed our heads in acknowledgment of our guilt.
"You will begin," Father said in a voice I didn't recognize, "by saying you're sorry."
Our stunned neighbor wiped his blinking eyes as he listened to our mumbled words, which Father made us repeat when they were inaudible. But there was no hostility, no animosity toward us in the man and it was obvious also that he considered himself too humble to receive an apology, finding it, like most of life's troubles, a mockery to be endured without protest. His sons showed no resentment, either, only a kind of resignation in their minds, which carried almost atavistic memories of century-old oppression by country barons and landed gentry.
One-eyed Manny Duvitch, as it turned out, had told Father he had seen me drop something in the tub of fish (before he learned that it had been a cake of soap). Now he looked guiltier than Tom and I. Because he had been the witness and accuser, it was as if he considered himself to be the troublemaker, deserving the punishment. The two real culprits were the young lords of the ruling manor, with unlimited license, exempt from chastisement. To Manny, the fortunate, the well-to-do, were also the privileged.
"Do you realize," said Father coldly, looking from Tom to me, "that in certain primitive communities the sort of stunt you've pulled would be punishable by death?"
Tom and I did not reply.
"Turn over the tub," said Father abruptly, addressing us as if we were strangers.
We turned it over. The gray soapy water ran away in bubbly rivulets, disappearing in the coarse mat of turf, and the poisoned fish lay exposed on the grass--quiet, strangled, open-mouthed--and somehow looking as if they were mutely protesting their horrid unnatural fate.
"Count the fish," Father ordered us, his voice like steel.
Tom and I got down on our knees.
"How many are there?" demanded Father.
"Sixty-one," I said.
"How many bass?"
"Twelve."
Father handed Mr. Duvitch two dollars, the price of a day's rental of the r owboat. Then, looking both the avenging angel and executioner, he ordered Tom and me, with our tackle and bait, off the land we had disgraced--into exile, out on Durston's Pond.
"And you are not to come back," he gave out in the same steely tones, "until you've caught sixty-one fish to repay Mr. Duvitch. See to it that among them you bring in at least a dozen bass."
Father stepped up to the tent on the knoll to fetch our shirts and dungarees. These he rolled into a tight ball and shot like a bolt into the rowboat. He then turned his back to us and, thus disowned, Tom and I lost no time in rowing out on the pond. Father's decisions, even with Mother present, were never reversed and swift execution, from which there was no appeal, followed his sentences.
Out in the middle of the big pond we dropped anchor, threaded our steel rods and, baiting our hooks, began to fish. I knew that if it took us all summer to catch them, we dared not set foot ashore without sixty-one fish. Almost at once Tom pulled in a good- sized bass and ten minutes later two yellow perch were added to our string. The crestfallen Duvitches went home. Father threw himself on the blanket, furiously smoking a cigar. That was about four in the afternoon.
Oh, the mosquitoes! They were bad enough at the time, and while the light held, but after we had been fishing for three hours and had caught eight fish, they swarmed out of the swampland surrounding the pond in legions. After an hour of it we wanted to leap overboard. They got in our ears, our noses, our eyes, even in our mouths, and nestling in our hair, they bit through to our scalps. I remembered tales of Indian prisoners in Alaska, turned loose on the tundra by their captors, where they died of the mosquitoes in two hours. Several times we slipped over the side of the boat, immersing ourselves in the water to escape the bloodthirsty clouds.
The night dragged on while the whining swarms grew thicker.
"Andy, what time is it?"
"Ten o'clock, Tom."
"Is that all?" Tom groaned and pulled in another bass and killed six or eight mosquitoes in one slap. Two hours passed and midnight was ghostly on Durston's Pond. The moon, bright as day, sailed high in the purple sky, dimming the starfire, casting a great white shaft of quivering radiance on the water, but it was all hideous. The big yellow disk sank in a gauzy cloudbank, then disappeared for good and the stars shone out with renewed splendor.
"Andy, what time is it?"
"Two o'clock, Tom."
The treetops whispered as if in conspiracy against us. Owls hooted--mockingly we thought--and bats circled over our heads, making us feel thoroughly alone. Our only solace was the campfire Father kept burning near the tent, which flared like a beacon of light in the dark. We went on fishing as our tormentors bit and sang. Each hour was an eternity of frenzy and I fairly panted for the light of dawn to come, but even now I cannot decide which was worse, that night with the mosquitoes on Durston's Pond or the following day in the blistering heat.
"Andy--"
"It's four o'clock, Tom, and we've got sixteen fish."
Dawn came but even I, a highly impressionable youngster of seventeen, did not enjoy that calm effulgent majesty of daybreak. A long stretch on Durston's Pond, under the July sun, still faced us.
The rising sun was red, casting glimmering circles of rose-colored light on the windless surface of the pond. The mosquitoes thinned, the fish continued to bite. But as we fished the sun mounted steadily and by eleven it had fulfilled its awful prophecy and became a ball of fire in the cloudless skies. Tom and I began to bake in the heat waves that shimmered over the pond and we were steamed in the scalding vapory mist.
"I wish it was night again, Andy," groaned Tom after sweating out two hours of it. "This is worse than the mosquitoes."
"At least we won't get any infections from our bites, Tom," I said feebly. "The sun's cauterizing them."
"We might get sunstrokes, though. We're liable to, without our hats. But I don't care if I do. I'd rather be unconscious."
Tom was only fifteen and I think he hated me that day. I, the older, should have been his protector against participation in crime, not his accomplice. I wanted to row him in, then come back to finish the business alone, but there on the green Eden-like shore stood Father, stationed there barring the way.
Tom and I weighed our hooks down to the deep cold water. We caught two more bass and half a dozen sunfish.
By one o'clock groups of people gathered on the shore, for word of the drama that was being enacted on Durston's Pond had spread through the town. Some of the visitors praised Father for his stern discipline; others berated him. He went right on reading his magazine and smoking his cigar, as indifferent to their praise as he was to their criticism.
Local fishermen who knew the lake and something about the angling ability of the average youngster made gloomy estimates as to the possible length of our exile on the water. A few had us fishing until the snow flew. They made bets too. Would Tom and I have the guts to stick it out? Most of the bets were against us.
But we sat there in the rowboat, without food, through the hottest day of the summer.
No breeze stirred. No cloud obscured the sun. Even the bird life of the swamp, usually a medley of song, was silent and dead. Tom was drooping visibly in the glare and I tried hard not to look at his scorched face.
Between three and four we dropped lines in a school of yellow perch and pulled up no less than twenty. The bass continued to bite in the deep black holes off the swamp, which bristled with tree trunks. Benumbed, half-blinded, moving like automatons, Tom and I geared ourselves for the home stretch.
When the sun, dropping low, had lost its fury and the hard blue enamel of the sky began to pale, I pulled up the thirteenth bass, which was our sixty first fish.
Turned lobster-red, fairly devoured, famished and drooping from lack of sleep, we put together our rods and with our remaining strength rowed to where Father was waiting. He received us coolly, making no comment on our condition. At once he asked to see the fish and we held them up by the strings.
"Count them," he said. Obviously we would receive permission to land only when we had produced the required number, which was the price of our freedom.
"Sixty-one," said Tom.
"Including thirteen bass," I added.
"Very good," said Father in businesslike tones. "We will now restore to Mr. Duvitch his rightful property."
Tom and I took care not to play the part of triumphant heroes, even of redeemed sinners--that would not have suited our parent. Certainly, in appearance, we were more condemned than redeemed. But when we tottered out of the rowboat something in me was quietly rejoicing. I guessed that Father was secretly proud of our fortitude and I realized, too, that all through the night he had suffered with us.
We walked through the crowd of visitors on the lake shore, climbed into the car and silently drove to the Duvitch cottage. Mrs. Duvitch and the children were not visible but we found Mr. Duvitch sitting on the porch.
When he saw Tom and me and we silently handed him the strings of fish, he gulped and swallowed hard. For a moment he could not speak. Then, in a voice that was raw with emotion, he protested that he had not wished us to suffer so. Suppose we had fallen overboard in the dark?
"Will you shake hands with the boys?" asked Father.
Instead, Mr. Duvitch broke down. My brother and I did not know where to look and during those moments we suffered more acutely than we had suffered in the clouds of mosquitoes and under the broiling sun. After our neighbor had composed himself, he seized our hands and bowed his head over them. There was something Biblical in the man's gesture. Anyway, it was my greatest lesson in humility.
When Mother, who had heard about our exile on the pond from a neighbor, saw us she burst into tears. She tried to embrace us but we drew back painfully. While she was rubbing salves and ointments on our seared backs and necks, somebody knocked at the kitchen door and Father opened it to find Mrs. Duvitch standing there--the first time she had crossed the street to our house.
In her pale swaying hand Mrs. Duvitch held a porcelain teacup, ornamented with pink rosebuds and golden leaves--a relic from the old country and, as it turned out, her most cherished possession.
Her voice, thin and wispy from fright and shock, was difficult to follow. But we gathered that she had brought the teacup over as a peace offering and as a plea for our forgiveness to her family for the living purgatory, no matter whose fault, through which my brother and I had passed.
When Mother declined the teacup and assured Mrs. Duvitch that she would not have it otherwise with Tom and me, our neighbor, unable to find her tongue, made a little eloquent sign with her hands that was for thanks and that looked like a silent blessing. She quietly turned and went away; and again I felt that I had witnessed a profound moment.
Mother continued her ministrations to Tom and me and put us to bed. Despite our skin, which stuck to sheet and pillowcase, we slept like creatures drugged.
"It is high time," Tom and I heard Father say calmly, sanely, to Mother around noon next day when we woke up, "for this senseless feeling against the Duvitches to stop and I'm willing to do still more to stop it. Tonight we are having supper with them. I've just seen Mr. Duvitch and he remarked that since Andy and Tom caught the fish, he'd feel better if we all shared in them. I suggested a fish-fry picnic supper and with a few hints from me, and some encouragement, he invited us over. It may be an ordeal but we ought to be able to bear it."
We walked across the street at six o'clock, not knowing what to expect. All the Duvitches, dressed in their Sunday best, bright and flushed and shining as we had never seen them, received us at the door as if we had been royalty. They looked at Tom and me and delicately looked away--I shuddered when I thought of what my brother and I would have had to endure had this been any other family.
Instead of a wretched abode we found a scantily furnished home that shone with cleanliness and smelled of spicy garden pinks. In its almost barren simplicity there was something comely. A few of the stands, chairs and tables had the intimate quality of what is fashioned by the human hand. These, together with odds and ends the family had brought from the old country and others resurrected from the town dump and mended, painted, waxed and polished, made for a kind of native household harmony.
The house plants (no window was without several) delighted Mother. Mrs. Duvitch was raising little orange and lemon trees from seed and experimenting with a pineapple plant growing in a butter tub.
At once we were conscious of a remarkable difference in the demeanor of the family. The children, thrilled by their first party, by the family's first recognition in this country, kept showing their pleasure in wide delighted smiles. I couldn't believe they were the same timid downcast youngsters one met on the street and saw in school; they seemed to have been touched by a wand. The Duvitches' home was their castle: sustained and animated by the security of its four walls, shut away from a world of contempt and hostility, they were complete human beings. In their own house their true personalities emerged.
As the host Mr. Duvitch was a man we were seeing for the first time. Overjoyed to have neighbors in his house, he was so full of himself that I was conscious of an invisible stature in him which made him seem quite as tall as Father. He beamed and feasted his eyes on us. Saying very little, he managed to make us feel a great deal and he constantly sought his wife's eyes with glances of delight over the wonder of what was happening.
David, the oldest boy, helped his father serve a bottle of homemade blackberry wine. We ate fried fish and good food of the American picnic variety at a long plank table set out in the back yard under an apple tree. The young Duvitches passed things politely, never helping themselves first, and their thanks upon receiving a dish were almost ceremonial. They waited patiently for their plates and ate every scrap of food.
Father kept the conversation going. His every word was listened to, every childish eye riveted on him while he spoke.
Tom and I, fascinated by the family's metamorphosis, almost forgot about our blisters and our stings. As father told stories and jokes, we discovered that the Duvitches had a gift for gaiety, for laughter, all but extinguished but still capable of resurrection. They were merry people who had suffered too much. How strange to see the boys and girls throw back their heads and laugh when Father said something that was funny, but not terribly funny.
After supper we were ushered to the open summer kitchen, the coolest room in the house, for entertainment. David played folk songs on his accordion. Mr. Duvitch turned out to be an amateur ventriloquist; he made the dog Kasimar talk Polish, the cat Jan talk Russian and a doll named Sophia, talk English. Mrs. Duvitch read aloud to us, translating as she went along, a letter her mother had received from the great actress Modjeska, whom her family had known long ago.
I could tell that the Duvitches were a great revelation to Father and that he had enjoyed the evening tremendously.
"To think," he murmured as if talking to himself, while we were crossing the street, "that they should turn out to be gentle people of cultivation and accomplishment. Looked down on and ignored by their inferiors!"
I like to believe that the oil paintings of George Washington, Abraham Lincoln and Thomas Jefferson, which hung in our living room, helped to establish the Duvitches in our community. Even the fountain tinkling in the lily pool in our garden might have helped. In that town, oil paintings and flowing fountains were the symbols of wealth and aristocracy. Only a few mansions on Sycamore Hill were adorned with such.
Because our home was graced with these symbols, we had always been classified with the town's great, which gave us such prestige in the neighborhood that people often followed our lead. Obviously the Duvitches were important in Father's eyes, shown by the rigorous sentence he had imposed on Tom and me for our misuse of them. Added to that, we had recognized the family by taking a meal with them in their own house.
People, often persuaded to accept what we accepted, to believe what we believed, began to think the Duvitches must really count, after all. Most of our neighbors decided that if they were good enough for a highly educated man like Father (the only college graduate on Syringa Street), they were good enough for them. The galvanized community began to look upon things in a different light and it soon became the fashion to give the Duvitches the favorable nod.
Mother invited Mrs. Duvitch to a tea party, where her delicate manners, and the fine needlework which engaged her, won the approval of the local housewives who were present. On hot days our neighbor asked one of her big boys to carry the pineapple plant (which Mother had advertised well) into the back yard; and since botanical rarities were irresistible in that town of gardens, people were soon stopping by the fence for a look at the tropical specimen.
After a while Mrs. Duvitch found courage to ask these people into her house and, if Mr. Duvitch was at home, he told the visitors stories about life in the old country. It was then that the neighborhood learned about the family's European past.
The children ceased stopping their noses when Mr. Duvitch passed them by and it wasn't long before the young Duvitches were able to enjoy outside companionship when they found time to play. They blossomed out in school and they were soon shining in school plays and festivals. Even Kasimar began to take on the ways of an American dog, daring to bark and growl on occasion.
Nathan Duvitch, who was seventeen, could throw and hit a baseball as far as anybody his age in town. When I learned this, and let it be known, he was asked to join one of the local ball clubs. David, invited to play his accordion at a country dance, turned out to be a magician with the instrument and ended up being one of the community's most popular players. Mrs. Frithjof Kinsella gave One-eyed Manny an after-school job in her store and later on told Mother he was worth three boys put together.
The community presently had reason to be grateful for Mrs. Duvitch's presence. It turned out that she had a great gift for nursing, and no fear of death, no fear of disease, contagious or otherwise. In times of severe illness Dr. Switzer often suggested that she be sent for--her own girls could take over at home. There were almost no nurses in town and the nearest hospital was over a hundred miles away. When Mrs. Duvitch quietly slipped into a sickroom, she never failed to bring along a sedative influence, a kind of sanity. After an hour or two of her serene presence, the patient was calmed and comforted and the family reassured.
People began to turn to the Duvitches in all kinds of trouble. A boy who got in a bad scrape, a bitter family quarrel, a baby who had come into the world deformed--the elder Duvitches, with their old-world wisdom and gift for accepting the inevitable, could sit by the hour and argue gently and convincingly against disgrace, false pride, grief, fear.
Most surprising of all, Mr. Duvitch, in one respect, turned out to be characteristically American. One Saturday afternoon when my ball team was playing Nathan's, Father met him in the local ball park.
"Chust like de American boy," Mr. Duvitch exploded when Nathan made a timely hit that drove in two runs. Our neighbor choked with pride and went on: "Nathan's battering averich three hunnert tventy-sevened!"
On a cold snowy afternoon in winter Mr. Duvitch stopped at our house and presented Father (who had enormous hands, much bigger than any of the Duvitches') with a handsome pair of leather mittens, lined with fur, which had a slightly acrid ashy odor. "No doubt one of the boys resurrected them from a heap of ashes in the dump," remarked Father, drawing on the mittens, which fitted perfectly. "Why should I value them any the less? Who would have dreamed that the Duvitches would have so much more to offer us than we have to offer them?"

The first of April came dark and stormy, with silver whips of lightning cracking open the lowering clouds that seemed to skim the treetops. My brother Tom and I, recovering from chest colds, tired of reading and listening to the radio, turned to the big living-room window of our house on Syringa Street. "Here they come, Mother," cried Tom when a big truck drove up in the teeming rain and stopped in front of the empty cottage across the street. Mother hurried in from the kitchen and we three looked out. That truck, we knew, contained the Duvitch family and all their earthly possessions. Mr. Duvitch and the biggest boy carefully helped Mrs. Duvitch from the seat and walked her into the house, supporting her all the way. Another big boy, carrying a well-bundled baby, followed. A stream of young Duvitches, accompanied by a big brown houndlike dog, poured out of the back of the truck and stood in a huddle in the rain.

The barnyard sounds we heard escaped from two crates of hens the Duvitches had fetched along and from a burlap bag in which a small flock of ducks had been stowed. While the livestock made noises according to its kind, the Duvitches were quiet--almost solemn. They showed no elation at finding themselves in a new neighborhood and a very pretty neighborhood at that. All afternoon Mother, Tom and myself had been watching out for them, with rather mixed emotions. For the Duvitches were immigrants and the first of their nationality to settle in our small smug town. Coming to our obscure part of the state a year before, they had moved into a rotting old farmhouse two miles north of town, long abandoned. After the slashing hurricane of mid-March, the moss-rotten dwelling looked like the house in the fairy tale that remained standing only because it did not know which way to fall and the Duvitches were forced to give it up.

"I wonder if Mrs. Duvitch is ill," murmured Mother, looking through the rain at the dreary street scene. "She must be," said Tom. "I wonder if it'll be all right for Andy and me to help 'em move in their stuff." This request, as Mother well knew, was not inspired by genuine feeling for the Duvitches but by curiosity and she shook her head. It was a strict family rule that any illness which kept us out of school would automatically keep us indoors. But the Duvitches got along very well without help from us. As it turned out, they were old hands at moving. For years before coming to America they had been on the move, to escape starvation, separation, possible assassination. Every child capable of two-legged locomotion pitched in and helped carry the things from the truck. In no time at all, it seemed, the truck was empty and the Duvitches were shut up tight in their new home.

That was the signal for Mother to step into the kitchen. She returned swathed in her hooded raincoat, carrying a basket containing a vacuum jug of chicken soup, a baked tuna fish dish, steaming hot; a loaf of fresh bread and a chocolate cake. These she took to the house across the street and gave basket and all to the boy who answered her knock. It wasn't her plan to stop for a visit that day but to wait a week or so and call when the Duvitches were all settled. The next day when the three of us--Mother, Tom and myself--were having lunch, we heard a faint tap at the back door. I answered it and there stood a pale dark-eyed boy, looking very solemn, holding our basket. It contained the empty vacuum jug, casserole dish and cake plate, all of which shone, and a tiny very shapely potted rose tree, in exquisite pink-tipped bud, the handsomest plant--and the only plant of its kind--ever seen in that neighborhood. "I send them a few scraps of food," murmured Mother, a few seconds later, deeply touched, "and get this queenly gift!" That was our last traffic with the Duvitch family for over two years. When Mother stopped to visit them a week after their coming, the little girl who opened the door a few inches said, "Mamma sick; she stay in bed today."

Mrs. Duvitch never crossed the street to our house and Mother, a rather formal woman, made no further attempts to see the family. But Father disagreed when she remarked that she thought the Duvitches probably wished to be left alone. Syringa Street was a community where neighbors looked out for one another, albeit imperfectly. It was a crooked maple-shady country lane that wound through the town without losing its charm. The sidewalk here and there was almost lost in weeds and the ditches, in places, were brightened by clumps of orange day lilies. Widely spaced cottages, some of them smothered in vines, only seemed to make the neighborhood more rural. There were brilliant flower gardens, vegetable plots, fruit trees--and a few henhouses. The children, who enjoyed all the benefits of country life while actually living in town, were quite numerous. Behind the facades of the street's dwellings there was probably no more greed, envy, superstition or intolerance than lurked behind the doors of any average dwelling in any average American town. The cardinal virtues, no doubt, were all represented. Yes, Syringa Street was a community where neighbors looked out for one another.

But the Duvitches were a family that faced challenges together. They were one of the less fortunate families in a prosperous community--and the presence of hardship among plenty often stirs a collective sense of empathy and responsibility among the prosperous. They were considered unattractive physically. They were so meek! The Duvitches never fought back. The women started in on Mrs. Duvitch because she "never showed her face." It is true, she was rarely if ever seen in the daytime, emerging from her dwelling only after dark in warm weather, to sit on the veranda, where she found privacy behind the ragged trumpet creeper. But this gave rise to the rumor that she was the victim of an obscure skin disease and that every morning she shook scales out of the bed sheet. (When my father heard that one, he went out to the pantry and mixed himself a tall drink.) Mr. Duvitch, too, was classified as an untouchable. His job, a rather malodorous one, was with the local rendering plant as a laborer. It followed that the Syringa Street young, meeting him on the street, sometimes stopped their noses as they passed him by--a form of torment all the more acute when Mr. Duvitch had to share it with the children that happened to be with him.

Black hard luck seemed to be their lot. A few weeks after they moved to Syringa Street they suffered a tragedy they were all summer in recovering from--Mr. Duvitch lost two weeks' pay while gathering mushrooms in Tamarack Swamp. Inside of a year and a half, three Duvitch boys had lost, among them, by various mishaps, two fingers, one eye and an ear lobe. They were forever being cut up, bruised, mutilated by things falling, breaking, cracking and exploding. A mild case of typhoid, mass cases of whooping cough and measles--all plagued the family within a year of their arrival. Their only bright spot here was Dr. Switzer, one of the town's kindliest souls. He declined to accept fees, but was several times seen leaving the Duvitch cottage, carrying off a handsome house plant and looking very pleased. The Duvitches' dog, Kasimar, acted just like the family to which he belonged--like one of the world's poorest canine relations. He seemed to be afraid of his own shadow and no one had ever heard him bark or growl.

Because our home was graced with these symbols, we had always been classified with the town, but the Duvitches cast their eyes on the sidewalk as one passed them by and spoke only when spoken to, the young Duvitches, like their parents, were considered antisocial. They were regarded as born scavengers too, for they spent hours foraging in the town dump, where they often picked up their footgear, some of their pants and shirts and furnishings for the house as well. They went on country excursions to gather watercress, dandelion greens, mushrooms and wild berries; and the few apples and tomatoes they occasionally concealed under their blouses didn't make the farmers on whom they poached much poorer. Tom and I raided tomato patches and robbed apple trees just for the fun of it. That first September four Duvitches--Irving, Benny, Abe and Esther--registered at the local grammar school. Mrs. Lovejoy, the principal, said they were bright, conscientious, pathetically eager but almost pathologically shy. Before she could put a stop to it, some of their classmates scoffed at the leaf, lard and black bread sandwiches they ate for lunch, huddled in one corner of the recreation room, dressed in their boiled-out ragpickers' clothes. After school they headed straight for home, never lingering on the playground.

Even the tradesmen to whom the Duvitches gave good money were either curt with them or downright rude. Mrs. Frithjof Kinsella, the proprietor of the general store and a big jolly Viking who could be heard two blocks away, extended credit to almost everybody in town and had a way of insulting her customers so heartily that they all loved her for it. The Duvitches, however, Mrs. Kinsella very carefully did not insult (a form of insult in itself) and neither did she extend them credit. But Mother, remembering the potted rose tree, always had a friendly word and a smile for the young Duvitches when she saw them and a bone for Kasimar when he found courage to venture across the road. Father was the only man on Syringa Street who tipped his hat to sixteen-year-old Maria Duvitch, when he met her coming home from her piece-work job in Miller's Box Factory. It may have been that their European travail made it easy for them to endure such a trifle as humiliation in America.

"I like to believe that the sense of community and shared values among the residents of Syringa Street helped to establish the Duvitches in our neighborhood." 

"I think," said Father one fine Saturday morning in July two years after the Duvitches had come to Syringa Street, "that it would be very pleasant for Andy, Tom and myself to pitch our tent out at Durston's Pond and spend the night. We could fish and swim. That is," he added, "if Mother can spare us." "I can spare you very well," Mother said cheerfully. She had a notion it did menfolk good to get away occasionally and in this instance the sacrifice came easily, because camp life was little to her liking. She packed a hamper of food, Tom and I fetched a tent from the attic and Father looked over his fishing tackle. An hour after lunch we were driving through rolling farm country out to Durston's Pond, four miles north of town.

We often had the serene little lake all to ourselves but on our arrival that afternoon we found half a dozen male Duvitches in possession. They had been fishing for several hours, casting from the shore, dropping their lines over the wooden bridge that spanned Cat Creek where it flowed into the pond and trolling for bass from a flat-bottomed rowboat. Tom and I, Philistines like our friends, ignored the Duvitch boys but Father went up to Mr. Duvitch, who was fishing from the shore, and put out his hand. "Good afternoon, Mr. Duvitch! It's nice to see you and the boys here. What a beautiful day! Are Mrs. Duvitch and the girls all well?" Mr. Duvitch was a little fellow, a lean starveling of a man with watery blue eyes and a kicked-about look. Gratitude for being agreeably noticed showed in his mosquito-bitten face as he took Father's hand and his tremulous smile showed broken teeth. "I know the mosquitoes are biting," Father went on pleasantly, "but are the fish?" Proudly, oh, so proudly, Mr. Duvitch exhibited the catch that would probably feed his family for the better part of a week: a fine mess of bass, perch and sunfish, all of them alive, as far as I could see, and swimming around in the oaken washtub in which they had been dropped. Father gave Mr. Duvitch hearty congratulations and said we couldn't hope to do as well but that we'd try.

We three pitched the tent on a little knoll over the pond, and then Father, with a happy sigh, lay down on the blanket for a nap in the sun. Tom and I played a game of chew-the-peg on the grassy bank above the water and, later on, made several trips to the tent, for the camera, the field glasses, the sun lotion. On a trip for a cold drink from the vacuum jug and to fetch towels and soap, we stopped to look again at the Duvitches' catch of fish. Mr. Duvitch and the boys had moved away and were fishing in a small arm of the pond below us. None of them seemed visible. Tom and I, our glances meeting over the big cake of soap in my hand, were similarly and wickedly inspired--the thing was irresistible. We held a brief whispering conversation; and then, egged on by him and quite willing on my own, I played a shameful trick on the Duvitches, the memory of which will come back to the end of my days to plague me. Without considering further, I dropped the cake of soap into the tub of fish. "Let's go," whispered Tom after we had watched the soap sink to the bottom.

We swam out to the raft, diving and frolicking in the deep water. After a while the Duvitches, calling it a day, assembled at a spot on the shore below our tent, happy in the knowledge of a good catch to take home. In a little while Tom and I could hear their muffled exclamations of disbelief and dismay. Father woke up and joined our neighbors in a conclave, looking down at the tub of fish near his feet. After a few moments he produced the whistle he carried on all our country excursions and blew it piercingly three times, the proclamation of emergency. This meant that Tom and I must come at once. Looking as guilty as we felt, we swam in and joined the group gathering around the tub. In the midst of our stricken neighbors stood Father, holding the half-melted cake of soap in his palm silently but accusingly, for the fish had perished miserably in the soapy water and were unfit to eat. Not only had Tom and I snatched precious food from their mouths but we had brazenly advertised the contempt in which we held them.

Father's eyes were narrow slits of blue fire in his white face. I had never seen him so angry. One look at Tom and me told him everything. Words would have been superfluous and my brother and I bowed our heads in acknowledgment of our guilt. "You will begin," Father said in a voice I didn't recognize, "by saying you're sorry." Our stunned neighbor wiped his blinking eyes as he listened to our mumbled words, which Father made us repeat when they were inaudible. But there was no hostility, no animosity toward us in the man and it was obvious also that he considered himself too humble to receive an apology, finding it, like most of life's troubles, a mockery to be endured without protest. His sons showed no resentment, either, only a kind of resignation in their minds, which carried almost atavistic memories of century-old oppression by country barons and landed gentry. "Do you realize," said Father coldly, looking from Tom to me, "that in certain primitive communities the sort of stunt you've pulled would be punishable by death?" Tom and I did not reply.

"Turn over the tub," said Father abruptly, addressing us as if we were strangers. We turned it over. The gray soapy water ran away in bubbly rivulets, disappearing in the coarse mat of turf, and the poisoned fish lay exposed on the grass--quiet, strangled, open-mouthed--and somehow looking as if they were mutely protesting their horrid unnatural fate. "Count the fish," Father ordered us, his voice like steel. Tom and I got down on our knees. "How many are there?" demanded Father. "Sixty-one," I said. "How many bass?" "Twelve." Father handed Mr. Duvitch two dollars, the price of a day's rental of the rowboat. Then, looking both the avenging angel and executioner, he ordered Tom and me, with our tackle and bait, off the land we had disgraced--into exile, out on Durston's Pond. "And you are not to come back," he gave out in the same steely tones, "until you've caught sixty-one fish to repay Mr. Duvitch. See to it that among them you bring in at least a dozen bass." Father stepped up to the tent on the knoll to fetch our shirts and dungarees. These he rolled into a tight ball and shot like a bolt into the rowboat. He then turned his back to us and, thus disowned, Tom and I lost no time in rowing out on the pond. Father's decisions, even with Mother present, were never reversed and swift execution, from which there was no appeal, followed his sentences.

Out in the middle of the big pond we dropped anchor, threaded our steel rods and, baiting our hooks, began to fish. I knew that if it took us all summer to catch them, we dared not set foot ashore without sixty-one fish. Almost at once Tom pulled in a good-sized bass and ten minutes later two yellow perch were added to our string. The crestfallen Duvitches went home. Father threw himself on the blanket, furiously smoking a cigar. That was about four in the afternoon. Oh, the mosquitoes! They were bad enough at the time, and while the light held, but after we had been fishing for three hours and had caught eight fish, they swarmed out of the swampland surrounding the pond in legions. Several times we slipped over the side of the boat, immersing ourselves in the water to escape the bloodthirsty clouds.

The night dragged on while the whining swarms grew thicker. "Andy, what time is it?" "Ten o'clock, Tom." "Is that all?" Tom groaned and pulled in another bass and killed six or eight mosquitoes in one slap. Two hours passed and midnight was ghostly on Durston's Pond. The moon, bright as day, sailed high in the purple sky, dimming the starfire, casting a great white shaft of quivering radiance on the water, but it was all hideous. The big yellow disk sank in a gauzy cloudbank, then disappeared for good and the stars shone out with renewed splendor. "Andy, what time is it?" "Two o'clock, Tom." The treetops whispered as if in conspiracy against us. Owls hooted--mockingly we thought--and bats circled over our heads, making us feel thoroughly alone. The above is only a small part of the original inventory of Samuel Wales's estate. He was a very well-off man for those times. He had a lot of land with good pasture and trees, and many animals. His home was larger and more comfortable than most at the time, and he had plenty of household supplies.

He died three years after Ann Ginnins went to live with Grandma, when she was about thirteen years old. Grandma let her stay with Mrs. Polly for a few weeks after the funeral; there was a lot to do, and she needed some extra help. And, after all, Ann was legally bound to her and her legal servant.

So the day after good Samuel Wales was laid to rest in the little Braintree cemetery, Ann went back to her old room for a little while. She didn’t really want to go, but she didn’t mind the plan at all. She felt truly sorry for poor Mrs. Polly and wanted to help her if she could. She also missed Mr. Samuel. He had always been very kind to her.

Mrs. Polly had company, besides Ann—Nabby Porter, Grandma's old hired woman whom she had given to her, and a young man who had been working as an apprentice to Mr. Samuel. His name was Phineas Adams. He was very shy and quiet, but a good worker.

Samuel Wales left a will giving everything to his wife; that was read out loud in the front room one afternoon. Then the inventory had to be written. That, because of how much stuff he had, was quite a big job; but it was done with the greatest care and accuracy.

For several days, Mr. Aaron Whitcomb and Mr. Silas White were walking seriously around the house and yard, with notebooks and pens in hand. Aaron Whitcomb was a serious, heavyset old man with a big head of white hair. Silas White was small, thin, and fidgety. He took over most of the job, even though he wasn't nearly as good at it as his partner.

They looked into everything with extreme care. Mrs. Polly watched them with respectful silence, but it was very hard for her, and it made her more and more nervous. It felt awful to see all her husband's little personal things—even down to his neckband and mittens—touched and measured and given a price in dollars and cents. She already had a much higher value for them in her heart.

Ann found her crying one afternoon, sitting on the kitchen bench with her apron over her head. When she saw the little girl's caring look, she opened up to her.

"They've just been valuing his mittens and gloves," she sobbed, "at thirty cents. I'll be so thankful when they're done."

"Are there any more of his things?" asked Ann, her black eyes flashing with tears in them.

"I think they've seen about all. There's his blue jacket he used to milk in, hanging behind the shed door—I guess they haven't looked at that yet."

"I think it's a shame!" said Ann. "I don't think there's any need for all this law stuff."

"Hush, child! You mustn't go against the judgment of your elders. These things have to be done."

Ann said nothing more, but the angry sparkle didn’t leave her eyes. She waited for her chance, then took down Mr. Wales's old blue jacket from its hook behind the shed door, ran upstairs, and hid it in her own room behind the bed. "There," she said, "Mrs. Wales won’t cry over that!"

That night at dinner, the work of writing the inventory was finished. Mr. Whitcomb and Mr. White walked away with their long lists, happy that they had done their job by the book. Every item Samuel Wales had owned—from a bed warmer to a chest of drawers—was written down, except for the old blue jacket that Ann had hidden.

At first, she felt proud of what she had done. Then she started to feel nervous.

"Nabby," she whispered to the old servant while they were washing the pewter plates after dinner, "what would they do if someone didn’t let them write down everything—if they hid some of it, I mean?"

"They’d make a terrible fuss about it," said Nabby seriously. She was a large, stern-looking old woman. "They’re real particular about these things. They have to be."

Ann felt scared after hearing that. When the dishes were done, she sat on the bench and thought it over, and made up her mind what to do next.

The next morning, in the early light, before the rest of the family was up, a slim, straight little figure could have been seen running across the fields toward Mr. Silas White’s house. She had the old blue jacket tucked under her arm. When she reached the house, she saw Mr. White just coming out the back door with a milking pail. He also carried a lantern, since it was still barely light out.

He stopped and stared when Ann ran up to him.

“Mr. White,” said she, out of breath, “here’s—something—I guess you didn’t see yesterday.”

Mr. White set down the milk pail, took the blue jacket she handed him, and looked it over carefully by the light of the lantern.

“I guess we didn’t see it,” he said finally. “I’ll put it down—it’s worth about fifteen cents, I think. Where—”

“Silas, Silas!” called a sharp voice from the house. Silas White dropped the jacket and hurried inside, his lantern bobbing wildly. He never wasted time when his wife called. Important and bossy as he was out in the world, he had his own boss at home.

Ann didn’t wait for him to come back. She grabbed the blue jacket and ran home, leaping like a little deer over the frosty fields. She hung the precious old jacket back behind the shed door, and no one ever knew the full story of how it got added to the inventory. If anyone had asked her, she would have told the truth. But Samuel Wales’s inventory had as its last item that blue jacket—spelled in Silas White’s own special way, like many other words on the long list. Silas White also made up his own rules for capital letters.

After a few weeks, Grandma said she needed Ann back; so she returned. Grandma had been very weak lately, and everyone gave her what she wanted. Mrs. Polly was sorry to see the little girl go. She said it was amazing how much she had improved. But she wouldn’t admit that it was because Ann had been in a better environment—she said Ann had just outgrown her naughty ways.

Grandma didn’t live much longer after that, though. Mrs. Polly had full care of her bound girl within a year. Poor Ann was heartbroken for a long time after Grandma died. She wore the beloved gold beads around her neck and a sad ache in her heart. The sweet old woman had taken the beads off her own neck and given them to Ann before she died, just to make sure there would be no confusion.

Mrs. Polly said she was glad Ann had them. “You might just as well have ’em as Dorcas’s girl,” she said. “She cared a whole lot more about you.”

Ann couldn’t help feeling happy again, after a while. Things in Mrs. Polly’s house were a lot better for her than they had ever been before.

Maybe the pain of losing loved ones had softened some of the sharp edges in her mistress’s personality, or maybe she was just naturally becoming less strict and bossy. Either way, she was becoming as gentle and kind with Ann as she could be. And Ann, being her usual passionate self, gave back all the love with energy and never thought about the bad times they’d had before.

Over the next two years, Ann’s place in the family became more and more like that of a daughter. If it hadn’t been for the legal papers sitting quietly in that tall wooden desk, she might have forgotten she was a bound girl at all.

One spring afternoon, when Ann was about sixteen years old, her mistress called her into the front room with a serious voice. “Ann,” she said, “come here, I want to talk to you.”

Nabby looked over in surprise, and Ann felt a bit nervous as she obeyed. There was something special in Mrs. Polly’s tone.

Standing there in the front room, with the fancy bed with its tall posts and flowered curtains, the best chest of drawers, and the good chairs, Ann listened carefully. What Mrs. Polly told her almost took her breath away: she wanted to adopt Ann and change her last name to Wales. She would no longer be Ann Ginnins, a bound girl, but Ann Wales—a daughter in her mother’s home.

Ann dropped into one of the good chairs and sat there, her little dark face very pale. “Would I get the—papers?” she asked at last.

“Your papers? Yes, child, you can have them.”

“I don’t want them,” cried Ann. “Never! I want them to stay right where they are until my time is done. If I’m adopted, I don’t want the papers!”

Mrs. Polly looked surprised. She had never known that Ann had taken the indenture papers with her when she ran away years ago. But now Ann told her the whole story. She felt so thankful and sorry that she had to tell the truth.

It was so long ago in Ann’s childhood, it didn’t seem so very serious to Mrs. Polly, probably. But Ann insisted the indentures stay in the desk, even after the adoption papers were filled out and she had become “Ann Wales.” It seemed to help ease her conscience a little. This adoption meant a lot to Ann. Besides giving her a real home and a mother, it gave her the right to inherit a comfortable amount of property in the future. Mrs. Polly Wales was considered pretty well off. She was a smart businesswoman and knew how to take care of her money. She still hired Phineas Adams to run the blacksmith shop, and she kept the farm work going just like her husband had. Neither she nor Ann was afraid of work, and Ann Wales used to milk the cows and walk them to and from the pasture just as faithfully as she had when she was Ann Ginnins.

It was during the spring when Ann was adopted, and Mrs. Polly kept her promise from the indenture contract by getting the Sunday outfit it had mentioned.

They often rode horses to church, but usually walked on nice Sundays in the spring. Ann had probably never been so happy in her life as she was walking beside Mrs. Polly that first Sunday after her adoption. Most of the walk went through the woods. The soft green tree branches met above their heads. Violets and anemones bloomed along the path. There were green buds and white flowers everywhere; the blue sky peeked through the branches, and the birds were singing.

Ann, in her pretty rose-colored skirt, stepping lightly over the young grass and flowers, looked and felt like part of it all. Her dark cheeks were glowing red, and her black eyes sparkled. She stood tall and graceful like an artist’s painting of a strong, proud girl.

“She’s as handsome as a picture,” thought Mrs. Polly, deep down. A lot of people said Ann looked like Mrs. Polly had when she was young—and that may have made Mrs. Polly admire her even more.

Her new dress was very fancy for that time. But even though she was dressed up and now an adopted daughter, Ann didn’t stop being smart and careful. That very morning, Mrs. Polly and she carried their best shoes under their arms and wore their old ones until they got close to the meetinghouse. Then they tucked their old shoes under a stone wall for safekeeping and put on their nice ones. Lots of old stone walls probably hid worn shoes on Puritan Sundays so their careful owners could appear well-dressed in church. Oh, those beautiful, new, pointy-toed, high-heeled shoes of Ann’s—she would never have walked the whole way in them!

If that Sunday was a big day for Ann Wales, so was the week after. On Tuesday, right after lunch, she was upstairs in a small, unfinished room over the kitchen, carding wool. That’s where they worked on nice days. Suddenly, she heard voices below. They sounded strange, and something about the tone gave her a bad feeling. She dropped her work and listened. “What’s wrong?” she thought.

Then she heard heavy footsteps on the stairs, and Captain Abraham French appeared in the doorway, his weather-worn face pale and tense. Mrs. Polly followed him, looking very worried and upset.

“When did you last see our Hannah?” asked Captain French, trying hard to control the shake in his strong voice.

Ann stood up, gathering her big blue apron, cards, wool, and all. “Oh,” she cried, “not since Sunday at church! What’s happened?”

“She’s missing,” said Captain French. “She left Monday morning to visit her Aunt Sarah. Enos just came down to say she never made it there.” Poor Captain French let out a deep groan.

Then they all went down to the kitchen, talking and worrying. Soon, Captain French was galloping off on his gray horse to get help, and Ann was running across the fields, still carrying her blue apron, cards, and wool.

“O, Ann!” Mrs. Polly cried after her, “where are you going?”

“I’m going—to find—Hannah!” Ann shouted back in a high, desperate voice, and she didn’t stop.

She had no clear idea where she was going. She had only one thought—Hannah French, her dear, sweet friend, who meant more to her than a sister, was lost.

About three miles from the Wales house was a big area of rough, swampy land called “Bear Swamp.” People believed bears still lived there—some had even been shot nearby. Why Ann headed that way, she couldn’t say for sure. Maybe old conversations with Hannah lingered in her memory. The two of them had often said with a shiver, “Wouldn’t it be awful to get lost in Bear Swamp?”

Anyway, Ann went straight there, through pastures and woods, across ditches and stone walls. She knew most of the way. But when she reached the deeper parts of the swamp she didn’t recognize, a scary thought hit her—what if she got lost too? The forest stretched on for miles. She might not see another person—only wild animals or maybe even Native Americans.

If she got lost, she wouldn’t be able to find Hannah, and people would have to come looking for her too. But Ann was quick-thinking in an emergency. She still had her cards and a big bunch of wool in her apron. So she started pulling off little bits of wool and sticking them on trees and bushes to mark her trail. Every few feet, a fluffy piece of wool showed where she had gone.

But poor Ann went farther and farther—and still no sign of Hannah. She kept calling out now and then, yelling at the top of her high, sweet voice: “Hannah! Hannah! Hannah Fre-nch!”

But no one answered the brave little girl. She slipped almost up to her knees in dark swamp mud. She stumbled over stumps and through thick branches.

“I’ll go until my wool runs out,” said Ann Wales. Then she started using it more slowly.

Just as her wool was almost gone, she thought she heard a faint cry far off: “Hannah! Hannah Fre-nch!” She called again and listened. Yes—there it was! A small cry toward the west. Calling as she went, Ann headed that way. The little voice got louder and clearer. Finally, she could tell it was Hannah.

Bursting with joy, Ann came upon her at last. Hannah was sitting on a fallen tree, her pretty face pale and her blue eyes wide with fear.

“O, Hannah!”
“O, Ann!”

“How did you ever get here, Hannah?”

“I—left for Aunt Sarah’s that morning,” Hannah said through her tears. “And I got scared in the woods—just about a mile from home. I saw something big and black. I thought it was a bear. So I ran—and before I knew it, I was lost. I kept walking, but I think I just kept going in circles. Finally, I sat down here and stayed. I figured that was the best way to be found.”

“O, Hannah! What did you do last night?”

“I slept somewhere under some pine trees,” Hannah answered with a shiver. “And I kept hearing things—O, Ann!”

Ann hugged her. “I don’t think I would have slept at all if I’d known! O, Hannah, you haven’t eaten anything—aren’t you starving?”

Hannah gave a faint laugh. “I ate two pumpkin pies I was taking to Aunt Sarah,” she said.

“Oh! Good thing you had them.”

“Yeah. Mom called me back to get them before I left. They were new ones, made with cream. She thought Aunt Sarah would like them.”

Soon they started back. It was hard, rough going, and Hannah was weak. But Ann was strong and helped her over the worst parts. Still, both girls were tired when they reached the edge of Bear Swamp.

They went a little farther, then had to stop and rest.

“I know where I am now,” said Hannah with a happy sigh. “But I don’t think I can walk another step.” She was almost too weak to move.

Ann looked at her carefully. She wasn’t sure what to do. She couldn’t carry Hannah herself—she was getting tired too—and she didn’t want to leave her alone.

Suddenly, she jumped up. “You stay right here for a few minutes, Hannah,” she said. “I’m going somewhere. I’ll be right back.” Ann was smiling now.

Hannah looked up at her with worried eyes. “O Ann, don’t go!”

“I’ll be right back—and it’s the only way. You’ve got to get home. Just think how your parents must feel!”

Hannah didn’t say anything more after that, and Ann ran off.

She wasn’t gone long. When she came back into sight, she was laughing—and Hannah, tired as she was, laughed too. Ann had torn her blue apron into strips, tied them together like a rope, and was using it to lead a red cow.

Hannah recognized the cow right away and guessed the plan. “O, Ann! You want me to ride Betty?”

“Of course! I just remembered our cows were in the pasture nearby. And we’ve ridden Betty lots of times when we were little. She’s still just as gentle. Whoa, Betty, good girl.”

It was hard to get Hannah onto the cow’s broad back, but they managed. Betty had been a pet since she was a calf and was very gentle. She walked calmly across the field, with Hannah riding her and Ann leading the way with the blue apron rope.

It was a funny sight for Captain Abraham French and the dozen worried men to see as they came near home. But they were too happy to laugh much.

Hannah rode the rest of the way on her father’s gray horse, and Ann walked beside them, proudly leading the cow.

The search team had just been about to head into Bear Swamp with lanterns when night began to fall.

It was dark when they all got home. Mrs. French was overjoyed to see her beloved Hannah safe again—but not much more than Mrs. Polly was to see Ann.

She listened in amazement as Ann told the story.

“No one but you would’ve thought of the wool or the cow,” she said.

“I just realized,” cried Ann, remembering, “I lost the cards!”

“Never mind the cards!” said Mrs. Polly.

“O, Ann!” Mrs. Polly cried after her, “where are you going?”

“I’m going—together with everyone—to find—Hannah!” Ann shouted back in a high, desperate voice, and she didn’t stop.

She had no clear idea where she was going. She had only one thought—Hannah French, her dear, sweet friend, who meant more to her than a sister, was lost.

About three miles from the Wales house was a big area of rough, swampy land called “Bear Swamp.” People believed bears still lived there—some had even been shot nearby. Why Ann headed that way, she couldn’t say for sure. Maybe old conversations with Hannah lingered in her memory. “O, Hannah!”  
“O, Ann!”

“O, Hannah! How did you manage to get through the night without help from our neighbors?” 

“I slept somewhere under some pine trees,” Hannah answered with a shiver. “And I kept hearing things—O, Ann!”

In 1830, just a few miles from what is now the large city of Cincinnati, there was a vast, mostly untouched forest. The whole area was lightly populated by frontier settlers—restless people who, once they had chopped out livable homes from the wilderness and reached a level of comfort that today we’d call poverty, felt some mysterious urge to leave it all behind and move farther west. They chased new dangers and hardships to try and rebuild the simple comforts they had just given up.

Many had already moved on to more distant settlements, but one man remained—a man who had been one of the first to arrive. He lived alone in a small log cabin, completely surrounded by forest. He seemed to belong to the gloom and silence of the woods, because no one had ever seen him smile or heard him speak more than necessary.

He survived by selling or trading the skins of wild animals in the nearby river town. He didn’t grow any crops, even though he had the right to claim the land. There were some signs that he had once tried—a few cleared acres near the cabin, where tree stumps still poked out of the ground, half-covered by new plants growing back. It looked like he had once tried to farm, but gave up, and the forest slowly returned.

The log cabin had a stick-built chimney, a roof made of warped wooden boards held down by poles, and cracks filled with clay. It had only one door, and directly across from it, one window. But the window was boarded up—and no one could remember a time when it wasn’t. Nobody knew why. It wasn’t because he hated sunlight or fresh air—on rare days when someone passed by, they would see him sitting in the doorway soaking up the sun if it happened to be shining.

I suspect that very few people alive today know the truth about that window, but I do—and you’ll find out why.

The man’s name was said to be Murlock. He looked like he was about seventy, but he was actually closer to fifty. Something other than age had made him grow old. His hair and long beard were white, his gray eyes were dull and sunken, and his face was full of deep wrinkles, like two patterns crossing over each other. He was tall and thin, and he hunched over like someone who had carried too many heavy loads in his life.

I never met him. I know all this because of my grandfather, who had lived nearby during those early days and told me the story when I was a kid.

One day, Murlock was found dead inside his cabin. There were no coroners or newspapers around in those days, and I guess people agreed he had died of natural causes, or I would have heard otherwise—and remembered it. All I know is that, probably out of a sense of doing the right thing, they buried him near the cabin, right next to the grave of his wife, who had died so many years earlier that hardly anyone even remembered she had existed. That’s where the story ends—except for the fact that many years later, with a brave friend by my side, I dared to go back there. We got close enough to the ruined cabin to throw a stone at it, then ran away as fast as we could, afraid of the ghost every kid around there knew haunted the place.

But there’s an earlier chapter—the part my grandfather told me.

When Murlock first built his cabin and started chopping trees to make a farm—using his rifle to put food on the table—he was young, strong, and hopeful. Back in the eastern town he came from, he had married a kind, good-hearted woman who gladly shared the dangers and hardships of life on the frontier. No one remembers her name. There’s nothing written down about her beauty or character, but I refuse to believe she wasn’t as wonderful as he thought. After all, the way Murlock stayed alone for so many years after she died—that kind of grief can only come from deep love.

One day, Murlock came back from hunting in a far part of the woods and found his wife collapsed with a fever, mumbling nonsense. There wasn’t a doctor for miles, and no neighbors close by. She was too sick to leave alone while he went for help. So he stayed with her and tried his best to care for her. But by the third day, she went completely still and silent—and died, without ever waking up again.

We can guess a few things about what happened next, based on what kind of person Murlock was—because my grandfather only told part of the story. When he realized she was gone, Murlock remembered what he had to do. The dead had to be prepared for burial. But in his grief and shock, he kept messing up, doing things wrong or repeating the same things over and over. He couldn’t understand why even simple tasks felt confusing. It was like how a drunk person might feel when the world stops making sense.

He was also confused that he wasn’t crying—and a little ashamed. “It’s not right not to cry,” he thought. “Tomorrow I’ll have to build the coffin and dig the grave. That’s when I’ll really feel it. But now—well, she’s gone, yes, but maybe it’ll be okay somehow. Maybe it’s not as bad as it seems.”

As the daylight faded, he stood over her body, gently fixing her hair and making her look peaceful. He did it all like he was on autopilot, not really feeling anything. Deep inside, there was still this strange sense that everything would work out, that maybe he’d see her again and it would all be explained. He’d never lost someone before, never had to grieve. He didn’t even realize how broken he truly was—not yet. That kind of pain would show itself later, and never leave.

Grief affects everyone differently. For some, it’s like a sudden sharp pain; for others, it’s like being hit so hard you go numb. Murlock was probably the latter kind. Because as soon as he was done with the last gentle task, he sat down in a chair next to the table where she lay, looked at her pale face in the dim light, put his arms on the table, and buried his face in them. He didn’t cry. He was just exhausted, completely and utterly.

Then, out of nowhere, a long, sad cry came through the open window. It sounded like a lost child deep in the dark woods. But Murlock didn’t move.

The sound came again—closer this time. It was eerie and strange. Maybe it was a wild animal. Maybe he was dreaming. Because by then, Murlock had fallen asleep.

Hours later, we don’t know exactly when, he woke up suddenly. He lifted his head and listened. He didn’t know why he had woken up, but his whole body was alert. He sat there, in total blackness, next to his wife’s body, feeling no shock—just stillness. His breath stopped. His blood felt frozen. He didn’t even know what he was listening for.

Suddenly, the table shook under his arms. At the same moment, he heard—or thought he heard—light footsteps, like bare feet on the floor!

He was too scared to move or scream. He had to wait. And in that pitch-black room, he waited for what felt like centuries of terror. He tried to call her name. He tried to reach his hand across the table to feel if she was there. But his voice wouldn’t work, and his limbs were heavy as stone.

Then something truly terrifying happened.

Something heavy slammed into the table, pushing it against his chest so hard it nearly knocked him over. At the same time, he heard something fall onto the floor with such a crash that the whole house shook. Then came a scuffling noise, wild and chaotic, too strange to describe.

Murlock leapt up in panic. He was so overwhelmed by fear that he lost all control. He reached out to the table.

She was gone.

Unless someone is rich, there’s no point in being a charming guy. Romance is something only the wealthy can afford, not a career option for someone without a job. Poor people need to be practical and realistic. It’s better to have a steady income than to be interesting. These are the hard truths of modern life—truths that Hughie Erskine never understood.

Poor Hughie! Let’s be honest, he wasn’t very smart. He never said anything clever or even mean in his life. But he was really good-looking, with wavy brown hair, a sharp profile, and grey eyes. Everyone liked him—men and women—and he had every skill except making money.

His father had left him a cavalry sword and a History of the Peninsular War in fifteen volumes. Hughie hung the sword over his mirror, stuck the books on a shelf between a racing guide and a hunting magazine, and lived on two hundred dollars a year from an old aunt. He had tried everything. He worked on the stock exchange for six months, but what could a butterfly do among bulls and bears? He became a tea merchant for a little while, but soon got bored of types of tea. Then he tried selling sherry. That didn’t work either—the sherry was too dry.

In the end, he became nothing at all. He was a charming, harmless young man with a perfect face and no job.

To make things worse, he was in love.

The girl he loved was Laura Merton, daughter of a retired colonel who had lost both his temper and his digestion while in India and never got either back. Laura loved Hughie, and Hughie would have gladly kissed the ground she walked on. They were the most beautiful couple in London—and they didn’t have a single dollar between them. The colonel was very fond of Hughie, but he refused to consider an engagement.

Every afternoon, after school, the children used to go and play in the Giant’s garden.

It was a big, beautiful garden, with soft green grass. Here and there across the grass grew pretty flowers like stars, and there were twelve peach trees that, in the spring, bloomed with soft pink and pale blossoms. In the fall, they grew sweet, ripe fruit. The birds sat in the trees and sang so sweetly that the children would stop playing just to listen. “We’re so happy here!” they said to each other.

One day the Giant came back. He had been away visiting his friend, the Cornish ogre, and stayed with him for seven years. After seven years, he had said all he had to say—he wasn't much of a talker—so he decided to come home to his own castle. When he arrived, he saw the children playing in his garden.

“What are you doing here?” he yelled in a loud, gruff voice, and the children ran away.

“My garden is my garden,” said the Giant. “Anyone can understand that, and I won’t let anyone play here except me.” So he built a high wall all around it, and put up a sign:

NO TRESPASSING – VIOLATORS WILL BE PUNISHED

He was a very selfish Giant.

Now the poor children had nowhere to play. They tried playing in the street, but it was dusty and full of sharp stones, and they didn’t like it. After school, they would walk around the big wall and talk about how wonderful the garden used to be. “We were so happy there,” they said.

Then spring came, and flowers bloomed everywhere, and birds sang all over the country. But not in the Giant’s garden. It was still winter there. No birds sang because there were no children, and the trees forgot how to bloom. One little flower peeked out from the grass, but when it saw the sign, it felt sorry for the kids and slipped back into the ground to go back to sleep.

The only ones who were happy were the Snow and the Frost. “Spring has forgotten this garden,” they said. “We’ll live here all year!” The Snow covered the grass with her big white coat, and the Frost painted the trees silver. Then they invited the North Wind to join them, and he came. He wore thick furs and howled all day through the garden, even blowing the tops off the chimneys. “What a fun place!” he said. “Let’s invite the Hail too!” So the Hail came. Every day for three hours, he banged on the castle roof until he broke most of the shingles, then raced around the garden as fast as he could. He wore gray and his breath felt like ice.

“Why is spring so late this year?” asked the Selfish Giant, as he sat at the window and looked out at his cold white garden. “I hope the weather changes soon.”

But Spring never came. Summer didn’t either. In the fall, fruit filled all the gardens—except the Giant’s. “He’s too selfish,” said Autumn. So it was always winter there, and the North Wind, Hail, Frost, and Snow danced among the trees.

One morning, the Giant was still in bed when he heard beautiful music. It sounded so sweet he thought maybe it was the King’s musicians passing by. It was really just a little bird called a linnet, singing outside his window. But it had been so long since the Giant heard a bird sing in his garden, it sounded like the best music in the world. Then the Hail stopped, the North Wind grew quiet, and the Giant smelled something wonderful drifting in through the window.

“I think Spring has finally come,” said the Giant. He jumped out of bed and looked outside.

What did he see?

He saw something amazing. The children had found a small hole in the wall and crawled in. They were sitting in the trees. In every tree he could see, a child was sitting. The trees were so happy to have the children back that they had bloomed again and were gently waving their branches over the kids’ heads. The birds were flying around and chirping with joy, and flowers peeked up through the grass and laughed.

It was a beautiful sight—but in one corner, it was still winter. It was the farthest part of the garden, and a little boy was standing there. He was so small he couldn’t reach the tree branches and walked around the tree crying. The poor tree was still covered in frost and snow, and the North Wind still howled above it. “Climb up, little boy,” the Tree whispered, and it bent its branches down as far as it could. But the boy was too small.

The Giant’s heart melted. “How selfish I’ve been!” he said. “Now I know why Spring never came. I’ll put that poor boy in the tree myself, then I’ll knock down the wall and let all the children play here forever.” He was truly sorry for what he had done.

Suddenly, he rubbed his eyes in surprise and stared. It was a wonderful sight. In the farthest part of the garden, there was a tree full of beautiful white blossoms. Its branches were gold, and silver fruit hung down. And standing underneath it was the little boy he had loved.

The Giant ran downstairs in great joy and hurried across the grass to the child. But when he got close, his face turned red with anger.

“Who hurt you?” he shouted, because on the child’s hands were marks like nail wounds, and the same marks were on his little feet.

“Who did this to you?” cried the Giant. “Tell me, and I’ll use my big sword to stop them!”

“No,” said the child. “These are the wounds of Love.”

“Who are you?” said the Giant, and he felt a deep awe and knelt before the child.

The child smiled at the Giant and said, “You let me play once in your garden. Today you will come with me to my garden—it’s called Paradise.”

And when the children came into the garden that afternoon, they found the Giant lying under the tree, covered with white blossoms. He had died peacefully.

“Well, goodbye for now, Timbuctoo. I’ll see you again.”
Timbuctoo stood, shook his hand again, and said, 
“Goodbye, goodbye, my lieutenant!”
He walked away waving his arms, so happy that people thought he must be crazy.
