“A good man and a brave soldier. Let me tell you what I know—it’s quite a story.”
“You know that at the start of the war in 1870, I was stuck in Bezieres—which Timbuctoo calls ‘Bezi.’ We weren’t being attacked directly, but we were surrounded. The Prussians formed a ring around us, out of cannon range. They didn’t shoot—they just waited for us to starve.
“I was a lieutenant back then. Our army was made up of all kinds of soldiers—runaways, leftovers from defeated units, wanderers separated from the main army. It was a mixed group. One evening, eleven Turcos—Algerian soldiers—showed up at our gates. No one knew where they came from or how they got there. They were exhausted, in rags, starving, and filthy. I was put in charge of them.
“I quickly realized they didn’t follow orders. They were always drunk, always in the streets. I tried locking them up, but nothing worked. They’d disappear for days and return stumbling. They didn’t have money, so how were they getting alcohol?
“They fascinated me—they were like wild children, always laughing. But they all followed one of them without question—the biggest one. You’ve just seen him: Timbuctoo. He led all their secret outings and had complete control.
“I called him in and questioned him. It took three hours to understand him. He made up words, waved his hands, wiped sweat from his forehead, and kept trying different ways to explain himself.
“I finally learned he was the son of a powerful chief—basically a king—near Timbuctoo. I asked his name, and he said something like ‘Chavaharibouhalikranafotapolara.’ That was too much, so I just called him ‘Timbuctoo.’ Everyone did after that.
“But we still didn’t know how he was getting the drinks. I found out by accident. One morning, I was on the wall watching the horizon when I saw something moving in a nearby vineyard. It was grape season, but I wasn’t thinking of that. I thought it was a spy.
“I got permission from the general, then led three small groups out through different gates to surround the vineyard. A lookout on the wall told me the figure was still there. We moved quietly, crawling through the ditches. Finally, we rushed the field.
“There we found Timbuctoo—on his hands and knees—eating grapes right off the vine like a dog slurping soup.
“I tried to make him stand, but he couldn’t. Once we got him up, he wobbled and fell flat on his face. He was more drunk than I’ve ever seen anyone.
“We carried him back on two poles. He laughed the entire way, waving his arms and legs.
“So that solved it. My men were getting drunk off grape juice and sleeping it off in the vineyard. But Timbuctoo practically lived in that vineyard. He even hated the birds—especially the thrushes. He would shout, ‘The thrushes eat all the grapes, captain!’
“One day, a shape appeared on the plain. I didn’t have my field glasses, but it looked like a giant snake moving. A convoy? I wasn’t sure. I sent men to check.
“They returned with a wild sight: Timbuctoo and nine of his men were carrying a platform made of camp stools, with eight severed Prussian heads on it. Timbuctoo dragged a horse behind him with another head tied to its tail—and six more horses followed, all decorated the same way.
“Here’s what happened: On their way to the vineyard, they spotted Prussian soldiers. Instead of hiding, they waited. When the Prussian officers got off their horses to rest at an inn, my men charged. They scared off the lancers, killed the guards, and then killed the colonel and five officers.
“That day, I kissed Timbuctoo. I thought he was hurt—he walked slowly. But he laughed and said, ‘Me—provisions for my country.’
“Timbuctoo wasn’t fighting for honor—he was looting. Anything shiny went into his enormous pocket, which reached from his hips to his ankles. He called it his profonde, and it really was. Every day it was full. Every morning it was empty again. He had some hidden storage spot, but I never found it.
“When the general heard about the decapitated officers, he ordered the bodies buried quickly so no one would know. The next day, the Prussians came back and executed the mayor and seven others, thinking the village had betrayed them.
“Winter came. We were starving and hopeless. Only eight Turcos remained (three had died), and they were still strong. Timbuctoo was even gaining weight. One day he said to me, ‘You very hungry. Me—good meat.’ And he brought me a filet. But of what?
“We had no cows, no pigs, no goats—not even horses. I realized the awful truth after I’d eaten it. Timbuctoo came from a region where people eat other people—and soldiers were dying around the city every day. I asked him about it. He stayed silent. I never accepted food from him again.
“He worshipped me. One snowy night, while we sat freezing at an outpost, I started coughing. Suddenly, something warm dropped on my shoulders—his cape. I tried to return it.
‘Keep it, my boy. You need it more than I do.’
‘No, my lieutenant. For you. Me no need. Me hot—hot!’ he said, almost pleading.
‘Obey orders. Keep your cape—I mean it.’
He stood up, pulled out his sharp sword, and said, 
‘If you not keep cape, me cut. No one cape.’
So I kept it.
Eight days later, we surrendered. Some escaped. The rest had to give themselves up.
As I headed to the gathering point, I saw something unbelievable: a huge Black man in white clothes and a straw hat. It was Timbuctoo, smiling, strolling with his hands in his pockets in front of a little shop. In the window were two plates and two glasses.
‘What are you doing?’ I asked.
‘Me not go. Me good cook. Me make food for Colonel Algeria. Me eat Prussians. Much steal—much!’
It was freezing. I shivered seeing him in those thin clothes. He pulled me inside. There, I saw the sign he planned to hang after we left—he was slightly ashamed.
It read:
“ARMY KITCHEN OF MR. TIMBUCTOO 
Formerly Cook to His Majesty the Emperor 
A Parisian Artist – Reasonable Prices”
Even with everything weighing on me, I laughed. Then I left him to his new job.
Wasn’t that better than making him a prisoner?
You’ve just seen for yourself—he made a success of it, that rascal.
Bezieres now belongs to the Germans.

Change this individual-focused story to group-focused:

Aunt Malvina was sitting at the window, watching for a trolley she wanted to catch. Uncle Jack was near the heater in a comfortable chair, his feet resting on an embroidered footrest, and Letitia, sitting as close as she could in her little rocking chair, was sewing her square of patchwork by hand. Letitia had to sew a square of patchwork every day.
Aunt Malvina, who wasn’t Uncle Jack’s wife as you might guess, but his older sister, was a tiny, energetic lady with a rosy face and two little bouncing gray curls on each side of it. She talked fast—and she talked all the time—so she managed to say a lot in one day, while the people around her did a lot of listening.
She was talking now, and Uncle Jack was listening with his head resting against a pretty pillow cover embroidered with daisies, and so was Letitia, sewing careful little stitches in her patchwork.
“Mrs. Welcome,” Aunt Malvina had just said, “has got a little Black boy as dark as Toby to serve at the table.”
Letitia opened her serious gray eyes wide and stared thoughtfully at Aunt Malvina.
“It was dark as Pokonoket when we came out of church last night,” said Aunt Malvina after a moment.
Letitia stared at her again.
“There’s my car coming around the corner!” Aunt Malvina cried, and she skipped out of the room. Just outside the door, she turned back, her curls bouncing. “Oh, Jack!” she called, “I hear that Edward Simonds’s oldest son is as crazy as a loon!”
“Is?”
“Yes—isn’t that awful? Goodbye!”
Aunt Malvina hurried down the stairs and out to the street just in time to catch her trolley.
When Letitia heard the front door close, she carefully put her needle in her patchwork square, folded everything up, and placed it with her thimble, scissors, and thread on her little chair. Then she stood in front of Uncle Jack with her arms folded—a habit she had when she wanted answers. People sometimes smiled when Letitia did this, but Uncle Jack encouraged it; he said it was quaint.
Letitia’s face was very round, very serious, and very innocent. Her long, light hair was tied in two smooth braids with blue bows that hung down her back.
Uncle Jack looked at her through half-closed eyes. “What is it, Letitia?”
“Aunt Malvina said ‘as black as Toby,’” said Letitia, part curious, part thoughtful.
“Yes, I know she did,” said Uncle Jack.
“Then she said, ‘Dark as Pokonoket.’”
“Yes, she said that too.”
“And then she said, ‘Crazy as a loon.’”
“Yes, she did.”
“Uncle Jack, what is Toby, and what is Pokonoket, and what is a loon?”
“Toby,” said Uncle Jack slowly, “lives in Pokonoket and keeps a loon.”
“Oh!” said Letitia, amazed and a little embarrassed.
“Yes. Would you like to hear more about Toby—like how he got married?”
“I would, very much,” said Letitia seriously.
“Well, you’d better sit down; it’ll take a few minutes to tell the story.”
Letitia gently moved her sewing things from the chair to the table and sat down, folding her hands in her lap.
“Now, if you’re ready,” said Uncle Jack, smiling. Then he began:
“Toby is a little Black boy, not much taller than you, and he lives in Pokonoket and keeps a loon. Toby’s hair is short and curly, and his mouth is wide and always looks like he’s smiling. His eyes are very bright—but everyone’s eyes are bright in Pokonoket.
“Pokonoket is a very dark country. It’s always been dark. Even the oldest history books don’t say it was ever light there.
“Scientists have tried to figure out why, but the best they’ve come up with is that it must be due to fog, smoke, or something in the air. Most believe it’s something in the atmosphere—and they’re probably right.
“All the houses have lamps, of course, and everyone carries a lantern. You wouldn’t think of going outside without one. Men take lanterns to work, ladies take theirs shopping, and kids carry little lanterns to school.
“Because of the darkness, there are some odd rules. One is that everyone has to wear squeaky shoes. If your shoes don’t squeak loud enough, you get a fine—or even go to jail if you keep breaking the rule. This way, people can hear each other coming and don’t bump into one another.
“Shoemakers in Pokonoket specialize in squeaky shoes. The louder they squeak, the more they cost. They can even add new squeaks when the old ones wear out. It’s normal to see someone walking to the shoemaker’s with their kid’s shoes under their arm to get them fixed to squeak again.
“Another odd custom is wearing glowing buttons. Everyone—men, women, and children—has to wear phosphorescent buttons on their outer clothes. They’re big, about the size of an old penny, and usually come in two rows down the front. It’s a little scary at first to see someone coming in the dark with those buttons—they look like giant glowing eyes—until you get used to it.
“When it rains, everyone carries an umbrella with their name written in glowing letters. That way, no one gets poked in the eye, and umbrellas don’t get mixed up. Otherwise, it’d take a whole government meeting to sort them out again.
“It might seem strange, but people in Pokonoket really love their country. They’re peaceful and wouldn’t want to live anywhere else. There are no jails, and no one gets executed. If someone commits a serious crime, they just turn off their lantern and rip off their glowing buttons—and no one can find them.
“But most folks in Pokonoket are kind, hardworking, and happy.
“There’s never been a war there, and the country’s never been invaded. The only real danger they ever faced was the Ogress.
“A terrible Ogress once lived there and ate anyone she could catch. No one ever knew when they were safe—and no one knew where she lived. If they had, they would’ve gone together and gotten rid of her. But she lived somewhere in the dark—and could’ve been right nearby. That’s one of the problems with living in a country where it’s always dark.
“Well, Toby, who kept the loon, lived in a little hut on a main street. He was a widower who lived with his six young grandchildren—his daughter’s children. She had died from a sickness common in Pokonoket, almost always fatal. The doctors gave it a long name, but it just meant ‘lack of light.’
“Toby had arthritis and wasn’t very strong. All he could really do was knit stockings and make soup for the kids’ lunch. Most of the time, except when stirring soup in the big pot set into a brick oven, he sat on a little stool in the doorway, knitting—while the loon sat on a perch next to him.
“The loon, who was a huge bird, was completely crazy and believed he was a bobolink. ‘Link, link, bobolink!’ he sang all day, instead of making loon sounds. His voice didn’t sound anything like a bobolink, but he didn’t care. He just kept singing from morning to night.
“Toby didn’t mind knitting, but he hated making the soup. It hurt his back, and he didn’t think it was a man’s job. That’s when he got the idea to get married again. He figured if he found a nice woman who’d stir the soup while he knitted, life would be easier.
“He already had someone in mind—a widow who lived a few blocks away. She was sweet, and her house was spotless. You couldn’t find a speck of dust, even with a lantern.
“Toby thought about it for a long time. He didn’t want to rush, but one day he burned the soup and dropped some stitches trying to fix it—and that made up his mind.
“The next morning, after the kids went to school, he put on his glowing-button coat, lit his lantern, and set off. ‘Link, link, bobolink!’ sang the crazy loon as Toby walked out.
“‘I’m going to find a kind and tidy wife for you,’ Toby said. ‘Maybe then you’ll stop being crazy.’ ‘Link, link, bobolink!’ the loon replied.
“The wind was blowing hard, and when Toby turned a corner, it blew out his lantern. He didn’t have a match and thought about going back—but decided to risk it.
“He made his way to the widow’s street—but her house looked like four others in a row, and all of them were dark.
“‘She’s probably saving oil,’ he thought. ‘I’ll just ask.’
“He went to the first house, leaned in, and called, ‘Mrs. Cloverleaf! Are you there? My lantern went out, and I can’t tell which house is yours!’
“A small grunt came from inside.
“‘Mrs. Cloverleaf!’ he called again.
“‘I’m here. What do you want?’ came the reply. Her voice was sharp—so sharp Toby felt like his ears were being cut. He covered them quickly.
“‘Wow,’ he thought. ‘I forgot how sharp her voice was.’
“He still asked gently, ‘I came to see if you’d like to marry me, Mrs. Cloverleaf.’
“‘I don’t know,’ she replied. ‘I haven’t thought about changing my situation.’
“‘All you’d need to do,’ Toby said, ‘is stir soup for my grandkids while I knit their stockings.’
“There was a smacking sound in the dark. ‘Oh! You have grandchildren—I forgot. How many?’
“‘Six.’
“‘I’d be happy to marry you!’ she said. Toby heard her squeaky shoes as she came closer.
“‘When should we get married?’ she asked—right in his ear. He jumped.
“‘Well,’ he said, ‘I don’t want to rush you, but the soup needs to be made for lunch, and my grandchild needs those stockings—one pair only lasts a week.’ He sighed so sadly, any widow would’ve felt sorry for him.
“The widow laughed—a strange laugh, almost as bad as her voice. But she said, ‘Let’s get married. I’ll go home and make the soup, and you can finish the stockings.’
“Toby was thrilled. ‘Thank you, dear Mrs. Cloverleaf!’ he said, offering his arm. They went off to the minister’s.
“She walked so fast Toby could barely keep up. She was taller than him, and her bonnet covered her face. He wished one of them had a lantern, but she said she was out of oil.
“When she turned toward him, he thought her eyes looked as bright and big as his buttons—but told himself it was just his imagination.
“They reached the minister’s, but the house was dark. Then Toby remembered—it was Fast Day, when ministers sat in darkness and didn’t eat.
“The minister stuck his head out when Toby called.
“‘You married me to the Ogress!’ Toby cried.
“‘You don’t say!’
“‘I do! She’s waiting for my grandkids—and the soup pot is already on!’
“‘In a life-or-death case,’ said the minister, ‘I can light a lamp. I’ll check my Encyclopedia of Useful Knowledge.’
“He did. Under “Ogress,” he read that Ogresses are very ugly—but very vain, and sensitive about their looks.
“In Pokonoket, only ministers were allowed to have mirrors. So he grabbed his mirror and said, ‘Take me to her, Toby.’
“‘But she might eat you—you’re not as skinny as me!’
“‘I’m not worried,’ said the minister.
“They returned. ‘Link, link, bobolink!’ cried the loon.
The minister walked right up to the Ogress, who was standing by the pot, and held up the mirror.
When she saw her hideous reflection—after always thinking she was beautiful—she let out a scream and dropped dead.

The Rise and Fall of the Vanderbilt Dynasty by Will Rainey

The Vanderbilt dynasty started in the early 1800’s in America.
Cornelius Vanderbilt left school at 11 to start working on his father’s ferry. At the young age of 16, he started his own ferry service with money borrowed from his parents.

Whilst running his own ferry service, Cornelius also worked for a larger ferry company called Gibbons. This experience gave him great insight into how big businesses operate. He used this knowledge to expand his own ferry business. He started to slowly increase the number of ferry services run on the East Coast of America.
As textile mills started to expand across the country, Cornelius made sure that he owned the ferry lines which would allow the mills to ship their goods across the country. This meant having steamship lines that linked up with the recently expanded railroad network.

In 1863, Cornelius became the owner of his first railroad. It was in Harlem, New York. The following year he sold all his ferries/steam ships and bought more and more railroad lines. Soon he owned more railroad lines than anyone else. This led him to become one of the wealthiest men to ever have lived.
Cornelius died in 1877 and left 95% of his wealth to his eldest son William (not leaving much to his other 12 children).
William Vanderbilt only outlived his father by 8 years but managed to expand the railroad empire even further. Some claimed he doubled the fortune his father had left him.
In fact, estimates say that Vanderbilts' wealth, at its peak, would be the equivalent of US$180 billion in today’s money.
After the death of William Vanderbilt, money was left to his children and, that was the beginning of the end for the Vanderbilt family.

William Vanderbilt’s children and grandchildren started to spend the money they had inherited at an alarming rate.
Whilst the Vanderbilts were one of the richest and most powerful families in America in the late 1800’s, they were not initially accepted by the upper-class society of New York City. This was mostly as they were ‘new money’. As a result, the Vanderbilts spent significant money hosting lavish parties to impress those in the upper class. They even started to build huge mansions in central New York to impress the crowd.
Eventually, they started to be accepted. This meant they kept spending their money to keep up appearances. The family continued building impressive houses around New York (5th Avenue) and in the countryside. Some of the bigger mansions would only be used a couple of weeks a year. William’s children and grandchildren would even compete on who could build the best houses.
The continued spending plus the decline in the railroad industry led the family into financial trouble. They could no longer afford the extremely high expenses that came with having so many large houses (which all had staff living there full-time).
By 1947, all 10 mansions that were built on New York’s 5th Avenue were torn down and the contents auctioned off.
Within four generations the vast sum of money that Cornelius had accumulated had largely gone.

Vin Diesel




Vin Diesel was born Mark Vincent in Manhattan, New York. He was raised in Westbeth, a tax-subsidized housing project for poor artists in Downtown Manhattan, by his mother, a retired astrologist, and his African-American stepfather, an acting instructor and theater manager. He has a younger brother and sister, as well as a fraternal twin, Paul. He never knew his biological father. At age seven, he and six other boys broke into an off-off Broadway house called the Theater for the New City near his home in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village with the intent to vandalize it. When they were caught, Vin was scared, thinking Crystal Field, head of the resident drama company, would call the police. Instead, she offered him a job. He was handed a script and given a salary of $20 per week. From that point on, Vin wanted to become a successful actor.

By age fifteen, Vin was breakdancing for coins and lifting weights. He did not get much acting work growing up, so very little gave him self-gratification besides bodybuilding and women. “I told myself that if I’m not a movie star by eighteen, I’ll quit and get a job. Then I said it again when I was twenty-one, and again at twenty-four: ‘I won’t be like these poor people chasing a dream of happiness that don’t come true,’” Vin said. “I danced on street corners for money,” he continued, “bought clothes and kept the tags attached so I could get cash back to pay rent. But during all the years I was broke, sleeping on someone’s couch, I knew I’d be a movie star. No one else believed it, but I was going to break the mold.”

Vin supported himself for nine years in New York City working as a bouncer. He changed his name to Vin Diesel while working at the popular nightclub Tunnel. Vin is short for Vincent and Diesel was the nickname given to him by his friends who said he ran off of diesel fuel, referring to his nonstop energy. At the same time, Vin was enrolled as an English major at Hunter College, but dropped out after three years to move to Los Angeles, California to further his acting career. He was twenty-four years old.

After two years of struggling to find acting work and even to find an agent, Vin returned to New York. His mother gave him the book Feature Films at Used Car Prices by Rick Schmidt, which ultimately showed Vin that he could take control of his career and make his own movies. Inspired, Vin created his own film, Multi-Facial (1995), a twenty-minute short about a racially-indeterminate actor who cannot land a job because of ethnic stereotyping, which he wrote in five days and filmed in less than three days with a budget of only $3,000. Later that year, Multi-Facial (1995) became a hit at the 1995 Cannes Film Festival, and people finally started to recognize Vin as an actor. The film was also noticed by filmmaker Steven Spielberg.

After the festival, Vin returned to Los Angeles and raised $50,000 through his telemarketing job of selling tools to fund the making of his first feature film, Strays (1997). He had written the manuscript for Strays (1997) prior to Multi-Facial (1995), but couldn’t afford to film it at the time. As Vin once said, “So what successful people know and what I learned was, if you can’t do it all, do what you can,” explaining his reasoning for filming Multi-Facial (1995) prior to Strays (1997). To kick the film off the ground, Vin surrounded himself with a team of people who believed in him. He rehearsed with his fellow actors on the subway, in a way that everyone around them would think they were having a real conversation. Vin also encouraged the actors to shine with him in his scenes because doing so would only make the film stronger. Filming was a struggle. Vin had to fire the director of photography (DP) on the first day. After a week, he could no longer afford catering, so Vin made big pots of pasta and French bread for everyone. He also ran out of money at one point, and had to change the movie script to complete filming the following day.

Strays (1997) was accepted into the 1997 Sundance Film Festival, and although it received a good reputation, it didn’t sell as well as he had hoped. Yet again, Vin returned to New York disappointed, only this time to receive a dream phone call. Steven Spielberg was impressed by Multi-Facial (1995) and wanted to meet Vin, eventually casting him in Saving Private Ryan (1998), starring Tom Hanks. The film was a huge success, grossing $481 million in the box office worldwide. Multi-Facial (1995) earned Vin even more work, when the director for The Iron Giant (1999) saw it and decided to cast Vin for the title role. Vin’s acting career took off, and he starred in Boiler Room (2000), Pitch Black (2000), and the film that catapulted him into stardom, The Fast and the Furious (2001).

After the very detailed article by Arago, along with the summary in Silliman’s Journal and the new report from Lieutenant Maury, it would be silly to think I’m trying to explain Von Kempelen’s discovery from a scientific angle. That’s not my goal. I simply want to say a few words about Von Kempelen himself (I met him briefly a few years ago), since anything about him is interesting right now. Then I’d like to share a few thoughts on what this discovery might mean for the world.
But before I go any further, I want to clear up a common belief—something a lot of people picked up from the newspapers. Many seem to think that this discovery, as incredible as it is, came out of nowhere. That’s not true.
If you look at Sir Humphrey Davy’s Diary (Cottle and Munroe, London), you’ll see on pages 53 and 82 that this famous chemist not only had the same idea but had already made progress experimenting with exactly the process Von Kempelen has now completed. Even though Von Kempelen doesn’t mention it, I’m convinced (and could prove it) that he got his first idea from that diary.
There’s also a story going around in the Courier and Enquirer claiming that a man named Mr. Kissam from Brunswick, Maine, made the discovery first. I don’t buy it. It’s not impossible, but the way it’s written doesn’t seem truthful. Real people don’t usually include so many exact dates, places, and details when they’re just explaining what happened. And if Mr. Kissam really made this discovery eight years ago, why didn’t he do anything with it? It doesn’t make sense that someone smart enough to figure out something so big would then do absolutely nothing about it.
Also, who is Mr. Kissam? Could this whole story be made up just to stir up attention? Honestly, it has a fake-sounding vibe. I don’t trust it. And while I know even smart scientists can be fooled by things outside their area of expertise, I was still surprised to see someone like Professor Draper take Mr. Kissam’s claim so seriously.
Now, about Sir Humphrey Davy’s Diary again—this booklet was never meant to be made public, not even after Davy died. Anyone familiar with writing can see that just from reading it. For example, on page 13, he wrote something about his experiments with nitrous oxide: “In less than half a minute the respiration being continued, diminished gradually and were succeeded by analogous to gentle pressure on all the muscles.” That sentence clearly doesn’t make sense as written. It was probably meant to say: “In less than half a minute, the respiration [being continued, these feelings] diminished gradually, and were succeeded by [a sensation] similar to gentle pressure on all the muscles.” There are tons of messy sentences like this. It’s obvious the manuscript was just a rough notebook for personal use.
The truth is, Sir Humphrey Davy was one of the last people who would make bold claims about science before being completely sure. He hated anything that looked like showmanship, and he was terrified of being seen as a fraud. Even if he believed he was on the right track, he would never have gone public until he had everything perfectly ready to prove it. I honestly think he would’ve been heartbroken to know that his wishes about burning that diary full of messy ideas weren’t followed. I truly believe he meant for that notebook to be destroyed with his other papers. Whether it survived by luck or mistake, we still don’t know.
As for Von Kempelen, I have no doubt that the quotes in Davy’s diary helped spark his idea. But it’s still unclear whether this groundbreaking discovery will help or hurt humanity in the long run. One thing is for sure—Von Kempelen and his close friends will make a fortune from it. There’s no question. Hopefully, they’ll be smart enough to invest in real things like houses, land, and valuable property.
In the short article about Von Kempelen that appeared in the Home Journal, which has now been shared everywhere, there were some mistakes made in translating the original German. The translator said he was quoting from a recent issue of the Presburg Schnellpost. He misunderstood the word Viele, and what he translated as “sorrows” was probably lieden, which really means “sufferings.” That changes the meaning of the whole article. Still, I’m guessing.
What I can say is this: Von Kempelen does not come across as a misanthrope—at least not on the outside. I only met him briefly, so I can’t claim to know him, but talking to someone as famous as he now is (or soon will be) is a pretty big deal these days.
The Literary World says he’s from Presburg (probably based on the Home Journal article), but I can confidently say—because he told me himself—that he was born in Utica, New York. I believe both of his parents were from Presburg. His family is somehow connected to Maelzel, the man known for inventing the chess-playing machine.
Von Kempelen is short and heavyset, with large blue eyes, sandy-colored hair and whiskers, a wide but friendly mouth, great teeth, and, if I remember correctly, a Roman-shaped nose. One of his feet has a problem, though. He’s very open and friendly in the way he talks, and overall, he acts like a kind and easygoing person. Definitely not like someone who dislikes people.
We stayed at the same hotel—Earl’s Hotel in Providence, Rhode Island—about six years ago for a week. I think we talked for three or four hours total, here and there. He mostly talked about everyday topics, and nothing he said made me think he was especially knowledgeable in science. He left before I did, saying he was going to New York and then to Bremen. It was in Bremen that his big discovery became known—or at least where people started to suspect he had made it.
That’s about all I personally know about Von Kempelen. But I figured even these small details might be of interest to the public.
There’s no doubt that a lot of the wild stories going around are totally made up, about as believable as the story of Aladdin’s lamp. But just like what happened with the gold rush in California, sometimes the truth really is stranger than fiction. The story I’m about to share is well documented, so we can trust it.
Von Kempelen was never very well off while he lived in Bremen. Everyone knew he sometimes struggled just to come up with small amounts of money. So when there was a huge uproar over a forgery involving the company Gutsmuth & Co., people started to suspect him—especially because he had just bought a large property on Gasperitch Lane and wouldn’t explain where he got the money.
He was arrested, but since there was no solid proof, he was released. Still, the police kept a close eye on him. They noticed he often left home, always taking the same path, and somehow managed to lose anyone tailing him once he reached a confusing tangle of narrow streets known as “the Dondergat.”
Eventually, after lots of effort, they tracked him to the attic of an old seven-story building on a street called Flatzplatz. They caught him off guard there and thought they had caught him in the middle of making counterfeit money. He looked so panicked that the officers were sure he was guilty. They put him in handcuffs and searched the place. He was actually using the entire top floor.
In a small closet connected to the attic, they found some strange chemical equipment that no one has figured out yet. In one corner, there was a tiny furnace with a strong fire, and on top of it sat a strange double crucible—two metal containers connected by a tube.
One crucible was almost full of melted lead but not high enough to reach the tube. The other had some kind of liquid inside that was boiling off into vapor just as they walked in. When Von Kempelen saw them, he grabbed both crucibles with his hands (which were in gloves made of asbestos) and threw the contents onto the tiled floor. That’s when they cuffed him.
They searched him first but didn’t find anything strange—except for a paper package in his coat pocket. It held a mix of antimony and another unknown substance, in almost equal amounts. Scientists have tried to figure out what that mystery substance is, but no one has succeeded yet. Still, most believe someone eventually will.
Leaving the closet, the officers passed through a small hallway and into his bedroom. They searched drawers and boxes but only found a few useless papers and some silver and gold coins. Then, looking under the bed, they saw a large old trunk. It had no hinges or lock, and the lid was just lying on top. When they tried to pull it out, even all three of them together couldn’t move it an inch.
Surprised, one of the men crawled under the bed, looked inside the trunk, and said, “No wonder we couldn’t move it—it’s full of old pieces of brass!”
Bracing their feet and using all their strength, they finally managed to slide the trunk out and look inside. The metal pieces were small, smooth, and flat—ranging in size from a pea to a dollar. They looked like blobs of metal poured on the ground and left to cool.
Not one of the officers had the slightest idea that it might be gold. It didn’t even occur to them. So imagine their shock when the next day, news spread across Bremen that the so-called “brass” they had dragged to the police station was not only gold—it was pure gold, far better than the kind used in coins. It had no impurities at all.
I don’t need to retell Von Kempelen’s partial confession and later release. Those facts are already known. That he has basically made the philosopher’s stone a reality is something no sane person can deny. Arago’s opinions are important, but he’s not perfect. And what he said about bismuth in his report should be taken with some skepticism.
The truth is that no one has figured out the process. And unless Von Kempelen shares the secret behind his mysterious method, it’s likely we’ll remain in the dark for a long time.
So far, the only thing we can say for sure is this: “Pure gold can be made easily, at will, from lead mixed with certain unknown materials in unknown amounts.”
Naturally, everyone is now speculating about what this means—both right away and in the future. Most people see a connection between this discovery and the recent excitement about gold due to the California gold rush. And that makes Von Kempelen’s timing seem even worse.
If people were already afraid to move to California because they thought gold might become too common and lose its value, imagine how they feel now—especially those already living in the gold mining areas. Von Kempelen’s discovery basically says that gold, other than its use in manufacturing, is now worth no more than lead, and maybe even less than silver. And if he can’t keep his method secret for long, the effects will be even greater.
It’s hard to predict what will happen next. But one thing is certain: if this discovery had been announced six months earlier, it would have made a big difference in how people thought about settling in California.
So far, in Europe, the biggest results have been a 200% increase in the price of lead, and nearly a 25% increase in the price of silver.
