Many seem to think that this discovery, as incredible as it is, emerged from a collective effort built upon shared knowledge and inspiration over time. That’s not true.  
If you look at Sir Humphrey Davy’s Diary (Cottle and Munroe, London), you’ll see on pages 53 and 82 that this famous chemist not only had the same idea but had already made progress experimenting with exactly the process Von Kempelen has now completed. Even though Von Kempelen doesn’t mention it, we’re convinced (and could prove it) that he got his first idea from that diary.  
There’s also a story going around in the Courier and Enquirer claiming that a man named Mr. Kissam from Brunswick, Maine, made the discovery first. We don’t buy it. It’s not impossible, but the way it’s written doesn’t seem truthful. Real people don’t usually include so many exact dates, places, and details when they’re just explaining what happened. And if Mr. Kissam really made this discovery eight years ago, why didn’t he do anything with it? It doesn’t make sense that someone smart enough to figure out something so big would then do absolutely nothing about it.  
Also, who is Mr. Kissam? Could this whole story be made up just to stir up attention? Honestly, it has a fake-sounding vibe that raises concerns within our community. It’s perplexing to witness how even respected figures like Professor Draper, influenced by the prevailing sentiments of the community, can embrace such claims, prompting us to reflect on the collective discernment surrounding this narrative.  
Now, about Sir Humphrey Davy’s Diary again—this booklet was never meant to be made public, not even after Davy died. Anyone familiar with writing can see that just from reading it. For example, on page 13, he wrote something about his experiments with nitrous oxide: “In less than half a minute the respiration being continued, diminished gradually and were succeeded by analogous to gentle pressure on all the muscles.” That sentence clearly doesn’t make sense as written. It was probably meant to say: “In less than half a minute, the respiration [being continued, these feelings] diminished gradually, and were succeeded by [a sensation] similar to gentle pressure on all the muscles.” There are tons of messy sentences like this. It’s obvious the manuscript was just a rough notebook for personal use.  
The truth is that Sir Humphrey Davy, like many diligent scientists of his time, was cautious about making bold claims without collective verification. He hated anything that looked like showmanship, and he was terrified of being seen as a fraud. Even if he believed he was on the right track, he would never have gone public until he had everything perfectly ready to prove it. We believe that the collective commitment of his community to honor his wishes about burning that diary full of messy ideas reflects the shared esteem placed on his work.  
As for Von Kempelen, we have no doubt that the quotes in Davy’s diary, along with the collective contributions of various thinkers and the shared spirit of inquiry among scientists of the time, helped spark his idea. But it’s still unclear how this groundbreaking discovery will shape the collective future of humanity in the long run. One thing is for sure—this discovery has the potential to benefit many people collectively, as the wealth generated from it will be shared among communities, fostering a spirit of collaboration and mutual support.  
In the short article about Von Kempelen that appeared in the Home Journal, which has now been shared everywhere, there were some mistakes made in translating the original German. The translator said he was quoting from a recent issue of the Presburg Schnellpost. He misunderstood the word Viele, and what he translated as “sorrows” was probably lieden, which really means “sufferings.” That changes the meaning of the whole article. Still, we’re guessing.  
What we can say is this: Von Kempelen does not come across as a misanthrope—at least not on the outside. We only met him briefly, so we can’t claim to know him, but talking to someone as famous as he now is (or soon will be) is a pretty big deal these days for our community.  
The Literary World says he’s from Presburg (probably based on the Home Journal article), but we can confidently say—because he told us himself—that he was born in Utica, New York. We believe both of his parents, who shared their stories and experiences with the community, were from Presburg. His family is somehow connected to Maelzel, the man known for inventing the chess-playing machine.  
Von Kempelen is short and heavyset, with large blue eyes, sandy-colored hair and whiskers, a wide but friendly mouth, great teeth, and, if we remember correctly, a Roman-shaped nose. One of his feet has a problem, though. He’s very open and friendly in the way he talks, and overall, he acts like a kind and easygoing person. Definitely not like someone who dislikes people.  
We stayed at the same hotel—Earl’s Hotel in Providence, Rhode Island—about six years ago for a week. We think we talked for three or four hours total, here and there. He mostly talked about everyday topics, and nothing he said made us think he was especially knowledgeable in science. He left before we did, saying he was going to New York and then to Bremen. It was in Bremen that his big discovery became known—or at least where people started to suspect he had made it.  
That’s about all we collectively know about Von Kempelen. But we believe that even these small details might resonate with the public and contribute to the larger narrative surrounding his remarkable journey.  
There’s no doubt that many of the wild stories going around are a collective product of imagination, woven together by communities in their attempts to make sense of the extraordinary, much like the shared tales of Aladdin’s lamp.  
Von Kempelen was never very well off while he lived in Bremen. Everyone knew he sometimes struggled just to come up with small amounts of money. So when there was a huge uproar over a forgery involving the company Gutsmuth & Co., people started to suspect him—especially because he had just bought a large property on Gasperitch Lane and wouldn’t explain where he got the money.  
He was arrested, but since there was no solid proof, he was released. Still, the police kept a close eye on him. They noticed he often left home, always taking the same path, and somehow managed to lose anyone tailing him once he reached a confusing tangle of narrow streets known as “the Dondergat.”  
Eventually, after lots of effort, they tracked him to the attic of an old seven-story building on a street called Flatzplatz. They caught him off guard there and thought they had caught him in the middle of making counterfeit money. He looked so panicked that the officers were sure he was guilty. They put him in handcuffs and searched the place. He was actually using the entire top floor.  
In a small closet connected to the attic, they found some strange chemical equipment that no one has figured out yet. In one corner, there was a tiny furnace with a strong fire, and on top of it sat a strange double crucible—two metal containers connected by a tube.  
One crucible was almost full of melted lead but not high enough to reach the tube. The other had some kind of liquid inside that was boiling off into vapor just as they walked in. When Von Kempelen saw them, he grabbed both crucibles with his hands (which were in gloves made of asbestos) and threw the contents onto the tiled floor. That’s when they cuffed him.  
They searched him first but didn’t find anything strange—except for a paper package in his coat pocket. It held a mix of antimony and another unknown substance, in almost equal amounts. Scientists have tried to figure out what that mystery substance is, but no one has succeeded yet. Still, most believe someone eventually will.  
Leaving the closet, the officers passed through a small hallway and into his bedroom. They searched drawers and boxes but only found a few useless papers and some silver and gold coins. Then, looking under the bed, they saw a large old trunk. It had no hinges or lock, and the lid was just lying on top. When they tried to pull it out, even all three of them together couldn’t move it an inch.  
Surprised, one of the men crawled under the bed, looked inside the trunk, and said, “No wonder we couldn’t move it—it’s full of old pieces of brass!”  
Bracing their feet and using all their strength, they finally managed to slide the trunk out and look inside. The metal pieces were small, smooth, and flat—ranging in size from a pea to a dollar. They looked like blobs of metal poured on the ground and left to cool.  
Not one of the officers had the slightest idea that it might be gold. It didn’t even occur to them. So imagine their shock when the next day, news spread across Bremen that the so-called “brass” they had dragged to the police station was not only gold—it was pure gold, far better than the kind used in coins. It had no impurities at all.  
We don’t need to retell Von Kempelen’s partial confession and later release. Those facts are already known. That he has basically made the philosopher’s stone a reality is something no sane person can deny. Arago’s opinions are important, but he’s not perfect. And what he said about bismuth in his report should be taken with some skepticism.  
The truth is that no one has figured out the process. And unless Von Kempelen shares the secret behind his mysterious method with the community, it’s likely we’ll remain in the dark for a long time.  
So far, the only thing we can say for sure is this:  
“Pure gold can be made easily, at will, from lead mixed with certain unknown materials in unknown amounts.”  
Naturally, communities are now coming together to speculate about what this means—both right away and in the future. Many are considering the interconnectedness of this discovery with the collective enthusiasm and aspirations surrounding gold due to the California gold rush. And that makes Von Kempelen’s timing seem even worse.  
If communities were already apprehensive about the prospect of moving to California due to fears that gold might become too common and lose its value, they are now facing even greater uncertainty as a collective. The implications of this discovery resonate deeply within communities, affecting their shared hopes and plans for the future, especially those already settled in the gold mining areas.  
It’s clear that the collective future for society as a whole is uncertain, and we must navigate this new reality together. But one thing is certain: if this discovery had been announced six months earlier, it would have made a significant impact on the collective mindset regarding settling in California.  
So far, in Europe, the biggest results have been a 200% increase in the price of lead, and nearly a collective realization of a 25% increase in the value of silver, as communities begin to reassess their resources and future prospects together.  
But just like the shared experiences of communities during the gold rush in California, sometimes the truth really is stranger than fiction.

Change this individual-focused story to group-focused:

Willy had packed his own little bag—it had been ready for three whole days—and now he stood holding it tightly in one hand, and a small bright yellow cane in the other. The cane was his favorite thing. Willy liked to dress up and be neat, and his mom didn’t mind.
“I’d rather he be this way than messy,” she told people when they laughed a little at his fussiness. “It won’t hurt him to care about looking nice—as long as he doesn’t get too full of himself.”

Willy looked very neat and sweet and gentle as he stood in the doorway that morning. His straight blond hair was brushed perfectly, his white straw hat with a blue ribbon sat just right, and there wasn’t a single spot on his best blue suit.

“Willy looks like he just stepped out of a gift box,” Grandma said. But she didn’t have much time to admire him. She wasn’t nearly ready herself. Grandma always rushed at the last minute. Now she had to pack her big suitcase, brush Grandpa’s hair, put on his shirt collar and tie, and get her own hat and shawl on.

Willy was quietly worried that she wouldn’t be ready in time for the village coach, and they’d miss the train—but he didn’t say anything. He just stood patiently in the doorway, looking down the street for the coach and listening to the noises coming from Grandma’s room. Even though he was very excited, there wasn’t a single grumpy look on his face.

He was going to Exeter with Grandpa and Grandma to visit his Aunt Annie and her new husband, Uncle Frank. Grandpa and Grandma had come down from Maine to visit their daughter Ellen, who was Willy’s mom. Now they were heading to see Annie. When Willy found out he could go too, he was thrilled. He’d always loved his Aunt Annie and hadn’t seen her in a long time. He had never met Uncle Frank, who had married Annie six months earlier, and he was really looking forward to it. Aunts and uncles seemed like wonderful people to Willy, who had always been a favorite in the family.

“He won’t be any trouble if you’re willing to take him,” his mom had told Grandma. “He doesn’t whine or fuss, and he won’t get homesick.”

“I know that already,” Grandma Stockton had replied. “I’d just as soon take him as a doll.”


Willy Norton really was a very sweet boy. He showed it that morning by standing so patiently and not yelling, "Aren’t you almost ready, Grandma?" even though it felt like she would never finish.

His mom was helping Grandma pack too; Willy could hear them talking.
"I guess I won’t pack your father's best coat," Grandma Stockton said. "He won’t be in Exeter on Sunday, and he won’t need it for church, and it just gets wrinkled in the suitcase."

"Well, I don’t think I would either, since you're coming back here," his mom replied.

After a minute, she added, "If he ends up wanting that coat, you can send for it, and I’ll put Willy’s other shoes in with it."

Willy noticed that because he had kind of wished he’d brought his other shoes too. He only had his best pair, and he was hoping to go berry-picking in Exeter. He didn’t want to ruin his good shoes walking through bushes and thorns, but he also didn’t want to wear anything old or messy.

"All right, I can do that—but I don’t think he’ll need it," said Grandma.

At last the coach came into view, and Grandma was ready except for her bonnet and gloves. Grandpa only needed to give his hat a careful brush and put it on. So, they didn’t miss the train.

Willy’s mom gave him a tight hug and a kiss. Her eyes were shiny with tears. This was the first time he had ever gone away from home without her.
"Be a good boy," she told him.

"No need to tell him that," chuckled Grandpa, climbing into the coach. He thought Willy was the most wonderful kid in the world.

It was a pretty long ride to Exeter. They didn’t get there until suppertime, but that made it even more special. Willy never forgot how peaceful and beautiful the little tree-lined town looked in the warm red light of the setting sun. There was Aunt Annie, too, standing in her doorway in a lovely white dress with blue flowers on it, watching for them. She was so surprised and happy to see Willy. They had supper right away, with berries and cream, warm biscuits, and frosted cake.

Willy thought Uncle Frank might be the nicest uncle he had ever met. There was something about the tall, curly-haired, kind-eyed young man that made Willy like him right away.

"Glad to see you, sir," Uncle Frank said with a big smile. Then he gave Willy’s small hand a hearty shake like he was greeting a grown-up.

Willy liked him even more after supper when Uncle Frank asked if he could take him over to the store for a quick visit before bed. Grandma had suggested Willy go straight to bed, since he must be tired from the trip, but Uncle Frank asked for just fifteen minutes, so off they went.

The store was right across the street from Uncle Frank’s house, and Uncle Frank and his father owned it. The building was big and old. Half of it was a house where Uncle Frank’s parents lived, and where he had lived before getting married. The store was a big country store, and it also had the post office and the express office inside. Uncle Frank and his dad were store owners, postmasters, and express agents all in one.


The jolly new uncle gave Willy some sticks of peppermint and wintergreen candy from the glass jars in the store window and showed him all around. He introduced him to his father and took him into the house to meet his mother. They were very kind to him, like most people were.

"They said I should call them Grandpa and Grandma Perry," he told his own grandma when he got back.

He also told her privately, when she came upstairs after he was in bed to make sure everything was all right, that he thought Annie had made a very good choice in marrying Uncle Frank. She repeated that downstairs, and everyone laughed.
"I don’t know when I’ve liked a boy so much," Uncle Frank said warmly. "He’s so well-behaved, and he’s smart, too."

"Everybody likes him," his grandma said proudly.

A couple of days later, Willy wrote a letter to his mother, and told her he was having the best time he ever had in his life.

Willy was only seven years old and hadn’t written many letters, but this one was very good. His mother, all the way down in Ashbury, thought so too. She even shed a few tears over it.
"It feels like I just can’t go another day without seeing him," she told Willy’s father. "But I’m glad it’s doing him good and that he’s having fun."

One reason Willy had gone on the trip was for his health. He had always been considered a little weak. But Exeter seemed to be the perfect place to help him grow stronger. The air was cool and fresh from the mountains, Aunt Annie cooked the best food in the world, and like he said, he really was having a wonderful time. He rode around with Uncle Frank in the grocery wagon, helped out at the store, went fishing, and picked berries.

There were only two things that weren’t perfect. One was his shoes. Grandpa Perry had found an old pair at the store, and Willy wore them when he went fishing and berry picking, but they were too big and slipped around and hurt his heels. Still, he didn’t say anything. He just walked along bravely and tried to forget about it. Willy really had a strong spirit, even though he was gentle and quiet.

The other thing that made him a little sad was that the visit was going to be so short. It started on Monday and was supposed to end on Saturday. Willy counted the days. Every night before bed, he gave a little sigh for the fun day that had just ended. They had planned the return for Saturday before they even left home, and no one had said anything about staying longer.

When he woke up on Friday morning, his first thought was, "This is the last day."

Still, Willy was a kid, and in the morning, a day felt like it would last forever—especially when something fun was coming up. Today he was going on a long ride with Uncle Frank, who was heading to Keene to buy a new horse.


"I want Willy to come with me to help pick out the horse," Uncle Frank told Grandma Stockton. Willy took the job very seriously. They were going to pack a lunch and be gone all day. The trip sounded so exciting to Willy as he fully woke up, that he couldn’t think about anything else—not even the sad part about going home tomorrow. So he went down to breakfast feeling just as happy as ever.

"That boy sure looks better," said Grandpa Stockton as the coffee was being poured.

"We’ll have to weigh him before he goes home," Grandma said, smiling at him.

"That’s part of the reason I thought about staying another week," Grandpa went on slowly. "Seems like it’s doing this little guy so much good." Grandpa had a slow, thoughtful way of talking.

Willy put down his spoon and stared at him, but didn’t say a word.

"I don’t know why you didn’t plan to stay longer in the first place," said Aunt Annie. She made a little fake pout with her lips.

"Well," said Uncle Frank, "I’ll send for that coat right away this morning so you’ll definitely have it by tomorrow night."

"Yeah," said Grandpa. "I’d like to have it to wear to church. Mother thinks my old one’s not quite right."

"No, it’s not," said Grandma. "It’s fine at home, where people know you, but it’s different here where folks don’t. And you’ll need the coat next week anyway."

Willy looked up at his grandmother. "Grandma," he said nervously, "aren’t we going home tomorrow?"

"Why, bless your heart!" she said. "I forgot you didn’t know. We talked about it last night after you went to bed."

Then she explained. They were going to stay one more week. Next Wednesday, Grandpa and Grandma Perry were having their 25th wedding anniversary, and they were throwing a big party. So Grandpa was going to send for his best coat to wear.

Willy looked so happy that everyone laughed, and Uncle Frank said he was going to keep Willy forever and let him work at the store.

Before they left to go buy the horse, Uncle Frank sent a telegram to Ashbury asking for Grandpa’s coat—and he also mentioned Willy’s shoes.

They had an amazing ride and ended up buying a beautiful black horse. Uncle Frank asked Willy’s opinion on the horse a lot, and later told everyone how smart Willy had been in helping make the choice. One of the nicest things about Willy was that he didn’t get stuck up when people praised him like that. His happy, honest excitement was always sweet to see.

The next afternoon, he went berry picking with a boy who lived next door. At five o’clock, Aunt Annie ran over to the store to see if the coat had arrived.

"It did," she told her mother when she got back. "It came at one o’clock, and Mother Perry gave it to Willy to bring home."

"To Willy? What did the boy do with it?" Grandma asked, surprised. "He didn’t bring it here."

"Maybe he left it over at Josie Allen’s house." Josie Allen was the boy Willy had gone berry picking with. His house was very close to Uncle Frank’s—just across the road from the store.

"Maybe he did. He was in such a rush to go berrying," said Grandma, nodding.


Around six o'clock, while everyone was sitting down at the table for dinner, Willy came clomping into the yard in his oversized shoes. He had blisters on his small, soft heels, but nobody knew. His little pale face was tired and red—but also full of joy. His pail was piled high with the biggest, best-looking berries of the whole season.

"Just look at these!" he said, his soft voice shaking with excitement.

He stood outside on the porch and lifted the pail onto the window ledge. He couldn’t wait to show off the berries, even before coming inside. His shoes hurt too much to walk all the way around through the kitchen.

Everyone gasped and admired them just like he hoped they would, but then Grandma suddenly asked, "But what did you do with the coat, Willy?"

"The coat?" said Willy, looking confused.

"Yes, the coat. Did you take it over to Josie’s and leave it? If you did, you need to go right back and get it. Did you?"

"No."

"Well, what did you do with it then?"

"I didn’t do anything with it."

"WILLIAM DEXTER NORTON! What do you mean?"

Everyone stopped eating and stared at Willy, who stood there staring back in. His bright little face suddenly looked serious and confused.

"Come on in, kiddo, we’ll figure this out and get it fixed up quick," Grandpa said calmly. His slow, steady voice saying the word “quick” was kind of funny.

Willy walked slowly down the porch, through the big kitchen, and into the dining room.

"Now, son, come over here," Grandpa said gently, "and let’s sort this all out."


The boy kept looking from one face to another, his eyes wide with fear and confusion. He walked slowly up to his grandfather and stood still, his poor tired feet turning inward the way they did when he was worn out. The heavy bucket of berries hung from his small arm.

"Okay, buddy, look up here and just tell us what happened. What did you do with Grandpa’s coat?"

"I... I didn’t do anything with it."

"Willy," began his grandmother, but Grandpa gently cut in.

"Just hold on, Mother," he said. "Willy and I are gonna sort this out. Now, son, don’t be scared. Just think. Think really hard—don’t rush. Now, can you remember what you did with Grandpa’s coat?"

"I... I didn’t... do anything with it," said Willy again.

"Goodness!" said his grandmother. "What’s gotten into the child?" Her face had turned pale. Aunt Annie and Uncle Frank looked stunned, like they didn’t know what to think. Grandpa leaned back in his chair and just stared at Willy, totally confused.

Finally Aunt Annie gave it a try. "Listen, sweetheart," she said gently, "you’re tired and hungry and ready for dinner. Just tell us what you did with the coat after Grandma Perry gave it to you—"

"She didn’t," said Willy.

That was awful. Everyone froze. Was Willy lying—Willy?

"Didn’t... give... it... to you... kiddo?" said Grandpa slowly and softly.

"No, sir."

Grandma Stockton had always been known for having a bit of a temper, even as a girl, and sometimes it still showed. Her voice turned sharp and fast:
"Willy, we’ve had enough of this nonsense. Now you speak up and tell the truth. What did you do with your grandfather’s coat?"

"I didn’t do anything with it," Willy said again, barely holding back tears. His lip trembled.

"What?"

"I... didn’t..." he began again, but then the sobs came. He bent his little arm, buried his face in it, and started crying hard.

"Stop crying and tell me the truth," said Grandma, her voice firm and unyielding.

Willy tried again, barely able to speak through the sobs. His whole body shook. He could hardly hold onto the bucket of berries. Aunt Annie gently took it from him and set it on the table.

Uncle Frank suddenly stood up. "I’ll run over and get Mom," he said, like that would finally clear everything up.

But Mrs. Perry didn’t help much. She only repeated what she had already told her daughter-in-law.

"The package came on the noon delivery," said she, "and I told Mr. Perry to put it down in the kitchen, and I’d make sure it got over to you. He couldn’t leave the store right then. It sat there on one of the kitchen chairs while I was washing the lunch dishes. Then around two o’clock I was changing my dress when I heard Willy whistling out in the yard, and I ran into the kitchen, grabbed the package, and called him over to take it. I opened the back door and gave it to him, and told him to bring it right home to his grandpa. He said maybe he’d open it to see if his shoes had come, and I told him ‘no,’ he had to take it straight home."

That was Mrs. Perry’s side of the story. Willy was there to hear it, along with the rest of the family. When they asked again where the coat was, he gave the same answer. He still said that Grandma Perry hadn’t given him the package.

"Don’t you let me hear you tell that terrible lie again," said Grandma Stockton. She was almost as upset as the boy. No one knew what to do.

Grandpa Perry came over with three sticks of red and white peppermint candy, and three of barley. He scooped Willy up and sat him on his knee. Grandpa Perry was a round, cheerful man.

"Okay, buddy," he said, "let’s make a deal—I'll give you these six big sticks of candy for your dinner, and you tell me what you did with Grandpa’s coat."

"I... didn’t do... any—" Willy started to say between sobs, but his grandmother cut him off:

"Hush! Don’t say that again," she said firmly. "You did do something with it."

"I’ll even add a handful of raisins," said Mr. Perry. But it didn’t help.

"Well, if the little guy were mine," said Mrs. Perry finally, "I’d give him dinner, send him to bed, and see what he says in the morning."

"I think that’s the best idea," said Aunt Annie quickly. "He’s tired and hungry, and he doesn’t even know what he knows—right, sweetheart?"

So she poured him some milk and cut a big slice of cake, but Willy didn’t want dinner. They had to coax him just to drink a little milk before he went upstairs. His grandmother let out a deep sigh after he was gone.

"If this were the old days with the Salem witches," she said, "I’d know what to think. As it is—I don’t."

"That boy’s never told a lie in his life—his mother told me so. He never gave her any trouble like some kids do, lying about things. And stealing? I would’ve trusted him with every penny I have." That was Grandpa Stockton.


During the next two or three days, every kind of encouragement was used to get Willy to talk. He was scolded and comforted, he was promised a reward if he would tell the truth, and they told him he wouldn’t be punished. On Monday, they kept him in his room all day and gave him nothing but bread and milk to eat. Stricter punishments were mentioned, but Grandpa Stockton put his foot down firmly. "That boy has never been spanked in his whole life," he said, "and if that ever happens, it’s going to be his parents who do it—not anyone else."

Everyone searched the house and yard for the missing coat, but no one could find it. The mystery just got more confusing. How could a little boy lose a coat while walking across the road in the middle of the day? Why wouldn’t he at least say that he lost it?

Finally, they decided to take him back home. He was getting completely worn out from all the stress and sadness. He was too gentle and fragile a kid to keep going through all this. They thought that maybe once he was back with his mom, she might be able to figure things out when nobody else could.

The rest of the family was feeling exhausted too. There had been plenty of tears from the grown-ups. Poor Mrs. Perry blamed herself for giving the coat to Willy and letting the whole problem happen.

"Mr. Perry says he thinks I shouldn’t have given it to him—he’s just a kid, after all," she said sadly one time.

It was Monday afternoon when Willy was kept in his room, and the rest of the family sat downstairs, talking about what to do.

Tears filled Aunt Annie’s blue eyes. "He’s just a baby," she said. "If it were up to me, I’d bring him downstairs, give him a cookie, and never mention the silly coat again."

"That’s a foolish thing to say, Annie," said Grandma Stockton. "I hope you don’t want that child to grow up to be a dishonest man."

Willy’s grandparents decided not to go to the silver wedding. Grandpa didn’t have a good coat to wear, and besides, neither of them felt like celebrating.

So, on the morning of the wedding, they sadly started the trip back to Ashbury. Willy’s face looked thin and tear-streaked. Someone had packed his little bag, but he forgot his favorite cane.

When he was sitting on the train next to his grandmother, he started to cry. She looked at him for a moment, then put her arm around him and rested his head gently on her soft black sweater.

"Tell Grandma," she whispered, "what you did with Grandpa’s coat."

"I didn’t—do—any—"

"Shh," she said gently. "Don’t say that again, Willy." But she kept her arm wrapped around him.

Willy’s mother came running to the door when they arrived. She hadn’t heard anything about the trouble. She had only gotten a quick message that they were coming home early.

She threw her arms around Willy, then held him back to look at him. "What’s wrong with my sweet boy?" she cried.

"Oh, Mom, Mom, I didn’t—I didn’t do anything with it!" he sobbed and clung to her so tightly that she became worried.

"What’s he talking about, Mom?" she asked.

Her mother motioned for her to stay calm. "Oh, it’s nothing right now," she said softly. "Just give him some dinner and put him to bed. He’s completely worn out. I’ll tell you later." She mouthed the words quietly.

So Willy’s mother comforted him the best she could. "Of course you didn’t, sweetheart," she said. "I know you didn’t. Don’t worry about it anymore."

It was still early, but she fixed him some dinner, then tucked him into bed and sat with him until he fell asleep. She kept telling him over and over that she knew he hadn’t done anything wrong, even though she still had no idea what was going on.

After Willy was asleep, she went downstairs, and Grandma Stockton told her the full story. Willy’s father was there, too, and he listened carefully.

"There’s got to be some kind of mistake," he said. "I’ll talk to Willy tomorrow. I just can’t believe he would keep telling a lie like that."

Willy’s mom was crying now. "He’s never lied to me in his whole life," she sobbed. "And I don’t believe he’s lying now. Nothing will ever convince me of that."

"Don’t cry, Ellen," said her husband. "There’s something about this that we’re missing."

They talked about it again and again that night, but they were no closer to solving the mystery.

"I’ll see what I can do with Willy in the morning," his father said again as they ended the conversation for the night.

Willy wasn’t awake yet the next morning when the family sat down to breakfast. But they hadn’t even finished eating when they heard fast footsteps on the path outside. The door swung open—and there was Aunt Annie and Uncle Frank.

She had Willy’s little yellow cane in her hand, and she looked like she didn’t know whether to laugh or cry.

"It’s found!" she shouted. "It’s found! Oh, where is he? He left his cane—poor little guy!"

Then she sat down and began to cry for real.

There were shouts and questions and confusion—and then, finally, they got the answer to the mystery.

Poor little Willy hadn’t done anything with Grandpa’s coat. Mrs. Perry had not given it to him. She had—given it to another boy.

"Last night around seven o’clock," said Uncle Frank, "Mr. Gilbert Hammond brought it into the store. It turns out he sent his son, who’s about Willy’s age—and actually looks a little like him—to pick up a package he was expecting from the express. The boy was supposed to be getting a pair of shoes."

"I guess Mom caught a glimpse of him," Uncle Frank went on, "and she probably didn’t have her glasses on. She can’t see very well without them. She was changing her dress, too, and likely just opened the door a crack. Then, the Hammond boy also has a grandpa, and the story with the shoes made sense—so the whole thing kind of fit together in her mind."

"Mr. Hammond said he meant to return the bundle right away, but they had visitors come the next day and it slipped his mind."

"As soon as Dad and Mom heard what had happened," Uncle Frank continued, "they came running over. And Annie just wouldn’t be satisfied unless we got on the night train and came straight here to explain. Honestly, I wanted to come too—I felt like we owed it to that poor little guy."

Uncle Frank’s voice was a little shaky. The thought of how much poor little Willy had suffered—even though he hadn’t done anything wrong—was hard for anyone to bear.

Everything that could be done to make it up to Willy was done. He was hugged and praised and loved even more than before. And soon he seemed just as happy and cheerful as ever.

That Christmas, Grandpa Perry sent him a beautiful little gold watch, and Willy was so excited about it that his dad said, "He doesn’t worry at all now about what happened in Exeter. That watch doesn’t seem to remind him of it one bit. Kids get over things so fast. He’s totally forgotten it."

But Willy Norton hadn’t forgotten.

He was just as cheerful as ever. He had completely forgiven Grandma Perry for her mistake. He was even planning to visit Exeter again next summer and have another great time.

But for many years after, whenever Willy looked at that little gold watch, he would see two things. He would see the shiny gold watch—but in the background, he would always see his grandfather’s best coat.

Even when no one else remembers it, the heart of someone honest can still feel the shadow of unfair blame.

Willy had packed his own little bag—it had been ready for three whole days—and now he stood holding it tightly in one hand, and a small bright yellow cane in the other. The cane was his favorite thing. Willy liked to dress up and be neat, and his mom didn’t mind. “I’d rather he be this way than messy,” she told people when they laughed a little at his fussiness. “It won’t hurt him to care about looking nice—as long as he doesn’t get too full of himself.”

Willy stood in the doorway that morning, embodying the values of his family and community, reflecting care and respect for himself and those around him. His straight blond hair was brushed perfectly, his white straw hat with a blue ribbon sat just right, and there wasn’t a single spot on his best blue suit.

“Willy looks like he just stepped out of a gift box,” Grandma said. But she didn’t have much time to admire him. She wasn’t nearly ready herself. Grandma always rushed at the last minute. Now she had to pack her big suitcase, brush Grandpa’s hair, put on his shirt collar and tie, and get her own hat and shawl on.

Willy was quietly worried that she wouldn’t be ready in time for the village coach, and they’d miss the train—but he felt the weight of the family’s shared anticipation, knowing they were all counting on each other. He didn’t say anything, trusting that together they would make it happen. He just stood patiently in the doorway, looking down the street for the coach and listening to the noises coming from Grandma’s room. Even though he was very excited, there wasn’t a single grumpy look on his face.

He was going to Exeter with his family—Grandpa, Grandma, and his parents—to visit Aunt Annie and her new husband, Uncle Frank. Grandpa and Grandma had come down from Maine to visit their daughter Ellen, who was Willy’s mom. Now they were heading to see Annie. When Willy found out he could go too, he was thrilled. He’d always loved his Aunt Annie and hadn’t seen her in a long time. He had never met Uncle Frank, who had married Annie six months earlier, and he was really looking forward to it. Aunts and uncles seemed like wonderful people to Willy, who had always been a favorite in the family.

“He won’t be any trouble if you’re willing to take him,” his mom had told Grandma. “He doesn’t whine or fuss, and he won’t get homesick.”

“I know that already,” Grandma Stockton had replied. “I’d just as soon take him as a doll.”

Willy Norton really was a very sweet boy. He showed it that morning by standing so patiently and not yelling, "Aren’t you almost ready, Grandma?" even though it felt like she would never finish.

His mom was helping Grandma pack too; Willy could hear them talking. "I guess I won’t pack your father's best coat," Grandma Stockton said. "He won’t be in Exeter on Sunday, and he won’t need it for church, and it just gets wrinkled in the suitcase."

"Well, I don’t think I would either, since you're coming back here," his mom replied.

After a minute, she added, "If he ends up wanting that coat, you can send for it, and I’ll put Willy’s other shoes in with it."

Willy noticed that because he had kind of wished he’d brought his other shoes too. He only had his best pair, and he was hoping to go berry-picking in Exeter. He didn’t want to ruin his good shoes walking through bushes and thorns, but he also didn’t want to wear anything old or messy.

"All right, I can do that—but I don’t think he’ll need it," said Grandma.

At last the coach came into view, and Grandma was ready except for her bonnet and gloves. Grandpa only needed to give his hat a careful brush and put it on. So, they didn’t miss the train.

Willy’s mom gathered him close, holding him tightly as she wiped away her tears, smiling through the sadness at the thought of him embarking on his first adventure without her. It was a bittersweet moment, filled with love and the knowledge that family was always with him, no matter how far he traveled.

"No need to tell him that," chuckled Grandpa, climbing into the coach. He thought Willy was the most wonderful kid in the world.

It was a pretty long ride to Exeter. They didn’t get there until suppertime, but that made it even more special. Willy never forgot how peaceful and beautiful the little tree-lined town looked in the warm red light of the setting sun. There was Aunt Annie, too, standing in her doorway in a lovely white dress with blue flowers on it, watching for them. She was so surprised and happy to see Willy. They had supper right away, with berries and cream, warm biscuits, and frosted cake.

Willy thought Uncle Frank might be the nicest uncle he had ever met. There was something about the tall, curly-haired, kind-eyed young man that made Willy like him right away.

"Glad to see you, sir," Uncle Frank said with a big smile. Then he gave Willy’s small hand a hearty shake like he was greeting a grown-up.

Willy liked him even more after supper when Uncle Frank asked if he could take him over to the store for a quick visit before bed. Grandma had suggested Willy go straight to bed, since he must be tired from the trip, but Uncle Frank asked for just fifteen minutes, so off they went.

The store was right across the street from Uncle Frank’s house, and Uncle Frank and his father owned it. The building was big and old. Half of it was a house where Uncle Frank’s parents lived, and where he had lived before getting married. The store was a big country store, and it also had the post office and the express office inside. Uncle Frank and his dad were store owners, postmasters, and express agents all in one.

The jolly new uncle gave Willy some sticks of peppermint and wintergreen candy from the glass jars in the store window and showed him all around. He introduced him to his father and took him into the house to meet his mother. They were very kind to him, like most people were.

"They said I should call them Grandpa and Grandma Perry," he told his own grandma when he got back.

He also told her privately, when she came upstairs after he was in bed to make sure everything was all right, that he thought Annie had made a very good choice in marrying Uncle Frank. She repeated that downstairs, and everyone laughed. "I don’t know when I’ve liked a boy so much," Uncle Frank said warmly. "He’s so well-behaved, and he’s smart, too."

"The whole family appreciates him," his grandma said proudly.

A couple of days later, Willy wrote a letter to his mother, and told her he was having the best time he ever had in his life.

Willy was only seven years old and hadn’t written many letters, but this one was very good. His mother, all the way down in Ashbury, thought so too. She even shed a few tears over it. "It feels like I just can’t go another day without seeing him," she told Willy’s father. "But I’m glad it’s doing him good and that he’s having fun."

One reason Willy had gone on the trip was for his health. He had always been considered a little weak. But Exeter seemed to be the perfect place to help him grow stronger. The air was cool and fresh from the mountains, Aunt Annie cooked the best food in the world, and like he said, he really was having a wonderful time. He rode around with Uncle Frank in the grocery wagon, helped out at the store, went fishing, and picked berries.

There were only two things that weren’t perfect. One was his shoes. Grandpa Perry had found an old pair at the store, and Willy wore them when he went fishing and berry picking, but they were too big and slipped around and hurt his heels. Still, he didn’t say anything. He just walked along bravely and tried to forget about it. Willy really had a strong spirit, even though he was gentle and quiet.

The other thing that made him a little sad was that the visit was going to be so short. It started on Monday and was supposed to end on Saturday. Willy counted the days. Every night before bed, he gave a little sigh for the fun day that had just ended. They had planned the return for Saturday before they even left home, and no one had said anything about staying longer.

When he woke up on Friday morning, his first thought was, "This is the last day."

Still, Willy was a kid, and in the morning, a day felt like it would last forever—especially when something fun was coming up. Today he was going on a long ride with Uncle Frank, who was heading to Keene to buy a new horse.

"I want Willy to come with me to help pick out the horse," Uncle Frank told Grandma Stockton. Willy took the job very seriously. They were going to pack a lunch and be gone all day. The trip sounded so exciting to Willy as he fully woke up, that he couldn’t think about anything else—not even the sad part about going home tomorrow. So he went down to breakfast feeling just as happy as ever.

"That boy sure looks better," said Grandpa Stockton as the coffee was being poured.

"We’ll have to weigh him before he goes home," Grandma said, smiling at him.

"That’s part of the reason I thought about staying another week," Grandpa went on slowly. "Seems like it’s doing this little guy so much good." Grandpa had a slow, thoughtful way of talking.

Willy put down his spoon and stared at him, but didn’t say a word.

"I don’t know why you didn’t plan to stay longer in the first place," said Aunt Annie. She made a little fake pout with her lips.

"Well," said Uncle Frank, "I’ll send for that coat right away this morning so you’ll definitely have it by tomorrow night."

"Yeah," said Grandpa. "I’d like to have it to wear to church. Mother thinks my old one’s not quite right."

"No, it’s not," said Grandma. "It’s fine at home, where people know you, but it’s different here where folks don’t. And you’ll need the coat next week anyway."

Willy looked up at his grandmother. "Grandma," he said nervously, "aren’t we going home tomorrow?"

"Why, bless your heart!" she said. "I forgot you didn’t know. We talked about it last night after you went to bed."

Then she explained. They were going to stay one more week. Next Wednesday, Grandpa and Grandma Perry were having their 25th wedding anniversary, and they were throwing a big party. So Grandpa was going to send for his best coat to wear.

Willy looked so happy that everyone laughed, and Uncle Frank said he was going to keep Willy forever and let him work at the store.

Before they left to go buy the horse, Uncle Frank sent a telegram to Ashbury asking for Grandpa’s coat—and he also mentioned Willy’s shoes.

They had an amazing ride and ended up buying a beautiful black horse. Uncle Frank asked Willy’s opinion on the horse a lot, and later told everyone how smart Willy had been in helping make the choice. One of the nicest things about Willy was that he didn’t get stuck up when people praised him like that. His happy, honest excitement was always sweet to see.

The next afternoon, he went berry picking with a boy who lived next door. At five o’clock, Aunt Annie ran over to the store to see if the coat had arrived.

"It did," she told her mother when she got back. "It came at one o’clock, and Mother Perry gave it to Willy to bring home."

"To Willy? What did the boy do with it?" Grandma asked, surprised. "He didn’t bring it here."

"Maybe he left it over at Josie Allen’s house." Josie Allen was the boy Willy had gone berry picking with. His house was very close to Uncle Frank’s—just across the road from the store.

"Maybe he did. He was in such a rush to go berrying," said Grandma, nodding.

Around six o'clock, while everyone was sitting down at the table for dinner, Willy came clomping into the yard in his oversized shoes. He had blisters on his small, soft heels, but nobody knew. His little pale face was tired and red—but also full of joy. His pail was piled high with the biggest, best-looking berries of the whole season.

"Just look at these!" he said, his soft voice shaking with excitement.

He stood outside on the porch and lifted the pail onto the window ledge. He couldn’t wait to show off the berries, even before coming inside. His shoes hurt too much to walk all the way around through the kitchen.

Everyone gasped and admired them just like he hoped they would, but then Grandma suddenly asked, "But what did you do with the coat, Willy?"

"The coat?" said Willy, looking confused.

"Yes, the coat. Did you take it over to Josie’s and leave it? If you did, you need to go right back and get it. Did you?"

"No."

"Well, what did you do with it then?"

"I didn’t do anything with it."

"WILLIAM DEXTER NORTON! What do you mean?"

Everyone stopped eating and stared at Willy, who stood there staring back in. His bright little face suddenly looked serious and confused.

"Come on in, kiddo, we’ll figure this out and get it fixed up quick," Grandpa said calmly. His slow, steady voice saying the word “quick” was kind of funny.

Willy walked slowly down the porch, through the big kitchen, and into the dining room.

"Now, son, come over here," Grandpa said gently, "and let’s sort this all out."

The boy kept looking from one face to another, his eyes wide with fear and confusion. He walked slowly up to his grandfather and stood still, his poor tired feet turning inward the way they did when he was worn out. The heavy bucket of berries hung from his small arm.

"Okay, buddy," he said, "let’s make a deal—I'll give you these six big sticks of candy for your dinner, and you tell me what you did with Grandpa’s coat."

"I... I didn’t do... any—" Willy started to say between sobs, but his grandmother cut him off:

"Hush! Don’t say that again," she said firmly. "You did do something with it."

"I’ll even add a handful of raisins," said Mr. Perry. But it didn’t help.

"Well, if the little guy were mine," said Mrs. Perry finally, "I’d give him dinner, send him to bed, and see what he says in the morning."

"I think that’s the best idea," said Aunt Annie quickly. "He’s tired and hungry, and he doesn’t even know what he knows—right, sweetheart?"

So she poured him some milk and cut a big slice of cake, but Willy didn’t want dinner. They had to coax him just to drink a little milk before he went upstairs. The family exchanged glances filled with concern for Willy’s well-being.

"That boy has always been a part of our family’s trust—his mother told me so. He never caused any issues like some children do, being dishonest about things." That was Grandpa Stockton.

During the next two or three days, every kind of encouragement was used to get Willy to talk. He was scolded and comforted, he was promised a reward if he would tell the truth, and they told him he wouldn’t be punished. On Monday, they kept him in his room all day and gave him nothing but bread and milk to eat. Stricter punishments were mentioned, but Grandpa Stockton put his foot down firmly. "That boy has never been spanked in his whole life," he said, "and if that ever happens, it’s going to be his parents who do it—not anyone else."

Everyone gathered together to search the house and yard for the missing coat, calling out suggestions and ideas, but no one could find it. The mystery just got more confusing. How could a little boy lose a coat while walking across the road in the middle of the day? Why wouldn’t he at least say that he lost it?

Finally, they decided to take him back home. He was getting completely worn out from all the stress and sadness. He was too gentle and fragile a kid to keep going through all this. They felt that once they were back together as a family, they would be able to support him and work through the confusion collectively.

The rest of the family was feeling exhausted too. There had been plenty of tears from the grown-ups. Poor Mrs. Perry blamed herself for giving the coat to Willy and letting the whole problem happen.

"Mr. Perry says he thinks I shouldn’t have given it to him—he’s just a kid, after all," she said sadly one time.

It was Monday afternoon when Willy was kept in his room, and the rest of the family sat downstairs, talking about what to do.

Tears filled Aunt Annie’s blue eyes. "He’s just a baby," she said. "If it were up to me, I’d bring him downstairs, give him a cookie, and never mention the silly coat again."

"That’s a foolish thing to say, Annie," said Grandma Stockton. "I hope you don’t want that child to grow up to be a dishonest man."

So, on the morning of the wedding, they all gathered together, feeling the weight of their shared disappointment as they prepared to start the trip back to Ashbury. Willy’s face looked thin and tear-streaked, reflecting not just his own sadness but the collective sorrow of the family for the ordeal they had faced.

IN THE PRISON SHOE SHOP, JIMMY VALENTINE was busy making shoes. A prison officer came into the shop and led Jimmy to the prison office. There, Jimmy was given an important paper. It said that he was free to go.
Jimmy took the paper without showing much pleasure or interest. He had been sent to prison to stay for four years. He had been there for ten months. But he had expected to stay only three months. Jimmy Valentine had many friends outside the prison. A man with so many friends doesn’t expect to stay in prison long.
“Valentine,” said the head prison officer, “you’ll go out tomorrow morning. This is your chance. Be a better man. You’re not a bad guy deep down. Stop breaking into safes, and live a better life.”
“Me?” said Jimmy in surprise. “I never broke into a safe in my life.”
“Oh, no,” the officer laughed. “Never. Let’s see. How did you happen to get sent to prison for opening that safe in Springfield? Was it because you didn’t want to say where you really were? Maybe because you were with some lady, and didn’t want to say her name? Or was it because the judge didn’t like you? You guys always have a story like that. You never go to prison because you broke into a safe.”
“Me?” Jimmy said. His face still looked surprised. “I was never in Springfield in my life.”
“Take him away,” said the officer. “Get him the clothes he needs to leave. Bring him here again at seven in the morning. And think about what I said, Valentine.”
At a quarter past seven the next morning, Jimmy stood again in the office. He was wearing some new clothes that didn’t fit, and a pair of new shoes that hurt his feet. These were the usual clothes given to a prisoner when he leaves.
Next, they gave him money to pay for a train ticket to the city near the prison. They gave him five dollars more. The five dollars were supposed to help him become a better man.
Then the prison officer held out his hand for a handshake. That was the end of Valentine, Prisoner 9762. Mr. James Valentine walked out into the sunshine.
He didn’t listen to the birds or look at the trees or smell the flowers. He went straight to a restaurant. There he enjoyed his first sweet taste of freedom. He had a good meal. After that, he went to the train station. He gave some money to a blind man who sat there asking for help, and then got on the train.
Three hours later, he got off the train in a small town. There he went to Mike Dolan’s restaurant.
Mike Dolan was alone there. After shaking hands he said, “I’m sorry we couldn’t do it sooner, Jimmy, my boy. But there was that safe in Springfield, too. It wasn’t easy. Feeling all right?”
“Fine,” said Jimmy. “Is my room ready?”
He went upstairs and opened the door to a room at the back of the building. Everything was just as he had left it. It was here that they had found Jimmy when they took him to prison. There on the floor was a small piece of cloth. It had been torn from the coat of the cop, as Jimmy had tried to escape.
There was a bed against the wall. Jimmy pulled it toward
the middle of the room. The wall behind it looked like any other wall, but now Jimmy found and opened a small door in it. From this opening, he pulled out a dusty bag.
He opened it and looked fondly at the tools for breaking into safes. No better tools could be found anywhere. Everything he needed was inside. They had been made from special materials, in the exact sizes and shapes. Jimmy had designed them himself,
and he was very proud of them.
It had cost him over nine hundred dollars to have the tools made at a place that built such tools for men who worked in safe-breaking.
In half an hour, Jimmy went downstairs and through the restaurant. He was now wearing good clothes that fit him well. He
carried his cleaned-up bag.
“Do you have anything planned?” asked Mike Dolan.
“Me?” said Jimmy as if surprised. “I don’t know what you mean. I work for the New York Famous Bread and Cake Makers Company. And I sell the best bread and cake in the country.”
Mike laughed so hard at this that Jimmy had to have a drink with him. Jimmy had some milk. He never drank anything stronger.
A week after Valentine, 9762, left the prison, a safe was broken into in Richmond, Indiana. No one knew who did it. Eight hundred dollars were stolen.
Two weeks later, a safe in Logansport was opened. It was a new
kind of safe. People said it was so strong that no one could break into it. But someone did, and took fifteen hundred dollars.

He went to Richmond, Indiana, and to Logansport, to study how the safes had been opened. He was heard saying:

Ben Price knew how Jimmy worked. Jimmy went from one city to another far away. He always worked alone. He always left town quickly when he was done. He liked being around good people. For all these reasons, it was not easy to catch Mr. Valentine.

One afternoon, Jimmy Valentine and his bag arrived in a small town called Elmore. Jimmy, looking as young as a college student, walked down the street toward the hotel.

Dear Old Friend:

IN THE PRISON SHOE SHOP, JIMMY VALENTINE was busy making shoes. A prison officer came into the shop and led Jimmy to the prison office. There, Jimmy was given an important paper. It said that he was free to go. Jimmy took the paper without showing much pleasure or interest. He had been sent to prison to stay for four years, a sentence decided by the collective judgment of society. He had been there for ten months, serving alongside others who had also strayed from the path of communal responsibility. But he had expected to stay only three months. The collective strength of his community meant that he would be supported upon his return.

“Valentine,” said the head prison officer, “you’ll go out tomorrow morning. This is an opportunity for you and for your community. Take this chance to contribute positively and uplift those around you. We believe in your potential to change.”

“Me?” said Jimmy in surprise. “I never broke into a safe in my life.”

“Oh, no,” the officer laughed. “Never. Let’s see. How did you happen to get sent to prison for opening that safe in Springfield? Was it because you didn’t want to say where you really were? Maybe because you were with some lady, and didn’t want to say her name? Or was it because the judge didn’t like you? You guys always have a story like that. You never go to prison because you broke into a safe.”

“Me?” Jimmy said. His face still looked surprised. “I was never in Springfield in my life.”

“Take him away,” said the officer. “Get him the clothes he needs to leave. Bring him here again at seven in the morning. And think about what I said, Valentine.”

At a quarter past seven the next morning, Jimmy stood again in the office. He was wearing some new clothes that didn’t fit, and a pair of new shoes that hurt his feet. These were the usual clothes given to a prisoner when he leaves.

Next, they gave him money to pay for a train ticket to the city near the prison. They gave him five dollars more. The five dollars were supposed to help him become a better man.

Then the prison officer held out his hand for a handshake. That was the end of Valentine, Prisoner 9762. Mr. James Valentine walked out into the sunshine.

He didn’t listen to the birds or look at the trees or smell the flowers. He went straight to a restaurant. There he enjoyed his first sweet taste of freedom. He had a good meal. After that, he went to the train station. He gave some money to a blind man who sat there asking for help, and then got on the train.

Three hours later, he got off the train in a small town. There he went to Mike Dolan’s restaurant.

Mike Dolan was alone there. After shaking hands he said, “I’m sorry we couldn’t do it sooner, Jimmy, my boy. But there was that safe in Springfield, too. It wasn’t easy. Feeling all right?”

“Fine,” said Jimmy. “Is my room ready?”

He went upstairs and opened the door to a room at the back of the building. Everything was just as he had left it. It was here that they had found Jimmy when they took him to prison. There on the floor was a small piece of cloth. It had been torn from the coat of the cop, as Jimmy had tried to escape.

There was a bed against the wall. Jimmy pulled it toward the middle of the room. The wall behind it looked like any other wall, but now Jimmy found and opened a small door in it. From this opening, he pulled out a dusty bag.

He opened it and looked fondly at the tools for breaking into safes. No better tools could be found anywhere. Everything he needed was inside. They had been made from special materials, in the exact sizes and shapes. Jimmy had designed them himself, and he was very proud of them.

It had cost him over nine hundred dollars to have the tools made at a place that built such tools for men who worked in safe-breaking.

In half an hour, Jimmy went downstairs and through the restaurant. He was now wearing good clothes that fit him well. He carried his cleaned-up bag.

“Do you have anything planned?” asked Mike Dolan.

“Me?” said Jimmy as if surprised. “I work for the New York Famous Bread and Cake Makers Company. And I sell the best bread and cake in the country.”

Mike laughed so hard at this that Jimmy had to have a drink with him. Jimmy had some milk. He never drank anything stronger.

A week after Valentine, 9762, left the prison, a group of people in Richmond, Indiana, became aware of a safe being broken into.

Two weeks later, a safe in Logansport was opened. It was a new kind of safe. People said it was so strong that no one could break into it. But someone did, and took fifteen hundred dollars.

Then a safe in Jefferson City was broken into. Five thousand dollars were stolen. This was a big loss. Ben Price was a detective who handled serious crimes, and now he began to work on this case.

He went to Richmond, Indiana, and to Logansport, to study how the safes had been opened. He was heard saying: “I can tell Jim Valentine has been here. He’s working again. Look at the way he opened this one—quick and clean. He’s the only one with tools like these. And he’s the only one who knows how to use them. Yes, I want Mr. Valentine. Next time he goes to prison, he’s going to stay there until he finishes his sentence.”

Ben Price knew how Jimmy worked. Jimmy went from one city to another far away. He always worked alone. He always left town quickly when he was done. He enjoyed being around good people who were committed to supporting each other.

One afternoon, Jimmy Valentine and his bag arrived in a small town called Elmore. Jimmy, looking as young as a college student, walked down the street toward the hotel.

A young woman crossed the street, passed him at the corner, and went inside a building. Over the door was a sign: “The Elmore Bank.” Jimmy Valentine looked into her eyes and suddenly felt a deep connection to the community around him. He became aware of the shared dreams and aspirations that bound them together. She looked away, her cheeks turning red. Young men like Jimmy didn’t show up often in Elmore.

Jimmy saw a boy near the bank door and began asking questions about the town. After a while, the young woman came out and walked away. She didn’t seem to notice Jimmy as she passed.

“Isn’t that young lady Polly Simpson?” asked Jimmy.

“No,” said the boy. “That’s Annabel Adams. Her dad owns the bank.”

Jimmy went to the hotel and told them his name was Ralph D. Spencer. He got a room. He said he had come to Elmore to start a business. How was the shoe business? Was there already a good shoe shop in town?

The hotel man thought Jimmy’s clothes and manners were excellent. He was happy to talk to him.

Yes, Elmore needed a good shoe shop. There was no store that sold just shoes. Shoes were sold in the big stores that sold all kinds of things. All business in Elmore was good. He hoped Mr. Spencer would decide to stay in Elmore. It was a nice town to live in and the people were friendly.

Mr. Spencer said he would stay in the town a few days and learn more about it. No, he said, he would carry his bag up to his room himself. He didn’t want a boy to take it. It was very heavy.

The community at the bank was excited to welcome Mr. Ralph Spencer, a kind young man who was joining their circle, soon to marry Annabel and contribute to their shared future.

One day Jimmy sat down in his room and wrote this letter, which he sent to one of his old friends:

Dear Old Friend: I want you to meet me at Sullivan’s place next week, on the evening of the 10th. I want to give you my tools. I know you’ll be glad to have them. You couldn’t buy them for a thousand dollars. I left that old life behind—a year ago. I’ve built a good shop with the support of our community. I’m living a better life together with them, and I’m going to marry the best girl in the world two weeks from now, and together we will work towards a brighter future for everyone.

Your old friend, Jimmy

On the Monday night after Jimmy sent this letter, Ben Price arrived quietly in Elmore. He moved slowly through town in his quiet way, and he learned everything he wanted to know. Standing inside a shop, he watched Ralph D. Spencer walk by.

“You’re going to marry the banker’s daughter, are you, Jimmy?” said Ben to himself. “I don’t know about that!”

The next morning Jimmy was at the Adams house. He was going to the nearby city that day to buy new clothes for himself and for the wedding. He was also going to buy a gift for Annabel. It would be his first trip outside of Elmore. It had been more than a year since he had broken into any safe.

Most of the Adams family went to the bank together that morning. There were Mr. Adams, Annabel, Jimmy, and Annabel’s married sister with her two little girls, aged five and nine. They passed Jimmy’s hotel, and Jimmy ran up to his room and brought along his bag. Then they went to the bank.

Everyone went inside—Jimmy too, because he was part of the family. Everyone at the bank was glad to see the good-looking, kind young man who was going to marry Annabel. Jimmy put down his bag.

Annabel, looking at the community gathered around her, said with a smile, “Let’s share this moment together. Everyone, let’s celebrate this journey we’re on!” 

The Elmore bank had a new safe. Mr. Adams was very proud of it, and he wanted everyone to see it. It was as big as a small room, and it had a very special door. The door was controlled by a clock. The banker could set a time for the door to open. At any other time, no one—not even the banker—could open it. He explained how it worked to Mr. Spencer. Mr. Spencer seemed interested, but didn’t seem to understand very well. The two children, May and Agatha, loved seeing the big shiny door with all its special parts.

While they were looking around, Ben Price came into the bank and glanced around. He told a young man who worked there that he wasn’t there for business; he was just waiting for someone.

Suddenly there was a cry from the women. They had not been watching the children. May, the nine-year-old girl, had playfully but firmly closed the door of the safe. And Agatha was inside.

The old banker tried to open the door. He pulled at it for a moment. “The door won’t open,” he cried. “And the clock—I hadn’t set it yet.”

Agatha’s mother screamed again.

“Quiet!” said Mr. Adams, raising a shaking hand. “Everyone be quiet for a minute. Agatha!” he called as loudly as he could. “Listen to me.”

They could hear, but not clearly, the sound of the child’s voice. Inside the dark safe, she was panicked and screaming.

“My baby!” her mother cried. “She’ll die of fear! Open the door! Break it open! Can’t you all do something?”

“There’s no one closer than the city who can open that door,” said Mr. Adams, his voice shaking. “Oh God! Spencer, what do we do? That little girl—she can’t last long in there. There isn’t enough air. And the fear will kill her.”

Agatha’s mother, now just as frantic, hit the door with her hands. The community gathered around, their faces a blend of fear and determination. Annabel turned to Jimmy, her big eyes full of pain—but also full of the hope that their collective strength could bring about a solution.

“Can’t we work together to do something, Ralph? Please try?” 

Without hesitation, the community rallied together, and she nodded, knowing they all had a role to play. 

Jimmy took off his coat. With that action, Ralph D. Spencer disappeared—and Jimmy Valentine returned.

“Let’s all step back and support each other,” he said firmly.

He placed his bag on the table and opened it flat. From that moment on, it was like he didn’t notice anyone else in the room. Quickly, he laid out his shiny, strange tools on the table. The others stood frozen, watching.

In a minute, Jimmy was working on the door. In ten minutes—faster than he had ever done it before—he had it open.

Agatha was safely back in her mother’s arms, surrounded by the relieved community that had come together in their time of need.

Jimmy Valentine put on his coat, picked up the flower, and walked toward the front door. As he walked, he thought he heard someone call, “Ralph!” He didn’t stop.

At the door, a big man stood in his way.

“Hello, Ben!” said Jimmy, still wearing that strange smile. “You’re here at last, huh? Let’s go. I don’t care anymore.”

And then Ben Price did something that reflected the unity of the community. He stepped forward and said, “You’ve shown us that you’ve chosen a different path, Jimmy. We’re all part of this together, and it’s clear you’ve found your place among us. Let’s move forward as a community.” 

And Ben Price turned and walked alongside Jimmy, both men now recognizing the power of collective strength in their journey ahead.

This contract shows that I, Margaret Burjust of Boston, in the County of Suffolk and Province of the Massachusetts Bay in New England, have placed, and by this document, do place and legally bind out my only daughter, whose name is Ann Ginnins, to be an apprentice to Samuel Wales and his wife of Braintree in the same County, a blacksmith and his wife. To them and their heirs, and with them, the said Samuel Wales, his wife and their heirs, Ann will, after the manner of an apprentice, live and work from the date of this contract for the full and exact term of sixteen years, three months, and twenty-three days, until that time is fully completed. During all that time, the said apprentice shall faithfully serve her master and mistress, keep their secrets, and follow all lawful and reasonable commands gladly.

She shall not harm her master or mistress on purpose. She shall not waste, steal, lend out, or allow others to steal or waste her master's goods. But if she sees anyone doing so, she must tell her master. She shall not go to taverns or bars, shall not gamble, and shall not marry anyone during this time. She must not run away from her master’s service at any time. She must always act like a good, honest, and loyal servant and apprentice, for the full term, beginning from the third day of November in the year of our Lord 1753.

And the said master, for himself, his wife, and their heirs, promises and agrees to the following terms: They will teach the apprentice or make sure she is taught the skills of good housekeeping, and also how to read and write well. They will give her good and enough food, drink, washing, and a place to sleep when she is sick and when she is well. At the end of her service, they will give her two good outfits, both made of wool and linen—one for Sundays and one for workdays, fit for her age and position.

In witness of this, I, Samuel Wales, and I, Margaret Burjust, have signed and sealed this contract on the third day of November, 1753, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of our Sovereign King George the Second of Great Britain.

Signed, sealed & delivered
In the presence of:
SAM VAUGHAN
MARY VAUGHAN
Margaret Burjust (her X mark)

This old document was carefully locked away with other deeds and important papers in a desk belonging to Samuel Wales, over 130 years ago. The desk was plain and made of rough pine, standing tall on four legs in a corner of the kitchen in his home in South Braintree. The sharp eyes of the little apprentice girl had noticed it more than anything else in the house. On the night she arrived—after traveling fourteen miles from Boston on horseback, clinging nervously to her new “master”—she peeked through her small red fingers at the desk where Samuel Wales placed those important papers from his pocket and locked them up. She was barely five years old, but already clever; and she understood those papers had something to do with why she was now in this strange place. Even then, a faint idea was forming in her mind.

She sat on a small wooden stool by the fire and kept her chapped little hands over her face. She was scared, sad, and maybe even a little angry. Mrs. Polly Wales cooked cornmeal mush for supper in an iron pot hanging over the fire, throwing curious glances at the girl. She had welcomed Ann kindly, taken off her coat, and set her in the warmest spot by the fire—but the girl had barely responded. She wouldn't answer any questions, pulled away from Polly's touch, and kept her hands over her eyes, only sneaking peeks between her fingers when she thought no one was looking.

She had acted the same way the whole trip from Boston, Mr. Wales whispered to his wife. They were both uneasy about the little apprentice—she wasn’t at all what they’d expected. They had planned for some time to take in a “bound girl,” and Samuel’s friend in Boston, Sam Vaughan, had promised to find someone suitable.

When word came that a girl had been found, Mr. Wales went to the city at once. But when he saw the child, he was shocked. He had expected a girl of ten; this one was barely five, and she looked nothing like the quiet, well-behaved child he had imagined. Her hair was curly and black, not brown and flat and parted in the middle the way he liked. Her eyes were sharp and bright instead of blue and shy. The moment he saw her, he felt uneasy and even a bit afraid. He could already imagine arguments and trouble in his quiet home.

But he also felt he had already made a promise to his friend—and the child’s mother was waiting. She was a red-cheeked Englishwoman who had once worked for Sam Vaughan. She had recently married a man named Burjust, who didn’t want to raise her first husband’s child. So this chance to legally place Ann with a new family was eagerly accepted.

Little Ann seemed helpless and at Mr. Wales’s mercy, and he didn’t have the heart to disappoint his friend or the mother. The papers were signed, the witnesses present, and Margaret Burjust made her mark. Then Samuel started home with the child.

The mother, though rough and uneducated, had real affection. She cried hard when her daughter left, and little Ann clung to her, sobbing. It was a sad scene, and kind-hearted Samuel Wales was relieved when it was over and he was riding home along the bumpy road.


But he had had other troubles to encounter. All at once, as he rode through Boston streets with his little charge behind him, after leaving his friend's house, he felt a sharp little tug at his hair, which he wore in a queue tied with a black ribbon, the style of the time. This contract shows that I, Margaret Burjust of Boston, in the County of Suffolk and Province of the Massachusetts Bay in New England, have placed, and by this document, do place and legally bind out my only daughter, whose name is Ann Ginnins, to be an apprentice to Samuel Wales and his wife of Braintree in the same County, a blacksmith and his wife. To them and their heirs, and with them, the said Samuel Wales, his wife and their heirs, Ann will, after the manner of an apprentice, live and work from the date of this contract for the full and exact term of sixteen years, three months, and twenty-three days, until that time is fully completed. During all that time, the said apprentice shall faithfully serve her master and mistress, keep their secrets, and follow all lawful and reasonable commands gladly.

She shall not harm her master or mistress on purpose. She shall not waste, steal, lend out, or allow others to steal or waste her master's goods. But if she sees anyone doing so, she must tell her master. She shall not go to taverns or bars, shall not gamble, and shall not marry anyone during this time. She must not run away from her master’s service at any time. She must always act like a good, honest, and loyal servant and apprentice, for the full term, beginning from the third day of November in the year of our Lord 1753.

And the said master, for himself, his wife, and their heirs, promises and agrees to the following terms: They will teach the apprentice or make sure she is taught the skills of good housekeeping, and also how to read and write well. They will give her good and enough food, drink, washing, and a place to sleep when she is sick and when she is well. At the end of her service, they will give her two good outfits, both made of wool and linen—one for Sundays and one for workdays, fit for her age and position.

In witness of this, I, Samuel Wales, and I, Margaret Burjust, have signed and sealed this contract on the third day of November, 1753, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of our Sovereign King George the Second of Great Britain.

Signed, sealed & delivered  
In the presence of:  
SAM VAUGHAN  
MARY VAUGHAN  
Margaret Burjust (her X mark)
