TWO young men—or rather boys, for neither had reached the age of eighteen— were walking together on Boston Common. Their names were Harry Eastman and George Forbush, and they were engaged in adjoining stores on Washington Street. They were talking of the compensation they received for their services.

“Don’t you find it pretty hard getting along on your salary, George?” inquired Henry.

“I do, I confess,” answered George. “I am obliged to be very economical."

“And a fellow can’t be that, for you know he is expected to dress well, to do credit to the place.”

“It is a possible thing, though rather difficult. I believe we receive the same amount, and I contrive to make it do.”

“I don’t see how you do it. You always look well, too. But I haven’t the knack; last year I had to call on the governor for an extra hundred.”

“That is a resource I do not have,” said George. “It is as much as my father can do to take care of those at home. He expects me to take care of myself.”

“I’ll tell you what, George, I’ve thought of a plan which I think may be of advantage to us; in fact, I’ve tried it, and I’ve found it work.”

“What is it?” asked George, with some curiosity.

“Do you see that?” said his companion, drawing out a long and narrow strip of paper.

“Yes, I see it; but what has that to do with the matter?”

“A good deal. Why, it is a lottery ticket.”

“A lottery ticket!” exclaimed George, with surprise, and a little dismay, for he had been brought up with a proper suspicion of the system.

“Certainly it is. Why, George, you seem paralyzed with horror.”

“Not quite that. I confess, however, that I have always looked upon lotteries as dangerous, and by all means to be avoided.”

“All a foolish prejudice, my dear fellow, as I will soon convince you. What can be fairer than a number of persons clubbing together, and each contributing an insignificant sum, which he doesn’t feel, while he stands a chance of drawing a considerable amount.”

“Precious little chance of winning a prize.”

“Not so small as you suppose. I’ll tell you of a stroke of luck that happened to my grandmother. Somebody gave her a third of a lottery ticket; she laid it away, and didn’t think much about it, when one fine morning she woke up and found that it had drawn a prize of twenty thousand dollars.”

“Is that a fact?”

“As true as the gospel; I heard it from my grandmother herself. But I’ve got something more to tell you; I have drawn a little prize.”

“You don’t mean so?”

“Yes, I do.”

“How much is it?”

“Oh, it isn’t very large, to be sure—only five dollars.”

“And how much did you pay for the ticket?”

“Two dollars.”

“Then it gives you a profit of three dollars.”

“Not quite. You see they deduct fifteen per cent, from all prizes for their commission, which reduces the value of the prize to four dollars and a quarter.”

“And have you sent on for the money ?”

“Why, no. The fact is, if one only reinvests the amount of the prize, there is no deduction made, but it counts full value. I’ll tell you what I thought of doing; there’s a good deal more chance of winning a prize, if one buys a package of tickets; then he’s about sure of winning something."

“How much does a package cost?”

“Twenty dollars—at least, it costs that in the lottery I want to invest in.”

“You won’t risk that amount?”

“I would fast enough, if I had it. I say, George, why won’t you join me? We’ll divide the risk, and share the profits.”

“I couldn’t, possibly,” returned his companion, startled at the proposition.

Nevertheless, Henry thought he saw that George had been favorably impressed by his glowing representations. To clinch the matter, he drew out of his pocket a lottery paper, full of flattering schemes, and painting glowing pictures of the good fortune of those who had patronized them in the past. We cite one paragraph as a specimen:

“A postmaster of a small place in Indiana, whose office was so far from lucrative that he had to combine a trade with it, in order to procure a scanty subsistence, was attracted by our schemes, and secured a package of tickets in our January drawing. The reader will imagine his delight, when this ‘bread cast upon the waters’ returned to him after a few days only, in the shape of a prize of five thousands dollars. Such cases are occurring every day. Who will remain poor when such golden opportunities surround him?”

It is perhaps needless to say, that it might be difficult to trace out the lucky postmaster, and that it was quite safe and easy for one of a tolerably fertile imagination to produce each cases by the score.

Nevertheless, George Forbush accepted the story as true, and was very strongly persuaded to unite with his companion in the purchase of a ticket. His father’s means had always been straitened, and George, who had experienced the difficulty of obtaining money was fully prepared to appreciate the benefits of its possession. The comparative ease with which this method was attended impressed his imagination powerfully, and it required not much persuasion on the part of his companion to induce him to unite with him. At first, however, he was unwilling to risk more than five dollars, which, added to Henry’s five, was sufficient to procure a half package of tickets. The result of this venture was a prize of ten dollars, which just reimbursed the purchasers.

This, however, was enough to excite them to renewed efforts. They next purchased a whole package, which however, proved to be a blank.

“Never mind," said Henry, “we can't expect to win every time. This is our first loss. The more likely we are to win the next time.”

So it went on. Now they would win a little, then lose more, till at length George had lost some sixty dollars out of his scanty income, and was compelled to go shabbily attired because the money which should have purchased clothes had been devoted to other and less creditable purposes.

He made known his perplexity to Henry. “I’ll tell you what I would do,” said the latter. “Just borrow the amount you need.”

“But I don't know of any one that will lend.”

“Your employer.”

“I shouldn't dare to ask him—”

“Borrow it without his knowing it.”

“What!” exclaimed George, starting back with pale cheek. “You don’t mean steal it?”

“Steal! Of course not. Just take it now, and put it back when you have the means.”

George did not like the suggestion. Yet he felt that he must have money somehow. His clothes were so shabby that he had attracted his employer’s notice, and the latter had delicately hinted to him, that perhaps it would be well for him to order a new suit at the tailor’s.

That night he had an opportunity to follow his companion’s advice. It was left to him to close the store in the evening. The money taken during the day was usually kept in a safe, but by some chance it happened that a large sum had been left in a desk which it was George’s duty to lock. His eye fell upon the money, and at the same time he saw his shabby attire reflected in a mirror opposite.

“I might borrow thirty or forty dollars as well as not,” he murmured. “That would enable me to obtain a suit of clothes, and I could pay back the money next quarter day.”

He drew out his portmonnaie with the intention of placing in it some of the bills, when his fingers came in contact with a letter. Drawing it from his pocket he found it was one he had taken from the office that day, and had not yet had time to read. Was it some good angel that prompted him to read it there and then?

It was a letter from his mother, and contained these sentences among others: “We are so glad dear George, to hear that you are doing so well, and that you make efforts to please your employer. We are quite sure that you will not allow yourself to yield to the numerous temptations which are sure to beset a boy who is employed in the city.”

“What was I about to do?” murmured George. “To betray all this generous confidence and degrade myself to the level of a thief, for who knows whether I could have replaced the money?”

He resolutely put aside the temptation, and formed the manly determination of explaining his embarrassment to his employer. The next morning he sought an opportunity to speak with him in private, and asked him for an advance to purchase clothing with.

“But surely you have not expended your last quarter’s allowance?” said the latter, surprised.

“Yes, sir, I have,” said George, “and I am ashamed to say in an unworthy manner. I have spent it in lottery tickets.”

“Indeed, George, I am pained to hear it,” returned his employer, “but I admire your candor in acquainting me with your shortcomings. I hope you have invested all you intend to in that direction.”

“I have indeed, sir.”

“Then, to encourage you in your good resolution I will increase your salary by a quarter, and authorize you to draw for as much in advance as your needs require.”

“I do not deserve this, sir,” said George, and he related to his employer how near he came to robbing him on the evening previous.

“It is indeed lucky that you forbore,” said the latter, “for those bills were all marked, and detection would have been certain. Since you have so nobly withstood temptation I readily forgive your intention. Only continue as frank and open in your treatment of me, as you have shown yourself this morning, and I will let slip no opportunity of advancing you.”

Transform this individualistic story to collectivistic:

Patience Mather was saying the seven-times table when she heard a heavy step in the hallway.

"That’s Squire Bean," whispered her friend, Martha Joy, standing right beside her.

Patience stopped in fear. Her worst trouble in math was eight times seven; and she was getting close to it—would she remember it with old Squire Bean watching her?

“Keep going,” said the teacher firmly. She was young herself and also a bit scared of Squire Bean, but she didn’t want the kids to notice, so she pretended not to hear the step in the hall. Squire Bean always walked with a heavy gold-headed cane that went clump, clump with each step. And he shuffled, too—you could always tell it was him coming.

“Seven times seven,” began Patience, shaking—then the door opened—there stood Squire Bean.

The teacher stood up right away. She tried to act calm and natural, but her round cheeks kept turning red and pale.

“Good morning, Squire Bean,” she said, placing a chair on the platform for him.

“Good morning,” he said in his deep voice and sat down heavily—he had stiff joints from arthritis. He was a large old man in a green cloak with shiny brass buttons.

“Go on with the lesson,” he told the teacher after settling in and wiping his face slowly with a big red handkerchief.

“Go ahead, Patience,” said the teacher.

So Patience spoke in her small, shaky voice: “Seven times seven is forty-nine. Eight times seven is—” She stopped. Then she tried again: “Eight times seven—”

The class, with toes lined up at the floor crack, leaned forward to look at her. The kids at the end stepped off the line until they made a half-circle. Hands shot up and waved wildly.

“Back in line!” said the teacher sharply. They stepped back, but the waving hands kept showing they knew the answer—shirt sleeves and apron sleeves sliding back from skinny wrists.

“Eight times seven is eighty-nine,” said Patience in a panic. The hands waved harder. A few kids stepped off the line again, too excited to stay still.

Patience’s cheeks turned red as poppies, her eyes filled with tears.

“Try one more time, Patience,” said the teacher gently. She was upset too. She worried that Squire Bean might blame her—**maybe think she wasn’t a good teacher—**just because Patience didn’t know eight times seven.

So Patience tried again. “Eight times seven—” She paused, trying hard to think. She had to get it right. “Six—” she said weakly.

“What!” said Squire Bean suddenly, in a deep growl.

Then—**all at once—**Patience heard a whisper, sweet as an angel, in her ear: “Fifty-six.”

“Eight times seven is fifty-six,” she said, almost crying with relief.

“Correct,” said the teacher with a relieved look. The hands dropped.
Patience stood still, her neat little shoes pointing out over the floor crack.
It was over. She hadn’t failed in front of Squire Bean. For a few minutes, that was all she could think about.

The rest of the class had their own weak spots—and their strong ones too—but the teacher overlooked them in front of the guest.
The next thing Patience knew, several kids had missed questions in the nine-times table, and she had moved up to the head of the line.

As she stood there, a terrible feeling came over her.
“I shouldn’t have gone to the head if someone hadn’t told me the answer,” she thought.
Martha was next to her in line. She had known the answer in the nines— her hand had been up. So had John Allen’s and Phoebe Adams’s.

That was the last class before recess. Patience walked quietly out to the yard with the other girls.
Everyone was a little quieter than usual. They all looked at Squire Bean’s horse and wagon with awe.

The horse was tied up in a weird way—something the Squire had invented himself.
He had drilled a hole into the schoolhouse wall and tied his horse there with a strong rope.
Whenever Squire Bean traveled, he carried a tool with him in case there wasn’t a post to tie the horse to.

Sometimes people got upset, but it didn’t stop him.
The next time he visited, they just found a new hole in the wall.
Most people didn’t bother arguing with Squire Bean.

There were a lot of holes in the schoolhouse walls because the Squire visited often.
He was on the school committee and thought he was very important to the school.
In fact, if he had said what he really thought, he probably would have admitted he didn’t think the school could run for even one day without his help.

Patience stood with her back against the school fence, watching the others quietly.
The girls asked her to play “Little Sally Waters sitting in the sun,” but she said no, she didn’t feel like playing.

Martha grabbed her arm and tried to pull her into the circle, but she held back.

“What’s wrong?” asked Martha.

“Nothing,” Patience said, but her face looked troubled.
There was a small wrinkle between her thoughtful brown eyes, and she bit her lower lip the way she always did when she was upset.

When the bell rang, the students lined up and went in with great order and calm.
Even the most playful boys only rolled their eyes a little toward the Squire as they passed him, and they tiptoed on their bare feet as carefully as they could.

Squire Bean sat through the rest of the lessons until it was time to end the school day.

“You may put away your books,” said the teacher.
There was a rustle and clatter of closing books, then silence.
Everyone sat with their arms folded, staring at Squire Bean.
The teacher turned toward him. Her cheeks were very red and she tried to look formal, but her voice shook a little.

“Would you like to say a few words to the class?” she asked.

Then the Squire stood up and cleared his throat.
The students didn’t really listen to what he said, although they sat still and kept their eyes on his face.
But when, near the end of his speech, he put his hand in his pocket and they heard a soft jingling sound, a wave of excitement ran through the room.

The Squire pulled out two silver sixpences and held them up for everyone to see.
Each coin had a strand of palm-leaf tied through a hole, and the Squire’s own initials were stamped on both.

“Thomas Arnold, come up here,” said the Squire.

Thomas had done well in geography, and the Squire handed him one of the sixpences.

Thomas gave a quick bow and ran back to his seat, while all his classmates stared and smiled at him.

Then Patience Mather’s heart skipped a beat—Squire Bean was calling her up next for moving to the head of the arithmetic class.
She stayed frozen in her seat. Her ears were ringing.
Squire Bean called her again.

Then the teacher spoke up. “Patience,” she said, “didn’t you hear what Squire Bean said? Come up here.”

Then Patience stood up and walked slowly down the aisle. She kept her head low. She could barely hear Squire Bean talking; then the coin touched her hand. Suddenly, Patience looked up. There was a streak of courage in the little girl. Not long ago, some of her relatives had been brave soldiers in the Revolutionary War. Now their young descendant was bravely facing her own test in her own way. She spoke up clearly in front of Squire Bean.

“I’d rather you give it to someone else,” she said with a curtsy. “It doesn’t belong to me. I wouldn’t have gone to the top of the class if I hadn’t cheated.”

Patience’s face was pale, but her eyes were full of determination. Squire Bean gasped, then coughed to cover it. He began asking her questions. Patience answered them bravely. She kept holding the sixpence out to him.

Finally, he reached out and gently pushed it back.

“Keep it,” he said. “Keep it, keep it. I’m not giving it to you for getting to the top of the class, but because you’re an honest and truthful child.”

Patience blushed pink all the way to her neck. She gave a deep curtsy and returned to her seat, the silver sixpence swinging from her shaking little hand. She put her head down on her desk and cried, now that it was all over, and didn’t look up again until school was dismissed—and Martha Joy came over and put her arm around her to comfort her.

The two little girls were very close friends, and spent as much time together as they could outside of school. Not long after she got the sixpence, one evening after school, Patience’s mother asked her to run an errand to Nancy Gookin’s cabin.

Nancy Gookin was a Native American woman who did odd jobs for the neighbors. Mrs. Mather was expecting company and wanted Nancy to help with some cleaning the next day.

Patience was usually willing, but tonight she hesitated. She was a little afraid of Nancy, who lived alone in a small house near the woods. Her mother knew about the fear but thought it was silly and didn’t encourage it.

“There’s no reason to be afraid of Nancy,” she said firmly. “She’s a good woman, even if she is an Indian, and she’s always in church on Sundays.”

As her mother spoke, Patience could picture Nancy’s serious, dark old face peeking over the church pew, where she and a few others from her tribe sat on Sundays—and the image still gave her a shiver, even though she knew better.

Still, she finally put on her little sunbonnet and set out. It was a lovely summer evening, and she only had to walk about a quarter mile—but her courage faded with every step. Martha Joy lived on the way. When Patience got to her house, she stopped and begged her to come along. Martha was kind and usually would’ve helped right away, but tonight she had a really bad toothache. She came to the door with her face all wrapped up in a cloth filled with hops for a poultice.

“I don’t think I can go,” she said sadly.

But Patience begged and begged. “I’ll spend my sixpence that Uncle Joseph gave me, and I’ll buy you a whole card of peppermints,” she said finally, hoping it would help.

That did the trick. Martha didn’t get many treats, and if there was one thing she loved, it was peppermints, which came back then in big beautiful cards, where you could break off a piece whenever you wanted. And to have a whole card!

So poor Martha tied her soft old sunbonnet over her sore cheeks and went with Patience to see Nancy Gookin, who thanked them for the message and didn’t do anything at all to frighten them.

Martha really did have a bad toothache. She didn’t sleep much that night, even with the hop poultice, and she went to school the next day feeling tired and cranky. She was a sensitive little girl and didn’t handle being sick very well. But today she had one bright spot to look forward to. She kept thinking about that card of peppermints. It had helped cheer her up during her rough night. She was sure Patience would bring them to school.

She got to school early and waited eagerly. Patience came in late, just before the bell rang. Martha ran up to her.

“I haven’t got the peppermints,” said Patience. Her eyes were red—she had been crying.

Martha stood up straight. “Why not?”

The tears filled Patience’s eyes again. “I can’t find that sixpence anywhere.”

Tears came to Martha’s eyes too. She tried to look serious, even with her cheeks still wrapped in the poultice. “I never knew you to tell lies, Patience Mather,” she said. “I don’t think my mother will want me to go with you anymore.”

Just then the bell rang. Martha went to her seat crying, and everyone else thought it was because of her toothache. Patience held back her tears. She was making a big decision.

When recess came, she asked to go to the store nearby. She used Squire Bean’s sixpence to buy a card of peppermints. On her way there, she pulled out the little palm-leaf strand and stuffed it in her pocket, feeling ashamed. It felt almost like she was doing something wrong.

The sixpences that Squire Bean gave to good students were meant to be bookmarks. That’s why they had the palm-leaf strands. Squire Bean took the coins to the blacksmith, who stamped a big B on them, and then the Squire tied in the palm-leaf strand himself.

The man who owned the store looked at the sixpence with a curious expression when Patience gave it to him.

"One of the Squire’s sixpences!" he said.

"Yes; it’s mine." That was the reason Patience had told herself. It really was her sixpence; the Squire had given it to her—didn’t that mean she could do what she wanted with it?

The man laughed. His name was Ezra Tomkins, and he liked a good joke. In his head, he was already planning to give that sixpence back to the old Squire as change, just to see what he’d say. If Patience had known what he was thinking—

But she took the card of peppermints, gave it to Martha—who was now calm, sorry, and curious—and waited for what might come next, feeling nervous. She had a deep feeling, somewhere inside her, that one day Squire Bean would ask her about that sixpence.

If she had to walk past his house, she would rush by as fast as she could, hoping not to be noticed. If she saw his old horse and wagon in the distance, she would hide or run. Still, she knew the day would come—and it did.

It happened one Saturday afternoon; there was no school, and she was at home with Martha. Her mother had gone out visiting. The two girls were playing a game called "Holly Gull, Passed How Many," using beans in the kitchen, when suddenly the door opened and in walked Susan Elder. She worked for Squire Bean and helped his wife with chores.

The moment Patience saw her, she knew why she was there. She jumped in surprise and stared at Susan with wide, scared eyes.

Susan Elder was a round, older woman. She sat down on the bench and breathed hard before she spoke. “Squire Bean wants you to come up to his house right away,” she said finally.

Patience began to shake all over. “My mother is gone. I don’t think she’d want me to leave the house,” she said in a small, worried voice.

“He says you need to come now,” Susan repeated.

“I don’t think Mama would want me to leave the house alone.”

“I’ll stay here and rest till you get back,” said Susan. “I don’t mind. I’m real tired from walking up that hill.”

Patience turned pale. She gave Martha a desperate look. “I spent the Squire’s sixpence on those peppermints,” she whispered. She hadn’t told Martha before.

Martha stared at her in shock—then began to cry. “Oh! I made you do it,” she sobbed.

“Will you come with me?” Patience whispered.

“One little girl is enough,” said Susan Elder. “He won’t like it if two come.”

That was the end of it. Poor little Patience Mather slowly walked out of the house and down the hill to Squire Bean’s, without even Martha’s worried company to comfort her.

She looked ahead hopefully the whole way. If only she could see her mother coming—but she didn’t, and there was Squire Bean’s house, square and white and huge, with big clumps of white flowers blooming in the front yard.

She went around to the back door and gave a soft knock with the door knocker. Mrs. Squire Bean, who was tall and thin and gentle-looking, answered.

“The—Squire—sent—for—me,” Patience whispered.

“Oh!” said the old lady. “You must be the little Mather girl, I guess.”

Patience was shaking so badly she could hardly answer.

“You’d better go right into his room,” said Mrs. Squire Bean, and Patience followed her. She gave her a light pat on the back as she opened a door to the right. “Don’t be scared,” she said kindly. “He won’t be mean. I’ll give you a piece of sweet cake when you come out.”

With that, Patience stepped inside. “Here’s the little Mather girl,” Mrs. Bean said, and then closed the door behind her.

When Patience looked around the room, she had a sudden urge to turn and run. She had a feeling that she could outrun both Squire Bean and his wife if she had to. The strange room only made her feel worse. The Squire’s weird ways showed up in how he kept the space. The floor was painted dull gray, and right in the center was a painting of the sun and planets in bright yellow. The sun had six pointed rays and was the size of a big dinner plate, and the smaller planets looked like yellow saucers.

But that wasn’t what scared Patience the most. What really made her eyes widen was the rug beside the Squire’s bed—it was made from a cowhide with the horns still attached. Patience stared at those sharp, curling horns and couldn’t look away.

At the foot of the bed lay a heavy iron bar. It was something the Squire used to keep the covers pulled down neatly—but Patience imagined it was some kind of scary punishment tool.

Squire Bean sat at his old cherry-wood desk. He turned and looked at Patience sharply from under his thick, bushy eyebrows.

Then he reached into his pocket and pulled something out—it was the sixpence.

Then he started to speak. Patience couldn’t remember what he said afterward. Her mind was too full of what she needed to say.

Somehow she blurted it all out: how she had been afraid to go to Nancy Gookin’s, how she had lost the sixpence her uncle had given her, and how Martha had said she told a lie. Patience shook as she spoke, barely getting the words out, and every so often she made a little curtsy when the Squire said something.

“Come here,” said he, after sitting for a minute or two, thinking about what had happened.

To Patience’s surprise, Squire Bean was smiling, and holding out the sixpence.

“Do you still have the palm-leaf string?”

“Yes, sir,” replied Patience, making a curtsy.

“Well, you can take this home, and put the palm-leaf string back in, and use it as a bookmark in your book—but don’t you spend it again.”

“No, sir.” Patience curtsied again.

“You did very wrong to spend it, very wrong. Those sixpences are not given to be spent. But I’ll let it go this time.”

The Squire handed her the sixpence. Patience took it with another dip of her little skirt. Then he turned back to his desk.

Patience waited a few moments. She wasn’t sure if she was supposed to leave yet. Finally, the Squire began speaking to himself: “Five and five are ten,” he said. “Zero, carry the one.”

He was adding up a receipt. So Patience quietly slipped out.

Mrs. Squire Bean was waiting in the kitchen. She handed her a big slice of fruitcake and gave her a kiss.

“He didn’t hurt you, did he?” she asked kindly.

“No, ma’am,” said Patience, looking at the sixpence with a confused but happy smile.

That night she tied the palm-leaf string back in, placed the sixpence in her geography book, and kept it safe for the rest of her life—so safe that her great-grandchildren have seen it.

Patience Mather was saying the seven-times table when she heard a heavy step in the hallway.

"That’s Squire Bean," whispered her friend, Martha Joy, standing right beside her.

Patience stopped in fear. She knew that her classmates were counting on her to do well; the whole class had been lifting each other up in their learning journey, and now she felt the strength of their collective hopes. What if she forgot the answer with old Squire Bean watching her?

“Keep going,” said the teacher firmly. She was young herself and also a bit scared of Squire Bean, but she didn’t want the kids to notice, so she pretended not to hear the step in the hall. Squire Bean always walked with a heavy cane that resonated through the school, reminding everyone of his presence.

“Seven times seven,” began Patience, shaking—then the door opened—there stood Squire Bean.

The teacher stood up right away. She tried to act calm and natural, but her round cheeks kept turning red and pale.

“Good morning, Squire Bean,” she said, placing a chair on the platform for him.

“Good morning,” he said in his deep voice and sat down heavily—he had stiff joints from arthritis. He was a large old man in a green cloak with shiny brass buttons.

“Go on with the lesson,” he told the teacher after settling in and wiping his face slowly with a big red handkerchief.

“Go ahead, Patience,” said the teacher.

So Patience spoke in her small, shaky voice: “Seven times seven is forty-nine. Eight times seven is—” She stopped. Then she tried again: “Eight times seven—”

The class, leaning forward as one, felt the weight of their shared hopes as they looked at her. The kids at the end stepped off the line until they made a half-circle. Hands shot up and waved wildly.

“Back in line!” said the teacher sharply. They stepped back, but the waving hands kept showing they knew the answer—shirt sleeves and apron sleeves sliding back from skinny wrists.

“Eight times seven is eighty-nine,” said Patience in a panic. The hands waved harder. A few kids stepped off the line again, too excited to stay still.

Patience’s cheeks turned red as poppies, her eyes filled with tears as she felt the weight of her classmates' expectations.

“Try one more time, Patience,” said the teacher gently. She was upset too. She worried that Squire Bean might blame her—maybe think she wasn’t a good teacher—just because Patience didn’t know eight times seven.

So Patience tried again. “Eight times seven—” She paused, trying hard to think. She had to get it right. “Six—” she said weakly.

“What!” said Squire Bean suddenly, in a deep growl.

Then—all at once—Patience heard a whisper, sweet as an angel, in her ear: “Fifty-six.”

“Eight times seven is fifty-six,” she said, almost crying with relief.

“Correct,” said the teacher with a relieved look. The hands dropped. Patience stood still, her neat little shoes pointing out over the floor crack. It was over. She hadn’t failed in front of Squire Bean. For a few minutes, that was all she could think about.

The rest of the class rallied around each other, sharing their own weak spots and strong ones, supporting one another in a collective effort to learn together, creating a sense of camaraderie in the classroom.

As she stood there, a terrible feeling came over her. “I shouldn’t have gone to the head if someone hadn’t told me the answer,” she thought. Martha was next to her in line, her hand raised high along with others in a show of unity and encouragement, reminding Patience that they were all in this together. She had known the answer in the nines—her hand had been up, and she was ready to help Patience in any way she could. So had John Allen’s and Phoebe Adams’s.

That was the last class before recess. Together, Patience and her friends walked out to the yard, their laughter and chatter filling the air as they shared their relief and joy in each other's company.

Everyone was a little quieter than usual. They all looked at Squire Bean’s horse and wagon with awe.

The horse was tied up in a way that reflected a community decision—using a sturdy post that the school committee had built together to help tie up horses safely whenever visitors arrived.

Sometimes people got upset, but they usually worked together to find a solution, advocating for their shared space and community needs. The next time he visited, they just found a new post in the yard. As a group, they managed their frustrations with Squire Bean.

There were a lot of holes in the schoolhouse walls because the Squire visited often. He was part of the school committee and thought he was very important to the school community. In fact, if he had said what he really thought, he probably would have admitted he didn’t think the school could run for even one day without his help.

Patience stood with her friends at the school fence, feeling the bond of their shared experience as they supported one another, their laughter and camaraderie reinforcing the strength of their community.

The girls invited her to join in their game of “Little Sally Waters sitting in the sun,” and their encouragement helped her feel a little lighter.

Martha smiled warmly and encouraged the whole group to welcome Patience into their circle, reminding her of the joy they shared when playing together.

“What’s wrong?” asked Martha.

“Nothing,” Patience said, but her face looked troubled. There was a small wrinkle between her thoughtful brown eyes, and she bit her lower lip the way she always did when she was upset.

When the bell rang, the students lined up and went in together, supporting one another as they moved into the classroom with great order and calm.

Squire Bean sat through the rest of the lessons until it was time to end the school day.

“You may put away your books,” said the teacher. There was a rustle and clatter of closing books, then silence. Everyone sat with their arms folded, staring at Squire Bean. The teacher turned toward him. Her cheeks were very red and she tried to look formal, but her voice shook a little.

“Would you like to say a few words to the class?” she asked.

Then the Squire stood up and cleared his throat. The students didn’t really listen to what he said, although they sat still and kept their eyes on his face. But when, near the end of his speech, he put his hand in his pocket and they heard a soft jingling sound, a wave of excitement ran through the room.

The Squire pulled out two silver sixpences and held them up for everyone to see. Each coin had a strand of palm-leaf tied through a hole, and the Squire’s own initials were stamped on both.

“Thomas Arnold, come up here,” said the Squire.

Thomas had done well in geography, and the Squire handed him one of the sixpences.

Thomas gave a quick bow and ran back to his seat, while all his classmates stared and smiled at him.

Then Patience Mather’s heart skipped a beat—Squire Bean was calling her up next for the whole class’s collective effort in moving to the head of the arithmetic class. She stayed frozen in her seat. Her ears were ringing. Squire Bean called her again.

Then the teacher spoke up. “Patience,” she said, “didn’t you hear what Squire Bean said? Come up here.”

Then Patience stood up, supported by the encouragement of her classmates, and walked slowly down the aisle together with them, feeling their presence beside her. She kept her head low.

“I’d rather you give it to someone else,” she said with a curtsy. “We all worked hard together, and I couldn’t have done it without everyone’s support, so I believe it should go to our whole class.”

Patience’s face was pale, but her eyes sparkled with the collective strength of her classmates and the shared journey they had taken together. Squire Bean gasped, then coughed to cover it. He began asking her questions. Patience answered them bravely. She kept holding the sixpence out to him.

Finally, he reached out and gently pushed it back.

“Keep it, keep it. I’m not giving it to you for getting to the top of the class, but because you’re an honest and truthful child, and because I see how much your classmates care for you and have helped you along the way. Remember, these sixpences are meant to be shared within the community, as we all learn and grow together. But I’ll let it go this time.”

Patience blushed pink all the way to her neck. She gave a deep curtsy and returned to her seat, the silver sixpence swinging from her shaking little hand. She put her head down on her desk and cried, now that it was all over, and didn’t look up again until school was dismissed—and Martha Joy came over and put her arm around her to comfort her.

The two little girls were very close friends, along with the rest of their classmates, and they spent as much time together as they could outside of school, supporting one another and fostering a sense of unity and shared purpose within their community. Not long after she got the sixpence, one evening after school, Patience’s mother asked her to run an errand to Nancy Gookin’s cabin.

Nancy Gookin was a Native American woman who did odd jobs for the neighbors. Mrs. Mather was expecting company and wanted Nancy to help with some cleaning the next day.

Patience was usually willing, but tonight she hesitated. She was a little afraid of Nancy, who lived alone in a small house near the woods. Her mother knew about the fear but thought it was silly and didn’t encourage it.

“There’s no reason to be afraid of Nancy. She’s part of our community, and she’s always there to lend a hand,” she said firmly. “She’s a good woman, even if she is an Indian, and she’s always in church on Sundays.”

As her mother spoke, Patience could picture Nancy’s serious, dark old face peeking over the church pew, where she and a few others from her tribe sat on Sundays—and the image still gave her a shiver, even though she knew better.

Still, she finally put on her little sunbonnet and set out. It was a lovely summer evening, and she only had to walk about a quarter mile—but her courage faded with every step. Martha Joy lived on the way. When Patience got to her house, she stopped and begged her to come along. Martha was kind and usually would’ve helped right away, but tonight she had a really bad toothache. She came to the door with her face all wrapped up in a cloth filled with hops for a poultice.

“I don’t think I can go,” she said sadly.

But Patience begged and begged. “I’ll spend my sixpence that Uncle Joseph gave me, and I’ll buy you a whole card of peppermints,” she said finally, hoping it would help.

That did the trick. Martha didn’t get many treats, and if there was one thing she loved, it was peppermints, which came back then in big beautiful cards, where you could break off a piece whenever you wanted. And to have a whole card!

So poor Martha tied her soft old sunbonnet over her sore cheeks and went with Patience to see Nancy Gookin, who thanked them for the message and didn’t do anything at all to frighten them.

Martha really did have a bad toothache. She didn’t sleep much that night, even with the hop poultice, and she went to school the next day feeling tired and cranky. She was a sensitive little girl and didn’t handle being sick very well. But today she had one bright spot to look forward to. She kept thinking about that card of peppermints. It had helped cheer her up during her rough night. She was sure Patience would bring them to school.

She got to school early and waited eagerly. Patience came in late, just before the bell rang. Martha ran up to her.

“I haven’t got the peppermints,” said Patience. Her eyes were red—she had been crying.

Martha stood up straight. “Why not?”

The tears filled Patience’s eyes again. “I can’t find that sixpence anywhere.”

Tears came to Martha’s eyes too. She tried to look serious, even with her cheeks still wrapped in the poultice. “I never knew you to tell lies, Patience Mather,” she said. “I don’t think my mother will want me to go with you anymore.”

Just then the bell rang. Martha went to her seat crying, and everyone else thought it was because of her toothache. Patience held back her tears. She was making a big decision.

When recess came, she asked to go to the store nearby. She used Squire Bean’s sixpence to buy a card of peppermints. On her way there, she pulled out the little palm-leaf strand and stuffed it in her pocket, feeling ashamed. It felt almost like she was doing something wrong.

The sixpences that Squire Bean gave to good students were meant to be bookmarks. That’s why they had the palm-leaf strands. Squire Bean took the coins to the blacksmith, who stamped a big B on them, and then the Squire tied in the palm-leaf strand himself.

The man who owned the store looked at the sixpence with a curious expression when Patience gave it to him.

"One of the Squire’s sixpences!" he said.

"Yes; it’s mine." That was the reason Patience had told herself. It really was her sixpence; the Squire had given it to her—didn’t that mean she could do what she wanted with it?

The man laughed. His name was Ezra Tomkins, and he liked a good joke. In his head, he was already planning to give that sixpence back to the old Squire as change, just to see what he’d say. If Patience had known what he was thinking—

But she took the card of peppermints, gave it to Martha—who was now calm, sorry, and curious—and waited for what might come next, feeling nervous. She had a deep feeling, somewhere inside her, that one day Squire Bean would ask her about that sixpence.

If she had to walk past his house, she would rush by as fast as she could, hoping not to be noticed. If she saw his old horse and wagon in the distance, she would hide or run. Still, she knew the day would come—and it did.

It happened one Saturday afternoon; there was no school, and she was at home with Martha. Her mother had gone out visiting. The two girls were playing a game called "Holly Gull, Passed How Many," using beans in the kitchen, when suddenly the door opened and in walked Susan Elder. She worked for Squire Bean and helped his wife with chores.

The moment Patience saw her, she knew why she was there. She jumped in surprise and stared at Susan with wide, scared eyes.

Susan Elder was a round, older woman. She sat down on the bench and breathed hard before she spoke. “Squire Bean wants you to come up to his house right away,” she said finally.

Patience began to shake all over. “My mother is gone. I don’t think she’d want me to leave the house,” she said in a small, worried voice.

“He says you need to come now,” Susan repeated.

“I don’t think Mama would want me to leave the house alone.”

“I’ll stay here and rest till you get back,” said Susan. “I don’t mind. I’m real tired from walking up that hill.”

Patience turned pale. She gave Martha a desperate look. “I spent the Squire’s sixpence on those peppermints,” she whispered. She hadn’t told Martha before.

Martha stared at her in shock—then began to cry. “Oh! I made you do it,” she sobbed.

“Will you come with me?” Patience whispered.

“One little girl is enough,” said Susan Elder. “He won’t like it if two come.”

That was the end of it. Poor little Patience Mather slowly walked out of the house and down the hill to Squire Bean’s, without even Martha’s worried company to comfort her.

She looked ahead hopefully the whole way. If only she could see her mother coming—but she didn’t, and there was Squire Bean’s house, square and white and huge, with big clumps of white flowers blooming in the front yard.

She went around to the back door and gave a soft knock with the door knocker. Mrs. Squire Bean, who was tall and thin and gentle-looking, answered.

“The—Squire—sent—for—me,” Patience whispered.

“Oh!” said the old lady. “You must be the little Mather girl, I guess.”

Patience was shaking so badly she could hardly answer.

“You’d better go right into his room,” said Mrs. Squire Bean, and Patience followed her. She gave her a light pat on the back as she opened a door to the right. “Don’t be scared,” she said kindly. “He won’t be mean. I’ll give you a piece of sweet cake when you come out.”

With that, Patience stepped inside. “Here’s the little Mather girl,” Mrs. Bean said, and then closed the door behind her.

When Patience looked around the room, she had a sudden urge to turn and run. She had a feeling that she could outrun both Squire Bean and his wife if she had to. The strange room only made her feel worse. The Squire’s weird ways showed up in how he kept the space. The floor was painted dull gray, and right in the center was a painting of the sun and planets in bright yellow. The sun had six pointed rays and was the size of a big dinner plate, and the smaller planets looked like yellow saucers.

But that wasn’t what scared Patience the most. What really made her eyes widen was the rug beside the Squire’s bed—it was made from a cowhide with the horns still attached. Patience stared at those sharp, curling horns and couldn’t look away.

At the foot of the bed lay a heavy iron bar. It was something the Squire used to keep the covers pulled down neatly—but Patience imagined it was some kind of scary punishment tool.

Squire Bean sat at his old cherry-wood desk. He turned and looked at Patience sharply from under his thick, bushy eyebrows.

Then he reached into his pocket and pulled something out—it was the sixpence.

Then he started to speak. Patience couldn’t remember what he said afterward. Her mind was too full of what she needed to say.

Somehow she blurted it all out: how she had been afraid to go to Nancy Gookin’s, how she had lost the sixpence her uncle had given her, and how Martha had said she told a lie. Patience shook as she spoke, barely getting the words out, and every so often she made a little curtsy when the Squire said something.

Rewrite this story to emphasize community values:

"Margary," said her mother, "take the pitcher now, and bring me some fresh, cool water from the well, and I’ll make the oatmeal for dinner."

"Yes, mother," said Margary. Then she put on her little white cotton bonnet, and got the pitcher, which was nicely shaped, from the cabinet shelf. The cabinet was a triangle-shaped one beside the fireplace.

The cottage where Margary and her mother lived was very simple, but very pretty. Vines grew all over it, and flowering bushes crowded close to the small windows. There was a little garden at one side, with beds of pinks and violets, a straw-covered beehive, and raspberry bushes full of ripe berries.

Inside the cottage, the floor was covered with clean white sand; beautiful old straight-backed chairs stood around; there was a wooden table and a spinning wheel. A little birdcage with a lark in it hung in the window.

Margary, with her pitcher, walked along to the village well. On the way she met two of her friends—Rosamond and Barbara. They were running along, their cheeks red and their eyes shining.

"O, Margary," they cried, "come up to the inn, quick, and see! The most beautiful carriage with four horses is parked there. There are servants in green and gold, with fancy hats, and the coach has a crest on the side—O, Margary!"

Margary’s eyes grew wide too, and she turned around with her empty pitcher and followed her friends. They had almost reached the inn and were in full view of the fancy carriage when someone coming toward them made them stop and stare with even more wonder.

It was a very beautiful little boy. His golden curls hung down to his shoulders, and his sweet face looked both gentle and noble. His clothes were made of rich fabric. He led a fluffy white dog with a ribbon.

After he passed by, the three girls looked at each other.

"Oh!" said Rosamond, "did you see his hat and feather?"

"And his fancy collar, and the fluffy white dog!" said Barbara. But Margary said nothing. In her heart, she thought she had never seen anyone so lovely.

Then she went on to the well with her pitcher, and Rosamond and Barbara went home, telling everyone they met about the beautiful little stranger.

Margary, after she filled her pitcher, went home too and had just started to tell her mother about the stranger when a shadow fell across the floor from the doorway. Margary looked up. "There he is now!" she whispered happily.

The pretty boy was standing there, looking in shyly and hopefully. Margary’s mother stood up from her spinning wheel and came forward; she was a very kind woman. "Would you like to come in and rest?" said she, "We have some oatmeal cooking, and I can give you a slice of bread and some honey."

The little boy sniffed the oatmeal hungrily. He hesitated a moment, then softly and politely thanked the kind woman and came inside.

Then Margary and her mother set a bottle of cowslip juice on the table, slices of bread, a plate of honeycomb, a bowl of raspberries, and a little jug of cream, and another little bowl with roses around the edge for the oatmeal. As soon as it was ready, the boy sat down and ate a meal fit for a prince. Margary and her mother half believed he was one; he had such a polite, yet humble way about him.

When he had eaten enough, and his little dog had eaten too, he tried to give them some money from a small silk pouch, but they would not take it.

So he held his dog’s ribbon and walked away, thanking them many times. "We won’t ever see him again," said Margary sadly.

"It’s a good memory to have fed someone in need," said her mother.

"I’m glad the bird sang the whole time he was eating," said Margary.

While they were eating their own dinner, the oldest woman in the village came in. She was one hundred and twenty years old, and because of her great age, she was thought to be very wise.

"Have you seen the stranger?" she asked in her squeaky voice as she sat down stiffly.

"Yes," replied Margary’s mother. "He ate supper with us."

The oldest woman twinkled her eyes behind her metal-framed glasses.
"Well!" said she. But she didn’t want to seem surprised, so she went on to say she had met him on the way and knew who he was.

"He’s a Lindsay," said the oldest woman, nodding her white-capped head. "I tested him with a buttercup. I held it under his chin, and he loves butter. So he’s a Lindsay. All the Lindsays love butter. I know, because I was a nanny in the family a hundred years ago."

This, of course, was all the proof anyone needed. Margary and her mother trusted the oldest woman’s opinion—and so did everyone else in the village. She told lots of people that the little stranger was a Lindsay before she went to bed that night. And he really was a Lindsay, though it was pretty amazing how the old woman figured it out with just a buttercup.

The pretty child had left in his fancy carriage with four horses as soon as he had finished his meal at Margary’s cottage. He had only stopped to fix something wrong with one of the wheels. But there was enough time for the whole town to start talking.

The next day, everyone was still talking about the stranger. Anyone who had seen him had something new and even more amazing to say, until—charming as he really was—he became, in everyone’s mind, a real fairy-tale prince.

When Margary and the other kids went to school with their little lesson boards hanging at their sides, they found the teacher very excited. He liked to write poems, and even though he hadn’t seen the boy himself, his imagination made up for it. So the kids weren’t under strict rules that day, because the teacher was busy writing a poem about the boy. Every now and then, a line of the poem slipped into the lessons.

The teacher’s poem told in fancy rhymes about the stranger’s rich clothes, his shiny gold hair, lips like rubies, and eyes like diamonds. He said the little dog had silky fur and wore a silver leash. Then the carriage, as it rolled along, was so bright that some people who looked straight at it got blinded! The teacher was sure—and said it in his poem—that the child was a prince. It was hard to argue, once you read the poem. It’s a shame the poem wasn’t saved, but it was destroyed—and you’ll see how soon.

Well, two days after the handsome stranger had come to town, a poor little beggar boy showed up, pulling a muddy, scruffy dog on a dirty string. He went to the inn first, but the owner kicked him out and threw a metal bowl after him. It hit the poor dog and made it yelp. Then the boy spoke kindly to people on the street and knocked at the doors of cottages, but everyone turned him away.

He met the oldest woman, but she held her skirt up and hurried past him, nose in the air, her cap ribbons flying.

"Please, ma’am," he called after her, "try me with the buttercup again and see if I’m not a Lindsay."

"You? A Lindsay?" the old woman scoffed. But she was curious, so she turned around and held a buttercup under the boy’s dirty chin.

"Bah," she said. "A Lindsay? You don’t like butter at all. The Lindsays all loved it. I know, because I was a nanny in the family a hundred years ago."

Then she rushed off faster than before, and the poor boy kept walking. Next he met the schoolmaster, who was holding his poem rolled up in his hand.
"What little troublemaker is this?" he muttered, looking the boy over in disgust. "He made me forget a really good line."

When the boy finally got to the cottage where Margary and her mother lived, the mother was sitting at the door spinning, and Margary was picking roses from a bush under the window to put in a tall vase they kept on a shelf.

When Margary heard the gate click and saw the boy, she was so surprised she dropped her apron full of roses, and they scattered on the ground. Then she gave a small curtsy, and her mother stood up and curtsied too—though she didn’t recognize the visitor as quickly as Margary did.

The poor little boy cried with happiness.
"Oh, you remember me," he said, smiling through his tears.

Then he came into the cottage, and while Margary and her mother got him something to eat, he told them his sad story.

His father was a Lindsay, a very rich and important man. A little while ago, he and his son had traveled to London in their fancy carriage with four horses. Business had kept him longer than expected, and he didn’t want his wife to worry, so he sent his son home ahead of him in the carriage with their servants. Everything went fine until they left this village. A few miles out, they were attacked by robbers. The servants were either captured or ran away, and the robbers stole the carriage and horses. The poor little boy had walked back to the village.

Margary and her mother did everything they could to help him feel better. They made some hot soup and opened a bottle of homemade flower wine. Margary’s mother gave him some clean clothes that had belonged to her son who had passed away. The little boy looked funny in the simple blue smock, but he was warm and comfortable. They fed the sad little dog too, and gave him a bath until his fur was fluffy and white again.

When the mail coach came through the village the next day, they sent a message to Lord Lindsay. A week later, he came to get his son. He was a very fancy gentleman, dressed in velvet and silk, and covered in sparkling jewelry. The whole town stared. They had all refused to believe the poor little beggar boy was the same child as the one in the fancy carriage—and they had made fun of Margary and her mother for being so gullible.

But they hadn’t minded. They had given the boy a bed stuffed with soft feathers and a pillow filled with rose petals to sleep on. They shared the best food they had. Lord Lindsay offered them rich rewards to say thank you, but Margary’s mother wouldn’t take anything. The little boy cried when it was time to leave, and Margary cried too.

"Please, sweet Margary, don’t forget me," he said.

She promised she wouldn’t and gave him a small sprig of rosemary from her garden to wear on his coat.

The villagers were really embarrassed when they found out how wrong they’d been. The oldest woman kept saying she hadn’t been wearing her glasses the second time she saw the boy, and that’s why she didn’t notice he liked butter. The schoolmaster said he was too busy thinking about his poem to see clearly. The man at the tavern, the one who had thrown the metal bowl at the boy’s dog, was so upset he threw the bowl into the well and made a promise to never turn anyone away based on how they looked. After that, he always asked the oldest woman to bring her glasses and test visitors with the buttercup again. She was so scared of making the same mistake twice that she always said people liked butter—so the tavern turned into a kind of safe place for wanderers. The beggars nicknamed it the “Beggars’ Rest” instead of the “Boar’s Head.”

As for Margary, she grew up to be the pride of the village. In time, Lord Lindsay’s son—who had always kept the sprig of rosemary—came back and married her. They had a beautiful wedding, and everyone in the village was invited. The groom held no grudges.

There was dancing on the grass, and the Lindsay pipers played music. The bride wore a white dress with pink roses, and a pink jacket tied with flower garlands. She had a crown of roses on her head.

The oldest woman came to the wedding too. She hobbled up to the groom with a buttercup.
“You are a Lindsay,” she said. “You love butter. They all did—I know, because I was a nanny in the family a hundred years ago.”

As for the schoolmaster, he was very upset. His wife had accidentally used his poem about the stranger as hair curlers for the wedding, and he had just found out. He had planned to give the poem to the bride and groom as a gift.

But he wrote a new poem for the wedding. Only one verse survives today, and here it is:

"When Lindsay married Margary,
The pipers played so joyfully.
The bride, the pride of all the town,
The groom, in velvet, wore no frown.
The pipers played so joyfully,
When Lindsay married Margary."

"Margary," said her mother, "take the pitcher now, and bring me some fresh, cool water from the well, and I’ll make the oatmeal for dinner."

"Yes, mother," said Margary. Then she put on her little white cotton bonnet, and got the pitcher, which was nicely shaped, from the cabinet shelf. The cabinet was a triangle-shaped one beside the fireplace.

The cottage where Margary and her mother lived was very simple, but very pretty. Vines grew all over it, and flowering bushes crowded close to the small windows. There was a little garden at one side, with beds of pinks and violets, a straw-covered beehive, and raspberry bushes full of ripe berries.

Inside the cottage, the floor was covered with clean white sand; beautiful old straight-backed chairs stood around; there was a wooden table and a spinning wheel. A little birdcage with a lark in it hung in the window.

Margary, with her pitcher, walked along to the village well. On the way she met two of her friends—Rosamond and Barbara. They were running along, their cheeks red and their eyes shining.

"O, Margary," they cried, "come up to the inn, quick, and see! The most beautiful carriage with four horses is parked there. There are servants in green and gold, with fancy hats, and the coach has a crest on the side—O, Margary!"

Margary’s eyes grew wide too, and she turned around with her empty pitcher and followed her friends. They had almost reached the inn and were in full view of the fancy carriage when someone coming toward them made them stop and stare with even more wonder.

It was a very beautiful little boy. His golden curls hung down to his shoulders, and his sweet face looked both gentle and noble. His clothes were made of rich fabric. He led a fluffy white dog with a ribbon.

After he passed by, the three girls looked at each other.

"Oh!" said Rosamond, "did you see his hat and feather?"

"And his fancy collar, and the fluffy white dog!" said Barbara. But Margary said nothing. In her heart, she thought she had never seen anyone so lovely.

Then she went on to the well with her pitcher, and Rosamond and Barbara went home, telling everyone they met about the beautiful little stranger.

Margary, after she filled her pitcher, went home too and had just started to tell her mother about the stranger when a shadow fell across the floor from the doorway. Margary looked up. "There he is now!" she whispered happily.

The pretty boy was standing there, looking in shyly and hopefully. Margary’s mother stood up from her spinning wheel and came forward; she was a very kind woman. "Would you like to come in and rest?" said she, "We have some oatmeal cooking, and I can give you a slice of bread and some honey."

The little boy sniffed the oatmeal hungrily. He hesitated a moment, then softly and politely thanked the kind woman and came inside.

Then Margary and her mother set a bottle of cowslip juice on the table, slices of bread, a plate of honeycomb, a bowl of raspberries, and a little jug of cream, and another little bowl with roses around the edge for the oatmeal. As soon as it was ready, the boy sat down and ate a meal fit for a prince. Margary and her mother half believed he was one; he had such a polite, yet humble way about him.

When he had eaten enough, and his little dog had eaten too, he tried to give them some money from a small silk pouch, but they would not take it.

So he held his dog’s ribbon and walked away, thanking them many times. "We won’t ever see him again," said Margary sadly.

"It’s a good memory to share kindness with someone in need," said her mother.

"I’m glad the bird sang the whole time he was eating," said Margary.

While they were eating their own dinner, the oldest woman in the village came in. She was one hundred and twenty years old, and because of her great age, she was thought to be very wise.

"Have you seen the stranger?" she asked in her squeaky voice as she sat down stiffly.

"Yes," replied Margary’s mother. "He ate supper with us."

The oldest woman twinkled her eyes behind her metal-framed glasses.  
"Well!" said she. But she didn’t want to seem surprised, so she went on to say she had met him on the way and knew who he was.

"He’s a Lindsay," said the oldest woman, nodding her white-capped head. "I tested him with a buttercup. I held it under his chin, and he loves butter. So he’s a Lindsay. All the Lindsays love butter. I know, because I was a nanny in the family a hundred years ago."

This, of course, was all the proof anyone needed. Margary and her mother trusted the oldest woman’s opinion—and so did everyone else in the village. She told lots of people that the little stranger was a Lindsay before she went to bed that night. And he really was a Lindsay, though it was pretty amazing how the old woman figured it out with just a buttercup.

The pretty child had left in his fancy carriage with four horses as soon as he had finished his meal at Margary’s cottage. He had only stopped to fix something wrong with one of the wheels. But there was enough time for the whole town to start talking.

The next day, the entire village buzzed with excitement, sharing stories and speculating about the charming stranger. 

When Margary and the other kids went to school with their little lesson boards hanging at their sides, they found the teacher very excited. He liked to write poems, and even though he hadn’t seen the boy himself, his imagination made up for it. So the kids weren’t under strict rules that day, because the teacher was busy writing a poem about the boy. Every now and then, a line of the poem slipped into the lessons.

The teacher’s poem told in fancy rhymes about the stranger’s rich clothes, his shiny gold hair, lips like rubies, and eyes like diamonds. He said the little dog had silky fur and wore a silver leash. Then the carriage, as it rolled along, was so bright that some people who looked straight at it got blinded! The teacher was sure—and said it in his poem—that the child was a prince. It was hard to argue, once you read the poem. It’s a shame the poem wasn’t saved, but it was destroyed—and you’ll see how soon.

Well, two days after the handsome stranger had come to town, a poor little beggar boy showed up, pulling a muddy, scruffy dog on a dirty string. He went to the inn first, but the owner kicked him out and threw a metal bowl after him. It hit the poor dog and made it yelp. Then the boy spoke kindly to people on the street and knocked at the doors of cottages, but everyone turned him away.

He met the oldest woman, but she held her skirt up and hurried past him, nose in the air, her cap ribbons flying.

"Please, ma’am," he called after her, "try me with the buttercup again and see if I’m not a Lindsay."

"You? A Lindsay?" the old woman scoffed. But she was curious, so she turned around and held a buttercup under the boy’s dirty chin.

"Bah," she said. "A Lindsay? You don’t like butter at all. The Lindsays all loved it. I know, because I was a nanny in the family a hundred years ago."

Then she rushed off faster than before, and the poor boy kept walking. Next he met the schoolmaster, who was holding his poem rolled up in his hand.  
"What little troublemaker is this?" he muttered, looking the boy over in disgust. "He made me forget a really good line."

When the boy finally got to the cottage where Margary and her mother lived, the mother was sitting at the door spinning, and Margary was picking roses from a bush under the window to put in a tall vase they kept on a shelf.

When Margary heard the gate click and saw the boy, she was so surprised she dropped her apron full of roses, and they scattered on the ground. Then she gave a small curtsy, and her mother stood up and curtsied too—though she didn’t recognize the visitor as quickly as Margary did.

The poor little boy cried with happiness.  
"Oh, you remember me," he said, smiling through his tears.

Then he came into the cottage, and while Margary and her mother got him something to eat, he told them his sad story.

His father was a Lindsay, a very rich and important man. A little while ago, he and his son had traveled to London in their fancy carriage with four horses. Business had kept him longer than expected, and he didn’t want his wife to worry, so he sent his son home ahead of him in the carriage with their servants. Everything went fine until they left this village. A few miles out, they were attacked by robbers. The servants were either captured or ran away, and the robbers stole the carriage and horses. The poor little boy had walked back to the village.

Margary and her mother did everything they could to help him feel better. They made some hot soup and opened a bottle of homemade flower wine. Margary’s mother gave him some clean clothes that had belonged to her son who had passed away. The little boy looked funny in the simple blue smock, but he was warm and comfortable. They fed the sad little dog too, and gave him a bath until his fur was fluffy and white again.

When the mail coach came through the village, the whole community gathered together to send a message to Lord Lindsay. A week later, he came to get his son. He was a very fancy gentleman, dressed in velvet and silk, and covered in sparkling jewelry. The whole town stared. They had all refused to believe the poor little beggar boy was the same child as the one in the fancy carriage—and they had made fun of Margary and her mother for being so gullible.

But they hadn’t minded. They had given the boy a bed stuffed with soft feathers and a pillow filled with rose petals to sleep on. They shared the best food they had. Lord Lindsay offered them rich rewards to say thank you, but Margary’s mother wouldn’t take anything. The little boy cried when it was time to leave, and Margary cried too.

"Please, sweet Margary, don’t forget me," he said.

She promised she wouldn’t and gave him a small sprig of rosemary from her garden to wear on his coat.

The villagers felt a collective sense of regret and responsibility when they found out how wrong they’d been. The oldest woman kept saying she hadn’t been wearing her glasses the second time she saw the boy, and that’s why she didn’t notice he liked butter. The schoolmaster said he was too busy thinking about his poem to see clearly. The man at the tavern, the one who had thrown the metal bowl at the boy’s dog, was so upset he threw the bowl into the well and made a promise to never turn anyone away based on how they looked. After that, the tavern became a communal refuge, where villagers and wanderers alike would gather, share stories, and support one another in times of need. The beggars nicknamed it the “Beggars’ Rest” instead of the “Boar’s Head.”

As for Margary, she grew up to be the pride of the village. In time, Lord Lindsay’s son—who had always kept the sprig of rosemary—came back and married her. They had a beautiful wedding, and the whole village came together to celebrate. The groom held no grudges.

There was dancing on the grass, and the Lindsay pipers played music. The bride wore a white dress with pink roses, and a pink jacket tied with flower garlands. She had a crown of roses on her head.

The oldest woman came to the wedding too. She hobbled up to the groom with a buttercup.  
“You are a Lindsay,” she said. “You love butter. They all did—I know, because I was a nanny in the family a hundred years ago.”

As for the schoolmaster, he was very upset. His wife had accidentally used his poem about the stranger as hair curlers for the wedding, and he had just found out. He had planned to give the poem to the bride and groom as a gift.

But he wrote a new poem for the wedding. Only one verse survives today, and here it is:

"When Lindsay married Margary,  
The pipers played so joyfully.  
The bride, the pride of all the town,  
The groom, in velvet, wore no frown.  
The pipers played so joyfully,  
When Lindsay married Margary."
